: Overall, I'd give this game an 6/10 – a barely recommendation due to the regular Steam price of $9.99 being awfully steep for what amounts to less than 10 hours of content, just rearranged a bit so that it looks like more. That, plus the annoying lack of a traditional save makes me say that there is better out there, but a lot worse, too.
Anomaly: Warzone Earth is a sort of reverse-Tower Defense game, where your role is the one who plans the loadouts and the routes.  You then run around like a chicken with your head cut off, grabbing all of the various power-ups that you’ll need to pass each level, and then place them appropriately, using the mouse to lead your character around a top-down, isometric map. It’s fast-paced, but route planning, purchasing additional units, and upgrading them, is done while paused, so it’s not quite as frantic as it sounds.
At first, the game felt downright stupid. The voice-acting, while in itself not all that bad, is written horribly. You know that weird, sort of fake way that Moss always talks in The IT Crowd? Well, that’s how the entire game is voiced. Add to that many attempts at what I assume was supposed to be military humor (often the same "joke", even), and…yeah, it’s bad. This is one of those games that I feel could have been improved dramatically simply by not having voice acting. It’s not an RPG, and it’s not a AAA strategy game, so there really is no point, and it just comes off as irritating and trite.
After a while, though, the gameplay started to win me over, despite the drawbacks, and the game drew me in enough to finish the campaign, which only took 8.5 hours (and I am sloooooooow at beating games).  The story was just interesting enough, and there is a certain polish that I wasn’t expecting. Gameplay-wise, it mostly felt balanced and well thought out, though I did discover that a fully upgraded crawler can one-shot the tower that makes up 80% of what you fight, so that made things awfully easy.
Other than the aforementioned voice acting, there were other things that were just distractingly bad. The story tries, but has huge holes in it. For example, very early on, you find out that the central plot is that there are two big energy domes over two pieces of things that fell from the sky: one in Bagdad, one it Tokyo. Your first mission is to go into one. Under an energy dome.
An impenetrable dome of energy.
During this mission, and all subsequent missions, you will receive air-drop supplies in the form of power-ups. As in, airplanes actually fly by overhead and drop them down to the ground. They will repeatedly tell you that ground forces are necessary because air strikes are completely out of the question, yet what happens when you blow up an enemy? Air drop.
Really? Couldn’t they have just left out the air drop part and left the normal dead-bad-guy-leaves-power-up nonsense that we all know and love in video games? It’s like literally all of the voice acting – completely unnecessary and it actually screws things up.
Also, the game has no save, and that is inconvenient since some maps can take up to 20 minutes or so. It only saves when you have cleared a map. It has a checkpoint system, but that can be a mixed blessing since your choice is to load the last checkpoint or completely restart the map. If you were doing great at checkpoint 1, and you just crossed checkpoint 3 with one half-dead crawler and there’s no way you can finish the map because there just isn’t enough ways to get resources to build back up, oh well! You have to restart the whole map. I understand the strategic element, but checkpoints don't make since, in this case. A normal save would have been better here.
If you're willing to tough out the weird gameplay long enough to see if you like it, and it shows up on a bundle cheaply, and you can ignore and/or laugh at the badly written British people calling everything alien a "tin can", then you might could have some fun with this.
The regular price is definitely not fair, but this game bundles often. By no stretch of the imagination is it worth $10, even though it is very polished, very flashy, and completely voice-acted. The content is just over way too quickly, and then all that are left are some pointless “kill X waves of enemies” fights, and some ridiculously hard and time consuming achievements that I’m not even going to begin to touch.
For a game that I acquired accidentally (seriously, not sure where it came from, I assume a bundle somewhere), the production value is pretty high, and I’ve never played a game quite like it. That said, I’m not sure I’d want to play another game like it. It was okay once.  That's probably enough. Maybe if I accidentally get the sequel.

The gameplay was stupid, then it was okay, then it was addicting, then it was getting boring, then it was over. All in 8.5 hours. I might go back and do some of the maps where you fight the enemies in waves, but that’s only because I don’t feel like starting a new game before my sleeping meds kick in.
The game is very polished, and mostly stable. I only encountered one crash, and that was when I alt-tabbed out. However, mix that one crash with the fact that there is no save ability when you’re in a map, and there is no windowed mode, and you can see how that might end up being bad. You’re basically locked into that game being on your screen until you’re done with that map, and that may not be okay.
The game is over 6 years old, but could pass as a new indie game. There are already sequels out there, but the last one was in 2014. The studio did hit it big with “This War of Mine”, though, so who knows, they might revisit the Anomaly series someday. As far as I can tell, this game hasn't been patched in a very long time, but I don't know that there is a need for one, either.
The main story is the definition of linear. The rest of the game is just fighting the enemies in waves and achievement hunting. In my book, that’s very little replayability. It's a 10 hour affair, and then you're on to something else.

Interesting variety of tower defense genre. You're in control of "invading" units in pre-built maps. At the beginning of each stage, you select your squad based on money you have. You can set/change route of your squad any time you want, change their formation, upgrade their abilities, sell/buy units during mission. You'll have different goals like getting to the end point, destroying some towers along the route, escorting safely some unit to the end, etc. Enemy towers doesn't respawn (in most levels), nor upgrade, so you can plan your strategy ahead.
Besides your squad "on rails", you control the commander - unit which can freely roam the field. His mission is to provide help to your squad with healing, diversions and air strike. He can also be killed, but he respawns after several seconds, unlike other units. Commander is equally important as your other units, so you must learn to use him wisely.
Once you get familiar with game mechanics, you can finish this game with almost same unit formation every time on any difficulty, but nevertheless, game is addictive and very fun to play. I highly recommend playing in combination with steam achievements which adds interesting tasks to do during missions (which also makes the game more difficult).
Overall, if you like tower defense games, you probably won't regret getting this game.

This game really is something different. It's a football simulation, but it also isn't. And it's a life simulator... But also isn't. It's a bit difficult to describe this game. The football side is not as overly detailed as Football Manager for instance, but then again, that would take the fun out. Here, you aren't just constantly looking at numbers. Not to say that the life simulation is all that. It's not on the level of The Sims. It is what it is. It's just... Different. Fresh. It's not for everyone, but I certainly enjoy it. Even though it might not be the best in either of the two genres it tries to combine. For instance, I see people complaining about how managing all the addictions isn't easy. But it isn't supposed to be. They're supposed to be humans, not mindless drones. The best moments in this game are when you just let loose a little bit. Sure, my main striker was staying out late pretty much every evening, not showing up for practice, starting conga lines in the streets or sleeping on the sidewalk. But he kept banging in goals and ended as the league's top scorer. So who am I to judge? I hope this game gets a sequel. Because there certainly is enough to improve on. But this game is also one with great potential to build upon.

I've had a few attempts playing this game, let me summarise:
At launch:  a buggy mess, a festival of bugs and crashes and AI/UI issues.  You could not place certain (crucial) structures like steps .. which would allow you to mount archers on the walls.  Archers did not return fire as mace-men approached your walls.  It was a ridiculous and frustrating mess.  Only positive I can say is I liked some of the gritty art style.
A few months later:  it seemed like the developer was as disappointed as most consumers .. there was apparently some advices saying they blamed the publisher who pushed for an early release, and that they would endeavour to give consumers the game that they deserve through patching and constant and consistent after-sale improvements.  (Apparently the game we deserve is 'poo poo' because even with them working through the list of problems, the game, although playable in some ways, was still deeply flawed.  Archers still wouldnt retaliate, still had issues placing simple things like stairs up to walls).
About a year after launch:  I decide to give the game one last try.  (Loved earlier Stronghold titles and the concept in general).  They made some improvements to the game .. archers could fire back .. structures could be placed .. overall the game became somewhat playable .. BUT .. even after all that work they really barely achieve 'passable' .. archers may retaliate, but there's no mechanic for wall cover, and they get no elevation bonus to range or accuracy .. so basically 20 archers attacking a wall v 20 archers on a wall .. probably the attackers would win because they are clustered into one big kill-group, firing all their arrows together accurately, while the wall guys are scattered about and some would be out of range to attack... but yeah, basically the ones on the wall get no benefit).  Also you'll place units on a wall and they will become un-movable.  Just plain stuck.
So basically, despite a good legacy and concept, the game sucks.

Not something most people have probably heard of, but this is a hero-based real-time with pause strategy game. And it's tough.
It's an interesting game because it really does reward positioning, clever use of debuffing as well as damage-dealing skills and picking the right targets. Many skills - including healing - will happily affect friend and foe, which means you have to have a considered approach to battles, along with have to dodge the range of enemy spells. And given that enemies have a ton of health, you have plenty of time to hone your skills. Outside of frequent battles there are some puzzles to solve and a very rudimentary loot system; characters only have 4 item slots and you can recycle the items you pick up to create new epic items. And that's your lot.
It's pretty good, although it does have some real issues. Firstly, each character has only 4 skills (though they do branch to create other options) but the cast don't really have greatly defined roles, which is probably designed to make you mix-and-match your team as their skills increase but because things are much of a muchness you'll probably just stick with a group of 4 and be done with it. Also, the lack of meaningful loot. Stuff is only found in the field and is generally crap (including Epic items). As noted, you can recycle stuff to create more Epics, but they are still crap so you probably wouldn't bother, and, because the difference in stats you get is so minimal you won't care about periodically upgrading stuff.
The biggest crime, though, is the whole of the second act because it is largely comprised of some really frustrating environmental puzzles and there are too many of them. There are 3 or 4 different types but they are all awful and just drag you down and sour the experience. And the ending is dreadful - abrupt, lacking in real closure and designed for a sequel that is never going to come.
It's therefore a title with some interesting aspects - genuine tactical combat being the biggest draw - but some poor/odd design decisions hold it back from being something to recommend - if there was that 'Maybe' option on here, it would get that.

I'll talk about this game and how it compares to the other 3D Sonic games I've played. I'll start with the basics.
Graphics: The graphics are nice, but they're certainly a step down from Unleashed. Thankfully, there are mods that remedy this. The game also runs at a decent framerate on my main PC and a silky smooth 60 FPS on my gaming laptop. This doesn't mean that the graphics aren't bad, by any means. The graphics look great and the cartoonish look suits the remastered levels well. Overall, Sonic Generations is a great looking game.
Audio: The sound effects feel like a huge step up from the Adventure trilogy (1, 2 and '06) and the previous two boost games. The soundtrack is composed of great remixes of past games and you can even unlock the classic themes as well as others from many past Sonic games (Classic series, Adventure series, spinoffs and even the Rush games, Chaotix and Sonic 4!). I personally prefer the soundtracks of games like Unleashed and '06 but it's a huge step up in terms of quality compared to the Adventure games and the sound design puts the new Sonic Forces to shame.
Controls (Classic): Feels like the Classic games but the spindash is mapped to its own button, a la the Adventure games. The issue with this is that the spindash is too overpowered and rolling doesn't work very well when not being used as an attack. Controls are snappy and responsive and the analog controls (besides a glitch) work great. Overall, not much to say here. It's Sonic from the Genesis games, like the Genesis games. Overall: Like the classic games, but the physics feel a bit off and the spindash is broken in an OP way.
Controls (Modern): The gameplay is a step up from previous boost games. First of all, the homing attack and jump dash are now mapped to the jump button like in the Adventure games, rather than the boost button. This means that you can now use the jump dash while your boost meter has a charge. Previously you would just air boost instead. This comes with one caveat: you can no longer double jump like you could in Colors. Thankfully, in my opinion having the jump dash is better than the double jump and helps platforming a bit more, something Forces needs to learn from. Also you can drift. You can't do that in Forces anymore. Overall: Best control in a 3D Sonic game. The moveset is great and Forces definitely took this a step down.
Level design: Easily the greatest of the 3d games, second in my opinion to only '06, and overall my fourth in the series overall. Only this time there are far, FAR less bugs worsening the overall experience. All of the levels have been changed and entirely redone and overall play GREAT! The levels have a great balance of speed and platforming and often blend the two together in areas. The levels have many paths and usually have a lot of opportunities to do things like drifting to maintain speed. Forces's levels often feel like the earlier parts of Final Fantasy 13. Like hallways. Thankfully, this game, the previous game, does not have that problem. You will definitely enjoy playing the remixed levels in this game.
Replayability: The replayability is great. You have multiple missions that you can do later and there is a TON of bonus content you can unlock, including the Super States, artwork, and extra music.
Sonic Generations is certainly an experience you will enjoy. If you're looking for a good 3D Sonic game you can play on PC, this should be your first choice. Or Adventure 2. That works too.

What you need:
First of all you need to download the latest community patch (i think it's 1.7.5) otherwise the game will crash (Where is the Guru? error) and the mobs will simply one-shot you. Unfortunately the game was forcedly released before is was complete so the base version is full of bugs.
After you have installed both the game and the CP you can play.
G1 G2 comparison:
Differs from Gothic 1 and Gothic 2, you still play as the nameless hero but:
No chapters. You have a few main quest to complete. There are 6 reputation in the game and you have to choose who you want to support. There are 3 different way you can end the game based on your decisions.
Attributes: Strength, Mana, Dexterity, HP (no longer increase with lvl up, you can raise them by using ability points), Stamina (NEW, for combat and sprint) Ancient Knowledge (NEW, for magic), Thief skill (NEW), Smith skill (NEW),  Alchemy (NEW).
The ability points can now be spent in talents. In order to learn a talent you need a specific amount of points in its attribute (ex: 1h sword II req. 150 str. ex: crafting mana pots req. 20 alchemy).
The combat mechanics is completly different. You can now dual wield 1h swords or using 1h sword and a shield. There are different attack types (it's not just left click spam all game long, unless you play on "very easy")  but the main difference is that you now have a stamina bar. If you are low on stamina your attaks will be slower, you can't parry/block properly, you can't perform some power attack,  you can't sprint.
Final Judge:
Even if the G2 NotR storyline is the best by far, in terms of pure gameplay i thinks G3 is better thanks to the new talents system. The map is really huge and filled with secret areas.There are a lots of different quests and even an easter-egg like the G1's. A single play can last 100h+ (i'm at 64h doing less than 2/3 of the map). The interface is more user friendly, you have a 10 item slot bar where you can put weapons, foods, magics and bind them with hotkeys (1->0). Now you can cook/craft huge quantity with just one click (it ask how many instead of left clicking on the fire 50 times) and also loot easly with the "pick all" button (or rightclick on corpes with CP). Pots and foods now restore a % of you max health/mana instead of a flat number.
Game Mode:
With the CP you can choose 2 different play style. The base mode and the advanced mode. The advanced mode rebalances the talent trees, so it's harder (probably impossible) to build a balanced hero that can do everything by unlocking all the talents.
I played as:
- 1h sword + shield warrior, both easy and boring since you can win any 1v1 duel but it's really hard when you're surrounded by enemies and so you have to do some cheesy pull to avoid that.
- mage, really funny. A bit hard in the beginning since you have to hit and run to regen you mana pool and the staffs deal less dmg than swords (obv.) but when you've learned the mana reg. talent and you have a decent mana pool it's really enjoyable. It's not broken as the G2 mage that one-shots anything or deals no dmg at all.
Others:
I know there are mods but i never tried them.
Good Soundtrack
Tips:
I do not recommend the highest difficulty for your first run since you need to learn the combat system first. If you really want to start with the hard mode, just save after the inizial cutscene becouse you're going to die a lot of times :P
Since the decisions you make can really impact the game, if you want to do the most quest possibile don't rush things, just talk with every one and accept as many quest as you can. Even if killing everyone is fun it may have bad consequence on your game plan.
You can open the inventory during a fight and the game just pause. So you can regen your hp by drinking pots or eating foods without getting attacked. I know this mechanic sounds really lame and it wasn't possibile in G1 and G2 but the game is almost impossibile sometimes without using it.

Breath of the Wild mixed with a bit of Stardew Valley and Harvest Moon is the best way to describe Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles.
It's also a deathless world, one void of despair.
Thats right, while it can be compared to those games, there is no combat whatsoever, the closest you get to any violence in this game is when you smash containers open for loot.
There's really only one dark element in this game and thats the "murk" a dark and murky substance that blocks off certain areas and treasure chests. Bar that, there's no demonic entities to fight like in Breath of the Wild, nothing hostile whatsoever.
Yonder's not a game for people who crave non-stop violence in their videogames, but its possible they could like it. Not every game needs a gun or weapons of any kind and Yonder proves this.
There wasn't a single time where I dreaded having to kill one of the various cute animals for their materials like in every other game, instead I merely had to befriend them, bring them to my farm and then make sure they were fed, getting their fur and milk etc in return.
Storywise is where the game fell flat for me, you start off on a ship which is wrecked, then end up at a nearby village where you help them out and then end up repairing the Cloud Catcher, thus dispersing the murk, all wrapped up with a surprise that I saw coming from a mile away. Its not a bad story, merely a dull one with no twists or unexpected events thrown at you. It could have been so much more.
Instead of one main farm as I had initially hoped, you have a number of them, one in each region bar two of them. While its a nice idea, it can be cumbersome travelling to and from each one to gather any materials produced. Sure, you have the sage stones which act as teleporters and a hub world where you can choose which one to go through, but even then you'll still be doing a fair amount of walking from one to get to your destination. Also a label of some sort for each sage stone would be a lovely addition, some of them I just could not tell where they lead to.
You can join several guilds in this, such as the tailor, chef, and tinker one. Joining them is simple enough: the master gives you some items and asks you to make a specific item for them, you make it and hey presto you're in. Then to advance to master of that guild you have to make 1000 value worth of items belonging to that class, easy enough right? Yeah, it would be if vendors stocked more than a small handful of items at a time, leaving you to wait for some time to restock or just farming basic items to make the kits, which are worth little. Either way it can be a nuisance mastering these.
Speaking of crafting, there are items such as mortar and nails that are required for crafting a variety of items but the only way (that I've noticed in my 20 hours) to acquire them is from vendors. So then you have to farm some items to trade with them to then get said items. Rinse and repeat until you just want to punch these vendors but realise violence is practically non-existent in this.
Fishing, mining, cutting grass, planting trees and smashing boulders are how you'll be collecting items in this outside of vendors, and fishing is easily my favourite thing to do in this. Considering that I don't like fish, its odd that I enjoy it so much but I can't help it when its so calming. Heck, I once spent nearly an hour fishing in this just because. Mining and the rest were merely pit stops for me as I traveled to the nearest watering hole.
Oh, I should mention there are collectibles in this, the most elusive being the cats. There are 55 of these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and some will only show up at certain times of the day, during a certain season and, most annoyingly, during a specific weather pattern. The 27 that I've found thus far was purely by just wandering from quest to quest and chancing upon them. You can build a cat totem once you've beat the story but all it does is place decorative cats in your farm. A shame, really.
The other collectibles are the animals, there's only seven of them which is a disappointment as they are truly adorable.One thing that I would absolutely love to be included in a possible future patch would be to ride said animals, I don't want to keep them cooped up in the farm all year but I see little point in taking them with me when all they can do is follow me around.
You also have sprites, think Navi from Ocarina of Time but the only time they talk is when you find them. They're found during the course of the story, by helping residents of the island with their requests, or by completing puzzles to bring them out of hiding, you can even change which one to accompany you but they're merely decorative.
Gemea itself is a beautiful island to explore, ranging from lush forests to beaches, an enormous mountain you can jump off and a wintery wonderland. The Unity engine is put to great use here and the art style alone is a great selling point for this game. The music is wonderful too, changing as you move from region to region or as the time of day changed.
Going back to the topic of quests, there is quite a lot of them, all of which can easily be tracked via your compass, but beware, because every time you accept a new quest it will then default to that one, forcing you to open the compass and go back to the one you were originally tracking.
Yonder is a beautiful game that can eat up 20-30 hours, maybe more depending on if you're going for full completion. You can call it a game for kids if you so wish but should there ever come a time where you want to explore a beautifully crafted world without having to fight every other minute, then Yonder is highly recommended.
Hopefully, with future patches (let me marry someone damn it) and additional content, if the devs intend to add some, the game could be even better.
Bonus: There's also an island that is populated with nothing but trolls and poop, with the trolls making satirical remarks about the game. Nice to see the devs have a sense of humour about people's reactions to the game.

Weaker in some aspects compared to Eastside Hockey Manager, stronger in others.
Pros:
- League expansion
- Fairly easy to mod and make custom teams/leagues
- Officially licensed by the NHL
- Dev team is active on the OOTP forums and updates the game regularly
- Contract negotiations are much more realistic than EHM
Cons:
- Generally much more "simple"
- UI can be difficult to navigate
- Player parity takes huge hits with little steps in attributes, ex. knocking 5 stat points off total from a 4 star player (like taking off 1 speed, 1 shot range, 1 aggression) will make them a 3 star player in some cases. Way too many 2.5 star players in the league but that can be solved with roster updates
- Slow simulation
- Still has bugs, on OSX I have occasional crashes out of nowhere and a lot of text glitches in emails
- Difficult to manage minor league teams
Overall, it's definitely worth a shot if you want some hockey management sim action. It's not quite at the level of EHM, but it will probably overtake it soon with the amount of work going into it. If you're on PC and you prefer the ability to customize your leagues and teams or want to take over an expansion team, this is your game. If you're on OSX, this is your only option, but it's still a pretty solid option. 6.5/10.

Got my hands into FHM3 for a few hours finally.  Big improvement on last year's game.  The main point of interest is the NHL license.  It adds a whole other dimension to the game, and allows you to immerse yourself into the role more.  Another big point for me, which actually caused me to stop playing FHM2, are the changes to the interface.  In FHM2, the interface was so bland and boring, text was so small, it was so difficult to focus on what you were doing and where you were supposed to look.  Though improvements could still be made in my opinion(certain font sizes, bolding, etc), the GUI is now wonderfully shaded with your team's colours - this has had a huge impact on my interest to learn the game more.
This iteration of FHM features more in-depth ratings and player stats, more logically and cleanly placed information and controls that are relative to what your task is and a great tactics system, which I'm learning to love.  I may be wrong about this, but it seems the game/match engine is improved quite a bit as well.

Franchise Hockey Manager 3 is developed and published by Out of the Park Developments. They seem to specialize on making sports management simulators such as the much better, Out of the Park Baseball 17. And I would have to be Out of My Mind to spend nearly 40 dollars on the “masterpiece” I’m about to present to you.

I haven't had this much fun since decorating my house. In fact, watching paint dry would probably make for a better review subject. Before you dismiss my unabashed opinion of this title as simply another review writing geek hating on sports games, I’ll have you know that my love affair with the ice rink goes back quite a few years. Now, that does not mean I was ever a professional ice skater or hockey player, but I wasn’t clueless about it either. To my major disappointment, Franchise Hockey Manager 3 is far worse than any cheap football manager I’ve ever played. Those had far better simulations of the games themselves. More on that, in a bit. You might think I’m comparing apples to oranges, but sports management video games are fairly similar in the User Interface department at least, if not game mechanics. Speaking of the UI, it’s as dreary as it can ever get. Micromanagement is a necessity even if you delegate an AI coach to deal with the players and their much needed training and tactics during the matches. In the end, it’s gonna come back biting you somewhere once you see just how bad your team fares and you will have to become the coach as well if you wish to stand any chance of finishing the championship in a dignified position.
Even if you have so many leagues to choose from North America, Europe and even a few Asian nations, it all plays the same and you don’t even have a randomized minimal visual style to differentiate one team from another (apart from a small logo). As for the hockey players, you don’t see any pictures or portraits with them at all. In FHM 3, only John Does seem to play no matter if you’re in a small town in Canada or in Japan The simulation of the hockey games made me think I’m play testing a game from the early ‘90s. You have the crude drawing of the Ice hockey rink over which a puck moves back and forth with some text below it with the commentator’s insights. It gets old really fast.
The title’s spartan approach in regards to its aestethics is sadly worsened by the lack of any sounds. I really wouldn’t have believed it if I didn’t actually try to play and “enjoy” this game. Even shovelware on Steam, costing 10 cents has more sounds than FHM 3. It’s beyond me, the dev team’s decision to esckew even a barebones repetitive tune or a crowd cheering. Anything is better than silence. Did I mention this game loads very slowly? Its sluggishness is inexplicable considering most modern CPUs. You’re telling me I can host lighitning fast 3D battles with thousands of soldiers in a Total War game, but a 2D hockey manager requires 10 minutes just to load all its database if you start a new game? Don’t even get me started on the game’s settings and resolution issues. FHM 3’s idea of fullscreen still implies that I hide the taskbar. Steam Overlay doesn’t even wish to start along with the game, not that I was just dying to showcase any screenshots with it.

+ Simulates the stress of being a sports manager/coach, I guess?
+ Steam Achievements & Steam Trading Cards.
- UI and basic Steam overlay issues
- Immensely overpriced
- Lacks almost any form of imagery
- No sounds
I don’t think I’ll need to play this genre for quite some time from now. I’ve had my fill and no matter how much of a fan I might be of simulations in general terms, sometimes arcades have their merits. Not having even a small measure of visual aid, harms such management games a lot. I knew they are a niche genre and I respect their well-accustomed playerbase, but there are enough alternatives to Franchise Hockey Manager 3. Even it’s predecessor, which is at the time of this writing 17 dollars cheaper, seems like a smarter choice. Asking $36.99 is just outrageous.

Corpse Party is a title that lives up to its name. Despite its seemingly simple premise, sprites and top-down perspective, Corpse Party manages to invoke a sense of fear and dread with every step of the way. It knows what you’re going in for, cranks it up, and gives you exactly what you weren’t expecting. This was what first got me into the series.
Corpse Party follows a simple structure: You navigate a cast of characters through the haunted elementary school, pick up various items, figure out puzzles and attempt to find a way home. The characters and situations you find yourself in change accordingly as the story progresses. There are no complex strategies to formulate nor enemies that you must defeat – your brain and intuition are all that matter. For that, Corpse Party uses simple control mechanics with both a keyboard and controller. Movements are sound and responsive (as what you’d expect from a top-down game) and any AI programmed into the game is fair to handle.
However, the same cannot be said for the entire game. Corpse Party offers many bad endings to its chapters alongside the true, canonical ones. The pre-requisites to obtaining the bad endings vary in circumstances and options given to the player. There are numerous times where the player may receive a bad ending by ignoring simple logic, going against their instincts or manipulating events in a manner they might not think of on their first playthrough. This can be rather unfair sometimes. Though some of them are relatively simple to figure out and avoid, others will test the player and get them to experiment with multiple runs. Saving can be essential.
The Steam port of Corpse Party is not the same as the PSP or 3DS versions. It was instead built off the PC version which came out a few years prior. This means that it does not contain the updated visuals, voice acting or CG scenes. Overall, the downgrade is not that bad, since the features are still good enough. It’s a preference over aesthetics. The lack of CG scenes is a bit disappointing, but they’re nothing that a simple internet search can’t fix.
Though Corpse Party is a relatively short game (roughly 8 - 15 hours depending on the player), it maintains a constant balance between characters and story. The atmospheric soundtrack and effects only add to its eerie setting. It is unarguably not for everyone, despite what outside impressions might look like. The series is one that is not afraid to get dark. If you can get past that and its graphic scenes, then Corpse Party will provide an immersive experience, and one that shan’t be forgotten.

TL;DR - Diet GTA in the middle of the 20th Century.
I loved this game. It's like a GTA Lite. Very much similar to the GTA games (unsurprising, since they're the same company) in the way that it plays during all the missions, although there isn't anywhere near as much to do in 'free roam' mode. There isn't a specific free roam as such, but you can do what you like in between parts of the missions. There are posters and magazines to collect (some of the mags are mission specific) and things to do, like robbing shops/buying clothes/stealing cars nd getting money for selling or scrapping them. Oter than that, there's the missions themselves - 15 of them - which when you boil it down, mostly involve driving and/or shooting, but they do feel different as you go through the game. Some are short, some long, many are broken up into seperate parts (leaving you the choice of going off and doing something else inbetween). The game is divided into several parts - which gives a nice variety to the game over time played - the music, cars, clothes and driving are different in wintry 1940s Empire Bay than they are to the summery 1950s Bay. There are also a couple of segues elsewhere, which add variety.
But it's the little touches that made this game much more than just 'average' for me - people slipping over in the snow, comments random people give you (in passing and in conversation), hubcaps flying off occasionally with dodgy driving, the radio news giving Newsflashes regarding things you've just done, the fact that you can 'open' doors, or kick them in and lots more 'little' things that add ambience to a game. Add this to a decent storyline, with some twists and turns, and good (if somewhat cliched characters) and it all makes for a game well worth playing. Plus, it still holds it's own graphics-wise. Definately worth buying, even more so in a sale.

This is my all time favourite game. It's everything I love about RPG's - the freedom, the story, the impact you can make and the interactions with others (NPC's).
But installing Comunity Patch is strongly advised, also modding might be interesting for some (more info on both can be found in the discussions).
Pros:
+ Great story line, that continues the adventures of our nameless hero from Gothic 1 and Gothic 2, but the game has dialogs for people who are not fammiliar with the first two games. If you meet someone  from the previous games, they will remember you, but you can ask them who tey are and usually with a whitty remark, they will remind you how you know them.
+ It's an RPG, so you have your standart RPG elements:
* You do quests, kill monsters, gain experience, level up, earn learning points and use them to learn a bunch of skills, like Hunting, Blacksmithing, Thievery, Alchemy, Magic (Anchient knowledge).
* Each set of skills has it's own attributes, like Hunting has archery, improved archery and master archery. Learning points can also be used to increase your hitpoints, stamina or mana.
* Wide vierity of weapons, also magic can be used in combat.
* You can make your own weapons, potions and food.
+ Fantastic soundtrack.
+ Open world. You can go where ever you want and do what ever you want (be ware of consequenses, some monsters are strong as hell and will kick your beginer♥♥♥♥♥.
+ Three different lands with different climate, different people, different culture and seperate stories that in one way or another intertwine.
+ You can beat up who ever you want (assuming you are skilled enough) and you can kill who ever you want (if you can beat them up or if you've learned Assasination).
+ If you start a fight in a town that doesn't know you and isn't friendly, others will kick your♥♥♥♥♥(unless you can kick all of their ases :D ). Towns have rules - no fighting (unless you are well known :D)
+ After you've beaten up someone and knocked them down, you can take their weapon and rob them.
+ If you steal something in a town people will start to suspect you, You can try to talk your way out, but they might or might not fall for that. IF they see you stealing, be prepared to fight.
+ If someone sees you killing someone in a town - be prepared to fight. If only one person saw you, you can kill him and get away with it, though others might suspect you're to blame, but just as with stealing, you can try to talk your way out of it. If a lot of people saw you, then you'll have to fight all the people in town.
+ Friends will join your fights and will support you. If you fight a friend, however, others will cheer. :D
+ You can pick sides. What will you choose. Who will you help. - it's up to you.
+ There are a lot of quests and a lot of different mods.
+ The moment you start a revolution...
+ Open ending. The main story gives you a choice on how you'll end the game. And your choice along with your other actions and choices, will determan what future will look like.
+ The game has one of the best gaming community and a Community Patch Team that has releaset the latest and final patch 1.75 that makes the game work and look a lot better. With the patch, you won't be able to tell that the game is so old. (More info on the patch can be found in discussions)
+ The game has mods.
+ The game has some surpises, like hidden diaries that tell a story no NPC knows.
Cons:
- Your decisions have consequences. This is a good thing, but it can actually ruin the game for you, if you did something and you don't know how it will impact the game. For example if you liberate too many towns before you do all the quests  for them, the town head will attack you and you'll loose dialogs and some quests.
- It's a massive game and if you wan't to play it as best as you possibly can, you need to know a lot of stuff. This includes who to kill and who to spare and when, where to look for items etc.
- Dialogs are important. This is nothing new and should be a norm, but sometimes gamers just like to skip dialogs and go kill beasts for no reason, but still get paid for it :D and in oh so many cases dialogs explain what and where you must do to finnish the quest, so skipping dialogs is unadwised. Luckily Quest log shows you the important parts of the dialog.
- At times you will need google to help you with quests. There are quests that conterdict each other and you'll have to choose who's side will you take.
- Some english voice acting is not the best. Other languages have it better.

NOTE: I finished this game, but played a majority of it offline.
If you think this is your generic RPGMaker horror game, think again. It is not very graphically intensive (usually a must for gore-fest horror games), but it more than makes up for that with a legitamatly interesting story, descriptive gore scenes
and great audio.
The game is split into 5 chapters. In each chapter, you make multiple choices which may effect the outcome of the chapter. There are multiple wrong ends for each chapter and only 1 "bloodcovered" end, which is the correct ending of the chapter. Throughout the game, you will have to solve puzzles to progress. For example, if there is an object at the bottom of a filthy pool, you will have to figure out how to get to that item which could be a key to room that you need to visit in order continue.
My only problem with Corpse Party would be that if you make a wrong choice early on in the chapter, you may not realise the mistake until near the end of the chapter. Chapters can take about 2 hours to complete, so if you don't have a save from before your mistake in one of your 3 save slots, I hope you enjoy replaying the chapter. It is also not always clear what your mistake was. Some say that figuring out where you went wrong is part of the fun, but some of the choices can be as acute as choosing whether or not to read something. If you do get stuck and have no idea what you've done wrong, I would recommend finding a spoiler free walkthrough of that chapter (although I never had to use one).
To conclude, this is an awesome horror game with an interesting story and good audio. If you can put up with its faults, it is an experience you wont regret.

Corpse Party is a fantastic horror title, but this one is marred by several issues. Others have already pointed out the downgraded art style (which went from realistic to overly chibi for some reason), but the dealbreaker is the voice acting. I'm sure the VA's are fine people who did a good job, but two issues arise:
1) I'm sorry, but the incredibly high-pitched anime voice is like jamming nails into my earholes. This isn't helpful when a whole lot of the dialogue is screaming or crying. A number of the scenes involve multiple talk bubbles of screams or sobs, and they're presented INDIVIDUALLY.
2) For no reason I can discern, quite a number of the dialogues later in the game don't let you speed through them, so you actually HAVE to listen to them be acted out in full time. It happens chiefly during the intro/outro scenes on the chapters, but also in other spots.
These are made worse by the fact that a whole bunch of those scenes that you can't speed through are just voice/text on a TOTALLY BLACK SCREEN. So basically you have to sit there and listen to a foreign language reciting dialogue you're already finished reading and just hoping it'll hurry the hell up and be over. CP is a dialogue-heavy game to begin with, but by stopping the player from being able to move at their own reading pace it brings a lot of it to a snail crawl.

I'm a big fan of games that try to do something different. Lords of Football attempts to marry the football management experience with a sims-lite player management experience. How successfully it manages that seems to vary on a person by person basis. It may not be spreadsheety enough for the Football Manager fans and not Simsy enough for Sims fans.
Personally, I love it. The unlicensed football-lite side reminds me of Sensible Soccer and the Simsy side... well yeah obvious. The point is, the resulting gaming experience is pretty unique and great fun. What's more, the dev team is taking the usual indie route of listening to players and working hard to improve aspects of the game. Consider the newly released database editor allowing you to fully customize all the teams and players to your heart's content.
Ultimately, I like this game. I think the IP has potential and the developer has potential. I've clocked up 63 hours of playtime and I'm not done with it yet. Your mileage may vary but if you want to try something different then give it a shot, you might just find yourself hooked.

This game is thoroughly enjoyable for anyone who likes open world games with elements of crafting and collecting. There is plenty to do and you'll not find yourself running out of stuff to do. For a small studios first game it looks absolutely beautiful, with a great user friendly interface. And that lends to the immersive experience I believe you are meant to have. The game isn't very large at all, and runs very smoothly!
The only real criticisms I have are that character interactions could have been a little more impactful and meaningful with depth. Combat isn't necessary but would certainly add more to the game (maybe in regards to hunting) but for it's Nintendo'esque child friendly style it is tolerable, and I suppose not every game has to have violence as a means to solve problems.
There's plenty of room for growth with this IP (I personally can think of many things I would love to see added) and I hope the devs get the resources to add more to the game, if not be able to make a sequel one day! It's definitely a rock solid foundation.
In context for what it aims to be, it is very successful and I think it deserves an 8/10. For its price I highly recommend it.

One day I was craving some open world, GTA type game-play, but browsing trough different catalogs, I couldn’t find anything to suit my needs, and when I almost gave up on my cravings, I found this gem in my steam’s library. Also since Mafia 3 is out right now, it would be right time to dive into this title, and to remember what this franchise is all about.
The story takes place in fictional city named Empire Bay. You’re playing as young man called Vito Scalleta, whose just been back from action in World war II. As Vito returns, he’s starting to look for a job, but soon he realizes, that doing regular job, won’t be enough to support his family and fulfilling his material needs, so trough his old friend Joe, Vito gets in to doing some illegal activities, and starts his way up into world of underground crime scene. Story is split up in two parts, first one being winter of 1945 and second is summer of 1951. Each one has unique elements for current time period, like cars, clothes style, music and so on. Main plot it-self, is well written and has some great moments and characters, but nothing out of the box. If you watched some gangster or crime movies, TV shows or been in to other media of such kind, a lot of things you’ll find familiar.  Same goes with characters some are quite interesting, funny and quite likable, while others are one-dimensional cliches. Story has some cool plot-twists and even couple a bit emotional moments. I personally  really enjoyed it, and it’s one of the best stories in last-gen games of such type.
On ultra settings, Mafia II run quite well, however there were moments were frame-rate dropped below 30 and stayed that way for couple minutes for no particular reason. Trough my play-trough, game crushed a couple times and I also encounter couple game breaking bugs, so I had to restart some levels from begging.  In the visual side of things, game looks great to this date, the draw distances are huge, lightning and environmental effects look great even 6 years later. Character models and animations look believable and lip-sinking also is done well, and environment has some angle of destructibility. Only thing to complain about, are textures, up close, a lot of them look quite ugly and low-res.  I also enjoyed sound design, the voice acting is well done, cars and weapons sound great and there are enough ambient sounds to feel it more like a real city. Also you can not mention the license soundtrack, which is just awesome.
Last, but not least – the game-play. Well some say that this game is considered open-world. I would disagree. Mafia II is as open world, as Fable is RPG game. So yeah, you have this city, which is a descent size. But besides story, there's not much to do, you can visit gun shops or clothing stores, you can go to restaurants or bars to have some meals, and you have some side activities, like stealing cars to earn extra cash, and that’s where the open-world aspect ends. Since it’s a gangster themed game, you’ll be doing a lot of melee fighting and shooting. Melee aspect of the combat is done OK, but could be done better, all the melee-combat is just fist-fights and there are no melee weapons like baseball bat in first game. Shooting is pretty much cover-based, like it’s done in ''Gears of war'' or ''Spec-ops -  The line'' and so on. It works great, weapons handle better than first game, and there are a lot more of them. Also the weapon management is improved. There are different types of pistols, rifles, sub-machines guns and explosives to choose. Only thing I didn’t like about shooting, is that it’s removed while driving, you’ll sometimes have someone in your car who will handle it, but you can’t do it yourself. And that brings me up to the last major element – cars. Cars in this game are still a bit clunky and sluggish to drive. But you can tune them up so they become faster and more easier to handle, also you can tune their appearance, and as you enter in to early 50’s the cars get better in every way. This game makes you focus on more “Drive safely” approach. Because police will chase you for speeding or hitting other cars. So quite often you’ll be driving by the rules, not to screw up the mission progress.
So to sum it up, game has some cool story, but it might be better and maybe element of choice could make it even more interesting. Gun-play and combat in general is done well and really improved over to the previous title. Car handling is more realistic, and makes you remember that your driving cars, from more than half-century ago. Game looks great to this date, but has some technical issues, that might not become pleasant. Overall the game is major improvement over first game, but it would be nice, if some game-play elements were left from first title. So yeah game is good, but some things could be done better. 9/10.
Thanks for reading.

Ever wondered what it was like back in the day when the mobsters still wore suits? Ever watched the Godfather and wished that there was a game like that (Well, besides the actual Godfather game)? Welp, Mafia 2's your game. Mafia 2 takes place in the 1940s, a time where the world is at war and the US is now getting out of the Great Depression. You play as Vito Scaletta, an Italian immigrant with a troubled past. When Vito gets back from the war, he comes home to debt and wants to be rich more than anything. He soon finds out that honest work isn't going to get him there so, he dives into the twisted nest of danger and adventure known as the Mafia.
The overall story is fantastic and has twists and turns that spice it up even more. The characters are also very memorable and likable. The game is split up into 15 chapters, and each one is unique. There are some things that you'll see a fair amount of the time, such as shoot outs, but it never really feels repetitive. The map is fairly large, so you'll usually need a car to get around. The cars in this game look amazing, being that this game takes place in the 40s and 50s, they're all classic. The driving mechanics are a tad bit old, but they're still good. You can also customize their paint and their license plates. In order to get one, you'll usually have to steal one. There's a lock picking mechanic in this game just for that. The lockpicking is pretty easy and satisfying. If you're in a rush, then you can also just break the window.
Like I said before, there are a fair amount of shoot outs. The shoot outs are tense and amazing. It feels like a good shoot out scene in an action movie. For shoot outs, you'll of course need some weapons. There are a variety of weapons, such as pistols, shot guns, rifles, assualt rifles, and some other weapons like grenades and molotovs. There's no limit to the amount of weapons that you can hold, so they're all yours. The sound design is pretty great, especially during these shoot outs. Thankfully, the shoot outs aren't overused, so it still feels special every time.
Another fighting mechanic is the melee combat. Now, the melee combat is pretty dated and is basically boxing. It's not super hard, but it's not all that satisfying. Thankfully, it's not used that much. There is a chapter where you'll have to do it about 3 times, but other than that, you won't have to use it too often.
Being that this is an open world game, there is a police system. The police in this game are actually decently realistic. Now, they won't bust you for running a light, but they do sometimes get you for speeding. If they catch you stealing a car, that car will be wanted, which means you'll have to change the plates. Also, if you're wanted, you'll have to change your clothes. It's a nice attention to detail that you typically don't see in other games. Granted, changing your clothes in real life when you're wanted wouldn't help, but this is a video game.
The music in the game is  also pretty fantastic and fits well. Being that this is set in the 40s and 50s, the music is appropriate for the time. Also, something extremely well  done is the time shift. Without divulging any spoilers, the game eventually shifts from the 40s to the 50s and it is awesome. They really have an eye for detail in this game.
One thing that people tend to complain about is that besides story, there's not much to do, which is true. You can go out to eat, buy clothes, and hold up and rob places, but other than that, there's not much to do. The story does keep you busy though.
If you've played Mafia 1, you'll probably catch the references that they make to it in this one. Also, there's a cameo from someone from the first game ;) In all, Mafia 2 is a fantastic game and is defintely worth checking out.

Don't let the RPG Maker graphics fool you, this is a horror themed adventure game and not an RPG.
A group of students decide to perform a ritual they found on the internet as a lark after class (Imagine something similar to saying "Candyman" three times). Unfortunatley for them, it turns out to be no urban myth and they are whisked away to the hell dimension that is Heavenly Host High School. Seperated into small groups they must try to survive and escape from this dastardly plane that is without doubt out to brutally murder them.
This game really isn't for the faint of heart, while I would not consider this game scary ala Amnesia the Dark Descent or SOMA, it most definatley disturbing. What the game lacks in graphics it more than makes up for in graphic descriptions of blood and gore. Especially some of the bad endings, of which there are many, are truly awful. So yeah, if you don't like your horror brutal and descruptive, maybe this isn't for you. If you like a good horror novel though, you are going to be right at home.
The story and characters are really quite engaging. While most of the characters generally fit into broad anime archetypes, seeing how they react to being inside the awfulness the is Heavenly Host makes it interesting and it's cool to see how they work together (or not) as things get more and more horrific and they deal with all kinds of really disturbing events. The story is broken into five chapters and each one builds on the last, slowy revealing each character's back story and the backstory to Heavenly Host itself. It's all well written and extremely engaging, almost every chapter ends with a shock revelation then a cliff hanger ending, meaning its hard to just stop at the end of an episode. You're going to feel compelled to start the next one just to see what happens.
It's also worth getting the bad endings, just for the extra insight they can provide on the plot. Not to mention this is where you are going to get some of the most gruesome stuff the game has to offer.
This is a really great game and I can't recommend it enough. If you are at all into this kind of thing you have probably seen the positive reviews on Steam itself and in other media. It really deserves the respect it gets, and if you can look past the 16 bit graphics, you are in for a hell of a ride.

I really do reccomend this game. After playing Sonic Forces, it made me want to go back and play this game. And my god, this game is stunning.
Graphics:
Graphics may not be the best. In fact, Unleashed and Forces have better graphics. It doesn't mean it's bad though. Graphics shouldn't really affect how fun a game is. And if you are bothered about the graphics, just download the UnleashedFXPipeline mod. There is a community page which contains the mod loader and mods.
Controls and Gameplay:
This is by far some of the best controls.
Modern Sonic - The boost is implemented well, the jump isn't too heavy or too floaty. The drift is a huge improvement from Sonic Unleahsed as it actually feels tighter and responds well. The Air Dash (or Homing Dash) is done well to. Just a slight adjustment hels you with the platforming in certain stages like Planet Wisp, Rooftop Run and Speed Highway. The Homing Attack is very quick and responsive. I never fell to my death by an unresponsive homing attack. Doing a chain is quick and fluent. The Air Boost is incredibly helpful for speed runs or trying to get across a large gap which a regular Air Dash wouldn't do. It doesn't last too long, so it isn't OP like it is in Sonic Forces.
Classic Sonic - Classic Sonic is simple. Jump, roll and spin dash (excluding unlockables). The jump isn't floaty at all. It feels almost the same as the originals. The Spin Dash is the main problem though. The Spin Dash is way too fast and lasts way too long, and getting the Skill 'Long Spin Dash' makes it incredibly broken. Not only that but there is a Spin Dash button, you don't have to crouch and spam the button. It's just like Modern Sonic's boost to where it can be used at any time. The roll is almost useless in this game. You don't gain ANY speed from rolling down a hill or slope. Most of the time, you'll be spin dashing to get the speed. You'll only be using the roll when there's an enemy and its a last second decision. The physics are broken as previously mentioned with the roll, but just simply running gains speed. And although it's not perfect, the physics are playable and you'll still have fun with it. Classic Sonic is definetly broken, but he is still fun. And if you're bothered about physics, download the Physics Mod.
Story:
None, This game is definetly lacking a story. It's basically 3 hours of nothing happening but running through levels to restore colour and life. I do wish there was a bigger story, but games like Mario have barely any story so i'm not too bothered about this. My main issue with the story is how short it is. I completed the game in just over 2 hours. And you'll never feel inclined to replay this game because of its story. It'll mostly be the levels.
Replay Value:
Now the story holds ZERO replay value. But the levels are just amazing. These are by far some of the the best levels we have seen in the Boost games. Not just the levels but there are so many collectibles to get too. Unlock concept art or music from the past games, which you can then listen to whilst playing a level. This is a great addition as you can change music in Chemical Plant to Toxic Caves or Sonic Boom. There'll be music which fits each level, and some which do not work and make the experience more funny. The collectibles are Red Star Rings and there are 5 in each stage. A total of 90 in the whole game. These can be difficult to find, but it's just increasng replay value more and more as when you're trying to find them, you'll be finding hidden paths along the way. The game also has challenges and these are little side missions. There are 45 with each Sonic, giving a total of 90 Challenges. Some are super easy, however some hold real challenge and this spices things up a little as the majority of the game is a cake walk. This game also has many years of mod support behind it. There are so many great mods, such as the Unleashed Project (All Act 1 Stages of Unleashed), STH2006 Project (All Sonic stages from Sonic 06), many character mods and there is a Real Tails mod which lets you fly! You'll never run out of mods as they are always being created and uploaded and this is what makes me keep coming back for more Generations.
The Rating:
There are many more things I could've commented on like Level Variety, level design, character development, humour etc. But this review is already long enough. I've covered the main points so it's good enough.
The game get a 9/10 for me. The Story was lacking and I never feel inclined to replay because of the story. The Online sucks as it's just leaderboards. The controls for Keyboard suck. You can't use a mouse, you can't use Shift or CTRL. The only keys tha tcan be used are letters, numbers and Spacebar. It's annoying if you are a Keyboard player as WASD isn't fully functional as you can't use Shift as boost and the mouse to drift. It's easy trying to play Classic Sonic with Keyboard but Modern Sonic is barely playable. At least for me anyway. If you have a controller.

. Another action-adventure addition to the evergoing Sonic the Hedgehog franchise.
In terms of story, Sonic and his friends celebrate his birthday in their present time. They are, however, interrupted and taken into a blank dimension by Dr. Eggman and his new diasterous entity from a corner of outer space known as the Time Eater. Causing havoc and bringing the past and present Sonics (and Tails) together, the quartet work to restore their respective worlds and put an end to Eggman's plans of total dimensional domination.
In terms of gameplay, players are orientated into playing two similar yet different styles. In Act 1 for every zone, you are granted access to Classic Sonic, whom plays much to that of Sonic in nostalgic times: his stages are all two-dimensional, your method of gaining speed is through charing spin dash, enemies can only be defeated via spin dash or bouncing atop them, and your goal is the original post sign at the end of the stage. In Act 2 for every zone, however, you have control over modern Sonic, whose gameplay fashions more closely to games like Daytime Sonic of
and
; the player is able to boost upon gaining power from rings, tricks such as the Homing Attack and Slide allow to advance through exploration of the wider map, areas of the stage alternate between three-dimensional and two-dimensional orientations, and your endgame is a shiny, larger ring.
Upon completion of each stage, Sonic rescues a friend that has been left frozen in a White Void (that serves as an "Adventure Field," if you will) and are able to explore, visit shops for new items, and see miscellaneous materials that have been unlocked throughout the game. After clearing three zones, there is an avaliable boss to traverse into three more.
This game's existence somewhat brings back semi-old memories of all Sega and Sonic Team have done and created that some fans of the franchise enjoyed. It featured notable characters like Amy, Knuckles, and Espio--whom has not been heavily showcased in any other games outside
--and lovable levels like Chemical Plant and City Escape. The game also brings back what many leveled about original Sonic: his starting roots in gameplay with solely 2D level design. The remixed music continues to be one of the best things about the frachise as well. In some areas, the plotline can be likened too.
Its missions are not too unbearable and provide extra game time, alongside hidden red rings throughout both Act 1 and Act 2 of every zone.
In Generations, the boss battles can either be short-lived and exhausting and can rarely find a middle ground; as one example, the Time Eater boss can last some time, especially if the players are unable to piece exactly what is happening and how to move in. Even on Hard Mode, the Shadow boss with Modern Sonic can easily be beatened without much difficulty in comparaison to the original fight from
. Though the missions can be funny, they do not break away from Sonic, much to my dislike, and provide at least one level that the player can interact with another character or somewhat relive a Treasure Hunt with Knuckles or Rogue, or a Race with Tails
.
--Hermix.

Throne Rushers is a 2D action-platformer game where the only goal is to get to the top of the map
which is including but not limited to: deceit, malpractice, taking extended naps, prostitution, and most importantly, murder. You double jump along the sides of terrain to climb and throw shuriken, because for some reason you and all your competitors are ninjas, even though nothing else on the map is ninja-esque. It's not even night time. You also have some sort of inner-fire thing with right-click that allows you to deflect projectiles. If you ignore the previous statement the game drives close to impossible because enemy shuriken fly at slightly-slower-than-light speed.
The gameplay is okay, a bit jagged at times but generally tolerable. It's simple and effective. The game is mildly entertaining at best, but there's really not a lot of reasons to keep playing aside from the character customization that the developer put in. Unfortunately, that quality is a good attempt, but not good enough to make the game worthy of playing for more than a couple of hours.
Another good quality is that the developer made the multiplayer expandable up to 30 simultaneous players on a locally hosted server. The downside is that none of your friends will play this game, but the effort is pretty good! Hit me up if for some reason you want to waste hella money and we'll host a Throne Rushers tournament. I'll buy pizza, or something.

The game is sound. It plays well and it's not boring. The story is a bit less than engaging, the controls are good, unique characters, linear and short which can be a nice break from the open world never ending variety. If I had any complaints, it would be that it doesn't let you play with friends.

The combat system in this game is its main selling point as far as I'm concerned and it is a fairly unique combat system that makes every fight a kind of puzzle challenge. The way the combat works is a mash up between party based real time with pause crpgs such as Pillars of Eternity or Baldur's gate with a MOBA. it does this by giving you 8 heroes to select from, 4 being useable at a time each with passives and 4 abilities that can be skill shots, AoEs or instants. the fights themselves play out in real time but the game is pause-able at any point and commands can be issued while paused. This turns every combat into a puzzle like encounter where you will want to read the enemy abilities, look at what buffs and debuffs can be applied, identify which targets need to be brought down first and aggro management which made almost all the fights engaging and require some thought instead of having completely forgettable trash encounters. The games length is perfect I feel for the combat system not to wear out its welcome at around 12 hours though I would be up for re-experiencing this combat system if used in another game or simply replaying this one. Issues come in unfortunately with the other aspects of the game such as the voice acting being pretty questionable, the characters being forgettable and the story feeling like its really just there to give a break from the combat sequences, which while appreciated I wish these elements were stronger as there is some cool design work and world building going on, just not enough is done within this rather compact experience. Overall this game left me feeling really positive towards it even if I had to question my competency many times from the frequent deaths I would suffer.

I have been playing sports simulations since the late 80s and basically buy all the newest versions of all the top sports sims out there year by year. I was excited when OOTPB announced they would be making FHM innitially, however i quickly dumped the first game. When #2 came out i simply ignored it, but decided to spend my hard earned $ on the 3rd edition. Personally i think this was a huge mistake, i have already deleted the game.
For one, this is a poor mans version of OOTPB, which is by far a more furnished and finished product in every single sense of the word. Considering FHM has the backing of OOTPB, i am shocked how the layout is so poorly setup. The colors and layout are painful to look at times. Just looking at this game is irritating, clearly not enough time was spent on the design.
The thing i hate most about this game in comparisson to OOTPB is their lack of editing and modding. If in that game you can basically edit everything, here you are very limited. In fact, you cannot even start a game without being forced to pick the NHL (i know that would be most peoples first option, but still). You cannot fiddle around with the teams and for some weird reason the game admin has decided to focus on a mode called Path To Glory which is basically even more limited to what you can edit and is slower paced, you cannot sim into the future like most sims allow you to do, which means a season takes a lot longer.
On top of all that, the game has crashed on me 3-4 times and i barely have played the game. Possibly i am a little spoilt after playing OOTPB and Football Manager every year, but i am dissapointed that this game has not progressed a lot more since it's first induction. The only thing going for this game at the moment is that it's only real competitor is a hockey game which is basically running on an engine which is over 10 years old and even then, it is a pretty even competitor.
Unless you are crazy about Hockey and love sports sims, i would refrain to buying this and buy a proper sports sim such as the 2 i mentioned above.

Franchise Hockey Manager 3 is a brilliant simulation of being a GM/Coach in the World of Ice Hockey. The improvement over the previous version is impressive with improved tactics,  international play, improved player development, much improved game ratings for players and also an improved UI that is easier to navigate. The choices of game modes have been expanded to suit the needs of how users want to play i.e modern day, historical or custom and the path to glory option. The game engine produces an impressive amount of stats not found in other hockey GM games and has also been improved in this latest version. Also injuries to players are less random. Players will be injured in situations that occur during games such as sustaining a broken nose or injured eye during a fight. All this plus other new features means that this game is much more than just an update to FHM2.
The game isn't perfect and there are still improvements that can be made but OOTP are committed to their products. Their baseball game OOTP Baseball is second to none but that took years to get to the point it is at now. FHM is a new series with a huge amount of potential.
The game is well worth buying and having secured an NHL license there is an added sense of realism to what is already a very impressive and immersive hockey simulation.

Could be a great game in the future.

Simply put; an absolutely lovely game with a pretty art style that is reminiscent of LoZ: Breath of the Wild.
Pros:
- Lovely soundtrack
- Amazing art style and graphics
- Sprites and Animal variations are interesting and unique

It will not challenge you with it's immense combat system and carefully planned out bosses (because there is none).
The game at it's simplest form is a retrieval and reward game combined with wacky characters; a rather large open world; puzzles and even a bit of farming.
Quests are numerous but short (which is good?). Having finished the main story, which is merely a group of side quests that give you a backstory of the game, I still have alot to do. I find it fun going around the towns, helping citizens and trading with people.
That brings me onto my next point, the trading. Trading is actually quite different in this game. Instead of "coins" like in other games you actually have to trade your OWN items for other items making hoarding worthwile. There are also coins in the game but they are only used for certain stores, not alot of those stores anyway. If you pay attention to what the NPC's say they actually tell you if something is in demand, for example "No point in going to blah-de-blah town for lumber, they are in surplus!". Some say they hate it but I think it is quite usefull to get suplies and other resources. As soon as you accept one of the "guild" side quests you can easily go to one of the traders, buy everything you need, and return the quest back in. This gives it sort of an MMORPG vibe which I enjoy.
Another point I would like to push forwards is the season system. It's basic but makes a huge difference in your gameplay. I have had many times where I couldn't do a certain quest for example the fish I needed was under an iced off lake and I would have to wait until summer for it to freeze. The weather makes a nice change to your gameplay, instead of being sunny skys all day long.
There are so many features I would love to talk about but it would surely get boring fast so i'm just going to do a quick overview of things I like. Farming; you can build your own farm with placeable objects to adopt many different animals of the island. Regions; there are a couple of regions ranging from sandy deserts to icy glaciers all with varying sound effects, music and animals. Exploration; there is so much to explore on Gemea and even after end-game I still have found places I have never been yet. Crafting; a plentiful crafting system with guilds that unlock new recipes. Customization; you can easily customize your character with backpacks, clothes, hairstyles and hats that make your character look how you want it to be (my favourite item is the Groffle Backpack).

I have only played a little so far, but is a nice relaxing game with no violence or combat, which makes for an interesting change of pace. The game world is beautiful and you really get to explore at your own pace.
Is it worth $25 (or the $19.99 I paid via the launch week special)? well, I have 2 answers for this, bearing in mind my short play time:
1) It feels like a $15 game to me, based on the approach and in game activities so far
2) I DON'T regret buying this at $20 and probably wouldn't regret it at $25 as it is the kind of game I could play with a headache and still get some enjoyment out of it. To me, the relaxed, chill atmosphere allows me to divert my focus from my headache without inducing a new tension/stress to the equation in terms of intense game-play mechanics.
Overall worth a try, good for the kiddies too.

Overall, this is a good game.
First off, it is the best hockey sim on the market, even though that market is small. The gameplay is very fun. When it comes to things such as stats and player progression, it is usually very accurate. The NHL License is also a very nice touch and helps make the game feel more complete. The "main" Path to Glory mode is a nice addition. While improving the simulation engine from FHM2, they gave a more realistic feeling to the game. Essentially it is like role playing a GM, where you get points to use that will affect how you do things such as train players, or make deals. It is an interesting spin on the normal game, that also shouldn't deter people. If you want more freedom, then sandbox mode is for you. If you want a more realistic feeling, then PTG is the better option. Both game modes are fun. One little thing i did enjoy was the slight upgrade to the UI. Not as nice as OOTP yet, but i do like the upgrade from FHM2
There are a few downsides to FHM3 however. One is that there are no online leagues. I personally never played them so idc, but if you are a person who strictly plays them, then sadly this game isn't for you. The developers said that they didnt feel right giving us an incomplete and bad online mode, and would rather work on it until it is up to their standards which i completly agree with and understand. The second thing that this game is missing is the vastness of customization options. I'm use to played OOTP17 which has many, however that series has been around much longer so it makes sense. I still love being able to create my own league, but the little things like fully personalizing league and conference set ups or determining draft order would be nice additions. The only other thing i have noticed is that the game can have slow loading times at points, but nothing game-breaking so far. I already see a good change frmo playing the beta the past few weeks however.
This series is only in its third edition, but has made very good improvements each time. The developers have shown this game has promise. The overall game play is good. With these types of games, getting the simulation engine to run smoothly is the most important thing, and FHM3 does a pretty good job at that. Even though it is lacking in customization options for people who enjoy more of a sandbox experience, and online leagues, that game is still enjoyable.
