If you are looking for a nice casual game, this might be a good fit for you.  I paid the promotional $20 for this game and I have already sunk 4 hours into it and I'm nowhere near completion.  So for that price, I would say this game was well worth it.  Like a lot of players that purchased this game, I was expecting a mix of Stardew Valley and Zelda.  This game is not that at all.  It's purely an exploration game that allows you to enjoy the beautiful scenary while crafting and running a lot of fetch quests.  There are lot of hidden items to find (such as those cute cats other reviewers also mention), some puzzles, and a move at your own pace and do whatever you want to do feel.
Pros:
-The game has a very cute style
-You'll feel relaxed after playing it
-There's no timeline or reason to rush any one task
-You can hire farm hands and pay them with food
-Simple and easy controls
-Your character can be customized more within the game by finding or earning clothes, accessories, and hair dye
-Finding the cute cats
Cons:
-All of the NPC are very shallow.  Some will give you quests but don't expect a story telling you why they need that quest done.
-A lot of time will be spent just running from point A to point B.
-The farming aspect is lacking.  You can place buildings and bring animals back to your farm, but you really don't do much on the actual farm.  Clean up poop and get your items is really all you can do.
-The map isn't labeled
-I found fishing to be difficult and a little annoying
-Not a lot of variability to animals
I read a few complaints about the trading system.  This game has no currency, so you are expected to trade equal values via items you collect.  Different towns have different items to trade and also value items differently.  While this can be tedious if you are searching for a specific item, I kind of like this realistic old timey feel.  The towns are themed so if you are looking to buy items to cook with, there is a specific town with a cooking guild and traders that trade food type of items.  The map is very widespread and not well labeled so if you are looking to complete a quest across the way and need an item, running to the town that you can purchase it is a pain.  However, you can eventually use portals to hop around to specific locations once you find them, so that helps a bit.
Another complaint I read was about the limited backpack space.  While you do have a limited inventory, you can have chests at your farm locations where you can store additional items.  Linking to the previous comment about map size, if you leave something at your farm that you need, traveling back to get it is again a pain.  I have yet to really run out of backpack space, however.  I think this game isn't meant to be rushed, so focusing on one guild at a time will help you with your storage space.
There is a lot of little details that I found to be a nice touch.  You gain badges from the various guilds that you can put onto your backpack.  You can have up to four badges on it at once and they actually appear on your characters backpack.    The artwork in the environment is beautiful.  I've seen a rainbow, light flowing through cave tunnels, and beautiful shallow water paths.
There is no tutorial and this game doesn't hold your hand.  It's a very simple game, however, so a tutorial really wouldn't be needed.  If you can't figure out how to make something/where to buy something, take a break and go exploring for a while.  You might uncover a new town or items that you need to discover first.
This game isn't going to be winning GOTY, but it can give you many hours of calmer enjoyment.  This is the game to play when you are winding down at the end of your stressful day.

Is the latest release in the Carnivores Franchise, essentially an update of Carnivores HD. And it's an okay game for a reboot of the franchise.
I am very neutral to the game, as I find it to be a lot of fun, but not without feeling that this game squandered most of its potential. This is where my neutrality plays its part, as I have a balanced like and dislike toward this.
To get down to it, the game is set on the series titular planet, UMM-UV32, evidenced by returning locations which only share their names with their original counterparts.
The maps are very lackluster and lack anything of interest, save pretty scenery in the
map, and the Basmachee Rocks map (my favorite in the game.) If you were expecting a wide variety of locations complete with their own unique fauna, Dino's and Ambiance, then you'll have better luck with a mod for Carnivores 2.
Maps are rehashed multiple times, with there being dusk and fog variant maps. In total there are three maps, but they have variations, boring and thoughtless variations with a few new dinos and a surprise one you wouldn't know was in it until you actually went looking. I would have loved a night-time map, or maybe something other than the same locations over and over again. An aviary or an old DinoHunt Corp facility would have been nice.
Essentially the butter to the games bread, the Dinosaurs in this game are anatomically correct, unlike Carn 1 and 2 (they were more artistic,) beautiful to look at, and they sound wonderful, except the Ankylosaurus, I didn't much like their roar.
They move wonderfully, shifting their weight and behaving with majestic splendour, and they sound lovely too.
That's about all the good I can say about them though. We get a roster of six Dino's, guess how many are carnivores...
The T.Rex and the Ceratosaurus are terrifying in this game, but only when you don't expect them, and encounters with them can be especially damning in the foggy map variants, but these are the only carnivores in the whole game, and it's really a shame they couldn't add Velociraptor, Spinosaurus, Coelophysis or many of the classics.
In my time playing this game over the past four days, I have taken time to admire the Dinosaurs, as well as occasionally revile them for some cheap deaths and loss of progress they can cause to the unwary. Their pathfinding could have used some work, especially since the Dino's needed more life. They sleep, they eat, they drink, the predators look for you, which can be scary, but that's all really, but they never really feel mindless.
I am disapointed at the lack of variety, they try to spruce things up with mutant Dino's but it's honestly very disappointing to encounter them, save the Rex though, fear the Rex.
No complaints here, this is an actual
They take a bit of time to get used to, there's no crosshair, so you have to rely on the reticle on the barrel, or rely on a scope, they don't hold your hand. This game isn't a shooter so don't expect to go in guns ablazing. There are lots of returning weapons, the X-bow, the Magnum and the Sniper Rifle are some (there's only four weapons.)
Essentially your lifeline, it's a device that you can use to keep track of Dinosaurs, call them, use as a telescope, call in evac, and claim trophy's, useful, and it makes playing a little more challanging as you can't have it up at the same time as holding gun.
These require gems, you get gems for knocking down Dino's and confirming the kill, these can be used to purchase hunting gear, player and M.I.S.T upgrades, as well as two of the three main weapons.

Calling this a neutral review is a stretch but my complaints are sound, and relatable to anyone who has played the game and thought the way I do. This game is fun, I have a lot of fun with this game, but it's missing a lot of things to make it fantastic.
It lacks a proper selection of Dinosaurs (six isn't much) and it gets boring with the options available after a few hunts. I feel that there was more planned, but the budget just wasn't in it. Maps feel lifeless, atleast in the older games there were ambient Dinosaurs, this game has none of that which takes a lot out of the game. I would'v elove to listen to Brachs singing in the distance, or something other than utter silence. And I'm not saying there should be music either.
Some of the things I would have done if I was lwad devloper, would add ambient sounds, more map selections, more weapons, and deffinitly more Dinosaurs. I'd've also added something memorable to each of the maps, something to make exploring worth while. Seems that wasn't on the table.
To conclude, this game, for me personally, is a lot of fun, I enjoy this game very much, despite every issue I have with it. This game lacks updates, DLC and mod support. This game could benefit from a modding community and it's a shame that's not currently possible.

Amazing game based off the old Carnivores games. Back when I got my first Win 98 PC I got Carnivores: Ice Age at a garage sale and played the hell out of it and later played the rest of the series. If you played the series you'll probably like this game.
Pros:
- Visuals are amazing and the simulation really feels realistic.
- The M.I.S.T. tracking hud was done perfect and has a great amount of options.
- Dino's look really good and their animations/sounds are perfect even down to the Dino dying the Dino will stagger.
- Lots of upgrades and a good amount of different places to visit.
- Aiming feels solid and how much damage or hit area a Dino can take feels realistic too.
- FPS is always really good for my gaming laptop.
Cons:
- Most Dino's are passive and will just run away when shot like a deer. To me this is more realistic, but some people wanting exact gameplay like the original Carnivores series might be disappointed.
- No nightvision. This is something that was a let down for me coming back from the old games. This is something that would have been easy to add to the game at later maps against aggressive Dino's for more excitement.
- Dino's will run into terrain every once in a while and get stuck on trees. This isn't something that happens a lot, but when it does it ruins the immersion.
- There is one error I get every once in a while that crashes the game. Its happened 2 times to me, but only happens right when starting a new hunt so no progress is lost so its not a big deal to me.
- Only 3 primary weapons in the game. While the amount of customization is good there's only 3 primary weapons you can get which is kind of disappointing. The gun you start out with will most likely become your favorite since it seems to be the best balanced.
9/10
Btw something to be weary of is that this game seems to always auto start in low process for me and I have to switch it higher. Another thing is make sure its using your best graphics card if you have a hybrid graphics card.

This game is an interesting reversal of the tower defense genre where you become the creeps trying to destroy the tower. Control-wise, I liked the mouse interface better than a keyboard one, and eventually mapped the entire control system to my mouse. It gave it kind of a minimalist fee, leaving more room just to enjoy the game. Graphics-wise it's stellar for a top-down scroller, with decent lower-quality modes for lower-end GPUs. The gameplay itself was unique and fun, with maps that require thought but can be attacked many different ways, integral power-ups that need to be rationed smartly, and several different types of towers all with a different weak spot. Overall Anomaly: Warzone Earth is a lot of fun for the price, and I'd recommend it to anyone who prefers careful strategy to simply mowing down the opposition

Mafia II is a game for those who love a good mob story. I would like to see more family drama but Vito's journey is a trip worth taking. Throughout the game, you follow Vito as he climb up the ranks of the mafia, from petty theft to mass murder. Behind the glamour of crime, money and prostitution is a broken man who's unsure of himself. You slowly start to sympathize with Vito, as he gets torn between his family and his job and the consequences of his actions becomes dire. His best friend, Joe, is also involved in organized crime but his likability comes from his carefree spirit and loyalty. The overarching narrative is divided into chapters, allowing the story to flow together nicely.
If you're looking for a good game, you're much better off playing GTA, or L.A. Noire if you're into the 40-50s era. Much of the main missions are pretty mundane and repetitive. You spend most of the game driving from Point A to Point B, to Point C and back to Point A again. Shooting sections are fun but ordinary. Mafia II has a nicely detailed period setting but some of the textures are rather lackluster and the open world is pretty empty. You can barely interact or do anything despite the size of Empire Bay. The gameplay is rather linear, which isn't a problem if the main missions had more variety and there are no side-quests to speak off. The playboy collectibles are a nice touch for any horny youngsters out there.
Mafia II may be a story-driven game but that shouldn't come at the expense of gameplay. There are loads of games that are both story and gameplay-driven, though I can't think of many that are set in the 40s, so if that's your preference, Mafia II isn't a complete waste of money. If you're hoping for a mafia version of GTA, you'll be disappointed.

Aarklash is for people who like real time with pause tactical RPGs that are extremely challenging. This game is very demanding of the player, asking of exact positioning, use of all your various abilities and strategies and punishing of mistakes. The difficulty is also set very high, it's not easy, medium, hard, it's more on the Super Hexagon Scale, hard, harder and harderest! Though I think the latest patch may have toned the difficulty down a little bit. But, don't let that scare you off as you'll miss one of the best tactical RPGs in years! Game play focuses primarily on a group of four characters, each of the characters have their own designated role within a group, such as tanking, healing and damage dealing. You will unlock more characters by progressing through the story mode however you can only have four characters in your group at any one time, meaning squad management plays a key role in success. Whilst each of the characters have their own primary role, there is some overlap with a few abilities, such as damage dealers may also have a healing spell to help out if needed, and healers will also have damage dealing spells. All characters have an “auto attack” which means your healers are still important when it comes down to burning enemies quickly.
Whilst the gameplay is mostly played in real time, the pause mechanic allows you to break from the mayhem in the fight to plan out your next wave of attacks and precisely move your group members around the battlefield. Certainly worth having in your library if you are into this type of genre.

Yes, Aarklash: Legacy is a hidden gem. It is definitely a game that is worth playing. It is reminescent of old games like Baldur's Gate. To think such a game was not marketed prominently goes to show that there are many hidden gems that lack the marketing clout of major game publishers. E.g. Witcher 2.
The gameplay is fairly simple. You control a Quorr (sounds like core), a group of 4 Wheel Swords (most likely Wield Swords). You have the archetypical 4 characters in a Dungeons and Dragons game. A healer, a tank, a mage and a rogue. Along the way, you can pick up more archetypes as the story progresses. So far, I got a lich and a dwarf gunner. Then I got an orc shaman and a big guy. You pause with the spacebar and issue commands to your heroes with QWER.
I will add more as I play through. At the moment, I feel like it's an incomplete game.It's currently missing itemization.
The main point of the game is to just focus on aggro, as long as your tank/healer doesn't die and you keep the aggro on the tank, you will win. If the enemies change their aggro target to the mages, it's over. This leads me to my next point, sub optimal AI. The AI should be targetting your mages as an optimal move and it should be the player's job to avoid, taunt or misdirect their attacks away from the mages. After a while, the gameplay resembles more of a World of Warcraft tank and spank raid, where you try to hold a giant bosse's aggro with a main tank. The crux is that it's all about your tank.If your tank falls, it's the end.
The puzzles are kind of simple though. Like turning 5 statues to point to the middle, teleportating red and blue squares. Simple does not equate to bad. The slightly harder ones can be solved pretty easily.
Conclusion, you can try the game for simple storytelling. You will not get tricked unlike Harry Potter and the Saw Series (if you are familiar with their storytelling styles). The story is kind of straightforward even until the end. Nella turning into a goddess was not an unforeseen conclusion due to all the ghosts speaking to her.
Note: Cyanide Studios is made up of former Ubisoft Employees. They have made other games such as Styx, Impire, Blood Blowl, Cycling Manger, Horse Racing Manager and Dogs of War Online. Aarklash Legacy is their first self-published game.
1. Beatiful artwork
So creative and beautiful that I would want to see more. The goblin was pretty well-designed. E.g. Denzil with his top hat and his rat in the hat.
2. Interesting Combat Game Design
In order to defeat the bosses, you have to click on them to study their weakensses. It's not a wail-on-bosses-to-win strategy.
3. Backstory
Every single one of the 8 heroes has one.
1. Complex Controls
I am not used to pausing a battle to find a tiny icon. I would prefer a tab option where I could cycle through each hero and stack their attacks.
2. Can't Run Out of Combat Zone
If you run too far, you lose.
3. Environment is Mostly Boring
Nothing to interact with. Everything is just flat and for show only. There are some interactable parts like the anti-mana regeneration orbs.
4.Pause Action Pause Action
It's actually really bad after a long time. You don't want to keep doing complex combos for minor mobs. Such complex actions are usually reserved for big bosses.
5. Boring Paper Doll Inventory
Every single hero dresses up the same way. You have 4 slots, a necklace, an ankh, a ring and a bow tie. Every single has the exact same slots.
6. Boring Items
A necklace, an ankh, a ring and an earring. That's it.
7. Tiny Status Numbers over Hero Profiles
How the heck do I make them out?
8. Cut-Scenes
Why do you need to cut-scene all 4 heroes before they enter a glowing door? Just let them in.
9.Only 1 Landscape Piece
Only Nella, Bo Lahn and Denzil? What about the rest?
10. Wheel Swords
I cringed at "Wheel Swords Alll"
1. Puzzles
Too simple but there's nothing wrong with simple.
2. Tank and Spank System
Tank and Spank is a simple system, easy for players to understand and exploit. However, I think gameplay has evolved greatly over the years so you can say that this is an archaic system.
1. Spice up the Paper Doll Inventory
You have goblins, humans, dwarves, etc. Do you think they all use and wear the same equipment? This isn't a one-size-fits-all t-shirt. Vary the items a bit.
2. Use Symbols for the Status Effects
Other than Fear, the rest of them have no clear symbol.
3. Automatic Dropdown
I want to see all the enemy's abilities immediately not click on a plus sign, then scroll over a tiny orb to read text.
4. Coloured Ability Names instead of Coloured Orbs for Enemy Descriptions
Why do I need to hover over tiny orbs to read them? You have only 4 active abilities and 4 passive abilities. Just give me the name and I'll hover over it to read a full description.
5. More Terrain Effects
Swamps that poison you, high ground advantage, rolling boulders, lava floor, creeping vines, healing auras etc... Put these things in.
6. Newer Forms of Gameplay Instead of Just Tank and Spank
Kiting, trickery and illusion, mind control.

Even though it is officially licensed by the NHL, it doesn't have all the rules. In example, you are limited to a roster size of 23 players during preseason. Until basics like that is fixed, I can't recommend this game.
More examples:
Olympic break is not long enough. NHL season resumes before the Olympics are over.
Submitting contracts is a bit wonky. For example, if you submit a entry level contract offer to a kid you've drafted, he will come back and say stuff like "I'd be happy to play for your team at these terms. But first let me see if there are any other teams interested in my services, before I sign. I'll be in touch." Sorry kid, this is the NHL and here we have rights. My team is the only team that can sign you. You are not allowed to talk to any other teams.
Another thing about contracts, I traded for Trouba, who is an RFA. I met his demands, asked for response and submitted my offer. A couple of days went by, and he came back and said he was going to sign for me if he didn't receive any better deals. Being an RFA, it's not very likely another team would give him an offer sheet, considering what they would have to give up to sign him. However, it's not 100% unlikely, so I withdrew my offer, and was going to give him a better offer, but now he doesn't want to sign, let alone talk to me.
...Which brings me to this. There has got to be a way to talk to players in a game like this. Look at EHM or FM(!) series.
Draft lottery rules are wrong. The top three top draft picks are part of the lottery. Not in the game, but not really a game breaker either.
Trades should not be limited to five players/draft picks for each team.
The UI is not the best. Now, it could come down to me being used to the UI of EHM, but it's surely not the sole reason of why I am not thrilled with the UI. A few examples.
*Inbox screen, why isn't there a "read next unread button"? Instead of this, I have to click on ever item.
*An option for saving different line and strategy setups is lacking. This should be a high priority, in my opinion as it is very time consuming the way it is now.
*There should be an option where the assistant GM just fills out the rest of the line up instead of only rearranging every player.

If I had to liken this game to something, it would be a cup of warm, soothing chamomile tea at the end of a stressful day.
This game will appeal to some, and not to others. It is only very, very, VERY loosely goal-oriented; your Main Goal is to find "sprites" hidden throughout the world and use them to cleanse the land. It is not a farming game. There is no fighting. Even the wild animals aren't interested in taking a nibble out of you. You can't even drown or die from fall damage (if you venture into deep water, you get ported back to the nearby point on dry land / if you fall from high heights, you pull a Mary Poppin and float down with an umbrella).
The NPCs do provide quests to nudge you along. But if you go into this game with the mindset of "pick up quest, go from point A to point B and get it done as soon as possible", you won't find it very fun. Instead, think of it as an exploration game.
See a funny shaped rock over there? Hop on over, you just might find a stone statue nagging you about your choice in clothing. Look, the water seems kind of shallow over there, perhaps I can juuuust make it to the next island without "drowning". And where on earth is that cat that keeps mewling!?
It's a... gentle game, in the sense that you are not pressured to do anything and there's no danger anywhere. There's no "right" or "wrong" way to play. Don't wanna farm? Don't. Don't wanna fish? Don't. Wanna complete everything in the pokedex? Go right on ahead.
If your idea of a good time is to blank out for an hour or so and submerge yourself in the simple joy of finding a new surprise in the landscape, I would recommend this game.
Criticisms that I do have.
- The world feels quite static; the NPCs mill around not doing anything else, the animals are basically backdrops to the landscape. I would love to see more dynamic interactions from the NPCs and animals. Eg. foxes chasing critters, or playing with each other. Those cute looking deer with ferocious antlers headbutting each other to win over a doe's paw in marriage(?). NPCs talking with each other. Etc. etc. It would make the world more interesting.
- There's not enough to explore and find, at this point in time. More Easter eggs please. There are some cute ideas out in the world, but they're not nearly enough.
- A minor quibble, but please turn down the default camera sensitivity...
- Yes I know the sprite in Zelda was annoying as heck, but since your sprite is there anyway, it'll be fun to have conversations with them. Or, they could have conversations with each other.

IT'S NOT STARDEW VALLEY PLEASE DON'T COMPARE IT TO STARDEW VALLEY IT'S NOT LIKE STARDEW VALLEY
Did we get that out of the way? Good.
So, now I'm going to say why this game is, in fact, a bit like Stardew Valley.
It's relaxing. It's got a very calming soundtrack. It gets me in a similar mindset Stardew Valley does - no hurry to do anything, just turn off half of your brain and let things happen.
That's it, really. If we were to compare this to other games, I'd say it's Animal Crossing meets walking simulators meets a "to-do" list.
In this game, you are a shipwrecked traveller, starting your journey on a coast of a beautiful new land. Your task is to explore it, find the lost spirits who will then help you clean it of the nasty purple goo that's appeared due to a past catastrophe. You go from town to town, do simple quests in the vein of "bring me x" and "take this to y". You can do some trading and repair farms dotting the landscape, you can fish, but mostly you will just wander around appreciating the views and collecting everything you can get your hands on.
And there are some really great views to appreciate - if anything, this game deserves applause for it's visual style. The landscape is amazingly varied and colorful, each season brings with it new weather effects and changes the 'feel' of the land completely. It's probably one of the most visually appealing games I've played. The music is nice too - perhaps not something you'd listen to outside of the game, but it goes well with what's happening on the screen.
So, in conclusion, if you are expecting deep, challenging gameplay, farming or advanced crafting and questing systems... don't bother. You will be disappointed. But if all you want is to relax in a peaceful world for a few hours and you enjoy ticking things to do off a list, give it a go! There are sights to see, cats to rescue and an island to save.
PS: if you want something like this but with more RPG elements, some combat and arguably more depth, Fantasy Life for Nintendo 3DS says hello.

I want to start off by saying that a lot of people are comparing this to the likes of Harvest Moon and Stardew Valley.
...I would like to respectfully disagree with them. Yonder is it's own game, and while there are farming aspects, it is not at the center of the game like SV and HM. I have more to say on that, below.
Yonder is a beautiful exploration game. There is an interesting story with curious NPC's to meet, many items to craft, and land to discover. The game doesn't hand you all of your tools, character customization... ANYTHING at the beginning. You find all of this along the way. The in-game bartering system is something that I really enjoy, although I do find that I need more inventory space...! I don't have a fishing addiction, I swear. =^)
As others are saying, this is a very relaxing game, there is no combat, no enemies at all, and I do enjoy that. I do feel a little limited in where I can go, if I land in deep water I'm respawned quickly (which is good!) and I can't climb up some places I feel like I should be able. Seasons pass really quickly... I notice them, I suppose, but boy they seem to pass in a snap. There doesn't seem to be any penalty for "dying" (like landing in deep water) or having a negative reaction to the weather -- my character was shivering in winter but no death or anything. Essentially you could really hand this game to a kid of any age and I doubt they'd run into any issue.
While I did not want to spend a lot of time on what Yonder isn't, I think it is important to note, particularly for the people that are undecided on buying and are hoping for something similar to HM or SV: This is a relaxing game, but it is not a farming sim. Farming is basically optional, and you can absoulutely shovel that work load off on to a farm hand, which you will likely do in favor of exploring and crafting. There is no relationship/marriage system in this game. And I don't think that's a bad thing. This isn't a Harvest Moon title, this is something totally different. It's a lovely game, and truly an enjoyable experience.

I'm not really sure why people are complaining about the price point or lack of content. For $20-25 this game is fine. Very fun mechanics and enjoyable exploration, combined with a decent amount of customization and wonderful design make it a very relaxing game. It reminds me of gamecube games where they weren't all about hyper-realistic graphics and killing everything. It's a fun relaxing game that allows you to wander and enjoy yourself without worrying too much about messing up or having to pay attention. The biggest complaint I see is a that the game lacks content, I agree and disagree with this point. The content is somewhat slim, especially if you just try to finish the main quests, but otherwise there's a decent amount.
In the time I've spent playing I went around doing side quests, exploring, mastering the crafting professions and finishing the main story. It took me 15 hours to do this and I still have a lot of things I'd like to do. I estimate when I get bored or am waiting for new content to be released I'll be around 30 hours played and that's more than enough to get my monies worth. People always complain about pricing, but don't realize even just movie tickets are $10-15 dollars or a decent burger is $8. Gaming as a whole is a very cheap way to get entertainment and I feel like most of the negatives are unwarranted. That being said there are some cons that do drag the game down a little bit in my opinion.
The inventory and space management is really bad, and on several occasions it has made me not want to play. What's the point in exploring and having a fun carefree time when you have to constantly manage your inventory and run back to your farm to store stuff? The amount of animals is a little slim and I'd like a way to increase the size and function of my farms. As this seems to be one of the main points of the game I feel that it's a little lacking. I'm fine with trading for goods instead of currency, if and only if, the inventory system is improved. Other than those fairly small complaints I don't have much negative to say, this game is fun and relaxing and I've had a good time so far.
All-in-all I'd say this game is a solid 8/10 and an enjoyable experience if you are looking to relax and don't expect some AAA story with tons of content. You should enjoy around 30 hours of playtime if you take your time and don't rush just to finish the main quests. The developers have also shown that they plan to add more content which is promising so you can probably expect some pretty decent updates in the near future.

I'd like to say this is a must have for Carnivores fans... but I do have mixed feelings. I've been playing the Carnivores games since the first was released and I own all the hard-copies: Carnivores, Carnivores 2, Ice Age, and CityScape (even played the ios version)... needless to say I'm a big fan and I'm glad the franchise is still around.
That being said... the game seems like it was left unfinished and has been seemingly abandoned? What a shame. There are actually very few dinosaurs in-game (6 huntable dinos total) which you are forced to 'farm' over and over again to progress. It gets old pretty fast. I was hoping with the game's popularity and positive reviews that we would see updates with more dinosaurs being added. Nope.
This game is very fun for me, but I feel like It -could- have been great.
PROS:
- Def and update from the graphics of the old games.
- Beautiful, high quality, immersive environments.
- Dinosaurs look good, move nicely (definitely not scientifically accurate).
- Great game for longtime fans.
CONS:
- Game is dead? No new updates for ages <<<BIG DEAL
- Very few huntable dinosaurs in-game. Especially when compared to the previous games (Carnivores 2 for example; had 9 dinosaurs and 6 ambient creatures).
- Repetitive gameplay gets old very quickly.
- Dinosaurs very retro looking and scientifically inaccurate.
- Dinosaur AI is very simple and mostly predictable.
Once again. It may be fun for fans, but doesn't make a lasting impression.

I grew up playing the classic Sonic games and only played a couple of the modern 3D titles but I finally purchased a copy of Sonic Generations as it seems an ideal game to compare the classic and modern era of the series. I would certainly recommend this game as you rediscover some old and familiar stages but with new level designs and remixed music plus some new mechanics.
Overall I quite enjoyed the game with a few elements of nostalgia here and there plus some good enhancements but there were quite a lot of frustrating elements so it might be a while before I decide to revisit this game in the future.
GAMEPLAY:
I like the concept of one act played with Classic Sonic and another with Modern Sonic, both have some unique moves although sometimes you forget when playing as Classic Sonic that you don't have boost or homing attacks. It's a decent length for a Sonic game and I like how there are different missions with some quite different level maps for each zone so even after you finish the main story you can continue to try and complete all the other missions.
I found it took a while to get used to the controls and quite often I found Classic Sonic quite slippery to control and frustrating when you are trying to jump. As for Modern Sonic, well I've never been a huge fan of 3D platformers and his controls certainly frustrated me especially in segments where you have to boost and switch lanes, plus moving platforms above bottomless pits are an absolute pain to navigate.
I loved the concept of Planet Wisp Zone especially for Classic Sonic, I don't mind a bit of a puzzle element in platform games and I thought the purple spike power up was really cool and fun to play. If Sonic Colors was ever ported to Steam then I would definitely consider playing it.
VISUALS & GRAPHICS:
Really nice and pretty maps especially for the more 2D gameplay which has been rendered in a more 3D style. One of my main criticisms though is that sometimes there is quite a lot of detail that you don't always know if a platform is in the foreground or actually part of the background.
STORYLINE:
Quite a simple story which is all the game needed really. I like the interaction between the classic and modern characters although maybe there could have been more dialogue reflecting on past zones.
BOSS BATTLES:
I like how you face different bosses from Sonic's past including "Dr Eggman" and the earlier "Dr Robotnik" plus Shadow, Silver, Metal Sonic and Chaos. The Death Egg Robot battle had a very nice concept in the latter part plus battling Metal Sonic was pretty fun. I wasn't so keen on Modern Sonic's battles except the Silver one. I don't particularly like the format of boosting just to get closer to the enemy then homing in, it got quite tedious especially once fighting the final 2 bosses. The final boss did provide a challenge but it got quite aggravating having to hear Cream, Vector etc. telling you to beware of homing shots and switching characters - when I defeated Time Eater I didn't even need to switch to Classic Sonic and I don't think I had fully sussed out how the mechanics of the battle worked by the time Time Eater was defeated.
MUSIC:
Overall pretty good. I like many of the remixes although I thought Modern Chemical Plant sounded really bad. Stand out tracks for me included Modern Crisis City, Time Eater Boss Battle, Casino Night DLC, Super Sonic Racing plus it was cool during one of the missions to hear a fusion of Sonic 3D's theme plus the end credit music from the Sega Saturn port - very well executed although it did sound out of place when completing a mission in the hell of Crisis City.
CONCLUSION:
A very nice homage to Sonic's past covering 20 years of the blue hedgehog's main titles with a few nice nostalgic moments. The gameplay controls could have been better with better physics for both characters.
I'd give it 7/10.

After going back and actually finishing this game, I can now rightfully say that this game is... well, great! Let’s look at some of the pros and cons of this game.
Pros:
- High Speed action that is almost always fun to go back and play
- Pretty decent control, aside from turning Modern Sonic
- Return to the Classic formula (although Sega doesn’t seem like they want to make this a 1 time gimmick and just milk it to the core)
- Great level design
- An amazing modding community that is still getting support today
Cons:

Got the whole series on a discount, I've had my eyes on these since the moment I saw Anomaly 2 on a random page. My interest in Tower Defense genre is not entirely the most enthusiastic approach perhaps, however these series with the idea and the great implementation of being the attacker seemed like a damn-good deal. So, I've been playing the Anomaly franchise for a while now, started from the very first Mobile Campaign game, to the Anomaly 2. Played them all in a row, didn't finish just tasted enough, and I'm impressed.
First of all, if you're not interested in buying the whole franchise, I would strongly recommend you to skip Anomaly Korea and maybe the Warzone Earth Mobile Campaign. Mobile Campaign might not the brightest example of a mobile port to PC, however it's technically consistent compared to the Anomaly Korea. But don't get me wrong, they're both pointless since they're just ports not adaptations. Which is a problem when it comes to PC Gaming.
Warzone Earth is an innovative Reverse Tower Defense game within an Alien Invasion setting on Earth which puts you as the commanding officer of a convoy of 6 different vehicles that you could purchase and upgrade by destroying your enemies. Pretty straight forward, nothing new. What makes it different though is that the game insists that you should not sit on your♥♥♥♥♥and let your convoy do the work. Nope. The only way to boost their attacking power is upgrading your units and from their types to their place within the convoy affects your survivalability. You will be constantly changing the Route you're taking, the Place of your Units, which Abilities you have to put on the ground in order to keep your units alive and their Tiers in order to beat a particular Mission. Which keeps you awake and well-aware of your surroundings, otherwise you fail. Plain and simple.
If you're a fan of the Tower Defense genre and/or you would like to try something out of your regular zone, Warzone Earth is not only an outstanding, a brilliant example but also an example for how you should reimagine, adapt your mobile game for PC Market.
Plus, it runs on GNU/Linux!

This game has been going through ups and downs when it comes to people reviewing it, the game suffers with too many negative reviews and I can totally understand why some people might be put off from this game. The game does have it's fair share of issues and Lichdom: Battlemage definitely isn't for everyone
The game does have its fair share of decent graphics however there was the odd weird texture here and there and some of the animations especially in the in-game cutscenes looked a bit janky
The game offers a nice spell crafting system, although quite complicated at first, you will get the hang of it in the end and when you cast a spell, it does have some nice spell effects

Lichdom: Battlemage. A game developed by Xaviant Games.
One of only 2 games produced by this developer, I believe the other to be "The Culling". It seems like an ambitious step forward into a genre, that hasn't been done in this way before.
Although this game has a relatively negative response ratio, due to its difficulty, and rather non inclusive description of how anything really works.
This game is what appears to be the love child of classic DOOM FPS style game play with the creative magic of the Elders Scrolls series. Where you can create magic and then visually cast if from your fingers like in Skyrim.
POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD.
You are what seems from the outside, A completely random stranger, with no affinity for magic or any type of adventuring skills. You step into a story from the beginning as a person either male or female, (in my case female). Where your sister has been kidnapped by what appears to be the lord of the lands you live in, You are left strewn in the street after attempting her rescue, and left broken to die, Until what appears to be a mage stands above you. You rise to your feet, and this mage offers you retribution and revenge. Giving you bracers that can conduct the forces of energy in the world. You then proceed to combust, freeze, corrupt, shock and completely obliterate thousands of people, creates and undead in your path. Assumingly reaching a climax of revenge.
Game Pros:
- The game plays extremely smoothly, Currently my FPS has stayed at a minimal of 60avg despite the ever increasing amount of enemies and spells flying about.
- The game gives you the ability to create and design your own spells from scratch, whether you want to throw fireballs into crowds or rain down ice in the form of blizzards is completely up to you, if you want it vice versa that seems completely available as well.
- The games overall story seems captivating enough to keep you intrigued, despite how fast paced the story telling can be (i'll get into that shortly) And seems from research to have a very reasonable story length for its price. (Approximately 20 hours while completing everything at a reasonable pace)
- The game makes you feel powerful, the spells you cast are extremely potent, but your ability to decide where and when to use them is the key to your survival.
- The locations are beautiful. Having this game operating at 60FPS and at 1080p looks absolutely brilliant. The world is finely detailed and delicately planned so that you are never really guessing where as to go to next. And the ability to venture back to locations via a Fast Travel system is an amazing concept for a "FPS" type game.
- The games combat is also very fast paced, very much in common with "DOOM16", You are often thrown into fights without warning. which test your ability to react to situations. But there is often plenty of preparation room in between larger scale fights to upgrade your spells and abilities.
Game Cons:
- I did mention previously that the game is fast paced as a positive, In the combat side of things this is entirely correct.
From a story perspective i find it rather a let down. You feel as though despite your characters previous inability to do any sort of magic (presumably) picks up the art form very easily which even the aged mage who helps you, has a hard time controlling his magic and energy, The areas also feels rushed, you lose a sense of anger you get from the intro to the story because it seems  like they are trying to pack too much information into the campaign.
- There is no real description as to what you can do with your spells and how to alter them, I found myself using the games "smart inventory" option to auto level most of my spells because i had no concept of how and with what.
- The enemies are very repetitive and often don't really change their move set, their are different types of the same enemy class that appear, that have increased hp, or do more damage. But by the time you've reached them they don't really pose a challenge at all.
- There is no armor customisation, the only customisation available is to the spells. But with the direction the game seems to lead, it would have definitely faired better as a whole experience if you had to craft and fashion your own gear, Or even the ability to choose melee magic, ranged magic or a combination of the two would have definitely increased the games overall stature.
I definitely recommend this game, but probably not at it's full price. It has/had a lot of promise to be a full fledged game in it's own right. but i felt like the end product was a little rushed. Its glowing triumphs of how to create a magical FPS are often overshadowed by the blazing speed of the story telling and boring enemy combos. If you are into the DOOM style of story, where you aren't really given one, and you just get to blast enemies into Oblivion. This game is definitely for you. If thats not your cup of tea, perhaps this is a pass, or at least a sale purchase only.

Finally, a single-player/multi-character RPG with real-time combat that isn't based on pen-and-paper games or owned by Bioware/EA.
Aarklash: Legacy is a party-based top-down isometric tactical RPG in the style of Dragon Age and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic - pause the game, queue up commands to your party, and then
unpause.
There are also a significant number of puzzles, but they aren't particularly frustrating and the worst of them are easily solved in under 10 minutes.
The awesome:
-Single-player/multi-character real-time combat with tactical pause for people tired of Bioware/EA's near-monopoly on the genre.
-Combines some of the best of MMORPG/MOBA mechanics with old-school design and puzzles.
-Mix and match 4 characters out of 8 total with no limits. 2 healers and 2 tanks? You can do that. 4 DPSers? You can do that. Reshuffle your party whenever you aren't in combat
-Unlike most classic or classic-style RPGs, there are no consumables. Your characters automatically regenerate all their health and energy outside of combat, unlike most classic RPGs that require you to
rest. The advantage of having no consumables is that you win or lose based only on skill and character builds. In a traditional D&D-style RPG, you could build and play your characters poorly and win by
throwing around entire bags of consumables, or you could have a perfect character build and lose anyway because you ran out of consumables. That doesn't happen in Aarklash: Legacy.
-Bioware loses its monopoly on the genre.
The good:
-Puzzles require some thought but they aren't frustrating.
-Intuitive and smooth UI design.
The bad:
-Game balance is somewhat broken. Boss enemies usually have abilities that instantly wipe characters. Control effects that take the keyboard and mouse away from the player last way too long (15 second
mind control or 10 second knockdown???). On the other hand, some characters have 10 second stuns too, so the bad balancing can also go the other way.
-Lack of character customizability. Each character gets a predefined advantage and disadvantage - instead I would rather have a choice of a few advantages and disadvantages, or even choose to have
neither. Character development is only 4 items with RNG stats and a tiering/affix system straight out of Diablo, plus a minimal skill tree. There are no skill choices, just variations on the same skills.
-Characters' run speed out of combat is somewhat slow and gets incredibly boring if you have to backtrack.
-Lack of hybrid characters, their roles are mostly rigidly defined as tanks, DPS, or healers
-A lot of the skills appear to be designed to artifically force your characters to work together. Giving characters skills that are useful on their own and even better when chained in a specific sequence
is one thing, it's another thing entirely to make characters almost completely dependent on each other.
-Characters have no AI if you aren't controlling them. If you want other characters to use skills or retarget you have to queue them up manually. If you were expecting something like Mass Effect or
Dragon Age where characters you aren't controlling remain somewhat competent, you will be disappointed.
-No story choices.
The unacceptable:
-The entire game is completely linear (see also: "rail playing game") with minimal alternate paths to the same destination and perhaps a few dead-end forks in the road with treasure - and it doesn't look
like there's any official modding support.
-Minimal replay value.
-Some types of enemies have narrow counters and it's very possible to get yourself stuck in a fight with the wrong characters. Save before every fight!
The verdict:
Aarklash: Legacy combines the best of new and old party-based RPG paradigms into real-time with tactical pause combat almost never seen outside of Bioware/EA games. Character and skill mechanics are
almost solid with a few large problems. Unfortunately: an almost linear environment, significant balance problems, and the lack of modding support weigh heavily on it.
The regular price ($20) is somewhat steep for the amount of content - I got this game on a large discount (somewhere between 80% and 90%) and I recommend buying this only on deep discount. At the very
least, wait for a 50% sale if you're impatient.
If you enjoy some aspects of classic RPGs with the tactical depth and real-time combat of MMORPG/MOBA style games,
I recommend that you buy Aarklash: Legacy... if you are also willing to overlook its design problems.
My suggestions to the devs:
-Add support for a nonlinear, respawning world.
-Add modding and custom characters.
-Faster running out of combat

This game completely tricked me into thinking it's something that it isn't.
Do you want to play a difficult, fast-paced puzzle game, where each enemy in itself is its own unique puzzle with randomized weapons, armor and abilities, as the game sells itself to be? Then don't play this game. This game is 100% a giant, 45-minutes-to-an-hour dice roll, with only luck involved. And it's all because of one mechanic: evasion. Each attack has a chance to miss, based on the enemy ship or your ship's evasion. This chance can reach up to 55%, literally meaning that each fight essentially becomes a 50% chance to win or lose.
If there were a way to remove this mechanic from the game entirely, this would be an amazingly fun and difficult rougelite puzzler that really puts your problem solving skills in a high-stress environment to the test, with an astounding OST to match. In fact, the OST almost convinced me to give this a good rating, but that one game mechanic sadly tears the entire thing to the ground.
tl;dr: If you like 45 minute dice rolls accompanied by a wonderful soundtrack, buy this game. But, if you want a rougelite that puts your problem solving and puzzling skills to the test, I'm deeply sorry, but you've come to the wrong place.

I'm not really sure why people are complaining about the price point or lack of content. For $20-25 this game is fine. Very fun mechanics and enjoyable exploration, combined with a decent amount of customization and wonderful design make it a very relaxing game. It reminds me of gamecube games where they weren't all about hyper-realistic graphics and killing everything. It's a fun relaxing game that allows you to wander and enjoy yourself without worrying too much about messing up or having to pay attention. The biggest complaint I see is a that the game lacks content, I agree and disagree with this point. The content is somewhat slim, especially if you just try to finish the main quests, but otherwise there's a decent amount.
In the time I've spent playing I went around doing side quests, exploring, mastering the crafting professions and finishing the main story. It took me 15 hours to do this and I still have a lot of things I'd like to do. I estimate when I get bored or am waiting for new content to be released I'll be around 30 hours played and that's more than enough to get my monies worth. People always complain about pricing, but don't realize even just movie tickets are $10-15 dollars or a decent burger is $8. Gaming as a whole is a very cheap way to get entertainment and I feel like most of the negatives are unwarranted. That being said there are some cons that do drag the game down a little bit in my opinion.
The inventory and space management is really bad, and on several occasions it has made me not want to play. What's the point in exploring and having a fun carefree time when you have to constantly manage your inventory and run back to your farm to store stuff? The amount of animals is a little slim and I'd like a way to increase the size and function of my farms. As this seems to be one of the main points of the game I feel that it's a little lacking. I'm fine with trading for goods instead of currency, if and only if, the inventory system is improved. Other than those fairly small complaints I don't have much negative to say, this game is fun and relaxing and I've had a good time so far.
All-in-all I'd say this game is a solid 8/10 and an enjoyable experience if you are looking to relax and don't expect some AAA story with tons of content. You should enjoy around 30 hours of playtime if you take your time and don't rush just to finish the main quests. The developers have also shown that they plan to add more content which is promising so you can probably expect some pretty decent updates in the near future.

Lets start off.
The PR guy let some things be said that will detract from the enjoyable content this game has to offer. This game is not like stardew or zelda. Though it does resemble the graphics from Wind waker, though thats about where the similaries end .. minus the link hat you can get from an npc.
This game allows you to explore the entire island, interact with the world minimally and even own several farms.
Exploration: This is the key focus of game play. The game is very pretty to look at more so with day/night cycle and seasons which give the world vibrant contrast. There is stuff called murk that will hinder you as well as areas that want you to build a bridge or even wait for the right season. Though the murk is easily disposed off by beings you find during your exploration called Sprites. These little guys are everywhere and are often clued to the player by blue sparkles .. something much easier to see at night. They are also inside of small mini puzzles that you can find through out the world.
Interaction: The main interaction with the world the player will be gathering of materials such as stone, wood and fodder. Most of this can be used to craft {The crafting system is very lite so you''ll more than likely just be buying for the npcs} or even trade with the npcs for items you need. NPC's lack a bit of depth and are just kinda there to make you wish you could push them off cliffs with how bland they can be.
Farms: Something that probably everyone was most interested in. Well they are there. They have very little in the lines of interaction after you set them up and get the animals you want in them. Hiring a farm hand will also make the whole farm 100% automataic allowing you to just pick up the goods produced. Some things such a seed planting require master carpenter to unlock {very easy}
The bottom line is the game is beautiful, simple and full of exploration. The devs are also greatly interacting with the community, listening and helping as well as listening to our ideas in what we would like to see within the game.
It's 20$ buy it.. experience it and enjoy the relaxing experience.

This game is not:
First of all, this game is NOT like Zelda, or Stardew Valley, or any other game you want it to be like. Don't listen to reviewers that claim this game is like any other and then proceed to compare it to these games. Honestly if you're looking for a Zelda/Stardew Valley game, then go play a Zelda/Stardew Valley game instead.
So, what is this game then?
This is a game that's all about exploration, cute animals, and feeling happy. There's no combat, there's no feeling of being rushed to do anything at all. In fact you'll get more out of the game if you slow down to look at things, or try finding all the little secrets hidden around. Rushing through this game quickly would be like using an item spawner to play Stardew Valley -- what's the point in that? Some people claim the game is completed in about 15 hours. I've played this game 26 hours so far and I'm nowhere near finished it yet. There's tons of stuff to discover and collect, it's a collectionist's dream and I'm happy with that.
This is the perfect kind of game to unwind to after a long stressful day at work. Also, this is a perfect game for kids of any ages and skill level since: there's not combat, no stamina limitations, no time restrictions, no violence, no scary moments, no controversy, no agendas.
Worth nothing is that the support for this game is strong, I wouldn't be surprised if some day the game world becomes even greater than it already is. The developers actively participate in the community and encourage players to make recommendations and share their experiences with one another. Every day so far there's been updates which fix bugs and implement player recommendations to the game. What more can you ask from a game developer?
I definitely recommend this game if you're stressed out and looking for something relaxing to play, or if you're looking for something to buy for your children. Don't buy it if you're looking for a specific popular game clone, though.

Eight minutes in, and the game's barely started. In fact after eight minutes the loading screen and opening cinimatics finally complete. At which point the tutorial begins. or rather, when what should be the tutorial begins. What actually happens is a couple pop up windows appear to barely explain the fact you have hotbars and use wasd to move. No mention is made of how to target an enemy or how to actually attack. This is during a pitched battle where you are taking damage, not a controlled setting where the player can learn the controls safely.
Then when you try attacking something, you instead sit down. How do you stand back up? Don't know, it doesn't explain. Is this because of that attack that hit you? Again it's never explained. How do you do anything now that you're sitting on the ground... in the middle of a battle? It doesn't explain, and trying every key on the keyboard and mouse does nothing. Why are you fighting these beings? Once again, you don't know cause nothing's been explained at all.
The story might be amazing later on. But I don't know, the game's stuck with me sitting during a heated battle right after the opening cinimatic. All in all, I'd say Gothic 3 is a huge failure.

Take Seaside Hill for example, Sonic starts off running and then the camera turns and boom. You can clearly see there are multiple routes you can take. You can keep going straight, boost off to the right onto the water, or do some little platforming to the left. The same kinda goes for Chemical Plant. Sonic starts off running, camera turns, and once again, multiple pathways to start off the stage. Once again, left, right, or straight. But even then, going straight will give you even more pathways soon after taking the path. You have to use your Homing Attack at the right time so grab onto zipline and go on top, which will lead to the 2D section of the stage. These 2 examples, although similar, shows what Modern Sonic's stages has potential in terms of design. It makes me want to go back to these stages, and see how my playthrough is differnet then me speedrunning. Though it may seem like Modern Sonic has great stages, it of course has problems, but not deal breakers in my opinion. The ending of Crisis City had potential. You speeding towards a fire tornado while dodging everything that it throws at you, left me wanting more. When I touched the Goal Ring for the first time in that stage, I said to myself, "WAIT WHAT IM DONE?! BUT I WANT MORE! COME ON SONIC TEAM, YOU COULD'VE MADE IT AT LEAST AT LEAST 5 MINUTES LONGER!" The only stage I actually hate is Planet Wisp. I'll admit, good design for the most part. But I just don't like you waiting on carts for something you might miss and wait all over again, how long it can be sometimes, just confusing sometimes for when I'm within the big 2D section of the stage. And that DAMN bug that shoots that yellow sphere thingy when it comes out of the ground, you know what I'm talking about if you played the game! I hate that thing! Regardless, MOST of Modern Sonic's stages are fun and great. But what about the boss fights? The first with Modern Sonic is decent. It's not terrible, but not actually fun. Except for when you can drown Sonic. Reminds me of Sonic drowning in the hotel pool in Sonic Adventure, unless... Ok I'm getting off-topic. The Rival Battle on top of City Escape, is 95% linear, but in a good way. It's just pure speed with some racing elements mixed in. And yes, Sonic is on his feet, not his car that he got off of eBay. 2nd Rival Battle on top of Crisis City, bad because it's the same patterns over and over again until you reach the final attack. Admittedly, the final attack is something that I think they should do again. The 2nd Boss Battle, I want to say I like it, but once you figure the pattern, it's boring. The final diving section can be make you say, "How did that hit me?" sometimes. The Final Boss of the game is more of a chore then a epic final battle. Switching between Classic and Modern Sonic is funky, both control badly, and getting the achievement from this stage took me so many tries cause in order to get it, you can't get hit by ANYTHING this foe throws at you. Parts of stages you've played will be thrown at you and you're supposed to dodge, but it's extreme hard to do so when you try to dodge and try to catch up to the boss and hit it's weak spot at the same time. It lasts about 3 minutes when you mastered the stage, but it feels like the same amount of time it takes to do a final exam at school. After beating the game, what can you do? Mods. Mods are the reason why I got the PC version of Sonic Generations instead of staying with my 360 copy. Stuff like the Unleashed Project, porting all of Modern Sonic's day stages from Sonic Unleashed. A entire game but for FREE and in 60 FPS, unlike the original 360 version I had. That's worth the money to get the full game, no argument about it. Even Classic Sonic got some love with some Werehog night stages for him! But him spindashing in 3D and crashing the game everytime he does it kinda ruins it. All in all, Sonic Generations is a game that has good stage design, simply fun, and incredible mod support by the Sonic community. One last note, the soundtrack is eh. I wouldn't listen outside of the game. But something like Sonic Forces and Sonic Mania, oh boy, a Sonic Generations 2 should take notes from these two...

Starting note: The version of this game available on Steam is "Corpse Party: BloodCovered", which was released for the PC episodically from 2008-2009 and 2012. No content has been added or removed from the Japanese version, and very little was changed from a gameplay standpoint (limited to unifying certain systems that changed from chapter to chapter, like the map titles).
Corpse Party is a horror game that sticks with you because of its strong characters. While some horror stories are quick to introduce and off unlikable characters just to show that there is danger, Corpse Party makes sure you actually feel the impact of each terrible situation. The first few deaths are not of people that had it coming, but characters that clearly didn't deserve to die. This sets up the threat and malice of the villains in a way that a straight-up slasher movie usually doesn't go for. Because of this, even knowing who will live or die doesn't make things any better. Those who die are the ones you wished could live, while those that survive are forever scarred by the experience.
Part of the popularity of this first entry into the modern Corpse Party continuity also lies in how it grounds its horror in the familiar, and doesn't rely on any single type of horror. The creator has admitted that the franchise is meant to have ero-guro content, but there is a lot more to the story than blood and gore. The setting of an old schoolhouse is something eeriely familiar, even outside of the original Japanese audience. There's something spooky about wandering the dark hallways at night, and Corpse Party takes it further by showing how such a familiar location could be home to horrible activities. This juxtoposition of the familiar and the strange/terrible is a staple of Eastern Horror, but this game is a great example of why that works and continues to be utilized.
The gameplay of Corpse Party: BloodCovered is relatively simple, using basic RPG Maker controls (a nod to its RPG Maker roots) and lock/key puzzles. The trick to Corpse Party is that the "locks" aren't always obvious, and sometimes not having the "key" item or choice will lead to a bad ending (stylized as "Wrong End"). However, these endings are as much a part of the story as the "clear" or "true" endings. Some aspects of the characters simply aren't seen outside of these alternate endings, motivating a collector's urge to see every potential fate. There are also more standard collectables in the form of nametags, but these are more for completionists and to hide a few easter eggs (such as the nametags of characters from Corpse Party Zero, or people that worked on the game).
For those that enjoy horror adventure games that rely more on character and story than trying to shock the player through jumps, Corpse Party is a great choice. It may not be the most "original" story, being heaviliy inspired by certain types of urban legends, but it is a story that can stick with you if you let yourself become attached to the characters. For those worried about the gore content, this version of the game is the least gory, as it relies on text descriptions or sprite animations for most of the deaths.
If you enjoy this version of Corpse Party, I'd also highly recommend playing its 3DS version (Corpse Party: BloodCovered:...Repeated Fear) and that game's sequels (Book of Shadows, Sachiko's Game of Love: Hysteric Birthday 2U [currently JPN only], and Blood Drive). If you want to see where the series began, picking up the original 1996 PC-98 game and a PC-98 emulator (or playing the fan remake "Corpse Party -Rebuilt-") is also a good idea.
And since I'm sure people want to know (and don't always look before asking), here are some of the major differences between BloodCovered (BC/this game) and BloodCovered:...Repeated Fear (BR 3DS):
Original version of Chapter 1-4
Revised version of Chapter 5 (2 new endings, 1 extended ending)
Extra Chapters 1-3, Tooth
Original Artwork
Amateur Voicetrack and Vocal Songs
Revised version of Chapter 1-4 (altered/added scenes, 1 new ending)
Original version of Chapter 5 (plus one ending from BC that was not in BR PSP/iOS)
Extra Chapters 1-14
Redrawn Artwork
Professional Voicetrack and Vocal Songs

Let me begin by saying that Carnivores and Carnivores 2 were my all time favorite games as a kid. I spent an irresponsible amount of time playing those games.
I saw yesterday that there was a remake of the game on Steam and almost fell over from excitement. I was disappointed for the most part after putting seriously hundreds of hours into Carnivores 1 and 2.
Pros
- I respect that they kept a lot of the features from the original games. The weird hovercrafts that take you to and from the game, the trophy room, even the map names.
- The upgradability of your weapons and character is neat, but the pursuit of upgrades seems to be the only driving force of the game.
Cons
- The graphics are very cartoony, I'd honestly prefer the original graphics
- The frame rate is capped somewhere between 30 and 50. I shouldn't be getting 40fps on a gtx1080. It stomps on the immersiveness of the game.
- The dinosaurs are laughably huge. So large in fact that the smallest dinosaur cannot easily run away from you in the woods because it's colliding with too much of the foliage.
- They cut the number of weapons in half
- The number of huntable dinosaurs was also cut in half. Which is a huge deal breaker.
- Gameplay feels like it should be a mobile game
I really wanted to love this game. And I'll continue playing it until I've unlocked all of the maps and all of the upgrades, but I'm going to stop immediately after that. Why? because there's no incentive to play after that. I am forecasting a lonely 4 hours of collective gameplay to finish. For the price, that isn't that bad. But it does not live up to the original games.

Honestly I am a little on the fence for this one. Some parts of the game, especially those where you are in jail, are quite enjoyable. If you like story - driven games, and mobster movies such as Godfather, Donnie Brasco etc. you might just get a kick out of it. Plus, with its fascinating vehicles and soundtrack the game captures the atmosphere of early 20th century America quite well.
Unfortunately, once you've finished the campaign (which takes about 10 hours at most, I imagine), there is almost no replay value whatsoever. The free-roaming world is nowhere near as expansive as the one in games like GTA, providing little incentive to do side activities, like robbing stores and so on. Why have a free roam world if you can't do anything noteworthy in it? Missions make about 95% of the game. Speaking of the missions, sometimes you have to spend too much time on tedious tasks in certain ones, eg. pressing a button to clean a prison toilet, turning off the lights, and so on. Because of this sometimes it takes a while to get to the action.
Overall, I would say Mafia II is worth a play but won't be bringing you back for seconds, unless you are crazy about these kinds of stories. That's why I'd wait for a sale.

Too many of negative reviews are way too uninformative. And I can totally understand why some people might be put off from this game. The game does have it's issues. And the game definitely isn't for everyone.
First and foremost, the game is hard. And by hard I mean dark souls levels of hard. It does return you to the last "checkpoint" and resets your "multiplier" for loot whenever you die. It does not fully explain all you can do. You have to put some of time into learning the game.
If you're someone who doesn't like games like dark souls, this isn't for you. If you're someone who doesn't like complicated skill systems, this game isn't for you. If you want to feel like a god because you're overpowered, this game may be for you.
However to feel like a god you start from the humble beginnings. You're given the means to become a god and become more powerful the further you progress. This game feels very rewarding, but only, if you put effort into it.
What makes it feel great? You get basically any possibly imaginable means to deal with enemies. Be it swarms of undead, squads of assassins, or just a giant beast. I haven't played long enough to say much more, however if you like games that don't hold your hand the entire time, are actually challenging and let you customize your arsenal, this game is for you.

Full Review

Lichdom:Battlemage is a first person shooter where an intricate spell crafting system replaces your usual pew-pews. Putting you under the skin of generic character #94857, the game will bring you through themed corridors and tempt you to try your craft by burning, freezing, electrocuting, mobbing and generally trying to make sense of game mechanics that favor quantity over quality.
L:B's crafting and combat are the two cornerstones of the game. Here, no ammo, no mana, no guns but a system where you apply shape and effect over basic elements to end up with freeze rays and poisoned traps. You can then juggle between three elements of your choosing and apply spells which can combo in interesting ways.
On paper, this system is novel and fairly appealing. The execution, though, falls flat.
All of the title's good ideas are marred by an sloppy execution which turn a potential complex and deep experience into a shallow tedium. Projectiles are incredibly slow, those with auto aim tend to target the wrong enemies and the rest suffer from poor aiming and collision detection. The slow build progression doesn't help, as grinding doesn't feel rewarding and doesn't encourage experiments.
It doesn't prevent from having fun during the first few levels, which lack challenge but let you discover the spell system... until the game's difficulty ramps up all of a sudden for all the wrong reasons.
There has indeed been a trend towards hard games lately, where players needs to understand patterns and learn from their mistakes, having nobody to blame but themselves for their failures (Doom 2016 does that very well on its harder difficulty modes). Unfortunately L:B isn't one of those, and the difficulty spikes originate from unfair, uninspired design.
If the game is rather pretty to look at, the art and story are too generic to justify its grindy and linear aspect.
Ultimately, the game would have benefited from some maturation in its concept and some scaling down in its mechanics (Halo, for instance, has proven that less can be more especially when it comes to weapons).
In L:B's current state, many players will chose to stick to one effective combo to fight against either boredom or impossible odds, and give up in face of the game's repetitiveness and less-than-mature design.
Not recommended.

The two defensive this game gives you is dodging and parrying. Parry is useless, you take a lot of chip damage and the "Galvanize" which is supposed to reward you for parrying is never worth the amount of health you lose when hit, the dodge is good, but after a certain point in the story every enemy has an impairing and homing projectile, disabling your blink for 10 seconds.
So yeah, it should be a fun game, but ends up being very amateur. And what's worse is the complete and utter neglect of the dev, I went looking for such discussions about these issues only to find SEVERAL threads since 2014, and that never got fixed. I can forgive amateurism, I can't forgive abandonware.
TL;DR It's a game where you can imagine how awesome it could've been, but it ends up unispiring and boring due to a good mechanic being strapped to a poor level and enemy design. Adding insult to injury, don't ever expect patches because the product will always be "as-is".

Especially with the great sale going on right about now, I certainly recommend people buy this game. Now, I will grant that it isn't perfect: it's long-lasting value is questionable, it's plot/storyline is not necessarily flourishing with detail and impact (I think), and the voiceacting I simply can't help but smirk at. But, this game definitely gets great points from me for innovation, presenting a new take on strategy and an innovative application of the tried tower defense genre. As the game progresses—at least in my case—you get the feeling that you've totally got this, but new features, units, and adversaries are constantly added and you are constantly expected to rethink your tactics to combat a threat that becomes less and less predictable and linear. Anomaly starts out simple, but eventually your ability to strategize is truly put to the test as more complicated battlefields filled with convoluted arrays of kinetic and non-kinetic threats appear.
On the practical side, this is a "tower attack" game (you play the role of a commander leading your squad of units through turret-infested landscapes), but with many innovative nuance, such as abilities that can buff your units or detriment your adversaries, the ability to purchase and upgrade your units to create a personalized squard as you move through the city blocks, and the opportunity to choose what path you want your units to take, giving you the choice of whether or not you want to try and score some bonus cash that is sitting in a swarm of defenders, or avoid combat as much as you can in order to survive through the finish. Missions are comprehensive and fun to play but are short enough that you can open this game just for a quick round, and its progressing difficulty and story keep it interesting from start to finish.
Oh, and let's not forget that this game was produced by a Polish company, and anything coming out of Poland has to be good (absolutely no bias whatsoever in this final statement).

Aarklash: Legacy is basically a group-based strategy/action RPG. You'll spend much of your time pausing live combat to issue commands to your units, such as heal, aoe, buff, silence, knock-down, etc. You control 4 units in your group at a time, but as you progress through the game, you'll find new characters that you can swap into and out of your group at any time that you are not in combat. You'll progress through a linear game that is filled with combat scenarios, and puzzles.
Enemies drop a combination of white/yellow/purple-named items (as usual in arpgs). You can equip your group with these items or destroy the item to build up a meter that will create a new rare item with random stats. Opening chests also drop random items. You can save the game before creating a new item or opening a chest, then reload the game in hopes of getting another item that is more favorable. It sounds like an underhanded tactic, but it's virtually required if you wish to gain items that each group member can use.
Each character has 4 skill trees to level up, which branch out into different paths, meaning you have some various in how you build your characters. I found the pacing of the leveling system to be rewarding.
The writing and atmosphere were unique. I wasn't sure if this game was based on a series of novels or already established lore, because some of the story seemed too unusual for a small video game, but I did not find any novels regarding Aarklash. I found the game to be satisfying. The graphics were surprisingly good, along with the music.
It's not a very deep game, being linear and relatively short for an rpg (around 20 hours), but the story was good enough. At $20 or less, I believe it to be a good value, and I hope to see a sequel or expansion.

Summary:
Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles is an extremely charming game with great graphics and quite a lot of content to offer. There are tons of places to explore and secrets to find. The problem is that nothing that you do will amount to much of anything. The world will remain largely unchanged, save for the fact that you will slowly clear the Murk out of it, as will your character. There’s no sense of progression guiding you towards greater things. There are no additional gameplay systems awaiting you, nor are there complex puzzles hiding out there, waiting for you to solve them and take the riches that they guard. It is a game that you could continue playing long after you’ve completed the main story, grinding through increasingly demanding quests and finding all of its hidden items, but chances are that you will not.
