It's hard to describe how much I really love Sonic Generations. Something about this game keeps me coming back and I can't really pinpoint what it is.
The colors are so bright and the game looks wonderful, and for the most part consistently plays smooth. The levels are all fast paced and move very quickly, and it is consistently exciting throughout. And while the story is not mindblowingly philosophical or extraordinarily written, it is certainly serviceable for a Sonic game and definitely improvement over some of the more recent entries. There's something great about being able to blast through all the levels at incredible speed, and this is really the only game that can fulfill that for me. The level design is certainly something that needs to be learned, but once you get the hang of it, nothing feels better. Competing with your friends for the best time is also definitely a plus (when it works, which I will get to later).
What I can't say I like as much are the 2D sections. Classic Sonic's 2d gameplay is not what I would pick over Modern's 3d gameplay, however it definitely isn't bad - just not really my cup of tea. I found myself looking forward to Modern levels a lot more than I did Classic. However, the 2D parts that really bring the game down are the slow and rough 2D Modern sections, and the transition between the dimensions is certainly not smooth. This consistently brought Modern's fun, exciting, and speedy gameplay down to a bore. I understand platforming is difficult and slippery in 3 dimensions, but that seems more a fault of the game design than it does an actual problem. The game also needs some bug fixes, as it will always crash when I select leaderboard levels.
Overall, Sonic Generations is definitely worth your time and money. 20 dollars is a steal for this game, and this game can be played for hours on end, especially if you have a friend or two to compete for the best time with. The story only lasts a few hours at most, and I put about 60 hours into the game and got every single achievement. If that doesn't show the game is quality, then I don't know what would.

Sonic Generations is a blast through the first 20 years of Sonic's history. It is a wonderful masterpiece of a game that has an amazing plot, stellar characters, and beautiful zones to run through, with two different play styles to boot!
So it's Sonic's birthday, and everyone came to celebrate. Then, all of a sudden, this wierd monster thing appears and sucks Sonic and his friends into a wierd white space that transcends time and space. Also, the monster kinda sucked all the life and color out of the zones and stuck them here. So Sonic must team up with himself (literally) and figure out what's going on!
So in short, this is  great game. I'd recommend you give it a shot sometime. It has planty of easter eggs and callbacks to earlier points in Sonic's history strung throughout the game that add a little slice of charm to it. The Zones are all amazingly designed for both acts, with different playstyles to fit both Sonics. The achievements here even help you to track your progress throughout the story, and I like that. SO whether you're a new face in the Sonic fanbase, or if you're familiar with the Blue Blur, I highly recommend giving this little beauty a whirl. You will not regret your decision.

Strategy RPG with puzzles thrown in here and there. It's difficult, but more or less fair. I'm not particularly great at strategy games, so I said more than my fair share of four-letter words while playing through on the normal difficulty setting. Aarklash: Legacy is a traditional RPG in that you have eight set characters to choose from. While you can change their function by realocating skill points (yay skill trees!), it's not what I would strictly call character customization. There are tons of synergies to find between various characters/skills and the game does expect at least some situational awareness (switching between skill variants based on what sort of battle you'll be in next, etc).
The story and characters didn't stand out much, but I found myself enjoying them regardless. I did manage to get twenty solid hours out of this game. Aarklash feels really good to play and I can recommend it to players who enjoy RPGs or strategy games. You can strap a time-bomb onto your tank to blow up all the enemies you've taunted. What more could you ask for?
This game has so much potential, the devs are obviously talented, but arrogant and thus will fail. A pity.

This game has been the surprise of the month to me. Bought while it was on sale, if memory serves, under ten dollars, I had limited expectations about this game when i first saw it was not but a rather delightful discovery.
To those looking over for a quick recap. Yes, Aarklash Legacy is worth your purchase and time. It is a solid rpg with engaging mechanics, it seems perfectly optimized.
And now, on to expand on the good...
The game has a good mechanic, basically, it is an over the head rpg in which one has the choice to pause and assign actions per each of the members of your four man team. I suppose that, in this aspect one could draw a parallel with the Dragon Age gameplay, but whereas the other characters could be controlled by AIs, this one expects you to micromanage each of the four character's actions, which i suppose makes the combat tighter and more demanding. The fights are a house of cards. One mistake, one character taken down because a buff is not applied or removed in the right time and the battle could turn into a loss, demanding your attention. Positioning plays a much bigger role in the game as some enemies have directional spells that must be dodging as they are casting them. Bosses have attacks that instakills those who are standing in the wrong place. And buffs play a bigger role here, affecting the combat from adding armor to reducing healing and potentially killing oneself, more than once a character died because there is a buff that "converts all heals into damage". So saving after each battle is highly recomended
You have a list of four skills per character, that can be upgradeable several times, and each tier has variations of the same skill, adding lettle details like damage, range, and status effects. All skills also have a branching path that alters the nature of the skill in different ways. The good thing is that there isn't actually a penalty for refunding the points you invest and putting them in the skills as you want.
The game looks great, with decent if not great quality in graphics and special level design. The ambience is said fairly nicely most of the time. Puzzles turn out inventive and amusing, nothing overly complicated but fun. And the game is decently optimized. Game loads fast and reloads are almost instant.
You will have up to eight playable characters to use (and this isn't a spoiler as it is announced in the trailer). Each of them with their special advantage and disadvantage, their unique set of skills, their own personality and backstory. They are just too good. The chemistry between characters is hinted through little lines and eventually you get to root for them in the short time they game lasts ...
Sadly, that leads me to the bad...
The criticism is that, the game 'feels' too short. And no, it isn't short, the first playthough took me 16 hours, minus one hour which i suppose condenses the time i was afk. But it does feel small because all the things that transpire, is but a small odyssey. I am trying not to spoil anything but i feel like the potential buyer should be warned about this. Basically characters are in trouble, gather up and go to solve the problem. It doesnt really help that the game split itself into just 3 acts.
My complain there is that it does feel like a wasted opportunity. There are 8 characters and u only travel in groups of 4. It is also convenient that there are 2 tanks, 2 healers, 2 spellcasters and 2 offensive characters. The idea of splitting them into groups was there but sadly it was barely used. The could've been more puzzles that required to use more than one character to complete (not that there aren't of those in the game, but could've been more)
I also wished to know more about the other characters. Each of them had their own motivations and reasons to be mercenaries as well as their unfinished businesses for that matter, i half hoped they would deal with them (of course, given that the story here is only a trip it makes sense those sidestories arent touched)
But then again, hopefully there will be a sequel and that it will continue the story. So far, this is a good game, and has a lot of replay value for those who want a bigger challenge.

This game is billed as a reverse tower defense game.  Unfortunately you get a handful of units against dozens of towers.  (Just a few at first then it increases each level)  You have to send your handful of units out on a designated path and you run around with a little guy who buffs or debuffs.  That's the entire game.  It's really just a babysitting game where you MUST debuff/buff at exactly the right place and moment.  There is room for error at first but by the later levels there is very little, if any.  I would have enjoyed being able to build creeps, making it more of an RTS game, which is what I was expecting.  In the end I found it irritating that I would cast my buffs at slightly the wrong location and my front units would walk out of the buff and get destroyed forcing me to try the level again.  Replay was expected in this game though, there isn't enough content to justify no repetition play.  It has cool ideas, like, having a buff unit that can run off road (anywhere really).  It isn't a bad game, just not good in my opinion.

Firstly, this game is very good.
The rest of this review is optional should you want to hear my opinions about what the game is like.
The game is a rougelike, real time strategy game that sees you in the role of the captain of the ship as opposed to the pilot (what you would normally experience in a space game). By putting you in the captain role, the game gives you almost complete control over every action that takes place on the ship, right down to prioritising which systems in the ship need power in the event that you don't have enough power to keep the entire ship online.
I will say that as much as I absolutely love this game, I have yet to actually defeat the final boss. The final boss is extremely difficult, regardless of which difficulty level you play on, and on your first few tries, it's perfectly normal to be completely obliterated before you even reach the last few sectors. Having played a reasonable amount of the game, I've found that the only real differences in the difficulty modes are found in how much scrap (currency) you earn, and how easy the enemies are when you find them in the main sectors; the final boss is always hard, even on easy mode. It may be intimidating to newer players that it is so difficult to actually finish the game, but the best stories usually don't come from beating this game, rather how long you were able to hang on when fighting against overwhelming odds.
The one criticism that I have with the game is that after some time playing it, it can get to the point where you think that you've seen all of the scenarios that it has to offer. All of the pirates seem to say the same thing, you'll have all of the ships, and you seem to play the game in the same way every time. When you feel as though this is the case, it's time for some mods! The game's support for modding (and the modding community) is very good, and you will find many mods for the game that will completely change the way that it plays; one of the best examples of this is the "Captain's Edition" mod, which completely overhauls the game in almost every way, whilst also adding in a whole host of new items. This will extend the life of the game, and it will make it much more challenging for more experienced players. It is also my understanding that mods are relatively easy to make for this game, so if you want something in the game, then you may as well make it (I say this with little to no modding experience though, so don't take my word for it).
With some of the best gameplay that I've experienced in quite some time, and excellent support for mods, this game is definitely worth it, especially when it is on sale. If you're anything like me, you'll be playing this game for a very long time.

Gothic 3 is♥♥♥♥♥♥ I loved gothic 1 and 2, I grew up with these RPGs. Gothic 1, while still rather clunky in its mechanics and controls, is still very enjoyable, thanks to the great world, characters and story. Gothic 2 took everything good from Gothic 1 and made it even better. Less clunky controls, smoothed out mechanics, bigger world, better story, more characters to like. It was pure Action RPG bliss.
While Gothic 2 from a technical standpoint was just a more polished Gothic 1, Gothic 3 has nothing in common with it's prequels, technically speaking. And it just ♥♥♥♥♥ over everything that made the original 2 games so great. The World is bigger? Sure, but it's also got less stuff to do in. The graphics have more polygons and stuff? Sure, but it looks so goddamn ugly and somewhere between plastic and rubber. The story? What story? You move from town to town, decide if you root out the rebels or the orcs, goto next town, repeat. Same for the Desert, except the factions names are different. In Gothic 1 and 2, stuff happened, there was tension, there was drama. In Gothic 3, nothing happens. Sure you liberate some cities and stuff, but it doesn't really tell a story, you just grind through progression.
The Combat in this game is one of the most hillariously broken messes I've ever seen. First of all, go full one handed melee in this. Archery or even magic is just not worth it. Which is ironic, considering how ♥♥♥♥ing overpowered enemy mages are. You'd think your level 20 hero would have no problem fighting a measly goblin mage. ♥♥♥♥ that noise, he deals an insane amount of damage. My only strategy left was to basically circle around him so that his fireballs miss me and hope I get close enough to pummel him into the ground before he incinerates me. And there was that one time I fought an Orc Shaman. He got stuck in a doorway and spammed fireballs at the nearby wall. So I just pulled out my bow and slowly chipped away his health from afar. As he was almost dead, he quickly pulled out a healing spell, fully healed himself and switched back to the fireball. That took him just a second. All my effort worthless.
It's unbalanced beyond believe. Wanna kill almost every humanoid in close quarters combat? Spam light attacks. Everytime you hit an enemy, they will flinch and then reset to normal combat stance, before they can strike. Flinching+striking takes more time than a light swing. You'll cut through anything with that. And as cool as poisoning your blade sounds, it's useless. In order to apply the poison to your enemies, you have to stab them by holding the attack button and pressing down. Normal strikes don't poison your enemy. But why would you do that, the stab takes way too long. Also dualwielding Swords is only usefull, because it allows you to attack with two swords at once with heavy swings, but not with light swings.
Overall: This game is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Be glad you don't have to play Version 1.0, that taught me to fear boars. They were able to bite faster than I could counter, so I was locked in an endless flinching frenzy, which only ended once I was dead.

My biggest problem with the game is that it eventually turns into the player quickly speeding through "trash" battles until they get to an overpowered boss battle which has no strategy to it other than reloading and getting lucky with one of your OP skills (like critical hits = one-hit-kill).
Bosses and some enemies have way too many attacks in one turn, most bosses I've seen with like 8-12, and they kill your party before you can do anything. This is fine if there was some strategy you could employ, but I didn't really see one.
Reviving your party members also destroys your CON stat, which i THINK is bad but I wouldn't know, this game has no MANUAL or any way to understand anything about it.
You basically just reload boss battles until the boss doesn't do something that seems completely unfair. Couple that basic gameplay loop with a bunch of weird bugs still in the game, obtuse mechanics which generally can be fun but often just leave you wondering if you've missed something important, and extremely discordant art styles, and this thing just doesn't seem cooked properly.
It's a shame because the underlying exploration, quest, and item systems seem very well done (though the inventory system didn't have to be so annoying imo). The writing is fun too. I'll come back to this game in a year or so if the developer keeps working on it.
The game was worked on largely by one person as far as I know, but the game has to stand on its own and can't get a pass just for that reason.

I really like the -idea- of this game.  I really hate this game.
tl;dr an amazing concept and good production value is ruined by awful writing, a lack of direction, bad combat balancing, and terrible repetition.  An essay follows.
On the plus, it looks pretty enough, with some relatively detailed environments and models.  The voice acting is mostly really good (thanks Jennifer Hale and Troy Baker and more).  The whole feel of throwing magic is fantastic, combined with all the animations, the "realistic" arm movements, the variety of spell effects conjuring in your hands, and most of the sound design, as well as the impact it has when enemies are smacked by it.  The idea of controlling magic so intimately is an extremely fascinating concept to me; having a direct control over the complex freezing rays, gravity bombs, and temporal blasts from a first person perspective sounds amazing.  And it is!
...For maybe 2 hours tops.  The story is a bit of a boring mess, and for a narrative so hell-bent on driving home strong feelings of hatred, revenge, and power, I've never felt so underwhelmed by what was supposed to be climactic fights.  They dragged certain emotions and events on FAR too long with no development within them.  The spell crafting system is awful.  The UI is bad, it's primarily driven by randomly generated drops which also serve to fuel as your progression of power, it's incredibly confusing and even once you figure it out you realize how downright stupid it is, and a large amount of the spells you can make are just useless!  Not just because they're bad or low strength, even though many of them are, but because of the terrible enemy design.
There are melee enemies, arrow shooting enemies, spellcasters, and flying enemies, along with rarer demons and minibosses.  All of the enemies have a high health pool and low damage, and to save some time, I won't list how they react to every situation.  What I will say, however, is that every melee enemy reacts the same, as does every archer, and every mage, and every rare flying enemy.  Suddenly, with everything having a high health pool and enemies extremely rarely grouping close together in groups more than 2, your AoE spells and Lightning as a whole are looking very lackluster.  I was sad because I just wanted to shoot lightning bolts, but it was so monotonous to do chaining-damage that did less to a single target that I stopped.  My slot for an Area spell was never actually used to hit an area because it was NEVER relevant.  I only used it in conjunction with a hard crowd control combination because them standing in my pool of Fire did more damage, faster, than actually throwing bolts of fire at them.
Aside from health pools going down, the progression in the actual pretty-looking areas are rather putrid.  In the latter half of the game (and maybe more, I took a hiatus between the first and last half), it was some RPG nonsense, except I wasn't earning anything.  Like clockwork, every 10 seconds of walking forward post-fight, new enemies would emerge from the woodwork in the huge, expansive, otherwise-empty levels.  It never changed in difficulty.  Nothing new ever happened.  There were no surprises.  It wasn't relevant to the story.  The "levels" you achieved in your spellcasting are menial.  It was just empty busywork that repeated itself, almost as if they thought repetitive combat was a good thing.  The areas were irrelevant except to give the artists a new palette to work with.  With my frustration set in and my faith in the game gone, I equipped a newly acquired and overpowered Ice bolt spell, summoned skeletons with Necromancy, and spat all over the intended combat systems by just running in circles and spamming left click to kill enemies in 4 - 10 seconds each.  For around 4 hours.  Nothing changed, nothing was introduced.  It was just an exercise in repetition.  Don't even get me started on the unwarranted difficulty spikes.
I'm starting and stopping on multiple points to just give the real sense that no one thing is wrong.  Everything concerning the combat system, everything concerning the story, the crafting system, the bosses, the flow of the game, is all so interwoven on so many bad levels it's hard to start and stop at one specific idea.  I stuck through it just to say I completed the game, and to really find out if it ever got better.  It didn't.  Upon completion of the game, I felt such a strong sense of disappointment and disbelief that I hadn't in a very long time, if ever.  The ending is absolute trash.  Indirect spoiler ahead:
The idea, the novelty, is legendary in my eyes.  The execution was just disgusting.

Lichdom: Battlemage is a decent, but monotonous game.
As I started playing my first reaction was: "Why I can't jump!?". It turns out - this game has no jumping mechanics. You can shoot fireballs, lightnings and other stuff, but you can't jump - it's to difficult for them mages.. I guess.
This game is very linear. Sometimes it has open spaces, but there is only one way to the main objective all the time. You can press a button to see the line where to go (that's always the wrong way if you want to explore the area and find its secrets ^^, but that's why I liked it, because you always know the right path + you will never miss something valuable if you go the other way).
The story is ... baaa... oook... decent enough. Nothing spectacular. The problem is how it is told. It's always in the same way - through some holograms from the (recent) past. Some dialogues/monologues are just dull and without any value. Everything feels so stretched out that in the end it just becomes really boring.
The graphics of this game is really good. Lighting, spell effects, enemy animations - everything is really well done (this actually saves the game from being bad).
Visually pleasant, but overall just ... empty game.
You can use 3 out of 8 different sigils (spell types) (can switch between them at checkpoints). Usually you can combo them for more efficient and faster killing. There is no loot in this game. You automatically collect all the "items" ... a.k.a. augmentations from the enemies you kill. You can use those to upgrade or craft new and better spells. It can be a bit hard to understand how all this works, but this game has some automated crafting system, so you don't need to waste much time here if you don't want to.
The gameplay itself is very straightforward. All you have to do is kite all the time and juggle through 3 different buttons. In other words - shoot, run, shoot, run, shoot, run (and sometimes die because of stupid bugs (knockback + damaging aura combos from the enemies doesn't help either)).
This game has really stupid bugs, You can make the enemies teleport from one area to another (randomly) by using one of the spells, but sometimes it happens that they teleport outside of restricted area and you can't kill them anymore and then you can't progress any further. Then you have to go back to the main menu and restart the area and waste another 5-7 minutes doing the same thing you just did.
Or you can fall off the stairs and get stuck between the wall and the stairs. Remember, that you can't jump in this game. Yeah. Time to reload once again...
I really liked those little hidden challenge areas. They each provide massive rewards but first you must fight through several waves of enemies and only then you will be able to collect all the loot. Most of them I managed to do in one go, but some are really challenging and you can die once or twice.
Oh, and this game has swamps too. Why so many games have swamps? I hate swamps. They should be deleted from the games forever. uhhh. But hey, it's linear so it's not THAT bad.
I only recommend this game if you are prepared to do the same thing over and over again for 20 hours and if you get this game on a big sale, otherwise - it's just a waste of your time and money.

I've played Cyanide games before and I can see how the gameplay in this is an iteration of the combat in Game of Thrones and Of Orks and Men but if the combat in those games turned you off trust me, it's much more responsive, fast paced, and gamer friendly than those other titles.
This is by far the best Cyanide game yet and a must-play if you're a fan of the old Infinity Engine games.

It's like playing a miniature wargame in real time. You control a band of units, each with its unique skills and abilities. You can usually swap them in and out of the squad freely (when not in combat) so you can experiment with different ability combinations (the plot assumes that all the characters are travelling together at all times so you're not missing out on any dialogue by sticking with one team, by the way). The fights are generally quite challenging, and boss fights sometimes feel like puzzles instead of actual fights. The equipment system is pretty bad - personally, I think the game would benefit more from an equipment unlock system instead of the random jewellery drops. The writing is nothing special but not particularly bad either, and some of the characters really grow on to you. The ability skill trees are pretty barebones as well - while some upgrades change the ways abilities behave, only four per unit seems a bit low. A huge plus is the ability to reset the skill trees when not in combat. The game seems a bit short, but the encounters are not repetitive. The game has an absolutely gorgeous art style and character design.
Overall, I would not buy this game at the full price. Wait until it's about half off.

Cyanide doesn't have the best track record when it comes to games, on this one though they have managed to pull ahead of the pack in some areas while falling far behind in others. With Aarklash Legacy they manage to provide an amazing tactical rpg experience at pretty much the cost of all other areas of the game. Real Time w/ Pause (RTwP) combat is where it shines and it is certainly the best isometric rtwp we've had recently.
I have read some stuff about people not liking the puzzles in the game, I found them fine. I enjoyed most of them and it was a nice change of flow to the endless barrage of fights.
The characters have lots of interesting attributes, E.G. the healer not able to regen mana, she has to feast on allies' hp to gain mana back. This skill can be upgraded so that the ally has buffs when feasted upon and even regenerates more than was feasted. Lots of tactical combat, having to carefully position your characters to avoid friendly fire and it manages it well. Rarely did I have an ally running into friendly fire unintentionally.
What it sacrifices is pretty much everything else, lackluster story, mediocre progression, (You max out your chars about halfway through the game,) sub-par to average voice acting, An item system that just seems tagged on, and very little immersion.
The game itself is pretty much a series of combats, you know that around every corner will be assorted bad guys and the plot comes up with a decent explanation for having skeletons fighting alongside humans, demons, angels, elementals, etc. If you enjoy RTwP tactical rpgs, then this shouldn't be a drag considering how well done it is. I was totally fine with it until about 3/4ths through the game, when there was no more character progression, all chars maxed out in levels, pretty much nowhere to go there. Just keep killing monsters at every bend in the path.
tl;dr Buy it on sale if you're a fan of the RTwP tactical rpg genre

Faster than light is a 2D Space Roguelike where you command a spaceship fleeing from a large fleet spreading across the galaxy. You explore systems encountering random events that shape your playthrough. The outcome of every encounter has different chances of success depending on crew and equipment at your disposal. Successful outcomes yield supplies like fuel, torpedos and scrap whilst bad outcome scan kill crew or damage your ship. Along the way you can upgrade your ship and buy things at stores with scrap. Your ship only has so much power, indicated by bars on your lower screen. Power is micromanaged depending on what you need to focus on like shield regeneration or weapon charging. Grimoire is a Wizardry 8 that never was. If you longed to plunge yourself into a proper Bradley's Wizardry game for the past quarter of the century, ever since the "industry" has decided to throw these games under a bus, you'd be a fool to miss this one.
If the words "proper Bradley's Wizardry" leave you puzzled, you probably should play something else instead, something about romancing derp personality and a fully voiced quest compass.

Grimoire is a tile based dungeon crawler that seeks to mimic Wizardry 7, one of the staples of the genre.
While it suffers from the usual problems a game made by a single person would... like some numbers needing to be tweaked here and there, some flags to be set for an item or an NPC, some UI quality of life additions... While all that, it manages to be a game game. A real game.
Today the market is overflowing with many Don Quijote's setting off to create one spiritual sequel after the other and the results are sadly vaporware. Not this game. This game is a game game. Was Arcanum buggy on release ? Yes. Knights of the Old Republic 2 ? Sure. VTMB:Bloodlines ? Most definitely. That didn't change the fact that they were squarely over that boundary that sets apart hobby projects and professional games. And Grimoire is too.
Let's talk about the tone of the game. Most people tell you about a game "it has charm" but they can't explain what that means... It's the tone. What's the tone of the game ? Some games are somber (Age of Decadence), some are lighthearted (Divinity:Original Sin), others are tragic (Planescape Torment). If a game is to have charm it has to set a consistent tone and back it up with an interesting plot and gameplay.
So what's the tone of Grimoire ? Does it have "charm" ?
It does. The best way to describe it to someone that hasn't played it is this: it's Monty Python's Quest for the Holy Grail. It's got a serious skeleton of adventure and exploration through a fantasy-medieval world but it never shies away from a silly gag to dispense some humor. Make note though, that just like Quest for the Holy Grail, the gags are there to complement the adventure, not to take it's place. You have to get the proportions right to get that special charm and Grimoire does exactly that.
What about gameplay ? Combat mechanics, itemization, all that stuff ?
Well... the game can be hard and it's mechanics require a good look over to comprehend, this isn't 'pret-a-porter' - in good tradition to its inspiration Wizardry 7, expect to play for a dozen hours and then think to yourself "Now that I get how stuff works, I need to restart and make a better party." - that's not a bug, that's a feature.
Also, to ride out the Monty Python analogy above, don't be surprised if you come upon a metaphorical holy hand grenade or a killer bunny wabit for that matter, this isn't a "grimdark" serious adventure, balance sometimes bows out and leaves the stage in favor of fun and a silly gag.
Starting to wrap this up... full disclosure time:
The UI is not great or good or even ok, it's mediocre. I'd rate it 5/10. It's not a bunch of endless windows of lists, this is still a game game not an RPG Maker project, but yeah, it could use some quality of life additions.
Bugs. Critical ones ? No. As I'm writing this, the game is stable. You may have heard about losing save games at one point... No. That was a one time thing, the game is stable, take it to the bank.
Are there some minor bugs left, a flag here, a broken script there ? Yes. At this point there are a few and those few have been reported and mapped. The next patch is already set to take care of that as well as some number tweaking to account for player feedback.
Home stretch. Should you buy this game ?
Yes. If you like the genre yes, you like RPGs, give it a shot.
Should you buy the game now or wait for more patches ?
Your call. I have no patience, I bought it on release. Patches come out, I don't have to restart, the game just gets better as I play, fine by me. Maybe you like to be more careful with your purchase, want that final experience from the get go. No problem.
Remember, your money your call. And if you decide to buy I hope you have as much fun as I'm having.

Carnivores 2 and Carnivores: Ice Age was the first games I got on my PC back in the day, and I played them to death. I even got my original copies somewhere...
I even got mobile versions of both games on my android phone and play them from time to time. Those versions are actually superior to PC, since they both run extremely well and got some new creatures thrown in for free (18 in mobile version as of time of writing this review compared to PCs 9).
So how does this hold up?
P.S. For short version, see TL;DR/ Conclusion at the end
P.P.S. Many people will probably compare this to theHunter: Primal, but I haven't played that so only comprarison you'll see here will be with previous games in Carnivores series.
Even though it's a port of PS3 version, it runs well on PC. I tried it on both a hi tech Alienware PC at my friends house and my 6 year old scrapheap, and didn't experience anything wrong with this game whatsoever. Settings are a little bit limited, but decreasing LOD and turning off advanced grass will make it run even on laptop without any hickups.
Graphics, while nothing amazing like Skyrim or Witcher, still look pretty well, even on lower settings. There are some neat effects here and there, and if you're observant you can even track a dino by following his footsteps and blood trails, which is awesome.
Sound design is pretty good. There are some great ambient sounds and one time, I almost started swatting at a fly which I thought was flying close to my ear even though it was in game. Believe me, it was that realistic.
Dinos also make different growls and sounds and even though Stegosaurus sounds like a bear, which I personally find a little bit silly, it works when you are trying to locate a specific dino by sound.
Animations on dinosaurs are pretty good and their movement feels natural. Watching Ankylosaurus in his defensive position, stomping and hitting his tail club on the ground was extremely awesome.
Speaking of dinosaurs, they look way better and are more "up to date" compared to mobile and and prequel counterparts. Don't get me wrong, those dinos weren't plain bad, but a lot of things has changed in the field of paleontology and some things like size and looks are a bit outdated. Ceratosaurus for example, is bigger than Spinosaurus, which is just plain wrong.
Devs probably didn't do their research properly or got something of it wrong, but they sure did it right this time, and it shows.
There is a "progression" system of sorts, where you can spend diamonds on upgrading your guns, player and Gadget. I say "progression" since upgrades are not permanent, and points can be taken away from one upgrade and be used on something else instead at any time or liking.
Shooting mechanics have been improved, and now, if you're skilled or lucky enough you can one shot dinosaurs if you aim at their weak spots, which will award you with more diamonds and better rating. Weak spots vary but with a little practice or with a help of one specific perk, you'll be be on top of things very quickly.
This game is also pretty cheap, NOT in early access, and support with more dinosaurs is already planned which is always nice.
First things first, there are only 6 dinosaurs to hunt...
Yes, you read it right, 6 dinosaurs. That was the biggest disappointment IMHO since, as I said before, mobile version has 18(!) completely different dinos to hunt. They really couldn't add more dinos?
There is also fewer weapons this time around.
Previous games had 6 (Pistol, 2 types of stotguns, 2 types of Rifles and Xbow) but this game only has 3 (4 counting Revolver sidearm perk). You could also carry all 6 if you could afford it, so why isn't it possible here? Your could go for a "realism" argument, but personally, I would like the option to be at least available.
AI on dinosaurs is pretty random as well, and feels like a downgrade compared to prequels.
When it works it looks great and all that, times when they manage to get stuck between  2 trees and rocks, are just... bad.
One time, this Stegosaurus I was hunting got stuck in a rock and when I got closer, managed to go through it and with some struggle, out on the other side. While I watched this "rebirth" my lower jaw almost hit the floor.
Sure, it doesn't happen too often, but when it does, it kinda ruins the immersion... COMPLETELY.
Their reaction to gunfire is also pretty random.
In prequels herbivores ran away like maniacs when they heard gunshots while carnivores looked at it like a dinner bell running up to you and chewing your face.
In this game however, Herbivores usually don't care if their mate is shot in front of them or close by, unless shot themselves. Carnivores are a little bit less relentless, which is a little bit disappointing.
Levels themselves while big, are still smaller and less varied compared to prequels. Some of them are also covered in this weird fog, which in turn makes hunting dinosaurs more frustrating than everything else, since you can't see them 90% of the time.
One thing that I also found annoying personally was that some maps doesn't feature all dinosaurs. For example, default map only features Stegosaurus and Ankylosaurus and nothing else. Want to hunt ALL dinosaurs on your favourite map? Can't do that! Must choose last map available!
My only questing to this is WHY?! In previous games you could hunt any dinosaur on any map, so why this feature is unavailable in this game is just bizarre.
Recommending this game is hard. With every step it takes in the right direction, it also takes a step back and if feels disappointing.
I like the new visuals, updated dinosaurs, sounds, upgrades and other new features but unfortunately, mobile version has 3 times the dinosaurs, double the weapons and environments are more varied and interesting.
I was really looking forward to this release of the game, but after 6-7 hours in this game, I had basically unlocked and upgraded everything this game had on offer and hunted all the dinosaurs, which is kinda disappointing compared to amount of hours I used on completing mobile versions.
I'll probably recommend this games to the long time fans of the series, but new arrivals will probably be disappointed and bored fairly quickly with the amount of content available at the moment.
I'll update this review as the game gets updated with more content etc.

Not sure how to feel about this one. For comparison, been playing a lot of The Hunter: Primal, to which this game is slightly similar to. There aren't that many dinosaurs to hunt, granted, but the guns feel very good and the scenery is downright gorgeous. The worst thing is how long it takes to walk around the environment and how hard it is to find ammo and how easy it is to die even after you've got good gear. It's rather unforgiving at times.
So with that said, Carnivores: DHR, has a little more on offer in my opinion. It's a more arcadey type of game, with cartoony art and a UI that looks like it was made for smart phones (because former versions were developed for iOS and Andriod in mind) for very casual gamers in mind. So far I have been having fun with it. There doesn't seem to be much consequence for dying and there isn't really much to lose.
Has way more dinosaur types than Primal does, though less guns, however there are attachments you can buy to improve your guns which outnumber the ones you can get in Primal. The gun handling itself also feels very arcadey.
Carnivores is also sadly SP only, while Primal you can hunt online with friends or strangers.
Arcade vs Realism isn't exactly bad, it's just a different feel. I'm not sure I can rate one game over the other even if they are similar. Carnivores is almost too easy though, so you don't really feel much risk as you do in Primal. It's a far more casual experience.
So to sum it up, TL;DR:
It's rather a very good game for what it is.
The good old days. Glad they brought this back.

Not much time in game yet BUT my first impressions are that it's an awesome game. The tutorial was informative enough to get started and have an idea of what to do, but it didn't feel over bearing either. One thing I had to do was turn up the brightness when I got in game, but that's a total nonissue. Game play is smooth, and as expected slow. But the slowness is what makes the hunts satisfying in my opinion after finally getting a kill, even more after getting it in one shot. Things such as wind direction, sound, movement speed all play a roll in how the hunt goes, so this game defiantly favors the patient player. There's no resupply points in game, or at least any that I've come across, so you have a limited number of rounds. If I remember right it's 15 until you purchase one of the perks. I think that this was a good idea on the park of the devs as this forces players to make each shot count if they plan on having a long hunt. In addition to the hunting mode, the game offers an observation mode that allows players to watch how their targets behave. I personally haven't used this feature yet, but I do plan to.
You start out with a bolt action rifle with no scope, and at first I thought that would be a sever limitation; I'm happy to say I was wrong. The starting weapon feels balanced enough to get started, although I feel that 500 gems to unlock the sniper rifle feels a little much at this point in the game, but I may change my mind on that. The game also offers a firing range to try out weapons, and targets will show the locations of vitals. I found this to be a very good idea, as this at least lets you get a working idea of where to aim on your target when you get into the field.
The AI is satisfying at this point, although the dinosaurs that I've hunted SO FAR have sounded like bears. Dinosaurs that I've encounter so far have acted pretty much how I would expect that species to act. One thing I did notice was that one of the little ambient dinosaurs would appear to almost clip when taking a turn while running around, but this didn't break immersion for me. The coolest thing, I think, is when the ship comes to pick up kills. The ship picks you up in the same way when you decide that it's time to leave the arena, an idea that I thought was awesome. There seems to be a decent selection of dinosaurs to hunt at this time, but from what I've read there are plans to add two more to the game.
Overall the game is very good, probably a few things that could be polished a little bit more, but nothing that makes the game unplayable or anything that is super distracting. With a $15 price tag it's worth picking up.

Call of Duty: World at War in my opinion is a fun game.
I have never really played a COD game (apart from COD 3 on the Wii) however after playing this it makes me want to play a classic COD game.
This game has gotten me intereset in the series (or maby just the WW2 aspect of the franchise) however some things in the game did annoy me.
At times I did find the game to be a bit cheesy, as it puts you upon a pedistall and the game says that you are the most important character out of this entire war. (This is even more clear when it comes to the end of the Soviet campaign) I don't really want this in a game about such a conflict, although this didn't bother me too much.
My least favourite campaign was the Pacific campaingn, it was also the one were my computer struggled a bit.
It was just going through trenches one after another burning everything in site. This is were my potato of my computer also nearly died. Throughout this campaign you will use a flamethrower and this killed my frames. One level in particular nearly set my computer alight. However if you have got a decent computer the game will run fine.
I was a bit dissapointed that there wasn't much variation in levels. I counted only two levels were you were in a vehical. All the other levels were just boots on ground. It did all start to feel the same after some time.
However that doesn't mean that I didn't enjoy my time with this game. The shootouts were fun to me, but might feel stale  to players who have played other COD games. In addition the two vehical levels were fun as well. There are few weapon variations but after some time in game I felt that all weapons fell into catagories of; Bolt-action, Semi-automatic, automatic and special weapons. (i.e. The flamethower or the Panzerschreck)
Overall I enjoyed most of my time with the game. Although this game might feel stale to people who have played other COD games. No, I haven't played the zombie mode, since I've got no-one to play with so I can't really talk about it.
I would give this game a 7/10.

Great game. I give it 8/10.
Pros:
-Puzzles to unlock goodies on about every level
-Awesome puzzles to complete storyline
-Good storyline
-Combat is intriguing and makes you think--must be very strategic.
-The number of companions that you can control and deck out with gear
-Pausing the game to plan out strategies
-Talent trees to cutomize for each companion; it adds a deeper level of gameplay
-Decent graphics
Cons:
-Game has some bugs--sometimes the abilities for a companion will not show up. Or, when you click on a companion, another companion's abilities show up. When this happens, you have to restart the game to fix.
...So, because of this, you need to remember to save the game after every battle!!
-Gear is simplistic--it doesn't seem to have gear specific to any one character, it doesnt change the look of your character, and it does not change or add abilities to any character. Basically. gear just adds passive stats.
-No end game. When you beat it, that's it. No unlocking of ubber mode, or anything, to find better gear for your characters. So, you can't really do anything else with the characters you have leveled up and decked out...not even restart and play the game again with your decked out characters.
Pro or Con?
-Easy to cheat to get gear. Just stand in front of a treasure box before you open it and save. If you don't like what you get, just load that save point and try again. You can do this when creating loot, too.
-Right before you beat the game, the storyline takes a drastic turn and ends, leaving you hanging.
What I would like to see in DLC or part 2 if they choose to make it, which devs should:
-Instead of still pausing, make it to where everything is in slowmo when you hit what is now the pause key.
-better gear
-some end game
-more challenges and hidden treasure
-more bosses
Tips if you decide to buy:
-Save Frequently
-Wendaroo is freaking awesome, so learn how to use her.
-Save before opening chests so you can reload last save if you don't like what you get.
-When creating loot, the last item is the item you will create.. it could've been my imagination, though, but it usually also had the last attribute of that item put into it too.
-Go for one target at first--usually the squishy magic type, like priests or mages. If you can't demolish it in 5 seconds,  split your damage amongst other targets.
..usually I tried demolishing one fast. But when that didn't work, I usually split dmg across two targets  in two seperate areas until one or the other was very low hp and then switched to full focus dmg on that one. This also helped me metigate inc damage better because I could see everything that was going on better so I knew who to heal and dispel and such.
This is not a lazy mans game

I look forward to and have high hopes of the return to Myrtania in the next true Gothic named sequel with Piranha Bytes at the helm again. With a lot of voice acting, multiple ways to play, and freedom to go wherever you wish, this game has managed to keep me occupied full of episodic gameplay that I can pick up and put down whenever I like. This is my first serious (mind the end) and public review on Steam.
Gameplay lengh: About 300-500 hours if you want to level high and see everything. 150 if you play through most content quickly.
Required skill level: Experience with RPG games and knowledge in oldschool RPGs. Studing how the game mechanics work but also keeping a cool head for hours.
Please note even if I'm merely clocking about 50 hours of it on Steam as of this review, I've already played through the game with the DRM-free version of it and it took me over a month of playing this game daily without any rushing through.
Furthermore this review has been written considering the following
mod, depending on how you see it. It is about as detrimental for the game as the game itself.
- Gothic 3 Enhanced Edition Patch v1.75 International release
It is
that you install this patch before you play this game.
There are a couple of other mods out there that enhance this game, like the "Questpaket" version 4.2, which has English subtitles available.
A lot of negative things can be said for a game like Gothic 3. It was released, as all releases of the Gothic series as a catastrophe. In 2006 at the time of release it was such a crash prone, bug ridden mess that almost nobody liked it, not even hardcore fans. Very similar to Gothic 1 it even was unbeatable because of the many bugs and problems. But since Piranha Bytes has a strong bond between them and the fanbase, they dicided to handle things over to the community. While some might argue that this is a rather lazy way of developing a game, a lot of others believe that the fans certainly knew for the best, sonsidering the unreasonably strict timeline publisher JoWood inflicted on Pyranha Bytes. After over 3 years of patching and care-taking, this game was finally able to become the greatness as envisioned by the developers but also the fans. It's considered the definite version of the game.
You also don't need to play through Gothic 1 and 2 in order to understand this games backstory. However, it can answer a lot of questions regarding the world, the Hero himself and his way to handle prople. Still, if you take your time reading through hundreds of pages of dialogues alone you can quickly grasps what happened around you.
Gameplay-wise this game has the typical Hack and Slash action formula with the twist of also adding role playing elements in a different way as people knew already from previous Gothic games. Imagine a Game like Diablo with the freedom from games like Fallout but in third person, and you get what Gothic 3 is supposed to be. That might be the best way to describe this game.
The main theme of this game can also be considered its main gameplay aspect, and that is the theme of freedom both in the storyline and gameplay-wise you'll find yourself in a world that doesn't explain much to you. Because of that you should properly always think about focusing your skills so you can live an easy life and Gothic typicaly this game is anything but easy.
For instance and without spoilering of course there are quests in which the player has to defeat hundreds upon hundreds of enemies with the help of maybe one Non Player Character. Quests can range from simple "Kill this Person or this Monster" and fetch quests, to whole adventures based on exploration. Even non Gothic fans know about the infamous "Where is the Guro?" questline that only people who truely enjoy exploration found as it's entirely optional regarding the entire game itself and the reward is to travel throughout the game while finding interesting and secret things. This doesn't mean that this game is boring, as Hacking and Slashing is the main focus and leveling up itself offers so many options to choose from.
To give a few examples, there are 39 spells to choose from, and there are 23 passive skills to learn just for doing physical attacks or to defend yourself and there are much more different skills ranging from smithing, to stealing from someones pocket. All of them need learning points and you get 10 of them with each level up and while this sounds simple it merely gives you free room so you tackle the immense hordes of hundreds of enemies in the middle game.
The Gothic series is known to be very challenging and hardcore games and the third incarnation is no exception from this. Almost all of the several hundred Quests are available from the start of the game where the only true requirement is to find them if the player chooses to wander around looking for important "named" Non Player Characters. It has to be noted that this game is totally MASSIVE. Apart from MMORPGs, most single player games don't come close to this in scale. This can be intimidating for newcomers of the genre, as there is no fast travel or any form of help other than a compass. It takes about an hour to walk from the lower left to the upper right corner of the entire game. About 40 minutes if you choose to run (about twice as fast as walking) and wait for the stamina to replenish.
As you can walk to almost every place right after the start of the game and due to the freedom of this game it's totally up to you on how to handle things entriely your own way. However, with this freedom a lot of mistakes are bound to happen. As the Hero shapens the way you can desire to choose whatever you want so it's recommended to always think about your next step, like what you would like to skill next or if you really want to follow a specific quest.
I haven't yet tackeled the general setting, but thats just because that this game is focusing on hardcore hack and slash gameplay that even hundreds of quests aren't exactly this eye-catching. The premise goes like this, you either join up with either the Orcs or Humans and kill those who are in charge of this entire ordeal. As every NPC is killable right from the start it's up to you to kill EVERYONE or follow the rules as set up in the beginning of the game. This may sound simple on paper but believe me its far from it, as you need lots of carefully planning to archive the main goals of this game.
Graphically this game was amongst the prettiest in 2006 and as it actually stood the test of time says a lot about its graphical fidelity. To be honest the grass landscape of Myrtana alone looks almost as good as Skyrims and considering the age and budget gap of both games I believe thats surely an achievement.
In terms of sound however, this is one of the best games for the PC, ever. Seriously, if you even just enjoy good music you have to get this game right now. Kai Rozenkranz is a genius when it comes to creating atmospheric music that fits spot on into the game. However, there is one song that stands out negatively and thats the Battle music. It's always the same theme when you're fighting a usual enemy and after a few hundred hours this may get on your nerves. This is forgotten when the player finally reaches the city of Ishtar, where argueably the best music in the entire game plays and you'll find yourself again after spending hours upon hours of your free time into this game without noticing that it's dark outside already, in the real world of course.
Gothic 3 is a very ambitioned game and I believe that its too bad the project was cut short for release due to the old publisher. With the user created patches and mods mentioned above however I believe that this might be one of those games that will stay fun even after decades to come. I highly recommend everyone to buy this game when a Steamsale comes along if you're still not sure if this game might be of interest to you. If you think this game is interesting and you enjoy huge in scale RPGs with an oldschool soul, get this now.

FTL is really really addictive. Theres only one "story" mode in the game, and it takes about 1,5-2h to complete the whole thing, but the catch is that it is really hard to beat, even on easy, and it is heavily RNG. It took me 20 hours to beat the game once, with about 18 runs in total. FTL for me is best played in small 2-3 h sessions, i usually play 1 to 2 games and then come back some other day. So its a great game to just pick up and play through a few runs.
The basic idea of the game is to upgrade the ship you have in different ways, there are lot of ways you can go with the upgrades, you can be really offensive or defensive, have different drones (repair, boarding, combat, defence etc)
or you could form a boarding party to take over enemy ships. Theres also "advanced" content (hence FTL Advanced edition)  that can be toggled on or off, which grants new weapon options and few new upgrades and playstyles (for you and the enemy aswell) for example Hacking enemy systems. The game looks complicated, but the basics are easy to pick up. Of course it takes a while to master the system, but it wont take long to get the hang of it.
Like i said, there is a lot of variety in how you want to go through the upgrades and theres also a limit of how much things you can have active, you need to power the different systems and play around with what system to power and how much. And obviously, you will need to get "scraps" or money to do that, which mainly comes from defeating enemy ships and certain events.  You also need to think about how much fuel you have, or missiles and droid parts, so you need to use your money on that aswell.
Your goal in the game is to deliver "critical" information to the Federation fleet, and you need to travel through about 9 "sectors" to reach them, some of the sectors are inhabited by different species or pirates etc, and each sector is full of planets, in most planets you need to fight different ships, but some of them includes quests, shops, different enviromental hazards, distress signals and so on, this is where the RNG comes in, you could end up with lots of good weapons, crew memebers or money early on, or you could loose exsisting crew mates due to certain events. Sometimes you just want to restart a run after few planets due to RNG slapping you hard enoug.  So basically you never know whats in store at the next planet. You also cant spend an eternity in the systems you are on, the rebel fleet is after you, and you need to keep moving.
There is some variety in the game of course, you have a bunch of ships you can choose to play with, and you will unlock more ships when you do certain quests etc. The ships very in layouts, and start with different equipments or devices and crew members, the crew members have stats that give bonuses when they man specific systems and you can assign them on different systems, for example, you can have on guy manning shields and one guy piloting the ship. As the crew mates man those stations, they get better in what they do, so if a member of your crew mans the shields for some time, he will grant a small bonus in shield recharge, because he has experience with that. And some species act differently too, the rock people are immue to fire and theres even a race that drains oxygen from the room they are in. So you do have some strategies with the crew also.
PROS:
-Simple idea executed well.
-A lot of variety in playstyles and ways to upgrade your ship.
-Pleasant good ol 8 bit style.
-Soundtrack fits the game perfectly.
- Cheap.
- A bunch of additional objectives, challenges and achievements for those who like that sort of thing.
-Nothing like suffocating space pirates by locking doors in your ship and letting the air drain out from the room.
CONS:
-RNG heavy (for some, this is a bigger con then to others)  but thats the idea when the game takes so little time to play through.
FTL is a great game, the idea is done really well, its dirt cheap and will offer you hours of entertainment, if you dont mind the RNG elements.

Anomaly: Warzone Earth (A:WE) is a hybrid reversed tower defense simulation crossed with a real-time strategy game developed by the company 11 bit studios with emphasis on combat and tactics.
+ Creative gameplay concept, where the player leads his attacking units through static towers.
+ Impressive balance between strategy and action keeps up the motivation.
+ Well-done art direction and particle effects.
o Solid background music.
o Alien design is rather playful.
+ Player escorts his convoy with an on-foot commander, who can collect and deploy tactical power-ups.
+ Coordination of the units, scouting out positions and deploying resources create a dynamic gameplay.
+ Strategic elements in form of route planning, convoy make-up and order of units.
+ Units can be upgraded up to three times increasing their effectiveness.
+ Additional spawning of enemy towers keeps the player on edge.
+ Challenging end boss fight.
o Column of vehicles is limited to six units.
o Game speed can be adjusted.

- Only six different models of enemy towers.
+ Original background story.
o Solid voice work.
- Limited identification of the player with the protagonist.
11 bit studios succeeds in reinterpreting the traditional concept of tower defense games. A:WE offers a lot of fun in trying to make the most efficient routes, that could cause greatest amount of devastation while minimizing both exposure and travel time.

Singleplayer achievements: 42
Multiplayer achievements: none

Absolver is one of those few games that come out now a days that makes so many promises, and actually delivers on all of them.
Absolver is a free flowing, mmo, pve, pvp, and fully customizable hodge podge of a game that I have accidentally fallen in love with. While this game is still in its infancy state, the amount of polish and promise that comes from this title is something unheard of. Bugs are nearly nonexistent, and the only one that seems as of 8/29 is a lighting issue. Absolver is a game that truly makes you rationalize nearly every opponents moves, and causes minute mistakes to lead to either catastropic chains or a waste of an opponents stamina. Everything falls into the hands of the player as it truly comes down to a mental chess match; each player locked in a mental battle of wills as they are thrusted against one another. The AI is programmed in a way to capitalize on your errors, and makes every scenario feel real.
The aesthetics of the game, while stylized are, in my opinion, beautiful. From the lush forests, to delapitated kingdoms, to the snowy tundra, and the engulfing deserts to even the telegraphing of attacks is meticulously detailed to give the player a sense of awe in every setting. The eye popping colors that telegraph the moves of an opponent are something I am so grateful to have because a single smidgen of color can tell so much once you learn it.
Progression does not feel hamfisted or grindy, but rather, feels just as natural as the combat. The leveling system, just like every other character aspect, is fully customizable to every stat. While I am certain that there will eventually be a "meta" in terms of stating in due time, as of now, it feels great to stat spread your own fighter.
Every combo chain, weapon chain, skill, move set, and focus is all dependent on how the player wishes to play and it satisfies all of my fighting game dreams. Something about the sheer amount of control a single player can obtain over time is astonishing, and for such a low price tag, it is no wonder I have fallen in love with this game.
TL;DR: While not "flawless" due to a minute graphical issue, this game is well worth the price tag of $30, and I feel like I am stealing money from the developers for buying this labor of love for so little. From customization to color pallet, the developers knew what they were doing, and seeing this brings a smile to my face. I have not had a game this fun to engage in since the For Honor Beta when Dedicated Servers were around.
A must have for anyone looking for a difficult yet rewarding fighter.

Back in the day I purchased the original Carnivores.  As a dino lover I was intrigued but didn't expect much.  But this became one of my most cherished hunting games of all time. Went on to get Carnivores 2 and Ice Age.  Now the reboot is out and I'm happy to say that all the wonder and awe from the when I played the original are back.  Beautiful and open hunting locations with freedom to roam around and hunt how you want.    Great sound design and graphics.  As you wander the lush jungle of the first few hunting locations you'll find a lush green hunting zone with scattered rock outcroppings (which you can climb for a good view).  Shadows of lazy flying dinos criss cross the ground below.  On a distant island an active volcano rumbles.   You'll hear the mournful moan of a herbivore as you walk or the growl of a meat eater who just sniffed out your scent.  It all adds up to a great immersive environment to explore.
GOOD:
Great graphics especially for a "budget priced" title.
Great sound design
If you bought the tag when you kill a dino you can put it in your "living" trophy room (and similar species of dinos will scale depending on their weight so that 3 ton stegosaur will look pretty big next to your 2 ton one).
Great reboot of a classic
BAD:
A few bugs here and there.
Sound of evac ship getting stuck in a loop on one expedition and drowned out all other sounds.  (only happened once in 4 hours of play time)
Deleting trophies from my trophy room seems buggy.  Maybe I'm doing it wrong but when I try to delete one nothing happens and then after several attempts then I lost 3 trophies.   Hmmmm like I said might be doing it wrong but if that's the case then boy is it not an easy task.
All in all it's a great title and great price for what you get.  If you're a fan of the original I don't think you'll be disappointed.

I have only just finished the first act, so this recommendation is a bit premature. That said this is a really good game. The combat system is reminiscent of Dragon Age Origins, but much, much better.
All the various party members play in very distinctive ways and while each character is limited to 4 skills the upgrade trees allow for surprisingly substantive changes in playstyle. There is a lot of interesting potential character/party builds and since you can respec and change the party any time you aren't in combat you are free to try them all.
Another feature I really like is that you can pull up the enemies stats and skills. Knowing what skills your enemy has is hugely important (particuarly for boss fights) and it is a lot of fun to plan around those obstacles.
Anyways, if you like the genre you should get this ASAP. The story is a little lackluster, but the combat is miles ahead of the competition and that more than makes up for it.

I think most of the negative reviews say the same: that Lichdom is boring and repetetive and I don't agree with that. Lichdom is underrated.
The story is not that stunning but it's good enough to be interesting and fill the game with life. Some breakpoints keep the tension. Nothing more to say. The game focuses on the fights.
The game, powered by Cryengine 3, really know how to wow you. The levels are very beautiful and crafted with a lot of focus on the details. Secrets are placed very good and you really have to search for some of them. Also, the different level themes (like harbour city, ice world or swamp) implement the corresponding atmosphere
by using different weather schemes, color saturation and so on.
Yes, the levels are in fact linear but I really doubt that an open world would have improved the game at all. This is not Skyrim.
I must say that I was really impressed by the whole fighting and spell thing. It's starting on a low level with weak fire and ice spells and you unlock many more different spells while doing progress in the story. I really like two of the spells: necromancer and delirium. While Necromancer will summon demons from fallen enemies that will help you, delirium will make enemies fight for you. I'm doing very well together with powerful fire spells.
Later in the game you can also combine two spells into Synergies, that must be charged but can for example cast large Hulk-like monsters fighting for you or a black hole as seen in the trailer. These spells are unique and may help you get around some boss fights where 'normal' spells are not enough.
Some reviews also state that all fights are the same and I don't really understand the point. Because the fights are not the same at all. Different enemies force you to change your tactics; you cant fight against three heavy tanks in the same way you fight against a large horde of weaker enemies. There are also very different types of enemies, from melee to ranged combat to enemies that are able to teleport themselves or also use ice spells against you.
The game is not easy but also not hard like Dark Souls. If you die all the time you simply use the wrong spells / tactics against the enemies.
If you are interested in magic fights, crafting and beatiful graphics you should really look into the game. I really recommend it!

FTL is really really addictive. Theres only one "story" mode in the game, and it takes about 1,5-2h to complete the whole thing, but the catch is that it is really hard to beat, even on easy, and it is heavily RNG. It took me 20 hours to beat the game once, with about 18 runs in total. FTL for me is best played in small 2-3 h sessions, i usually play 1 to 2 games and then come back some other day. So its a great game to just pick up and play through a few runs.
The basic idea of the game is to upgrade the ship you have in different ways, there are lot of ways you can go with the upgrades, you can be really offensive or defensive, have different drones (repair, boarding, combat, defence etc)
or you could form a boarding party to take over enemy ships. Theres also "advanced" content (hence FTL Advanced edition)  that can be toggled on or off, which grants new weapon options and few new upgrades and playstyles (for you and the enemy aswell) for example Hacking enemy systems. The game looks complicated, but the basics are easy to pick up. Of course it takes a while to master the system, but it wont take long to get the hang of it.
Like i said, there is a lot of variety in how you want to go through the upgrades and theres also a limit of how much things you can have active, you need to power the different systems and play around with what system to power and how much. And obviously, you will need to get "scraps" or money to do that, which mainly comes from defeating enemy ships and certain events.  You also need to think about how much fuel you have, or missiles and droid parts, so you need to use your money on that aswell.
Your goal in the game is to deliver "critical" information to the Federation fleet, and you need to travel through about 9 "sectors" to reach them, some of the sectors are inhabited by different species or pirates etc, and each sector is full of planets, in most planets you need to fight different ships, but some of them includes quests, shops, different enviromental hazards, distress signals and so on, this is where the RNG comes in, you could end up with lots of good weapons, crew memebers or money early on, or you could loose exsisting crew mates due to certain events. Sometimes you just want to restart a run after few planets due to RNG slapping you hard enoug.  So basically you never know whats in store at the next planet. You also cant spend an eternity in the systems you are on, the rebel fleet is after you, and you need to keep moving.
There is some variety in the game of course, you have a bunch of ships you can choose to play with, and you will unlock more ships when you do certain quests etc. The ships very in layouts, and start with different equipments or devices and crew members, the crew members have stats that give bonuses when they man specific systems and you can assign them on different systems, for example, you can have on guy manning shields and one guy piloting the ship. As the crew mates man those stations, they get better in what they do, so if a member of your crew mans the shields for some time, he will grant a small bonus in shield recharge, because he has experience with that. And some species act differently too, the rock people are immue to fire and theres even a race that drains oxygen from the room they are in. So you do have some strategies with the crew also.
PROS:
-Simple idea executed well.
-A lot of variety in playstyles and ways to upgrade your ship.
-Pleasant good ol 8 bit style.
-Soundtrack fits the game perfectly.
- Cheap.
- A bunch of additional objectives, challenges and achievements for those who like that sort of thing.
-Nothing like suffocating space pirates by locking doors in your ship and letting the air drain out from the room.
CONS:
-RNG heavy (for some, this is a bigger con then to others)  but thats the idea when the game takes so little time to play through.
FTL is a great game, the idea is done really well, its dirt cheap and will offer you hours of entertainment, if you dont mind the RNG elements.
