Like Sonic Colours, Sonic Generations is what I perceive to by SEGA's attempt at making a comeback with Sonic. Unlike Colours though, Sonic Generations is a celebration of the Sonic Franchise as a whole, giving the player the chance to experience levels from past Sonic games and play through them with either modern or classic Sonic.
The game's graphics are really beautiful, and really help to bring the levels to life - from the lush fields of Green Hill zone to the fire-scorched buildings of Crisis City, each level has its own unique style to bring to the table. At times it felt like I was playing through a movie rather than a game.
Graphics aside, the gameplay in Sonic Generations revolves around the player completing the levels themselves, along with mini-games based on the level itself. Overall, the mini-games are okay, but they're not really anything special, although they do add a little replayability to the game I guess.
Now, the controls. Frankly, I'm not a big fan of the control scheme used in Generations - playing as modern Sonic feels quite stiff, and not at all fluid like in the Adventure games. For instance, if you use the homing attack to clear a gap, there is no way to control sonic whilst he's airborne, which can lead to falls if you don't position yourself properly. Classic Sonic also suffers from a similar problem and feels somewhat strange. Of course, this may just be me, but it's one thing that I find somewhat annoying.
Like almost all Sonic games, the soundtrack is excellent and gives us some remixes of some old and new Sonic tunes. You can also collect additional music by completing challenges, which you can then choose to listen to when you're playing any level.
Level design is generally good - the first two sets of levels are relatively challenging, but still enjoyable. However, the last set really ramp up the difficulty and some, such as Crisis City, require a few playthroughs in order to get an idea of the level layout. Planet Wisp, the final level in the game, does become a little frustrating due to its length and having to use Wisps in order to complete it, but enough perseverance should get you that S rank you're after.
Overall, Sonic Generations may have its flaws, but it is a very well-made game and I highly recommend any Sonic fan picks it up if they don't already own it.

It's a good game. It has Classic and Modern Sonic levels that all play well and the levels have their gimmicks that help distinguish themselves from one and other. Both characters control relatively well, not much is wrong with Modern Sonic but Classic Sonic feels off in the physics and control department but overall it isn't too bad that I dread playing as Classic Sonic. The Stage themes feels samey with 4 urban levels, 4 clear day levels and 3 levels with grassy themes to them.
It would have been better to have some more level variety like:
Ice Cap Zone from Sonic 3.
Twinkle Park or Lost World from Sonic Adventure.
Hang Castle or Bingo Highway from Sonic Heroes.
Dragon Road from Sonic Unleashed.
Aquarium Park from Sonic Colours
Not even considered for DLC. The game also doesn't have Steam Workshop support either so it sucks that people will have to use a mod tools program and download them off from the internet.
Going back to gameplay, I'm not a big fan of the Boost feature since it feels like an invincibility power up you can use at the press of the button but thankfully it is not required to beat the game so if you're like me and you don't like the boost, you can do without it and can either slide (Why isn't this a Spin Dash instead?) into enemies, drift into them or do a classic jump on top of them. I would much prefer if they added a speed metre that when you reach maximum speed, the boost feature would then activate to reward the player for doing a good job getting through the level.
The game however is dash pad heavy which is used to keep the speed up but it comes off as automated and feels like the game is playing for you when you should be playing the game.
This game also has Skills you can use like Acceleration that allows you to get to full speed faster, Sure-footed that allows you to get back up on your feet instantly after being hit, exclusive abilites like an Endless boost for Modern Sonic and the unfortunate exclusivity to the skill shop of the elemental shields and not placed around the levels. After you complete the Story, Super Sonic in regular levels which is great for Classic Sonic but Super Modern Sonic is just trash where if you boost, you lose rings faster to the point that it's only a 10-second transformation and because of the boost, there is not much point to the Super form for Modern Sonic anyway.
Overall, it's a great game but it has it's flaws that keep it from being an amazing game. Sega loves to experiment on Sonic and this game is the exception which i'm glad but they could have made a better game in my opinion. I'll give this my recommendation for the fact it has mods to keep it alive but if you play it vanilla, it'll only be fun for the journey but there will be nothing else to keep you coming back to play it.

Anomaly: Warzone Earth is a top-down Tower Defense type game, where you play as the commander of the 14th armor battalion, and direct your convoy of vehicles through streets, using various powerups and tactics, all in real time. You alone control a 14th Platoon soldier on foot who picks up decoys and smoke-screens, repair kits and uses these items to protect and heal the convoy. Your convoy is attempting to penetrate anomalous zones around the city, which surround parts of an alien spaceship that crashed to earth.
Visually the graphics don't look bad at all. There is alot of switching back and forth from your minimap as you plot course corrections for the convoy depending on what obstacles are thown your way in real time. The game feels like it may have been made for a handheld initially and then ported to the PC, but if that is true they didn't do a bad job. While not exactly a tower defense game, more of a tower attack game, Anomaly: Warzone Earth can be fun to play. There are multiple difficulties to choose from, so I recommend the most difficult for the best experience.

I followed this game for a while, then, bought it upon launch.  After two solid hours, I opted for the refund (while I still could).  I have played many similar types of games over the years (Ultima, Wizardry, Bard's Tale, Proudfoot games, Magic Candle, etc., etc.).
I really, really wanted to like this game, but, I can only recommend this to people who want a (unique) Wizardy 7 clone; otherwise, be very cautious with your time and your money!
Everything from character generation to party management to combat is needlessly, counterproductively, difficult and cumbersome.  Twenty years in development?  The graphics are good for 1992, but, poor for 2017 - hold on, I also enjoy Moria/Angband games, so it is not about flash, it is about quality.  The music is OK.  The sound effects are tortuous.
Combat, even on the easiest setting, is ridiculously difficult.  Challenging combat is the heart of this genre.  Grimoire is so difficult, that it is stupid - solely on the basis of completely overpowering foes and a cumbersome (am I repeating?)  interface.  Game design is unbalanced and inefficient.
Do you love Wizardy 7?  If so, you should try this game, no doubt!
(Otherwise, if you love classic CRPG, then, Helherron has been updated and re-released!  Battle Brothers?  Dragon Wars is on Steam.  Darklands anyone?  IDK, but, you will have strong feelings with this niche game.)

After a rough start, things have settled down and the game now seems stable. Restarting twice because of patches was not my first choice, but I now have a much better party after learning more about the game.
I have never really liked playing more than 4 characters in a party, and never like phased combat. This game changed my mind on both of these. I am having a blast, even with some of the remaining rough edges and clunkiness.
If you like the Wizardry games, this is a must-have. If you like RPG's in general, it is still worth the price, imo.

While there are a lot of options when it comes to block-mode dungeons crawlers (old and new), there are far less when it comes to non-real time options and even fewer when they combine dungeon crawling and open world design. Apart from Wizardry 7 the only others are the early Might & Magics, Fate and Dragon Wars and some of the goldbox games, yet none of them had the system complexity of Wizardry (combat, spell system, NPC interaction, character development, etc). Wizardry 7 is a classic because it stood in a league of its own (W8 is an evolutionary offshot, good but different), that is until now.
Grimoire is a love letter to W7 that has learned its lessons but still strives to be more. The maps feel a bit tighter designed with more to do, the puzzles less obscure and where Wiz7 felt expansive with lots of empty wilderness, Grimoire just hits you over the head with content upon content.
Mind you, it's not perfect, the UI takes some time to get used to, there is the occasional bug and balance is rough around the edges (also the art-style can be inconsistent, from monster graphics that look neat to some I couldn't stand). But overall it's charming as hell, plain fun to play and addictive as ♥♥♥♥.

This review is based on a total of 31 hours played.
Grimoire is a game with a lot of history. Both it and its creator have had a lot of controversy surrounding them. Whether it be the extremely long development time, the broken promises, or the creator's personal (but publically) stated views. All of that has sparked a very active flamewar for the past 20 years. I ask that fellow gamers disregard all that stuff, or if you wish to enter the flame war, well, no one can stop you, but do not let your own personal opinions change your view of this game.
I'll start it by saying I haven't finished this game. Not even close. 31 hours in, while save scumming and asking for help and I've just barely completed the first area of the game, and something around a 10th of the main 'quest' in the game. My location flag has barely moved on the world map. The creator promises 600+ hours of game time, which I can barely imagine. The least that can be said about this game is that it is imaginative in scope.
Gameplay is brutal. While you have a total of 8 characters in your party, all of them custom made, and still, a single encounter that goes badly can still ruin your day. Even random encounters unprepared can seriously turn into a challenging fight. Characters WILL die, and you'll revive them, only to have them die again. Depending on how badly it goes, they might even end up dying permenantly!!!! Loot is rare, good loot is even rarer. You'll jump for joy at finding a weapon that is better than what you started with, or groan in desperation when a new weapon that looks awesome turns out to be cursed. You'll scream at the screen as your best damage dealer does 0 damage to an enemy because they're too tired, and probably cuss when your mage blows all his mana on a spell that fizzles in the end. Yes ladies and gentleman, this is an RPG of the old school variety. It gives you all the time in the world to pick every single action for your characters, then laughs at you after failing.... or applauds you for succeeding.
This is an RPG of the old school variety. Party development is reliant entirely on the player. Characters do not have amusing stories to tell, save the ones you create in your head or ones that happen in the game. Stat and skill points are doled out in dribbles, and it is up to you to share them around on a horde of skills that you might need. Every decision matters, and the game does not suffer fools.
This is not Dragon Age, or Mass Effect. This is not a 3d movie wrapped up in action scenes, this is not a loot fest like the Diablos. Not that those games are bad, but they are all an RPG and something.... Grimoire, on the other hand, is RPG. Only RPG.
So put on your wizard robe and wizard hat, bring out your dice, and start rolling up your party. I promise you, you will not be disappointed.
PROS:-
- Old school RPG
- Huge
- Fiendish puzzles
- Developer is quick to respond to bugs and issues
- Interesting races/classes
CONS:-
- Sound is repetitive and annoying
- NPC interaction takes a while to get used to
- Some bugs are bound to crop up (one man team made this)
- You'll feel lost.... A LOT.
P.S. A lot of people have complained about the price of the game. I'm 31 hours into the game and have just finished the first 'area' and started on the second (so you're talking a minimum of what? 300-600 hours of game)... Either way, it seems to be way bigger than most triple A games, so IMO, it is worth the price.

The timeline of buying a game for twenty of my filthy, filthy dollars, playing it until it stops being fun, and then uninstalling has never gone by so quickly. Looking so inspired and pretty on the store page is really all this trap project has going for it.
- Confusing, unattractive maze of a UI. You will be holding down a lot of wheels.

- Very clunky AI. Your Gruntz-esque Bricktrons(?) hobble into each other constantly, dropping rocks and logs all over the dang place because I hit the wrong thing again, I guess. I feel way too relieved when my units actually do what I want because I don't have the degree in engineering required to understand this game's needs.

So I had previously wrote a review for Absolver, right after release. I think I can add a bit more so here it goes...
Absolver nails in most of the things we (?) expected it to nail:
- Its combat is amazing, deck building is very rewarding and movement looks very polished to me.
- It's an amazing fighting game with RPG elements where you can completely costumize your fighting style (once you've unlocked the movements, ofc).
- Music is quite good if you're into that sort of stuff and the possibility to play Offline is definitely a plus, if you'd rather haver the singleplayer experience
- Maps are gorgeous, although far from being huge; you won't be doing much exploration, cause there is really not that much to explore. Expect to run around looking for enemy spawns/players.
Absolver has a few things that get quite annoying after a few hours of gameplay:
- I'll start with the 30fps cap. It is what it is, you should know it works this way before you buy it.
- The camera is crunky af. Seriously, this has been the most annoying thing throught the game. It's bearable when you're just 1x1-ing, but once you get to fight versus +2 enemies you see what I mean. Enemies corner you against walls or push you off ledges and you won't even see it coming, cause you'll too many times be staring at the ceiling (almost) completely oblivious of your whereabouts. This NEEDS to be fixed. I can't stress it enough.
- It lacks content, regarding objectives besides becoming an Absolver. It has easily 20-30h of gameplay before you get there, but I imagine myself stop playing by then cause there's really not much to do.
7/10

Is this game an ARPG? Maybe. Kind of.
Is it a shooter? Yeah, more or less.
I rate this game positively, but I didn't really feel like finishing it after getting about halfway through.
Is it fun? Well, that can be debated. While the spellcasting and spellmaking is neat, it isn't exactly fun to actually play. Don't get me wrong, a lot of work went into this game. The graphics are quite polished, and the environments are pretty interesting, if a little stifling in their hallway-esque design.
The spellmaking, more or less the main feature of this game is fairly robust. You take a basic sigil (fire, lightning, ice, necromancy, etc) add a shape (is it a grenade, a ray, some kind of trap?) and finish it off with various modifiers that determine damage or debuffs or whatever. The game's tutorial sucks at explaining itself, so I had to go look at how to do it on YouTube. That said, it is pretty fun --- if you're into shooters.
That's the thing, this game straddles a pretty weird line between being a shooter and an action RPG. Yeah, there are numbers flying over enemy heads and stuff, but it feels like you're just battling the same dudes over and over again while either seeking cover, putting up your shield, or dodging. I'm not the biggest fan of shooters, but I do love RPGs, while the RPG elements were enough to get me to play the game, I didn't stick around enough to actually finish it. The level design just seems to ask us to go from point A to point B and shoot up a bunch of stuff. That's great, or whatever, but it didn't really pull me into the game and make me feel like a badass wizard, which, is what I feel that the game is aiming for.
Part of this is the story. I do not care at ALL about it. Like, it has the cheesiest, silliest baselessly evil villain with no redemptive features that pretty much defines the story. I couldn't care less, and I like a little cheese to go with my vidya. That said, if you're looking to turn off your brain and blow up zombies and cultists with the fury of a mage with infinite MP, go for it. You will probably have a decent time of it.
Overall, I would say get it. On sale, this game is super cheap. Just don't expect to be blown away.

I've been on an open-world game kick recently, and figured I would check out Mafia II before the sequel came out to see what all the fuss is about. Mafia II has moments of greatness and and some weird design quirks.
The biggest quirk seems to be that it's not really an open world game as there is no sense of exploration, no real gameplay systems that exist on their own, and time only passes to serve the main plot line. You get the idea that either it might have been a true open world game given an extra year to develop it, or that 2K games at that time just wanted everything to be open world no matter what so all that work was shoved in there for no reason.  The majority of linear mission set pieces aren't even part of the open world locations, taking place on rooftops or warehouses or different locations entirely.
Which is confusing because what little exists of the open world is fantastic and had a lot of work put into it. The technology is really quite good for 2010. The seamless roads, distant LODs and number of pedestrians is up there with anything. The winter in the 40's feels exactly like how the movies show NYC. Snow and grime builds on your cars and everything inside has a cozy vibe. The dimmed sense of color and snow everywhere gives an almost black and white vibe, with Dean Martin's let it snow playing on the radio (despite not being period accurate... in general the game is not). The soundtrack is enormous (137 tracks from the era, vs fallout 4's 37). It is cool to walk around in an three piece suit and overcoat and also be in a crowd of other people wearing the same thing. Simiarly the cars are old-fashioned 80 hp steel death traps and drive and sound appropriately. Later on when things become a bit more vibrant sticking to your 3 piece suit and hat gives it a mad men feeling.
I found the writing quite solid, but is ultimately limited by the linear nature of the gameplay as well as the game developer mindset of this time where people tried to turn games into movies. All of the interesting stuff happens in cutscenes and you just ferry between them. I am glad they didn't try to whitewash history when it came to racism and such, but they also fell into quite a few tropes of their own which are areas for improvement.
It is worth picking up for cheap. Even if all you do is play the first couple hours it is worth it to check out the city a bit.

Quick review:  Complicated game with no way of knowing what you are doing.  Wait until they write a manual.  It’s like if you joined a group playing The World of Synnibarr table top rpg but you didn’t own any of the books.  Creating a character is hopeless without the books so you were given a character to play but you still had to make a few choices to round out that character.  With no way to understand any of the choices you simply guess and hope for the best.  The game play is just like the character generation.
My personal story: I love deep complex games and I love the old-school feel (reminds me of Bards Tale.)  However, I have requested a refund because I have no idea what I'm doing.  Complexity is great but if I don't understand the consequences for the choices I'm making during character creation (which was most of my game experience) then it doesn’t add to the game.  It feels like there is no rhyme or reason to any of the numbers.  I made several parties and they all end in frustrating death with a tough random encounter in the first area.  My groups usually have a couple high hp fighters, a thief, a bard, a cleric, a wizard, a sage, and some other random class for fun so I feel like I had a good balanced party.  On my second to last run I got into a fight with 2 groups of bugs and a fungus.  I knew this would be a swift death for sure but I wanted to play through it just to see.  My entire group took out the fungus and one bug except my thief (a Rhattu I think) with 12ish hp ended up soloing 5 bugs.  I just held down enter and clicked battle over and over waiting for the thief to die.  After an insane number of rounds, where he was paralyzed half the time, my little thief cut the bugs down and got like 870 xp and a ton of skills and 1 attribute point to spend. This is easily the best version of the least bad 3D Sonic game since the first Sonic Adventure. However that's not to say that it's without its flaws both as a game and as a port. Fair warning: this is going to be long & nitpicky.
When it launched it appeared to be based on a different build than its console siblings. There are a number of glitches & oddities in its scripted physics which were fixed before release on console but remain even with the latest PC patch.
One particular ramp in classic Crisis City springs to mind since Sonic is clearly supposed to launch into the air but simply keeps running & falls on PC.
There are graphical glitches too. I'm sure the downhill skyscraper chase in Speed Highway isn't supposed to look how it does on PC. Some of the reflections in the level seem off too.
Those are nitpicks but the port also has issues with controller support; at least anything that's not an official 360 Controller. The worst is probably that in some 3D segments, usually ones that suffer framedips, Sonic may go mad and start quick-stepping over & over. This only seemed to get worse with each patch.
I believe there's either a fan fix or workaround for the issue but it's sloppy regardless.
The leaderboards are somewhat infamously glitchy & not only full of times that aren't legitimately possible, though it's hard to tell which are "hacked" because there's exploits which outright break the timer, but they're also known to cause stability issues & crashing in the port.
Lastly the port seems to have optimisation issues. It'd be nice to expect a locked 60fps but even on hardware well in excess of the recommended requirements there's no guarantees. Conversely even on hardware a little below those requirements there's a slim chance you'll get smooth 60.
Reports were mixed to say the least. I'm in the former camp, particularly in Chemical Plant and Seaside Hill. Something about water seems to cause issues even while Sonic's on dry land.
The devs responsible for the port did produce numerous patches but I'm not sure what those patches achieved. If anything the game seemed to get less stable & eventually Sega stopped paying to try fixing the port.
Even with all these problems the mere fact the port runs mostly at 60fps makes it hugely preferable. The PS3 version, capped at 30 with frequent drops, just feels bad in comparison. In fact, going back to it, it honestly feels more juddery than Sonic Unleashed's day stages (Adabat aside).
The other big improvement over consoles is unofficial (but officially acknowledged) mod support. It turns out making new content for the Hedgehog Engine isn't easy so support isn't quite as widespread as you may hope but there are some decent ports of levels from Sonic 06 & Unleashed; in both cases by far the best way to play them.
So that's the port's issues & a couple strengths out of the way.
The game itself is a refinement on Unleashed with a couple of odd regressions; combined with an unfinished recreation of classic Sonic's gameplay.
I like the slightly slower & tighter default feel to modern Sonic compared to Unleashed. Drifting seems actually useful & the fact stomps kill your momentum make them useful for precise stops. Homing attack & boost and light dash & stomp  are no longer mapped to the same buttons which is far more sensible. There's no more insta-death QTEs.
In place of QTEs are Rainbow Rings which let Sonic perform optional tricks to earn boost meter, Sonic Rush style.
Water still means instant death if modern Sonic gets submerged in 3D but simply running on it drains Sonic's speed and boost far more quickly than in Unleashed; making taking shortcuts on it a more interesting matter of risk vs reward.
However, wall jumps can now only be achieved from certain clearly indicated tiles and the light dash is restricted to certain glowing ring trails & also overly finicky about timing. Rail switching, while more intuitive, also seems less reliable.
It remains a refinement of Unleashed's Day Stages. If you liked them you'll probably like Generations. If you hated them then you probably won't be swayed.
Sonic is still slippery at low to medium speeds & stiff to control at high speed. Many of the same set-pieces & forced-running-segments are still used. There's still a lot of fully 2D segments. It's a shame 3D gameplay wasn't given more chance to shine to differentiate the Sonics.
There’s still a lot of invisible walls and elongated corridor-like design preventing you from finding fun shortcuts.
That said I think work was put into improving his level design. Green Hill, Chemical Plant and Rooftop Run are mostly bland but his other levels each throw in some 3D platforming. I was honestly surprised at how much I enjoyed Seaside Hill & Sonic's slipperiness is hardly out of place in a level returning from Heroes.
Classic Sonic provides an OK 2D platformer but, though he looks like classic Sonic in HD, he doesn't play like it. He has a very heavy jump; rolling consistently slows him down; his spin-dash is a boost-lite & it can even be used on steep slopes. Though he has momentum while running on slopes, in every other sense, this is arguably a step down from even Sonic 4.
I do still like some of his levels though with Sky Sanctuary and Rooftop Run being particular highlights.
Both modern and classic Sonic are hugely reliant on scripted physics that can seem natural if you're boosting or spindashing everywhere but look very awkward as Sonic suddenly goes from 0 to Sonic-speed if you're not.
The game's other big problem shared by both characters is just how easy it all is. Both Sonics only lose some of their rings upon taking damage and the only insta-kills are drowning for classic Sonic and pits for both. By default the game is covered in obnoxious tutorial prompts including floating warnings near every pit but luckily this can easily be turned off.
The ranking system feels as though it wasn't play-tested and is almost insultingly easy. There are levels where you can put the controller down for over 3 minutes and still easily receive an S rank. It'd be one thing if the ranks were tied to some unlockable that it might be unfair the inexperienced gamer couldn't reach; but they only exist for "bragging rights".
One thing I do like about the game, applying to both Sonics, is the Skill Customisation system. Want the insta-shield for classic Sonic? It's there. Want a homing attack or Sonic 4's lack of momentum for Classic Sonic? OK. Want a faster modern Sonic like Unleashed or a glass cannon with infinite boost? You have that option. Want the peel out or for classic Sonic's rolling to carry momentum? Oh. Tough luck.
I'd love to see customisation return & be expanded upon in Forces. Who wants to bet it'll be limited to the Custom Character?
Generations was a good correcting step after Unleashed but it really needed to be capitalised on & further refined. Lost World didn't pull that off. Will Forces? I've got to say, I don't have high hopes from what I've seen, but it's too early to tell.

is a visual novel that takes place in 19th century New Zealand, at a time when it's still a frontier wilderness.  Despite its setting, it is not a purely historical visual novel, as there are supernatural and horror elements in it.  You take on the role of Cassandra "Cassie" Winter, a Falconer who has volunteered to take on the job of investigating the town of Moonlight.  As a Falconer, Cassie must find out if the unfortunate accidents in town are human in nature or the work of a "Culler," an insect-like monster that attacks and kills the humans in these frontier towns.  Will Cassie be able to save the town of Moonlight and its citizens or will she fail her first solo mission?
Now, that we have an idea of the story, let's move on to the critique.  I really liked
.  Cassie is such a strong female protagonist and that's always a plus for me.  I will admit, though, that there are times that she does make stupid decisions but they aren't overly idiotic.  They're decisions that she would make because it is her first solo mission so they can be forgiveable.  The art is absolutely beautiful and I love the certain animations in it, such as the collapse of the mine.  Of course, there are plenty of CGs and you can view them in the gallery once you unlock them.  (Also, you can replay scenes you've already viewed in the gallery.)  I do need to give a warning that, due to the nature of the story, some of the CGs and scenes can be quite gory so if you don't have the stomach for it, you may want to just keep this in mind.  The music is nice to listen to as well and the soundtrack has just the right number of exciting and sad scores.  I do like the story, too, although there is a critique I must make (in addition to what I already said in regards to Cassie's decisions at times).  Despite that there are a total of three different endings you can get based on the choices you make, I feel like
might have been better off developed as a kinetic novel rather than a standard visual novel.  For two of the endings, they only slightly differ depending on a certain choice and the other ending, well, I won't reveal what it is although you may be able to guess what it is.  Also, at times, despite that I would make certain choices, there would be later dialogue which wouldn't make sense based on the choices I made earlier.  This didn't happen often but it did happen.
With that said, though, I really did enjoy
overall.  It does have its flaws but its positives more than outshine them.  (Oh and there is no romance involved but I don't think that's a bad thing.)  Whether I think it's worth the price?  I think so although if you feel that it's a bit steep, then waiting for a sale on it isn't a bad idea.  It goes without saying that if you're a fan of visual novels and don't mind the lack of romance, give
a try.  ^^

The game has choices, true, but sadly except of the occasional alteration of the text they are 100% meaningless. What I could perhaps even forgive if only the game wouldn't make the impression of a decent detective story where the player's job is to identify the culprit from the clues he gets. Alas, I even managed to do so correctly but the game never asked for my opinion and the protagonist made the 'wrong choice' anyway. At this point I pretty much lost the interest and quick-clicked through the rest, confirming myself I indeed didn't miss anything. The only choice which actually matters is the one at the very end offering the usual most boring binary choice between two endings, ignoring everything what happened before. Disappointing to the core, unless you like basically 'kinetic novels' and want to just read a (mediocre) book with pictures on a PC. There is also no alteration of the character based on the choices and whether you act as a bully or a cunning detective, your behavior is hard-coded thruout the whole game save for those 1-2 sentences following each of such choices.

If this was the pilot episode of a TV show, it would make one hell of an introduction to Cassie Winter. Our protagonist is freshly solo and eager to prove her competence, riding into town to solve a crime. By your choice, she can be warm and trusting - the better to coax information from soft hearts - or tough and professional, more convincing to those who respect a show of force. This is her first independent mission as a Falconer, and it's a doozy.
showcases both lovely artwork and tasteful use of animation, embellishing what is a solidly compact, suspenseful story. It took me roughly 3 hours (with skipping) to see all 3 endings and get the achievements, so it's worth being thorough and exploring all the options.
As for world building, the game provides just enough detail to immerse the reader - considering its brevity, there's not room to go overboard with superfluous descriptions. Overall it felt an appropriate amount for the length, though I found myself wanting to learn more about the Falconers and their trade secrets (Farlan's remedy, anyone?), as well as their targets, the Cullers. The unconventional setting and the characters were all interesting enough to merit revisting, perhaps in another game.
All in all, I'd say it's definitely worth the money. Well-told and nicely illustrated, with solid fleshed-out characters. If you don't mind the length, you won't regret the purchase.

1. The World of Adal is not as open world as they make it out to be, with the tag of being a MMO type of game you would figure there was going to be a lot more to the world around us, it does not. The paths do branch off but all lead back to the main central areas, sometimes the terrain is so confusing and it has no bearings at times that it can all come off looking the same. Aside from the world being unique and artful in it's own way it still does have this flaw of feeling like you are roaming aimless.
2. The combat against the A.I is a little...how should I say, sluggish. Against players? infuriating. Definitely when they do their guard breaks or gang up tactics. The one on one is sometimes good, and other times too easy or just cheated. DODGING IN THIS GAME IS WAY TOO UNBALANCED I tried every style and mix to dodge punches and kicks only to still get knocked around like a rag doll, the side strafe and the four way dodges all just don't seem to work that well. Since you cannot voice chat or speak to others you cannot coordinate your attack patterns against a gang of enemies, also when you sometimes attack an enemy together or in the same area you can still hit and damage one another which automatically will cause Friendly to go Neutral to eventually Hostile without discrepency. With the combination of dodging not being worth a damn and some how spamming hits stagger your efforts everytime, and others fully heal on victory while somehow you don't is all just ifuriating. Can do this cheap stupid two punch spam moves against your opponents all the time for cheap wins. The game is so biased in PVP combat that if you stray away from good conventional set fighting styles you are practically screwed.

But Fox, is there good things about this game...? Yes. Definitely there is some great things about this game. First off it is very different from most RPG's we are used to, the old hack and slash of World of Warcraft or Everquest type of deal. In this game its all about learning and honing your skills in true martial art combat across a world. It is definitely a good buy if you are into Kung Fu, Mystical Stories and practice the arts yourself - I could see it than being worth in your collection. Yet your crew will also be breathless as they fix holes, put out fires and learn the very important “how to make that ship over there a fleck in the flotsam of space debris” all delivered in a concise tutorial. It also covers how to tweak the balance of reactor output and shipboard system requirements juuuust right, the basics for the mission ahead: Warn your allies of the marauding fleet of rebels at your tail sweeping the system clean of Federation remnants. Your crew, aligned the remnants, must scrape their way across the galaxy picking up what modifications they can to survive. Garnered by ruthless or noble means, rewards in weapons, upgrades, new crew members,  fuel, and precious scrap are random and might do or doom a play through dependent on how your RNG rolls fare. Reaching a sector store will give refuge from pirates and the chance to re-equip and repair at your leisure, but only if you have the scrap. The reprieve of not being shot at for a turn also happens when you find a barren system, a small flutter of text describing your crew's wistful gazes into the stars, which you might find lovely if your crew weren't busied by the sucking holes pirates felt best accented your ship's exterior.
The emphasis on text-based imagery keeps that 9th grade reading level sharp and the perky tone doesn't fall flat; whether being threatened by pirates, rebels, or other species, it is an interesting mote when opposing captains turn out traitors, zealots, pirates seasoned or desperate bandits. If only this was a hint at what kind of battle was going to happen, then it might be a more welcome accent.
One aesthetic I did find pleasing was how well the soundtrack complimented the theme. “Cosmos (Explore)” from the soundtrack I found particularly well-suited. As my crew was once again busy with breaking out the ship bandages, I could feel the tension of depleting oxygen with more impact when I noticed a ticking sound. I paused (a life saver of a feature to have in this rogue-like) wondering if it was some stealth bomb planted by enemies, when suddenly flashbacks of watching
flooded. Specifically the scene in which the crew find their first potential terrestrial colony and must debate whether sacrificing decades of earth-time for hours on the surface is prescient. These torturous moments waiting for my ship to reach stable condition thrilled me. I relished the designer's choice in this piece, yet wondered, further spirited by my love for the Nolan film: what if a game similar to this added a time constraint and forced the player to make a decision of how certain system's orbits might subject the crew to time dilation? How holding a fun house mirror to the timeline of the game might add for a more immersive component and with enough planning could leave room for alternate ending. Perhaps an endless mode where a ship borne onward through time and space, might entrench the impact of a space-faring survival sim exploring the gravity of these psychological scars. The prospect gives me space chills.
EDIT: I've also been wondering how new objectives or player back stories might be an exciting, but then caught wind of their new project
and am excited for what looks like a more story centric strategy game with time travel!
While
has tested me, I look forward to seeing what it has in store (and space), what subtle details I may have missed, and what lies ahead in the updated content boasting more races, playable ships, and soundtrack from the team at Subset Games. Until then I will cast my lot to the void, and, hopefully, not so many of my crew.

The concept seems fun. First-person point & click adventure game featuring a private eye who is investigating a murder.
However, the execution from both a gameplay and writing standpoint are really poor.
The dialogue is very obviously translated, and it comes off as stiff and robotic, with odd grammatical quirks here & there, and even some odd lines that seem like mistranslations. The voice acting is serviceable, but given the lines they're working with, it sometimes comes off a little wooden.
All of this makes it very difficult to get invested in the story.
On top of this, the game controls poorly. You have a cursor that you have to move to the edges of the screen in order to turn. Think Wii Motion controls for a first-person-shooter, except you're using a mouse instead of a wii remote. It's feels sluggish and makes playing the game feel like more of a chore than it should.
I also didn't much care for the amount of interactivity. With only one of two things for you to inspect in each area, it felt very limited, alomost like the game didn't want you to explore the environments, but just push forward.
Overall, this game feels like a chore to play, and since the story isn't as captivating as it needs to be, it's a chore for pretty much no reason. The game doesn't hold up today whatsoever, but even when compared to other adventure games of the era such as the Nancy Drew games, Myst III, or even one of Microids' other games, Siberia, Post Mortem just doesn't cut it. You'd be better off spending your time playing something else.

Very good game if u read the spell crafting instructions in order to actaully do good damage/control.  Don't use SMART INVENTORY past Sigil Tier 5. You'll have plenty of time to farm after the campaign section so keep the good spell bases with the most augments in your inventory until you know for sure you don't need it anymore for a specific map's fighting strategy.  During the campaign you have to be a bit of a miser with them to get them crafted best.
The NGP HUB after the campaign is still fun because it remains challenging even with the drops capped at Tier 20.  If anything it's harder on some of the open terrain maps (due to some crazy ranged enemies) which is good since you have to actually work at completing them; changed sigils/spell combos up depending on the portal type.  I found the game balanced enough to keep playing, and there's enough sigils and augments to keep you guessing which combo works best for max dps and the easiest/best synergies.  The missiles were the easiest targeting spells to use (I highly recommend), be careful of crafting too many rays since they tended to bind the hands up and slow you down when you needed to do real quick Nova blocks or to just run like hell.
No regrets buying this one (especially after all the patches had been completed before playing).   I didn't have any real tech issues other than having to back out of the spell crafting menu to get upgrades working correctly; i.e. wasn't recognizing an upgrade was possible, but no crashes, or major bugs in game-play/crafting like some other reviews/community discussions mentioned; pretty fluid game IMO.  Regardless, it's polished enough to play the campaign or the NGBs a few times every so often.

The game plays much like candy crush if candy crush were a 1v1 game. You match symbols to collect mana to empower your minions so that they can launch attacks against opposing minions. You win by defeating all opposing minions.
It was entertaining at first until I reached the frustration I've encountered in previous games...grinding.
Proceeding through the PvE portion of the game requires no amount of skill; instead, it requires inhuman levels of patience because AI opponents are overloaded with health and shields to the point that in order to reduce them to an acceptable level, a player must revisit previously beaten levels and beat those levels...repeatedly.
Rewards are incredibly RNG based and most of the time players are rewarded with points they may use to level up their minions. These add up fast, especially for those who visit PvP a few times. Eventually, players have no use for these points until after they've overcome a series of PvE challenges.
Levelling up minions is entirely pointless; in fact, because minions are all set to level 10 in PvP. It's only PvE in which minion levels somewhat matter and I say "somewhat" because the fake difficulty presented by High HP enemies is the excuse provided for players needing to grind. If enemy HP levels are lowered enough then minion levels can be rendered nearly pointless altogether.
As far as gameplay goes...there is some illlusion of fast-paced gameplay, but it is all too easily shattered by the number of interruptions players suffer through whenever a cinematic attack from either side is used during which time the game stops altogether just so both sides can "enjoy" seconds of an attack animation that they will see many more times throughout whatever amount of time they spend on the game. These hiccups as I like to call them often ruin whatever focus is needed to win.
And whatever skill is involved in actually defeating other players is removed by the fact that should either player fail to see any possible match on the board, the game will helpfully and automatically highlight an available match.
At best, this game is a colorful and bright distraction.

First of all: the directing is excellent, and for me it's the standout quality of this VN. Heavy use of 3D camera work and animations make the game feel dynamic and alive in a way VNs usually don't. Every shot is constructed with cinematic intent, which also gives the game visual variety and great mileage out of its art assets. There are some parts in the middle that are less polished than the beginning and the end, but overall I think the effort put into the presentation makes it worth its price point even if it's fairly short for a VN (took me around three hours to complete it).
The story itself is enjoyable. The beginning is slow, but once it hits its stride about 1/3 of the way in, it picks up a lot. The plot is well paced with strong progression of developments and a good balance of action and investigation. My biggest complaint is that I found the prose writing very overwrought in places, but the dialogue is quite good, and all the characters are distinct and well written with interesting backstories and motivations. Some of the themes are heavy-handed, but overall it's an entertaining story that effectively carries your interest to its conclusion. If you're looking for romance, there are hints of it here, but only hints.
Sound design and music do an effective job of setting the atmosphere without being intrusive, and some of the tracks are pretty catchy, although the majority of them are fairly forgettable. The art overall is strong as well, although I think the anime proportions + realistic shading looks kinda strange on some of the characters' faces.
Overall, this is easily one of the best English VNs I've played. The good story paired with the great directing makes for a tense monster-hunting action romp, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes VNs, westerns, or supernatural action stories. The main caveat is that it's a little shorter than some people expect VNs to be, but I personally prefer short games and don't find that to be a problem.

Pros:

- Sound design
- Believeable Characters (and fun too. I <3 me some Biddy)
- Refreshing setting
Cons:
- A bit on the shorter side. About 3 hours for one playthrough.
- Limited replayability. Only three endings.
Overall, I recommend this for people who enjoy well-written stories with a strong protagonist and beautiful artwork. Worth the money hands down.

This is an alpha/beta quality game that should have either been released as Early Access or given an Alpha/Beta phase.  Neither happened and now we're looking at a lot of bugs that would've been caught and fixed before release if there had been.

There have been reports of updates rendering old saves unusable (and for a game that claims 600 hours of gameplay, that's not acceptable).
If you're interested I would instead put this on your wishlist and give it 6 months while everyone else plays unwilling beta tester for the developer.
I personally refunded my money as I'm not one to purchase Early Access games.  There are just too many games out there for me to justify spending time working around bugs while trying to play.

"Sonic Generations" is the thirteenth console Sonic platformer, and approximately the eighth of them that people agreed on liking. Ported to PC, there's limited graphical options as well as (currently untested) mod support, and the latter fact is significant given that brevity is the game's main issue. "Generations" is about six to seven hours long if you just play the mandatory levels, and while most of these levels are layered with extra paths and side challenges to make replaying them satisfying, it's easy to be left wanting more, which the PC version's mod support thankfully provides. I've not played any, so I can't make recommendations.
I also played this at below the recommended specs, so I experienced occasional slowdown, and some of my runs overheated my laptop. If you have a better setup with proper cooling equipment, you'll probably be fine, but "Generations" isn't optimized to run on weaker hardware to my knowledge, and after a point the only way I could turn the settings further down was to decrease the screen resolution, which might not be desirable.
The gameplay of "Generations" is generally satisfying. Its levels are designed around optimizing button presses, and once you've figured out all of a level's tricks, repeating it to gain a higher score is genuinely exhilarating. The game is visually stunning, and of its nine stages, seven of them are thorougly satisfying, with only Crisis City and Planet Wisp standing out for unneeded frustration. It also has the usual Sonic problem of speed coming at the expense of platforming, which at times compromises mobility and often reduces gameplay to tapping A at the right times. However, growing accustomed to the level layouts and control scheme makes experimentation easier, though it's still easy to miss opportunities.
Classic Sonic is still fairly linear and speed-focused, so despite a different control scheme, it keeps most of the pros and cons of the modern stages, and the classic levels aren't as satisfying to explore as those of the Geneisis titles or, to a lesser extent, the first "Sonic Adventure." As mentioned, though, this straightforward design is satisfying in its own right, and lends itself particularly well to the increasingly intricate setpieces of the later stages. City Escape and Rooftop Run, in particular, contain some extremely memorable sequences which involve little more than reacting to a near-indestructible enemy.
I played very few of the extra challenges, but excepting a few races, they're mostly a wash. One particularly tedious one introduced a new gimmick where you need to stop a cursor in the right spot, which wasn't especially difficult but was hardly fun either. I played more of the race challenges than any other, because they emphasize the speed which the game excels at and provide an excuse to replay familiar levels. You'll need to go elsewhere for any deeper critique of the extra acts.
Finally, the bosses are split into two categories: three "races," which are all fairly satisfying, and four "bosses," which are almost all underwhelming. The third boss poses some challenge, and the first at least requires some critical thinking, but the second is nearly automatic and the final boss is more tedious than difficult. These, alongside the irritations of Crisis City and Planet Wisp, are the main issues with a competent, fairly tight game which generally pushes the series in the right direction. It's over before you know it, and I wish Sonic would focus on more than just speed, but when everything's working, "Generations" is a blast.

I recommend this game, but with some reservations.

My opinion is a bit skewed, because I first played the game when I was younger and really enjoyed it at the time. It was the first adventure game I had completed 100% by myself and felt very proud about it! I had found the story engaging and the atmosphere accordingly suitable.
Fast forward 15 years later, it seems my mind spins in a different direction and had to consult a guide in a few bits. Still, the various puzzles make perfect sense, but I mostly didn't have the same patience to solve them by myself. I think the story pretty much holds its own and I never felt lost as to what happens next or what to do. The game even provides you with alternate paths to approach the story, either in the places you visit or the dialogues you choose. (
has 3 different endings!)
A minor inconvenience is the resolution, which is stuck at 800x600 and in some scenes it's ok, and in others it's a strain for the eyes! :)
But my only major qualm, and a reason to
recommend the game is that Steam offers it "as-is". On my laptop (at least), with Winows 10, the game "as-is" does not start. The obvious solution is to "wrap" it with dgVoodoo (or any other DirectX emulator, if there is one). Well, with the latest version of dgVoodoo the game didn't start, with an older one the game started but the hotspots were pitch black and couldn't solve puzzles, and about half-way through I decided to try another
version, that turned out it worked fine!
Well, in all honesty, that's not a way to sell a game. Why couldn't these games come pre-packed with a DirectX wrapper, like even older adventures are with ScummVM or DosBox?

I gave up on this rather quickly (after about an hour anf a half), though not without reason.
First off, I love 'film noir' style point-and-click games, so I had good hopes for 'Post Mortem'. Though the rather generic plot is to be expected ('femme fatale' at the door asking you to solve a murder...), it is the game mechanics that ruined it for me. The bulk of it consists of conversations with NCP's, and you navigate with the familiar 'dialogue trees'. Aside from having different topics to choose from, you can also select the manner of speaking (charming, curious, direct, et cetera). Sadly, picking the wrong options will bring about an abrupt end to the conversation. Since the game gives you little to no clues on how to engage with the characters, this is a problem. Whereas succes is unsatisfying, failure is downright frustrating, and the game will punish you harshly with a dead end if you're not careful.
The graphics are nothing special, but that's forgivable in this genre. Voice acting is decent (I played the game in French).

Post Mortem is nice, but sometimes the game mechanics are flawed.
I had some fun with this murder mystery game. The story is compelling and really interesting. I also liked the art design, even though the graphics are of course outdated. However, I believe the graphics are still good enough.
The sound, music and English voice acting is quite good, though sometimes characters mumble slightly.
A very positive aspect is that you can choose different dialogue options and make progress in various ways, and this really influences what happens.
The reason why I would give a rating of only 70 % are the sometimes odd game mechanics. For example, some puzzles are very hard and one is especially annoying because you have to use exactly the right combination even if others seem very reasonable as well. So I had to consult a walkthrough several times. By the way, the walkthrough in the Steam folder of the game is a joke: you can only find pictures of the puzzles but no detailed explanations about most of them.
All in all, if you like point and click adventures with a good story and nice characters, you can give it a try, especially when it is on sale.

I have an addiction to point and click games and have learned to accept clunky gameplay, frustrating puzzles, confusing stories, and comparatively poor graphics. But every point and click game I've played until PM had some modicum of immersion, atmospheric details, charm. Even the dime a dozen Nancy Drew games had lively cheesy voice acting.
Post Mortem is not all bad - a few neat integrations of puzzles and mature themes that are present, but understated. But overall, undercooked branching storyline, poor inventory interface, even poorer dialogue and narrative organization, overall bugginess and uninspired voiceacting dragged this game to the depths of tepidness. No attachment to the characters, not enough attempt at atmosphere, and unsatisfying puzzles. Still Life 1 is still the best in the series, Still Life 2 was at least interesting to play. They developed the elements that PM introduced, but did not bother to follow through on.

Let me be straight. Unless you bought this game as part of the "Dollar Ultra Bundle" or any other similiar bundle where the game was merely a part of the deal, stay the hell away from this mess!
If you had any previous experience with RPG Video then I genuinely wonder why you even considered plunging into another of their grammar riddled products. If not, Back To Basics Gaming being the publisher should be enough reason to not give this game another thought. If you look at the list of games Back To Basics Gaming published, you will notice mediocrity and a couple of dollars is all it needs for your product to be published by them. So if you are looking for quality games that will entertain you for a while, anything listed under their name won't fit that criteria.
If for some reason you are still here thinking maybe I'm just biased, here's a summary of what's wrong with the game itself:
The game starts in a tiny window and instead of having actual settings on the title screen, you have to change the properties. There you have the options to change the screensize to full screen and get a short summary of the controls. Something you normally would expect to fnd ingame as well. Turns out you don't. Not even once do you get a single explanation.
Now that you figured out that pressing Z opposed to Enter is more comfortable you start exploring the map with your arrow keys. After a couple seconds you should notice that you have seen the mapstyle, the characters and models in pretty much any beginner-like RPG maker game, because apparently charging money for generic assets is fun! The music is also not unique and neither are the enemy sprites unfortunately.
The dialogues vary from straight out of a text book to throw away lines you heard in any cliché plagued B movie. What they have in common is the abysmal spelling and grammar. A speech bubble that doesn't lead to you calling the suicide hotline is a rare and pleasant encounter. The developers probably threw a coin when to use "was" and "were" because consistency isn't part of their vocabulary.
While grinding is fairly common in games like this one, the people behind it clearly didn't give the level curve any thought whatsoever. Not only do you need tripple the average exp you would normally expect, but the amount of gold you generate doesn't support grinding in a reasonable matter. The enemy scaling is a mess and the rigged RNG doesn't help either. There's a right way to implement a thrilling challenge and there's pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Land of Dashtir heavily favors the latter one.
The first area featuring random encounters (the mines) has enemies that can literally oneshot you before you even get a turn, if RNG isn't on your side. Be it zombies that hit three times on one turn or Ghosts spamming fire magic before you even get the chance to attack or guard, fun is not something you will have especially after you notice that you get a measly two XP for killing them, but need 50-ish to level up.
There's literally no reason why you should stock up on antidotes, ironically an item that heals any negative status effect in the game, because the first boss will bombard you with blind, sleep and confusion far outlasting any stock of items you may have prepared. In fact he throws disabling spells at you even after you have already been hit by them because six times gotta be the charm!
Said fight is neither fun, nor challenging. Just frustrating because the SP you need for special abilities that you unlock from level two onwards isn't a consistent value like it would be in any other game that has common sense. You generate SP by being attacked (that includes being struck by status effects) and by causing damage yourself while depleting it when you walk around. You get to keep whatever tiny bit you had left during normal encounters, but the entire gauge gets depleted when you start a boss fight because there wasn't enoguh artificial difficulty in the game yet.
Once you are tired enough of the mindless grinding post killing the boss, you check your inventory to notice you aquired a key item. In this case the empty bottle needed to get some magic water from a spring. An item half the village feels to remind you about. It seems your character is one hell of a dofus and can't remember aynthing for more than five seconds.
After backtracking to the area where the spring is you try to use the bottle just to get a dialogue prompt telling you that your character would like to get some water but he doesn't have a bottle. The hell?
If you made it that far into the game without breaking your keyboard in two, odds are the police has surrounded your house because your neighbour called them after hearing a disturbing noice and animal like sounds. Instead of going on a murder rampage leading to your early death or jail time which definetly would be more fun than playing this game, press the uninstall button and call it a day. Crying in a corner afterwards may help.
There's a slim chance that like me you consider giving the game still a shot after reading all that, don't! Having nothing else to do you feel like going to the next plot area while also taking care of some quests so our old friend oneshot returns to remind you why this game is crap. Leveling and better gear don't mean anything if RNG once more won't let you attack. Countless reloads later you beat up another generic boss that follows the same scheme as the first one, while still bombarding  you with horrendous dialogue lines.
That was also the point where I had enough and uninstalled the game because the story didn't reach any meaningful point and Terret's smug face started to bug me more than sitting on an anthill.
It's a disgrace that Steam would allow this unfinished garbage to be sold. Nothing works, the game has no plot and is full of grammar errors.

Single-player mode is great, fun to play and you feel you're making progress just by playing.
PvP on the other hand has some of the worst drawbacks I've seen in a game like this.
1. The game effectively pauses when a strike attack is being made, which leads to erratic gameplay.
2. Both players use the same field to play. So if one player is a fraction of a second faster to make moves you can effectively get locked out of doing anything. In addition to that, to that the pausing between strikes allow the opponent to move faster and stack strikes after one another leaving you to simply watch without ever getting to interact with the game.
3. Daily quests only progress during PvP fights that you win, which if you get unlucky with matching makes them impossible to finish.
It's early access and some of these things should really be looked into and improved on, because in the current state it's hardly playable or fun.
I'm not into matching games at all...But this is addicting and it feels great to beat people in PVP, It's all about how fast your brain reacts to certain patterns.
I recommend this game. But be careful, it can be addictive, you always want to do a better score.

Easily the most solid game in the entire series. The port is decent, but there's a nasty bug where the battles just hang. Thankfully, the game has an auto-save feature, so if you hit continue on the title screen, it'll take you to the last place where you transitioned screens, even if you hadn't saved.
Decent story that touches on a lot of touchy subjects, especially for a game that presents itself more like a light-hearted fairytale ( a kid confrontin his own mortality and a teenager basically dealing with depression and identity crisis being the highlights of this and some of the game's strongest moments.)
You WILL hate some bosses that seem to be able to que up 3 actions before yours go through, but honestly, not a hard game. Also, there's the in-game cheats, in case you just wanna see the story.
Game will probs take you about 40 to 60 hours, depending on how much you grind and what sidequests you pursue. I got it on sale for half-price, so i feel it was well worth it. 20 bucks for that kinda gametime might not be worth it to you, in which case, wait for a sale. Also, do not be intimidated by the sword-fighting minigame at the start of the game. It seems to have been tweaked, since it was even easier than the psx version to get 100 out of 100 approval rating. Also, unbelievable music ( and probably the best Nobuo Uematsu has written).
In short, get it.

FF9 is a game that pays homage to its Final Fantasy's roots. It's the classic FF world that we imagine: fantasy world, airships, black mages, and a large vartiety of people and races.
A standard-fare JRPG story that starts with a simple enough plot that turns into an epic adventure of saving the world. The game system is a mix of the various games before it: nothing revolutionary.
Despite it's been-there-done-that core, this game manages to summarize the entire FF series well into one package. The characters are charming, varied and deep. The story keeps you engaged with it's new developments throughout, right until the very end. The game manages to let you be as casual or hardcore as you want, and you are rewarded either way. All-in-all, it was a fitting end to the Playstation 1 generation of Final Fantasy games.

What can I say? This game is amazing. It isn't perfect, but most games aren't. This game is for you if you love tycoon games and selling drugs to random homeless men and women, which actually kind of makes the game sound boring, but believe me it isn't. I give this game an 8/10 and here is why:
Pros:
-The game simply has an amazing concept which I enjoy and find sometimes comedic which is to sell drugs. Simple, but I love that about it. It isn't complicated and takes almost no time to get a hang of, but I love it.
-Good looking game. It has good graphics and I do understand it is a pixel game but it just looks nice. It is appealing to the eye which makes it easier to binge on for a few hours.
-Still being updated. They update the game and I only got the game today but to my understanding they update it either often or in big updates at a time, since the game is rather new and has still changed a lot since it came out. I finished the game and I cant wait to play it again when they add new exciting things to do.
-Casual. It isn't a very difficult game to play and is kind of relaxing when you get into it... Well as relaxing as a drug cooking and dealing game can be...
-Replayability. It is decently replayable. I am not going to replay the game 50 more times and waste 100 hours of my life on it (at least not until they update it again) but still decently replayable.
Cons
-Repetative. Even though it is replayable, after a few run throughs, I'd imagine that it would become very repetative, which is why I hope they continue to update the game.
-Short. It does not take very long to beat the game especially if you tried. I kind of messed around a bit and still beat the game in less then 2 hours. If I really tried I could do it in less then 1.5 hours.
-Easy. Yes I did say it was casual but I really hope they add maybe a difficulty option or some way to make it more of a challenge after beating the game the first time. I beat it once and now I want to beat it again, but I want it to be harder then the first time and give me a good run for my money.
-No content. It is in early access which is why there is less content then a full fledged game would and should have but it is also most likely cheaper then the game will be in the future and is almost an investment in a game in hopes it will become even better.
Overall, great game. It needs some work but it is early access so don't get it and immediatelly refund it because wait a week or two and they will already have some new stuff to try out. I actually found out about this game from a youtube video by Sips and I decided to get the game. If you are uncomfortable getting an early access game then don't. If you are unsure remember that you will be getting an unfinished game but you will also be supporting the developers and speeding up progress at the same time. I hope everyone who gets the game enjoys it like I did and it now eagerly waiting for the next update.

I have just finished Wizardry 6 and wanted to start 7, but the sudden release of Grimoire made me put such plans on hold. Grimoire does everything that made me love Wizardry games of the Bradley era, but does it better. It has the depth of 80s and 90s fantasy rpgs like RoleMaster, the challenging gameplay of classic D&D campaigns, and rampant imagination of a teenage Dungeon Master. It also has a dated GUI and swarms of bugs, but Cleve is keen on fixing his mistakes and updates the game almost daily. This game is a rough gem - buggy, but also addicting and full of content. Heck, I had more fun with character creation than many games nowadays.

What can I say? After waiting decades for this game, I am not disappointed. I couldn't care less about the folks who have downed or doubted it. All that matters is I get a taste of what I miss from the 90's. I also don't care about any drama related to the dev. It's a game folks and a damn good one. It's like Picasso: you either get it or you don't. If you don't, go away and let me enjoy it. It isn't perfect and has a bit of roughness to it. There have been bugs that, for instance, allow me to play the game one day and the next, it won't even load. But that's the nature of gaming. There have already been updates and bug fixes. I cannot currently recommend this game in its current state.  Since its launch, saves have been wiped several times, along with user created charactors resulting in the loss of many hours of play.
There are numerous game stopping bugs that simply wont let you progress through the game.  The developer is constantly patching and breaking save games and other features and there is no steam option to roll back to a previous version like other games.
If you buy this you are essentially playing an early access game that does not have all the features as they will be added later.  There is no mention of this in the store description.
At its price tag and hype, its simply not a recommendable game to play right now.  In fact, 2 of the days since launch, patches have rendered the game completely unplayable for everyone (fights on every single step including when resting made the game broken and unplayable, has since been fixed but this is an example).  The patches are not tested before deployment and it seems the developer just updates at a whim without any testing.
I admire his dedication and there certainly are a lot of fans jumping on the band wagon here but the criticisms are legit.  I like the game, i imagine that in a few months it will be very good.  But it in its current state, its a horrible mess right now with bugs everywhere and broken patches being released every day that reset your progress.  Teh game touts a 600 hour completion time but there are only 24 hours in a day before your game gets wiped again.
This game should be listed as early access as anyoen buying right now is essentially bug hunting for the dev.  Nothign wrong with that but if i had known that before dropping my money, i would have waited.
The beginning of the game consists of groups of enemies that are simply impossible to fight at level 1.  You will reload your save file after every single action you take because at any point in time one of these groups of enemies could spawn on you causing you to have to reload.  There are no tactics or party composition that will allow you to win, half your team will die and there is absolutely nothing you can do but reload.  Its not fun.  Its a reloading simulator.  Im a save scummer just like the rest and dont mind a reload now and then when a bad decision is made, at this point its RNG deciding if you should reload or not.  No amount of skill or knowledge will get you over this hump.  Im sure there is a lot to be had here but its pretty hard to get to the potential this game has to offer.
I will update this review if the developer ever gets things ironed out and he is clearly dedicated to the game so i am sure it will happen.  But right now, avoid this mess.  Go play something playable.

I'm giving it a thumbs up not because it's a great game, because it's not. People have posted it's not a stronghold game, it is, just not a very good one. If your a die hard stronghold fan, thank you should explore it at least.
The game felt like it wanted to be Stronghold two, where you develop your castle into more of a town, but they left out all the decorations. More so, unlike the other Stronghold's, there isn't one stage where you start from scratch and build how you want to build.
Don't expect to build an epic army just to meet another epic army in the middle of the battle field and try to outwitt the AI all the while having another army building.
Most of the game is simply surving.  Your always on the clock with a limited amount of days before the task is met or you made it through the attacks.
What I didn't like was the limited amount of usage of the higher end units like swordsmen and knights, even crossbow men. Most of the game you use peasents as cannon fodder to protect your spear men. Though they added the ability for the spearmen to do a good amount of damange to soliders by throwing their spears, they are still the weak spearmen we all know.
They did add a new type of soilder, the Ranger but since you only get to use the Ranger unit twice I never got the chance to explore the unit.
If you look back to Crusaders and even stronghold legends, they have less units. No fighting monks and no mercs like the slaves that can burn down buildings or the archers on horse back. In fact there really is no use for the "well".
The sieges are way to hard. You litterly have a handful of men and not enough seige weapons. It almost feel's like a puzzle and a touch of stealth when your taking down a castle.
The one interesting aspect of the game I did like was the honor system. You buy statues and have varrious special buildings that allow you to throw a party which gives you honor which is needed to use higher end units like knights, swordsmen, macemen, but oddly enough not pikemen.
For Multiplayer this is a great effect, it makes it so you just can attack right away like in so many other RTS games. By the time you can build a half way decent army, your going to have to go against the other players castle...But oops, if your lucky enough to find someone online playing, it's buggy once you both get building.
I did like the fact that taxes actually were worth rasing and mining for materials paid a lot less which made it a must to have to build your own weapons. Unlike the other strongholds you do build weapons faster.
The graphics are better, but not really haven't made leaps and bounds since the orginal. The stronghold series has never been about the graphics. I rather have had the game graphics dumb downed when the game first game out.
It's pretty safe to say Firefly is finished with this game despite the few bugs it has. The only good thing that came out of this stronghold was the honor system, which is actually bearly used.
Perhaps the only saving grace for stronghold 3 will be if the makers do a crusaders verison of the game.

I had heard good things about Still Life and when I went to buy it I found it was part of a trilogy so I started here. However I am not impressed with this first instalment.
For a start there are technical issues with this game. The game’s resolution is hard coded, low and in 4:3 aspect ratio (and for some reason Nvidia defaults to screwing up the aspect radio and stretching the display). If your game loses focus for any reason it crashes. This happens all to easily when you are playing in a window or have multiple monitors as the controls to look around are to move the mouse to the edge of the screen but there is nothing to stop your cursor moving out of the game. Further more I had issues where the game would periodically just lose focus for no apparent reason.
The game itself is excruciatingly slow. Every other point and click game I can think of off the top of my head has fixed camera angles so you can easily see what is in each location. This however is displayed in the first person and you don’t have full free movement you just click to the next predetermined location you can move to. This means you have to click to take a step look round with the slow camera controls then take the next step. It also has lots of pointless dead dead ends and elongated corridors to waste more of your time. Even disregarding this the story is so slow; after the initial exposition nothing much happens for ages. The first chapter of the game is basically mundane police work of taking witness statements and establishing a description of a suspect. There were some plot developments in the latter part of the game but I was too bored by that point to be paying much attention.
The user interface is really not intuitive either. For example it is not clear how to give items to people. The lock pick puzzle gives you no hint of what to do, you have to click about randomly till you figure out what the puzzle is before you can solve it. The worst moment for me was the fresco puzzle, the game makes it clear that you need to use a candle on the fresco but won’t let you do that until you have found some seemingly unrelated item which unlocks another dialogue option which in turn unlocks the puzzle actually working.
This game also has one of my personal point and click bugbears and that is things that change at locations seemingly unrelated to the player’s actions. On a couple of occasions new items appeared at locations I had already visited without any logical link to anything I had done. This really annoys me as once you know the game does this each time you get stuck you have to go and revisit every location to ensure nothing new has appeared unnecessarily dragging out the game.
I really hope this game is not indicative of the quality of the sequels.

The problem lies in the puzzle and dialogue structure. In relation to the puzzles, if you miss one hidden object, you are stuck. And some puzzles are extremely illogical (e.g. a puzzle with two dial wheels where one wheel is not being used at all). But the even bigger problem is the dialogue: Most conversations simply don't make any sense. Some times you can ask people about things they still haven't mentioned. Other times it would be logical to ask them a relevant question, but you can't. And some times you are stuck with saying something that doesn't make any sense at all; e.g. blaiming right in the middle of a very friendly conversation. And it goes both ways. For instance a hotel manager might end up getting angry and banning you from the hotel. But the next time you meet him, he's friendly and you are free to ask questions and to enter the hotel. The next time you meet him he'll ask you to leave once again. The dialogue structure is simply awful and it wrecks the game. You end up just clicking some random statement because all the options are equally meaningless.
Sad, because the game had some potential when it comes to atmosphere and some story elements and characters.
