While the game is older, it really harkens back to a lot of the FPS/Strat game designs we see so successful today. Innovations such as the timed Force-enabled hero that can hack and slash through the legions of enemies (otherwise known as time-based leadership mechanics). Archetypal weapon loads like the shock troop, sniper, and engineer were as well developed into what we might see in today's games. As well, vehicle combat is exceptionally well implemented for a game of its time. The only other game I can remember immersing vehicles with fps combat around the time this game came out was Battlefield 1942. Sadly though, on no more than all occasions except my first multiplayer experience after the first server I logged into after buying the game, I've been unable to play with any other players. Single-player works flawlessly, however. If you're looking for a nostalgic reminiscence with respect to a Battlefront single player experience, then you'll get your money's worth with this classic. If you expect to play with other people on a regular basis - well...it's a game from 2005, what do you expect? Setup your own dedicated server!

Lichdom: Batlemage brings a great concept on the table... But fails to deliver on many aspects.
When I saw quotes like "Never has magic felt as powerful", I expected a lot from this game... But here are my pros and cons:
Pros:
- Amazing graphics. Excellent use of the CryEngine engine, locations feel real, many details, beautiful overall.
- Magic feels very good, visually.
- The whole "magic" part is based on a very good (and new) concept that has an amazing potential.
- They tried really hard to make you care about the lore, the characters, the past events, but...
Cons:
- Linear levels with some "goodies" on the side.
- Repetitive x1000.
- I honestly couldn't care less about certain characters or events. While I understood the story, I didn't feel "in it" at all.
- The inventory and the crafting system.
The problem is that, after a while in the game, you just keep doing this:
>be at checkpoint
>go forward onto the path that you cannot divert of
>ennemies spawn of the ground around you
>usually some running weak minions, some stronger various flying/walking/beasts/archers and eventually a lieutenant or mini boos
>combo, kill, dodge your way out of the fight
>go forward 50 meters
>repeat
Sometimes you'll find yourself at key points in the story and you'll have to fight a boss... And that's kinda all.
If the levels were to be shorter and the magic really more
, the whole "repeat" thing wouldn't be such a problem. But here, since even the slightest minion levels up as the game advances, it still takes the same freaking time to eradicate them, especially when you consider that at the start of the game you would have dealt 50 damage with a particular combo, and at the end 16'000 !
So yeah, given the fantastic possibilities of this magic system, I would have loved a game that actually make me feel like a badass - mid-game and onward, you should have been able to oneshot whole enemies waves with well executed combos, instead of that, you're just doing the same thing over and over again.
Sooo... Recommended, yeah, because I still had some fun playing it.. But only if you are into this type of games and only if it is on sale.

10 hours in and I've only just reached the 4th area (there are 4 more after this). The encounters become more difficult, enemies become tougher (not necessarily smarter, although they do seem to understand cover mechanics, or more diverse, just more health/damage/extra abilities).
The crafting system is engaging and combined with the tougher encounters, demons and bosses I face, the game really keeps me coming back. I just keep wanting to move to the next 'checkpoint' and gather a few more crafting materials for that one upgrade.
The graphics really don't disappoint, the different areas are diverse and detailed, and this adds to the fun.
- Visuals are great! Not just the spell effects, but the scenery as well.
- Gameplay is engaging; the crafting of spells and your loadout seriously alter how you play your mage.
- The game runs really smooth (R9 290 ran this at 60FPS on maximum settings, but more on this below).
- The story isn't half bad either
- There is an interesting loot system (the further you get without dying, the better the drop rate).
- There is NG+ for those who can't get enough.
- Great tutorials - after the tutorial part of the game, these can be revisited from the menu.
- The voice acting is great, and quite funny :P
or actually, mediocre.
- I have a bit of an issue with falling through a crack/hole in the floor while blinking around, which causes insta-death.
- RNG ... I hate RNG when it comes to loot. It really isn't too bad here, lots of loot, but still...
- It can get a bit repetitive once you've found your favorite spell combinations.
So, we have 8 different types: fire, ice, kinesis, lightning, corruption, necromancy, delirium and phase.
There are 3 different types of casting: AoE, targeted, and 'nova'.
I think there are 3 variants to each of the types, for example: targeted has a trap, lob and missile, AoE has a pool, trap and rain. I don't really know about the nova though...
And each cast type can be altered in 3 ways: mastery, control and destruction.
Considering all these options, if we do a little math, we get a total of:
8 * 3 * 3 * 3 = 216 different spells + a bunch of 'unique' spells, that combine 2 types and cause a unique effect, like a fire+ice tornado.
Of these roughly 230/235 different spells, you can equip only 9 at a time...
Next to that there's also a very important gameplay component, your shield. This one too can be crafted. You have 3 different shield types, each with it's own strength and weakness. This one will mostly guide your gameplay, whereas the others will be build around how you want to play. A certain type of shield is best for keeping distance, while another type is more build around getting up close and personal.
So, I was running this game at a very stable 60FPS on highest settings on my FX-8150 (OC'd to 4GHz), R9 290 (Asus OC edition) and 8GB DD3. I did not experience a single frame drop, except during certain in-game cutscenes. These dropped the framerate to 50. As soon as they were over, even during fights, the game would hold up a perfect 60FPS.
A second however: my midi-tower heats up a lot. The game is optimized for AMD, and I had this before with running Sniper Elite 3 on max settings as well. The GPU runs it perfectly stable, but very hot. After about an hour, the GPU would be about 80 degrees Celsius, after 2 hours it was 84 degrees, which made me decide to lower the settings a nodge, to preset High. This did not really impact visuals (I didn't notice any change, really), but it allowed my GPU to relax a little for some reason and the temperature started dropping immediately. Now, I haven't thoroughly tested this yet, because I entered a new area shortly after changing the settings, but in the new area, the temperature stabilized at 69 degrees. That's a 15 degrees drop, but considering it's in a new area, I can't say what exactly caused this...
Considering all of the above, I would say this game is definitely worth 15-20 bucks.
For a single playthrough, I'm expecting the average player to take between 15 and 20 hours.
If you're sure you'd like to try all spells and have fun with NG+ and the extra challenge modes, the game is good for at least 25 to 35 hours of fun - I'm estimating.
Be sure to check out my profile and see what kind of games I like, in order to be able to interprete my review better. This game is probably not for everyone.

Got this game during its early development and continued to revisit periodically.  I have a craving for a game with true freedom of spell creation and with a "total badass" mage.  Something that's challenging, but you can move through a horde and leave bodies strewn across the battlefield.  That's not this game.
The spell crafting system is essentially a weapon crafting system.  Here's the base spell, increase its special effect or damage.  Combining spells?  Nono, your mage isn't smart enough for that.  You can't even equip two different elements for each type of attack, such as ice on main and fire on aoe.
As for gameplay, it sucks.  Yes, it is graphically beautiful and clearly alot of effort went in to every detail, but not so much on variety.  Once you're in a level, which can span an hour or two easily, everything looks the same.  Each cave you passed looks just like the one before.  That ice mountain before you, exactly the same as the last three.  Enemies are all the same as well.  There's skeletons, humans, ghost thingies, etc, but they're all really the same.
The only real strategy for this badass of a mage is to kite and shoot.  Shoot what?  That's up to you.  Ice and you'll live longer, fire they'll die faster.  Add in some necro and things will get distracted, but the pets don't really do much damage.  Fire/Necro's my perferred path, and I'm not sure my undead ever actually killed anything.
When I bought it, I paid $20, and it's probably worth that much.  With the new price tag at 40, wait for a sale.

Sonic Generations, in my opinion, is the best Sonic game outside of the original Genesis/Mega Drive trilogy and Sonic CD (as of July 2017).  It gives a good compromise in what is often referred to one of the most broken bases in video games, providing both the classic Sonic gameplay, and modern Sonic boost gameplay in about even amounts.  The nine stages and various boss fights are re-imaginings of zones from Sonic’s past console adventures of his first 20 years; there are no brand new zones in this game as a result.  However, don’t let that deter you, since each stage features a new level design, with the set pieces and gameplay gimmicks of the original stages, with re arranged music.  Even though I’ve played all of the levels in their original games, it was a fresh experience playing the Generations versions with the new challenges that they presented.
One disappointment I had was the lack of DLC for more zones.  However, this game’s expansive mod community fills in that gap.  Another was the story, while entraining and funny, felt lacking, as many opportunities were missed for callbacks in the script throughout.
A single play through can be finished in about four hours, and 100% can be easily done in under 12 hours depending on your skill level.  However, this game has a high replay value, I can see myself going back to the game to replay levels with both styles on occasion.  There’s also a pinball machine in Casino Night, which is a nice little extra.
In short, if you like Sonic, pick this game up.

text:
This game shows all of the great things about Sonic.
Unfortunately, it also shows all of the issues that modern day sonics have had.
Pros
- There is only one Sonic (there are actually two in the game but you get what I mean), and playing as the blue hedgehog is a rewarding experience.
- The initial levels are really fun and interesting, with the classic Sonic levels really being done well.
- The nostalgic experience of remembering any of the levels you played is really fun, particularly with the really excellent soundtrack.
- A good looking game, with few visual issues (that don't really effect gameplay)
- The 'home world' area is a cool idea, with some cool exploration challenges
- Great sound design
Cons
- Whilst the Act 1 and Act 2 ideas are nice, if you play through Act 1 and Act 2 of the same level, the level can feel a bit too similar and a little boring.
- Some of the levels are outright mean, and leave you feeling cheated. More of a problem with this than other Sonic games I've played, where just as you start to pick up speed, a nearly unavoidable enemy is put in the middle of the track.
- Bosses aren't particularly tough or rewarding. Often feature repeating of similar mechanics and often those mechanics are not well explained. Make sure to listen carefully to what Omochao is saying if you want to finish a boss quickly. The last boss is also awfully explained and relatively confusing (but still somehow easy ????).
- May be an individual issue, but some control inputs were not registering properly (using a Logitech F310 and never had any issues with other games). Particularly an issue for a platforming game that tries to rely on quick reaction jumps.
- Weird movement quirks really stand out and punish on some 'New Sonic' levels (Act 2), as the lock-on mechanic cannot lock on until it is too late, resulting in an insta-death, or it can (on rare occasions) hit you into objects, again, resulting in a fall to insta-death, which always feels somewhat cheap.
- Controls can feel a little weird and flighty as well, not really allowing for a responsive feeling Sonic. 'Old Sonic' is generally fine, but the 'New Sonic' levels can leave you feeling a bit out of control.
- Often the game feels like they just shoved more content into it. So, if you're not the #1 Sonic fan in the world, you might struggle really getting through all of it. Could technically say that this game has hundreds of hours of content, but it is often challenges on already completed content. Exploring around the home-world is cool in a way, but also feels relatively pointless once you have completed the necessary challenges.
Summary
This game certainly has its moments. Particularly the earlier stages of the game, which is where most people will have fond memories of Sonic. However, the later you get into the game, the more issues appear, the content looks more and more repetitive and the challenge of the game does not feel like it changes at all. If you're a big Sonic fan, you've probably already picked this up, but if you're not, I'm not sure I could recommend paying full price for the game. If it goes on sale, it could be a few hours of entertainment, but don't expect to have a crushing urge to progress past the initial few levels. Any controller issues you may have really feel horrendous due to the speed of the game, and none of the bosses are particularly enjoyable outside of the first one.

A strong 5/10, but not enough to recommend purchasing this game

I was lucky enough to get this game on the Steam Summer Sale for like 6-7 dollars, and at that price, you'd be crazy not to buy it. But don't sweat it if you didn't because you're not missing too much, either.
Sonic Generations is an anthology of levels from past games, including those from the Genesis up to the Dreamcast and now. It's basically Sonic Jam 2 - you're not playing an original experience as much as you are a selection of parts from other games that legally passes as a complete product. That's not bad or anything but don't expect it to be like the Adventure series or the Genny classics in that regard. You are playing Sonic's Greatest Hits Collection.
Right away, I have to point out Generation's understanding of what makes a true Sonic game for the third dimension. This is something I don't think enough people appreciate. The amount of attention to detail and design here is incredible. It's absolutely obvious that the developers knew what they were doing, and after years of seeing them pump out crap or making lukewarm experiences at best, it's honestly mind blowing. Like, it's not just good, but eerily good. Both Modern and Classic levels are built around the formula of speedy platforming, throwing in alternate pathways and areas to explore. The way you transition between pathways, both high and low and left and right, is brilliant and leaves me in awe sometimes. I have to just sit there and appreciate it for a couple of seconds and laugh. This also cooperates with the game's art design, which blends so brilliantly and colorfully with the levels that both background and foreground exist together seamlessly. This is extremely apparent in Sky Sanctuary and Planet Wisp; rather than the surrounding environments just existing behind or around the level tracks, it feels like you're actually running through the environments, themselves, and the pathways just happen to be there. You'd also think the boost function would break the 'momentum-building' rule in Sonic games, but the levels are designed so that you can only use it during specific points, or else you'll lose rings or die. The boost feature is perfect for Sonic and I'll take it over spamming levels with dash pads, any day.
I could do with less emphasis on the F1 Racing-style levels, though, and the overuse of 2D sections on Modern stages. The levels also, at times, feel automatic, which makes the game way too easy and serves as its biggest weakness. It also could've used a lot more exploration and a lot less blasting mindlessly through all the beautifully designed levels. Still, though, its great. You are looking at the purest, most lovingly made gameplay in the entire series.
So, with all of that being said, Sonic Generations sounds perfect, doesn't it? It clearly has a lot going for it. I'm even still recommending it. What could be so wrong? Well, that's a little hard to answer. Remember when I said that Sonic Generations understands what makes a true Sonic game in 3D, despite its few flaws? That's true... except that's pretty much all it does and nothing else. The game's levels exist literally and figuratively in a white, lifeless void, occupying nothing except a hunger for nostalgia. Characters from the past are thrown in without context or for any reason. The story is stagnant dialogue between levels because, again, its only there to serve the nostalgia-driven experience and you don't really care. Aside from the fantastic soundtrack, there is nothing else going on. It's just you, a literal empty void of nothingness and some really great retro revival Sonic stages. That's it.
I'd like to put something into perspective that's also slightly embarrassing: as a child, Sonic was my religion. He was the most amazing video game character that ever lived, period, and at that time I had a reason to believe it. I remember being so young that videos were in a quality too low to numerate and a 2-minute video of Sonic and Shadow racing each other in Japanese took 2 hours to load. I remember getting to see the King Boom Boo fight, then telling my sister to come and watch it and not realize that she didn't care and I was annoying her. By the time I got Sonic Adventure 2 in my Gamecube, I was hyped for some sort of nirvana-level God-ascenting enlightenment with which the likes I'd never experienced before, nor would I ever again. Maybe it wasn't perfect, but there was a story to follow, there were characters to be engaged with and mysteries to uncover, and some fantastic levels. There were Chao gardens and kart races and cool music and Shadow and multiplayer and way too much stuff to pile into one paragraph. Now as an adult, stuff like that doesn't really happen to me anymore (except with Freedom Planet), but my point is that I got to see a game that existed for itself and in itself and not for something else.
So imagine Sonic Adventure 2, but instead it hands all the levels over to you - no more than 9 because that's what you get in Generations - and you're inside a void of nothingness. Characters up to that point in the series (and not new ones) can be seen standing around, dispensing basic game hints when you walk by. All the levels are from past games. The final boss sucks and then that's it. Except... the actual levels are pretty good. Amazing, actually. Everything about them is amazing. But everything else is so lifeless and unengaged. Do you really care?
If you enjoyed this game in all its purity and believe it to be one of the greatest Sonics, then that's fantastic. For me, it's hard to even compare it to the Adventure games. Again, it's like this by virtue of being an anthology collection with a handful of stages, so that's not necessarily bad.
Basically, you should get this if you really like Sonic games. Or just get Freedom Planet, which is a much better game, anyway. Both are recommended!

Okay I changed my mind.  My review is officially negative unless the developer addresses many of the concerns I have.
It's alright.  I mean, the gameplay is pretty good considering we are not dealing with something AAA.
Drawbacks:
- Controller mapping does not work as intended.  I can't figure it out, and the default controls are not ideal (X on 360 pad is for accellerate while triggers don't really do anything).  I can sort of change some settings, like changing the throttle to a trigger was okay, but when I go to set handbrake to 'B' it will skip back to the previus menu as though I hit 'B' at any other time.  If I hit 'enter' on the keyboard on any button it thinks there is an axis on the controller pressed slightly somewhere and every button will get mapped to that axis if you try.  Luckily the default controls are manageable enough to play.
- Controls are too sensitive, basically unplayable without a way to lower sensititivity dramatically.  I was able to get through a few races by just tapping left and right ever so slightly, and it's not too much to ask since the races are mostly straight.
- Crashes often.  Every 2 races my game locks up.  Very unstable.
- Graphics options don't make a lot of sense, but they're serviceable I guess.  Crank it up and hope for the best, it at least can play at a high framerate and look decent.
- Things in the background flicker like crazy.
- The entire game can glitch out.  One time I went to race and my car wouldn't go, you could hear my engine rev but my car wouldn't drive.  Same with everyone else in the starting line, we were all frozen in time at the starting line and slowly creeping backwards (I assume the wind) and all turning ever so slightly into each other.  For like 10-15 seconds and then suddenly we all got our gas working and we sped off and raced.  HIlarious game.
- The reversing in the car doesn't make a lot of sense to me.  I can't seem to figure it out, I keep hitting the wall and not knowing how to back up.  You press a button and 10% of the time it seems to back up.  It says you are in the reverse gear.  But it's okay because the AI is pretty broken and they are dealing with the same issues.  A few of the cars will just be stuck in random places and you're never lonely on the side of the road.
The Upsides:
- The tires look amazing.  Before you race, you can steer left and right and you can get a glimpse of those tires!  They truly look great!  Very high poly models and the rain on them just looks amazing.
- It's pretty fun racing, considering how bad it could have been.  It's playable, it makes you want to keep playing to unlock all the cars and levels.  If we could get a few control tweaks it would be even better.
- Everything is locked by default, so it's fun to sit through it to earn new cars to drive.  Plus they all have different paint jobs.
- THERES TWO SUZUKI VITARA'S IN THIS GAME.  Can't wait to unlock those.  Is there any 4x4ing though?  Seem sort of out of place.
The game is obviously broken as hell but I'm glad it exists.  If you catch it on sale sometime definitely pick it up.  I can't recommend full price but it's got potential.  A lot of it's issues can be fixed.

Grimoire : Heralds of the Winged Exemplar is simply a wet dream for everyone who enjoyed any of the other titles mentioned. While the look and feel of the old DOS games is there, everything is function normally in a Windows enviroment and you can use the mouse to enter menu's like in modern games.
There is the classic old skool music, but without the sound of an old 56k phone modem.
As for the highly detailed artwork that is not all static and high resolution fonts and screens.
All info is in the game like quest logs, party management, inv management, crafting, spellbooks, maps, making notes etc etc
As you can read on the storepage the game is huge on content. While I try to keep following all gaming news in specific genres I missed the 20 years this game was in development. I never heard of this title before I was searching the upcoming Steam titles and my eye catched the description of this project.
As soon as I entered the Steam forums there was an active discussion going on and I found out that there was not only a 20 year development cycle, but a 20 year during controversy as well. Many believed the game was Vaporware, not existing at all or the dev would be never able to finish it. Probably I was one of them if I was following active development for 20 years. I wasn't so I missed the controversy.
But I believed there was a game and I believed it will be released somewhere this year. I trusted it because the very pure and authentic forum post of a dedicated developer creating his lifetime project and dream in an crazy world with a lot of hostile people.
Everything I hate in life and in gaming is everything what is only being done because of money and greed or made by managers instead of artists. This game is the opposite from all of that. An exceptional long development time (Who cares development was not done in a 6 month to make the most cash out of it). A developer who react like an human being in the forum (Who cares he doesn't write fake lines of text as instructed by the marketing departement), a game of unacceptable huge proportions (no other company should ever take the risk to put so much content in a product that they can sell only once to every customer).
It's like smoking a cigarette on places where it's not allowed. To buy a packet of cigarettes for a 13 year old, to f*#k two different people at the same day or to use public transport without ticket. Good luck we are all good people who never ever do such things. We are just slaves in a scripted world and one day we can't have nice things because everything is regulated. How many hours a development cycle can take, how much content a game can have max etc etc
And exactly that is why it's so incredibly fun and motivating that there are people who really don't care and just turns their creativity into a game we can use to escape reality instead of using alcohol or drugs.
All those other reviews atm are about fullscreen not working correctly at first start, the manual not finished yet (what is really a shame since we probably have to wait another 20 years for it) and the game is around 40 dollar.
It shall take a few days before reviews coming in from people who really played the game a few days and my advice is to not buy the game based on my review for gameplay alone.
I recommend the game mostly because of the style, the art, the idea that it is still possible to create in freedom, the controversy, the trust and the way the developer communicates. This game is Sophisticated Cult. I'm hypnotised.
Its not perfect but it does exactly what i want...be hard and fun as f***

Been playing it for about 2 hours with the first update.
Runs nicely on my Win10 laptop, tho I chose windowed mode.
The clicking when starting the first fight is indeed oldskool functionality, but after setting it for all your characters once it's getting really easy in the next turn. You can easily review which character is left out from doing stuff in the battle turn.
I've walked around in the first two areas in the game, fighting some, and just on novice level it's already challenging like it was on Wizardry 7. First hours will pass with trial and error.
As I played W7 through twice, for me it's easy to get what's needed to do in a battle, but I'm sure for those who are new to this, it's rather cryptic with abbreviations. We need the manual ASAP.
I recommend this for those who love the genre of oldschool CRPG's where it's hard to get along.
The automapping is very well done.
The graphics for monsters is really fitting the oldschool style, and I like them, cartoonish, just like it was back in the 90's.
Here and there the graphics could be a little bit more polished, like the character's body color green is not my taste.
But the tiles and the monsters are well done, retro!
Music..well in that department I'm hesitant to say, but I find it mediocre. I loved the tunes in Wizardry 7. This one is okayish.
Sounds: I like em so far. A little bit annoying sometimes, rather cartoonish again. But it fits well the aura overall (so far).
I haven't had a crash yet on windowed mode luckily, and couldn't yet find a gameplay bug.
Hopefully the little quirks on some machines are already ironed out or soon will be. From my perspective this is recommendable.

Alright, Final Fantasy IX. This is a game that I have played more times then I care to count. First on Playstation a long time ago and finally on Steam. This game has a story that clutches your heart strings, a soundtrack that can sooth your very soul and make you relax and just enjoy life, and such lovable characters that you never want to do them wrong. Each playthrough of the game makes you notice more and more about the backstory and just the little details in it that make it a fantastic game. Now yes this game is dated and yes it has some really annoying things about it (Jump Rope Mini Game I am looking at you...) but with those things, you will not regret buying this game. You will love it, you will cry with it and you will come away with a smile and some damn catchy tunes in your head... Seriously if you don't believe me then listen to "Jesters of the Moon", "Black Mage Village", or "Rose of May".

Ever since I first played FFIX on my PS3 I have considered it to be my #1 favorite Final Fantasy game. Not long after starting my first playthrough of the PC version I confirmed this fact.
This is an amazing game; the music is (in my opinion at least) some of the best in the entire franchise, the story has a perfect balance of seriousness and lightheartedness and I love all of the characters (especially Vivi.)
I found the equipment learning progression system very simple and enjoyable (albeit a little grindy). My only problem with it was that party members can die easily and quickly if they have a weak piece of gear equipped in order to learn any available abilities. Yet, this issue can easily be addressed through various means and can be considered a very minor complaint.
This is by no means a perfect game, but there is so much I love about Final Fantasy IX that I cannot recommend it enough to any fan of Final Fantasy or RPGs in general.

If you like classic RPG's like Wizardry 7, this game is for you. If not, don't bother.
I played earlier versions of Grimoire and enjoyed it a lot. It is complex, huge, unforgiving at times and takes time to figure out and become good at. All positive things in my book.

(EDIT: be warned that this game is still undergoing heavy development and issues remain. Manual is still not out. My review below is about an initial run of 23 hours, but for now I'm waiting until the game is more polished and the manual is released. My review is positive because of the uniqueness of the game, but you must understand what you are buying.)
Much like a Terminator, Grimoire has been delivered to you via a time machine straight from the 90s. Be aware that this is not a "retro" game made to look like the classic, it *is* an RPG from the mid 90s that arrives 20 years late. Some will not understand this and criticize the "balance", the UI or whatever, but if you know and love the genre, this is your chance to enjoy a gem that evolves diectly from Wizardry 7, ignoring the "modernities" in which dungeon-crawlers fell after it.
This may also mean this game is not for you, so I advise to read various reviews and decide for yourself. I am a lover of the genre and I find Grimoire a blast, but as the game isn't cheap, I tried to put together a comprehensive review all things considered.
First and foremost, the content is huge, detailed, and quite imaginative (and often funny). Cleve is a worthy heir of D.W. Bradley as a writer and designer; the flavor text feels like a treat every time I find a description.  Each encounter and short dialogue feels unique and pulls you in. They're very humorous and original and just like one would expect from such a work of love, it is full with small hidden details and surprises.
Yet despite the above, the game doesn't lose focus on what really should be the center of it: exploration, mechanics and combat. that's where you'll spend 95% of the time, not reading. that's why you look forward to finding new lore in the game rather than feeling it's a chore.
Character creation alone can entertain you for hours. Combat is tough, even on easy mode you'll die if you just default-attack the first monsters... but that's alright. It was the same in the last game I played (M&MIII) and this is not a "retro" game pretending to look like the classics: it is a game frozen in the mid 90s. You need to try your best to avoid dying quickly.
The world is huge. 12 hours in, the Atlas tells me I've explored a 5% of areas. The first person that completed the game reported doing it in 90 hours, although he abused certain exploits (now fixed), so in the end completing Grimoire will probably take a few hundred hours to the average player.
The game sorely misses a manual: there's almost no information regarding how attributes or skills work, nor details about classes and races. I find myself making blind choices all the time. Damage penetration mechanics seem to be very frustrating in the early levels, making combat too slow. Hopefully, the manual (coming soon) will help with that. Still, the game should provide more information as contextual help, manual or no manual.
Mechanics are very similar to Wizardry 6&7, but sometimes they're a bit wacky and pointless. This becomes more evident in the mid-game, when several areas come down to "Oh, so you didn't cast Armorplate buff? then your chars die on every other hit". While hard-counters are a mechanic I generally like, when it comes down to repeating a buff over and over it gets cumbersome and just not fun.
UI is clunky and overcomplicated. Probably this can be easily solved with keyboard shortcuts, but only to some extent; a more modern UI with integrated help, more use of hover/right-click etc would make the game more enjoyable. In particular, the inventory "bar" is quite terrible.
Some sound effects can get annoyingly repetitive during combat. Art has very variable quality; some of it looks amateurish (luckily for me I couldn't care less about that). There are some fullscreen/windowed mode problems; the changed option doesn't seem to kick in until I restart.
I read other people is having trouble with screen resolutions; I am playing fine on a 1920x1080 monitor in windowed mode.
I've read some negative reviews from alleged old-schoolers mentioning how arbitrary and unfair is the difficulty... after less than one hour played. Hilarious. You need to learn the ropes to beat the enemies in games like this. Didn't you die a dozen times at the beginning of Wizardry 6? Please go back to Fallout 4 or Skyrim, where everything will gently scale to your level and nothing will disrupt your power fantasy.
Still, it is a fact this game will need a lot of balancing and tweaking. If you want an easy start, choose "Sanctuary" as the default starting area in Settings, and make sure you read some of the guides about party generation (Cooper's one is brief and useful). However the best advice regarding balance is to wait for it to be fully completed. IMHO the wait is worth it.
If you loved Might & Magic 1-5 and Wizardry 1-7, very likely this will feel like a miracle that will bring tears to your eyes; otherwise you'd just stare blankly at a screen wondering what the hell is this and why you keep dying. First look at the videos and screenshots, and if that doesn't push the right buttons for you, let it go. Sadly, incline is not for everyone. You had to be there, and all that. A game with a fairly uninspiring story and run-of-the mill generic characters, this game is held up solely by its combat and crafting.
The gameplay consists mainly of horde-style arenas where you go from place to place, and a bunch of enemies spawn which you have to kill to ge to the next area. Corridors, roads and passages serve as both opportunities to get fed some story from your companion AI character (who serves only this purpose, (s)he never actually participates in combat), and as a way to take in some scenery. The dialogue is fairly standard but executed with a good degree of skill, which prevents it from becoming annoying and keeps the game from becoming too stale.
The two main draws of this game as, as mentioned earlier, the combat and also the crafting system.
As you kill enemies, loot "chests" and destroy random things you are awarded spell components that come in several varieties, which you combine to create all new spells for you to use in combat.
The spell creation system can be a bit daunting until you figure it all out, but thankfully the game comes with an "auto-craft" function that can automatically upgrade your spells for you at the touch of a button. You'll frequently resort to this in the beginning, but as you progress to the mid and late game you'll gradually start to understand how it all fits together and start to fiddle with it to create some pretty nice spells that combo with eachother to explosive effect.
This is the cycle of the game, really. You kill stuff to get more spell components, which you craft into spells used to kill more stuff to get more components.
The game lets you select a new Sigil (which is kinda like an element such as fire or ice) to use as a base for your spells at the end of a level, and spells created with them can have very different effects since they're good at different things. While you can switch which 3 of these you can have equipped at a time, you can change them at any savepoint to spice things up if things gets too repetitive.
The game also features some rather brutal boss fights, and if you're unprepared you WILL get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you.
There are plenty of strategies available on the net to use if want, but if i were to give one piece of advice then it's this: never use a shield power that does not allow you to dash, and practice the blocking manouver on smaller enemies beforehand so you get it figured out before you actually need it.
At the end of the day, what's going to decide it for you with this title is if you like magic or not. I play a spellcaster in nearly every RPG i get that allows me to, so I'm very biased towards games that glorify the class. I liked Battlemage quite a bit, even if it was a bit frustrating at times.
I'll definitely keep an eye out for a sequel, if they ever make one, to see if they iron out the issues this one had. In the meantime, if you can handle the steep learning curve and actively seek variation to combat the repetetiveness, then you could definitely do a lot worse than this game.
You should probably wait until a sale, though :)

[Note: This is one of those times when a 'maybe' button would be useful - see explanation at the bottom in regards to the negative review.]
Basement is, in a nutshell, a reversed Sim Tower meets Breaking Bad. As of the current release, you play an unnamed scientist with the aim of bringing the entire city/urban area/whatever it is under your control. The game is bare bones right now, and goes something like this:
- Build new drug labs/security checkpoints.
- Hire new chemists/henchmen.
- Send henchmen to neighboring buildings to take them over: be prepared to send two or three truckloads, as they tend to die in rather short order.
- Send henchmen back to previously conquered locations to fight off police raids (or bribe them if you're making money hand over fist)
- Take over every building on the map; you win!
The game is lacking in content at the moment - my playtime represents a single game start to finish, with the only replay value being in the randomly generated maps. You have a very small selection of room choices and no upgrades or real variety for your chemists and henchmen (beyond very small stat changes that are tied in to the hiring cost/upkeep of them). On the plus side, the developers seem on the ball with patches and rolling out content, so this should be remedied sooner rather than later.
However, I can't recommend it at this time - I think more than a few people would be disappointed by the lack of content for the price. If you want to support the developers, buy it, play it for a bit, and shelve it until you start seeing updates. If you're on the fence, or just know that you'd rather purchase it in a more complete state - just put it on your wishlist and come back in three months.

Story time:
When this came out, I had just started my absence from gaming. Unable to purchase consoles from around '99-2006 due to money and time issues this one totally slipped under the radar. It wasn't until while playing FF XI online that people were rememebering how awesome this was and I was reminded of it's existence. By the time I was able to play it on an original PS1 I couldn't deal with the ugly (for the time) graphics and put it back down. FInally purchased it here and am blown away!
The updated smooth characrer models look great
Backgrounds are still those pre-rendered, somewhat fuzzy models from the PS1 days, but they are cleaner
Music is freaking amazing (as any Nobuo scores are)
Pacing has been markedly improved with the speed-booster to rn between places on the map
Story is getting better and better as the game goes on
Unfortunately, still a little grindy (unless one uses the gameshark-like stat/gil boosts)
While achievements are great, I find myself stopping and re-starting areas a lot so I don't miss things for these collectibles.
All-in-all a great port (for me at least) and looking forward to finishing the story.

I played the original on PS1 and the Playstation store download on PS3; this version is a big improvement on both. The character models are not blurry/fuzzy anymore and I can make out details on them; like, did you know Blank has stitches and frankestein skin going on? The scenery still retails its blurriness/fuzziness though, so a new issue arise, whether you consider this good or bad: treasure boxes and other items of interest have higher detail than the environment around them, which makes them stick out like a sore thumb. The surprises were not ruined for me because I have played through the game before, but I can see a certain spoilery element at work here for new players.
The controls were really annoying at first on the keyboard, but after playing around with the settings, I prefer the keyboard and mouse controls over the original controller. One thing to mention about controls, however, is that the multi-target spells button is the same as the camera rotation buttons, which the game never tells you.
The combat/gameplay was improved as well. The ability to turn off start-of-the-match camera intros cuts time spent on random encounters by nearly half, increasing the pace of what was once a notoriously slow game (I remember running to grab drinks at the start of battles before). I am also very happy with the Max AP setting in the config menu: grinding AP was the worst aspect of this game in the past for me. It was not fun in my opinion to get cool new weapons and armor and be forced to use the weaker/old stuff until you learned the abilities off them.
As for writting and story, FFIX could use some improvement. I found Zidane's "girls, girls, girls, and we are men" personality to be more annoying than funny, but I suppose some players out there found it interesting. There are also several continuity errors where some characters who should not know each other do know each other, like Garnet and Marcus. Despite the fact that Garnet and Marcus only have a brief encounter during the play at the beginning of the game (without introductions no less), they somehow know each other plenty later in the game.

Well, after playing several hours of this game, I think I am now qualified to make a little review about it. I'll make a little pros and cons list to start this off, then add my more detailed opinion afterwards.
Pros:
- The controls are fairly solid and responsive (if you have a computer that doesn't lag too much).
- The magical effects are amazing, so much so that I just want to launch fireballs in all directions just to watch them explode.
- The graphics are superb; the game in itself is a form of eye-candy and makes gameplay all the sweeter.
- The art style (which mostly shows in the cinematics) is brilliant and fits the style of the game quite well.
Cons:
- I found that the game was riddled with glitches, such as my companion character constantly phasing through walls, getting caught on things, and, at one point, going in mid-jump to teleport only to freeze in the air for a while. However, this could just simply be due to my computer and I have not been able to compare this with other's experiences.
- There is very little explanation in the game at all for most things, especially the magic crafting system. I found it to be bizarre and confusing and mostly just wanted to give up on making any spells.
- The game is very linear; while this is not a bad thing in and of itself, it becomes very boredom-inducing when it is coupled with a rather uninteresting story. Half the time, I couldn't even follow the story and was more concerned about figuring out which of the linear paths I was supposed to take to get to the next checkpoint. Which brings me to my next con.
- The checkpoints are placed in odd portions of the game, areas that are too far apart from one another or just bizarre. I found that this irritated me many a time when I died just before the next checkpoint and was sent ALL the way back to the last, which was what felt like half a continent away.
- The gameplay, although fun and engaging at first, quickly becomes mundane due to a lack of diverse enemies and a strange tendency to throw in enemies which seem far too powerful for the level.
In short, I would recommend this game only when the prices is reasonably low. I somewhat regret buying it for however much it was ($40 or so I think) way back when. It's not too bad a game and has some really cool and interesting gameplay mechanics, but lacks in an engaging plot and consistently-entertaining gameplay. But, overall, it's not a must-play by any means.

I got really excited when I frist heard about this "reverse tower defense" or "tower offense" game. I played the first few levels and then it took me YEARS between then and ever feeling motivated to play the game again. I finally did and finished it and to my surprise it's only a couple hours long. Even doing everything I wanted to (bonus missions, mission-specific achievements, etc.) did not add that much time.
But I'm thankful for the short length, because I did not enjoy it.
The game's
is great, but the
is not good. Despite the fact that the game keeps introducing new enemies and units right up through the last mission - which actually sucked because you never had the full system figured out until the very end - I found myself oscillating between two very undesirable points.
The first was more common: most levels were so easy as to be boring, even on higher difficulties. The second was shear frustration: getting stuck. The checkpoint system is totally inconsistent, as in some levels it will repeatedly reward you the same check point an infinite number of times, so that you can just get it as many times as you want, even every 10 seconds. But in other levels you'll go 15 minutes of gameplay without one and then have to reload. Frustraing. Annoying. And because of the set paths and limited resources if you do get a checkpoint late in a hard level where you don't have much money or health or abilities it might actually be impossible to finish the level and you have to restart. Accepting that is a painful process, but in some cases it's the only way forward.
So for such a short game with a cool concept I feel like I got disproportionately frustrated and annoyed.
The icing on the cake is that the story and the dialogue are abysmal.

The original FFIX will forever be listed as one of my favorite games of all time so buying the PC port was literally a no brainer. This port offers many ways to enjoy the game to tailer to new players looking to enjoy the story to old players looking for challenges. There are also two major minigames that this game has that I spend hours enjoying (part of the reason I don't think I could ever do an Excaliber II run)- Card Battles and Chocobo Hot and Cold. There is also an NPC that will randomly quiz you called the Ragtime Mouse so make sure you pay attention to all the small things in the world. It really helps out.
As great as this game is, this port is not without faults. The first would be with the background graphics. Even though the character models are touched up to look a lot smoother, the background looks identical to the PS1 version of the game which can be a little disorienting. Second, I have encounted some weird bugs with timer based activities in the game (mainly the timer not dropping for whatever reason) but that is usually fixed by reloading the game.
Even with those two faults, I feel like this is still an amazing game and if you are a fan of classic JRPGs, this would be one you should not pass up.

Already being a fan of the previous Final Fantasy games (IV~VIII, T), this was my first time on Steam, and playing IX.
Storywise, hard to top my previous faves (VI and VIII), but it was cute and enjoyable. I liked the music and the environment; I remember when it came out, way back when, there was a commotion over "returning to fantasy setting" but it's really more like steam-punk, hah hah. I felt like I was playing Howl's Moving Castle.
I see negative reviews that are really particular about the quality of the port, but since I never played it on PSX, I didn't "miss" anything. The only issues I had was a glitch where the program would hang on a black screen upon entry to battle and I would have to ctrl-alt-del. This occured for me usually a few hours into playing, so if you leave the game and return to it, this may happen. My computer also crashed at the veeeery end. These aren't complains, per se, just my experience as a reminder to SAVE OFTEN!! Call that Moogle!

I guess it could be a good "first" Final Fantasy to introduce someone to the series, moreso for younger players.

This is a very charming game, I really like the design of the world and the characters. The setting of the game feels like it has the most thought put behind it, it doesn’t feel like a jumbled mess like pretty much all the other games in the series before this one. I have yet to play any game in the series released after 9 but so far this is by far my favourite in the franchise (I’ve played and beat 4,6,7 and 8). It’s the first game that I actually like and I think is good. It’s got by far the best story, setting and characters. Characters that I like and that have actual personalities that I find interesting which is a first for me in this series, characters that have good story arc’s and good character development. The writing is very decent, it’s got humor and wit, you understand what the characters are saying and where they are coming from. The dialogue didn’t make me cringe and say to myself wtf am I playing like it did in 7 and 8. I’m praising competency which I shouldn’t be doing but I feel like I have to. The story however gets very convoluted and silly two thirds into the game which is kind of final fantasy tradition honestly and I wish it would stop, I just kind of tuned out for most of it but I did like the ending. The gameplay is very traditional JRPG turn based combat nothing really to say there. In the end it’s a very slow paced JRPG, it’s not a very exciting or entertaining game to play today and the story overall is decent, nothing great. FF9 is a good game and so far the only one in the series that I think is worth playing.

So GRIMOIRE is out. It's a little late, since it was delayed from its original August 1 release date, which was delayed from its June release date, which was delayed from its original March 2013 release date, which was delayed from its 2005 release date, which was delayed from its 2000 release date, which was delayed from its 1997 release date. So it's been a long time coming! In the meantime, Cleve "Neanderthal" Blakemore has espoused his opinions on many things, like game design and black people and the fact that satanists designed television to make women to go crazy and eat Ben and Jerrys Ice Cream and this causes men to become stupid because they can't have sex with women who are eating ice cream so much. It's definitely a real problem, which is explained on his blog here
. Fortunately men playing videogames for 600 hours doesn't affect women or themselves in any way, so Cleve is definitely NOT a hypocrite for making an endless CRPG and that's not a big deal. Phew!
Anyway, I don't want to get sidetracked with discussing Cleve's opinions, like how he thinks Stephen Hawking secretly died and was replaced by a duplicate or that black people are intrinsically stupid. Let's discuss the game! If you are familiar with CRPGs from the late 90s, you know that Wizardry 7 was to many people the pinnacle of game design and dungeon crawling. It's a well-designed product, and stands out from the other games that came out at the time, most of which tried to improve on the formula by adding bad gimmicks or lots of meaningless stats or changing the combat in ways which were detrimental to the experience. For example, FATE "improved" on Wizardry by making everything enormous for no reason, which allowed them to claim 200 hours of gameplay even though most of the world was empty or contained repeats of other areas because they simply didn't have time to make a game that big and put interesting things in all of it. Grimoire fits right into this period of CRPG design, because it's clearly based on Wizardry -- and Wiz7 in particular -- but changes the formula in ways that make it worse.
Let's talk about party composition. Wizardry had six party members. Grimoire has eight! EIGHT IS MORE! IT'S BETTER BECAUSE MORE!!! Anyway eight characters attacking an enemy at once would be a bit much if they remained the same as in Wizardry or Bard's Tale or whatever so as a result Cleve has to weaken party members and buff enemies. The result is over a long term the same balance is maintained, but in the specific case random encounters can simply kill your party members with no recourse and with nothing you could have done to prevent it. This is mostly true early on, of course, before you get spells and skills to mitigate it, and before you grind out the levels to improve your characters. If you're a big Bard's Tale fan you won't mind having your party die for no real reason over and over again early on. Anyone who's used to newer RPG design, or early RPG design in actual good games, should stay away. This ain't Might & Magic; it's more of a Wizards & Warriors. I was originally going to call it Dungeon Lords but that's, frankly, too harsh for this game. Cleve Blakemore may believe that Europeans are genetically predisposed to avoid jaywalking and Americans jaywalk because of all the non-white people poisoning our genes but even he doesn't believe David W. Bradley's Dungeon Lords is good.
Anyway! If you like shoddy Wizardry ripoffs that overpromise on everything but more or less deliver some dungeons and places to explore and items to puzzle over, and you don't mind giving your money to an insane white supremacist, then you should buy Grimoire Heralds of the Winged Exemplar. I can't say you should buy it if you like Wizardry, because those games are too good to really serve as a measuring stick. This is a game for people who have exausted every CRPG series already, for people who struggled through every other game there is. This is a game for people who think insect noises that repeat every half a second, layered for every insect in a six-enemy stack so that they make you want to kill yourself, and which you can't turn off without also turning off the music because apparently coding SFX and BGM meters separately is too hard even for a Neanderthal Supergenius, are good and cool. This is a game for people who like Eye of the Beholder -- not the real one, the GBA one -- or I guess for people who really really hate Aboriginal people. If you fit both those descriptions, buy Grimoire immediately. You will never find another game as perfect for you as this one. Hell, maybe someday Cleve will add custom portraits and you can make everyone look like Pepe or something and then you'll never need to play another game as long as you live! Mazel tov!

I really want to like this game, but the most important thing standing in my way is the interface.
I don't fancy playing in creative, so my view is from the survival aspect. In survival you have to quickly start building a castle and defend it against wave after wave of ever-increasing numbers of attackers. The key word here is quickly.
There is no pause, so you cannot stop and plan your castle out and then set your people to work, so you are instantly stressed. This could be fine if the interface otherwise supported speedy planning and building, but it does not.
The game seems very much built for consoles (or at least using a controller) because it just about only uses the mouse totally disregarding the keyboard for anything but camera navigation. In a game with so many things to build, getting even the simplest things made is a pain.
In order to build anything you have to first click the right mouse button and hold it for about 1 second. Then choose build mode. Then right click and hold for about a second again to get a radial menu where you then select the category of things you want to build and then you can finally select the specific item you want. So even building the simplest little storage box quickly takes 3-4 seconds. If you then want to switch items you want to build, you have to again hold the mouse and go through the waiting once more. In a game where you have 10 minutes before the first wave of attackers and ever less time before the next attacks spending 3-4 seconds per item you want to place into the world will make you frustrated beyond compare.
Again, I love the style and the idea, but the interface just kills it.
It seems like the designers like a sleek no on-screen menu interface so much they are willing to sacrifice a lot to get it. I urge them to reconsider seeing as any amount of waiting for menus in a no-pause survival game is infuriating and stressfull and is bad game design. Please, dear designers, consider adding a toolbar at the bottom and more use of the keyboard so the all the waiting for menus goes away, or at least add a pause function. A pause function would not remove the irritating wait time, but it would remove the infuriating stressfulness.

Ember Strike is a match-3 with some interesting twists. It doesn't do a great job (right now, at least) of explaining how its systems work, but once you get it, it's surprisingly fun. It blends PVP and single player together quite well, rewarding the player for doing both but not neccesssarily requiring both to progress. It does suffer from a few mobile game tropes (like a constantly shaking "BUY GEMS" button at the top of the screen), but as a F2P game, it seems pretty fair. Hopefully with a bit more time in early access, the game will become a bit cleaner and easier to grasp and the F2P elements will stick to time savers and monster chests (which are basically like card packs that can be earned in game or bought a la Hearthstone).

I couldnt decide what to write in this review , so im gonna share with you guys my favorite apple pie recipe Enjoy! :
Pastry
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt
2/3 cup plus 2 tablespoons shortening
4 to 6 tablespoons cold water
Filling
1/3 to 1/2 cup sugar
1/4 cup all-purpose flour
1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg
1/8 teaspoon salt
8 cups thinly sliced peeled tart apples (8 medium)
2 tablespoons butter or margarine
1) In medium bowl, mix 2 cups flour and 1 teaspoon salt. Cut in shortening, using pastry blender (or pulling 2 table knives through ingredients in opposite directions), until particles are size of small peas. Sprinkle with cold water, 1 tablespoon at a time, tossing with fork until all flour is moistened and pastry almost cleans side of bowl (1 to 2 teaspoons more water can be added if necessary).
2) Gather pastry into a ball. Divide in half; shape into 2 flattened rounds on lightly floured surface. Wrap in plastic wrap; refrigerate about 45 minutes or until dough is firm and cold, yet pliable. This allows the shortening to become slightly firm, which helps make the baked pastry more flaky. If refrigerated longer, let pastry soften slightly before rolling.
3) Heat oven to 425°F. With floured rolling pin, roll one pastry round into round 2 inches larger than upside-down 9-inch glass pie plate. Fold pastry into fourths; place in pie plate. Unfold and ease into plate, pressing firmly against bottom and side.
4) In large bowl, mix sugar, 1/4 cup flour, the cinnamon, nutmeg and 1/8 teaspoon salt. Stir in apples until well mixed. Spoon into pastry-lined pie plate. Cut butter into small pieces; sprinkle over filling. Trim overhanging edge of pastry 1/2 inch from rim of plate.
5) Roll other round of pastry into 10-inch round. Fold into fourths and cut slits so steam can escape. Unfold top pastry over filling; trim overhanging edge 1 inch from rim of plate. Fold and roll top edge under lower edge, pressing on rim to seal; flute as desired. Cover edge with 2- to 3-inch strip of foil to prevent excessive browning.
6) Bake 40 to 50 minutes or until crust is brown and juice begins to bubble through slits in crust, removing foil for last 15 minutes of baking. Serve warm if desired.
Enjoy!

Sonic Generations brings the best of old and new sonic games in one nice little bundle.
I thought I would give this game a try considering that I absolutely loved Sonic Adventure and even older sonic games like sonic & knuckles, sonic 3d etc. and boy has this game found a place in my heart ,and exceeded expectations having way more pros to cons.
Pros:
Updated graphics that are way better than '08, adventure, sonic unleashed and many other later sonic games
great level design that means even if you don't go the fastest route you can always get up to there.
artwork and music unlocks from previous sonic games that have been made, it's very cool to see the concept art in any game, and this game is no different
Sonic is back with his witty slapstick humour yet again, most main characters are back to really bring back some nostalgia and thier voice acting is decent and memorable. (Thank goodness they took out Big the Cat and froggy, it was like Knuckles from sonic boom, dull and uninteligent)
the sountracks for each level is composed very nicely and sits well with both modern and older sonic fans.
The casino nights dlc is free (well right now due to a steam summer sale)
The gameplay is fun and enjoyable, and you learn how to be faster at completing stages (levels)
I also liked how when you complete an area it colours it in for you instead of the white monochrome scheme
great modding community, and the mods are of high quality and bring back old stages from other games like Emerald Coast from Sonic Adventure (one of my favourite stages)
no rpg elements to the game like Sonic Adventure (I hated talking to npcs as it would take away from the thrill of fast paced sonic, which is what he is known for)
Cons:
occasional lag due to running too fast and using boost with modern sonic
sometimes I feel like the game just goes too fast to really keep up, like when you first start a stage you want to go fast, but it is a bit hard to focus on where sonic is sometimes, so you'll fly off a cliff or something.
not nearly as many levels as I would have hoped for, sure there is a lot of stuff to collect, but they maybe could have added in some more stuff (thankfully mods add more stuff to the game)
you have to launch steam big picture to configure a controller for the first time then you won't need to open big picture all the time to play Sonic Generations with a controller...
texture issues can occur, like they did in Chemical plant with classic sonic, making it so you can't finish the stage (but was fixed easily by verifying game cache)
not being able to roll in a ball down a hill while jumping with classic sonic like the old sonic games like sonic & knuckles
I strongly recommend this game if you love the old sonic games from the megadrive era, to die hard sonic fans, or even people that enjoyed the new sonic games. It's the perfect harmony between old and new. Really all you have to do now is just practice to go at the speed of sound ;)

Like many, I have waited many years for Grimoire. I have waited many years for a spiritual successor of D.W. Bradley 's Wizardry 6 & 7, and Grimoire is finally here.
Even with some ?BUGS?, my experience with the superdemo from 2015 gives me enough confidence to warmly recommend the game to any old school RPG connaisseurs, or to anyone who wants to travel in the past and delve in a world of high adventure.

Main Menu music is okay but going into configuration menu, turning it to 0 on the music slider, and hitting apply doesn't actually change the music volume.
All of the menus look pretty bad. Something that would be seen in a early access game or early tech demo.
No obvious way to make a new party. The library button seems to be where that is located. The party creation screen itself is extremely simplistic in design. There is no way to save a party, changing heroes is done on a sliding bar, and the list of available portraits is very limited even when it shows Dragon portraits for a human character.
Character creation is tedious and hardly seems worth the time. Compared to other CRPGs this is worse than something from the 90s.
No tooltips on any buttons so you have to just randomly click things to see what they do. The story writing is decent at best. "You wake up and cant remember anything (how original lol) ooh but you feel danger for a second but then you cant even remember that"
Basically every aspect of the interface and menu is awkward to use. The ESC button doesnt exit you from menus and a dozen other things.
Combat is just not engaging at all and really slow. The enemies I ran into didnt even damage my quick start party which all had almost the exact same attack spells. With no manual or explanation of game mechanics at all its just about randomly trying things to see what happens.
The dev claims 600 hours of gameplay and I believe them. It would take you almost half of that just to learn the clunky interface, irrational stats, and random crashes.
All of the graphics are terrible. I don't mean like because its 8 bit or whatever its terrible, I actually like the retro look in games, I just mean its terribly and lazily done. The animations are a joke with things just disappearing or showing a red star shape as a explosion when they disappear which looks like it was pulled out of ms paint.
The starting area is really boring with one or two textures used in the entire thing. its no wonder the game is less than 100mbs, there is very little content here that isnt just text.
Tried to exit to post this review and there isn't even a way to leave the game. No exit button, esc key does nothing, and after clicking on everything on the screen I just gave up and closed it through task manager.
TLDR:
There are so many better games to play out there right now. This one isn't worth the time. The dev promised to deliver a well polished gem but this is a unpolished turd that is hardly different from the super demo he released years ago.

so far the game is pretty tough, even though i chose the easiest difficulty setting. in particular, enemies can disease your characters, or kill them in a few hits (one of my characters started with 1 hp, max), and there doesn't seem to be a way to revive or cure disease at the start. there's no town to return to to get healed, that i can find yet anyway. so i tend to save after every battle in case a battle destroys my party. there are also some things i haven't yet figured out how to do, such as opening a treasure chest that i found, despite being familiar with the genre; i wish there was a manual (maybe there is, but i haven't found it). overall though it seems fun so far despite that (or perhaps because of that, i don't mind games where i need to figure it out as i go along).
EDIT: later on, through reading the forums, i learned how to open treasure chests, how to identify items, and even how to get a really strong fairy npc to join my party in the first area, and how to cure disease, which made the game a lot easier at the start. there really are a lot of interesting secrets in this game, so if you know what you are doing and know about them, the game is a lot easier than it first appears. i also learned that there is in fact a manual being planned, but it's not out yet, supposedly it'll be released next week but with this game's history of delays i'm not sure i'd trust that release date for it.
there are some cumbersome elements to the UI as well. for instance, no way to list 'all spells' that you know, you need to cycle through each of the many elements until you find the one or two spells that you actually know. a way to list all the spells at once, at least at the beginning of the game, would speed up battles enormously.
what seems to be this game's unique point is length and complexity; supposedly it's 600 hours to complete the game from start to finish. i've played rpgs that were 100 hours long, but never a 600 hour one, i want to see if it lives up to that claim.
also, i like that talking to npcs uses a chatbot type system where you type to them and respond. i haven't seen that in a rpg before, it's pretty interesting. it goes beyond a simple keyword-response system that other rpgs used, and feels more like it interprets grammar as well.
one thing i do like is having 8 characters on your party at once; that's pretty rare in rpgs (even dungeon crawlers) and having a party that size is something i've always wanted to see. there are some side effects of that however (such as necessarily making your party members easier to kill and more expendable; perhaps you are expected to create new characters and add them to your party when one dies? who knows). but it's a nice, bold choice, that i'm happy it made, despite its consequences or how difficult it is to balance something like that.
overall, this game is like classic dungeon crawlers, except a lot bigger, more complex, more cumbersome, more confusing, harder (i've heard it called "the dark souls of dungeon crawlers"), and perhaps to some, more interesting. if you have played through the eye of the beholder, bard's tale, and the wizardry games, and liked them and still want more, try this game. if you haven't, play those games first, or perhaps play the grimrock games, which are more recent, easy dungeon crawlers that appeal more to modern tastes.

Before I dig in here, I should probably mention that I got this game in a $5 bundle with some other stuff. So I paid less than a dollar for what normally retails at $40 as of writing. Obviously that allowed me to lower my expectations a ton.
Though deeply flawed and repetitive to the point I almost wondered if the game was joking sometimes, Lichdom: Battlemage managed to do enough to make me enjoy it. It's hyped up and marketed as the next big thing in AAA fantasy gaming but
. It took me a little while to realize it, and it's still fun, but its production values are weirdly out of sync with its overall design and had I bought into hype and pre-ordered this one at full price I'd probably be writing a long-winded rant right now instead. But with the mediocre reviews and huge discount,
. Funny how that works.
It puts its best foot forward with its impressive visuals and professional-quality voice acting, with Troy Baker and Jennifer Hale as the fairly likeable interchangeable player or support characters. It looks poised to set up an interesting revenge story, but that falls apart pretty thoroughly The magic looks and feels good. It's easy to control. I wouldn't say they nailed the "unshackled mage" feel they were going for, but
. At first, the crafting system seems impressively deep, and it's fun to tinker around with it to try out new ways of using each type of sigil until you settle on the playstyle you like. I played around with every different element, crafted hundreds of different spells, and never really settled into using the same strategy until fairly deep in the game.
It does a poor job explaining itself and new players will likely craft themselves into a corner if they don't know what they're doing. Plus, though the illusion of complexity is there, it really is pretty simple when you get down to it. It plays itself up with its elaborate stats and systems, but
, just a different colour. There are some exceptions, like the nifty corruption that grows big gross hives on your enemies rather than just directly damaging or debuffing them, but others are less creative. You can play around and do some cool things, but in the end the most effective strategy was just debuffing the enemy to take more damage then fireballing their face off. What could have been a drawn-out battle using corruption and necromancy or other more interesting elements became just zap, boom, dead, over and over.
And the battles being over fast was a very good thing, I eventually found. The game is pretty long, and not because it's loaded with ideas. The levels are pretty, but they go on for ages, walking you from room to room, spawning the same enemies on you a hundred times, with no unique strategies ever required other than exploding them all yet again. With level design that's basically corridor, room battle, corridor, repeat,
. The same enemy types keep appearing all throughout the whole game, with the same annoying battlecries shouted at you each time, going down to the same spells, every time. A bit of exploring is possible with some hidden secrets and extra optional fights to get you more crafting loot, but the game doesn't have many ideas other than "use spells to defeat enemies!"
Though I had fun for the first few hours, the repetition really sets in after a while.
, welcoming the same enemies so I could try a new strategy on them. But once I found a setup much more effective than others I tried, combat was a bore, and crafting was a pain. They were just things I had to do to get them out of the way, which is bad, because that's all the game actually has you doing. I'd groan when new enemies would spawn in, and eventually was tired of spellcrafting to the point I just kept using the same ones, using the (not very) smart inventory system to handle the upgrades for me.
I guess this doesn't exactly sound like a recommendation so far, but it's still a game that's worth trying and a worthy purchase at the deep discount I got it for. I've seen it sell for 90% off during Steam sales, and it's worth those four bucks. You'll have fun and enjoy the scenery and fancy magic explosions even if you don't ever end up finishing it. The performance for a game like this minimal really shouldn't be bad, but it bogs down after only a few minutes. That makes it even more difficult to play.
Even worse, the AI is frustratingly dumb. In a game like this, I would've fixed and polished that first, even if the UI wasn't ready. The little workers spend way too much time in a stupor when time is often of the essence. When they do work, it's often not very efficient. They can build themselves and others into a corner. Stockpiles can fill up with worthless junk while the vaulables sit untouched nearby. Often they fill up the nearest stockpile instead of the most full, giving you a bunch of half-full and unusable piles. One missed or misplaced block (or even one closed door) can render an entire castle useless.
Just needs way more polish and actual listening to feedback. With the updates coming every few months and not really seeming to do much, I wouldn't hold out much hope. Avoid this and go buy something fun.

This review is going to be a little biased.  Final Fantasy is really the series that took my RPG virginity.  I'd played the original Zelda once before at my cousins house but I dont really count that game as I got nowhere and never had the time to explore.  I played through FF9 several times on the PlayStation 1 before purchasing it on here and with that said here we go.
It was difficult to get accustomed to the updated character models in tandom with the original backdrops but after the first hour or so it stopped bothering me and I started to enjoy seeing these great, well designed characters in greater detail.  I have yet to see any porting issues or controller delays.  The game, other than the character model upgrades and autosave feature, is pretty much the exact same one as the original PS1 release from what Ive been able to tell.  Its also nice to have the option to speed up the game when your trying to grind levels or to turn off encounters after you've had your fill of combat and leveling for a while and want to go get other things done.  Random encounter rate does seem to have been turned down slightly from what I can tell.  Combat is unchanged in all of its Active Time Battle glory.  Up to four characters can complete a party.  Each character is his/her own class with their own set abilities which I've always found more compelling that just making each character do everything.  Abilities are learned from equipping weapons, armor, etc. and need to accrue enough points from battle to fully learn that move before being able to still know that ability when changing that piece of equipment out for something else.  Great characters help fill out a world with a lot of personality and intrigue.  Great storyline as well which is expected from not just JRPGs in general but the Final Fantasy series as a whole...mostly(A discussion for another day).  Soundtrack is amazing as Nobuo Uematsu delivers yet another masterfull piece of work to help bring the game even more alive.  If you enjoy the oldschool JRPG formula of grinding, deep story and vibrant living characters, searching out hidden sidequests you will love this game.  I know I do.  Highly recomment this as I think its among the best in the series and the genre.

I love replaying one of my favorite Final Fantasy games. This game was the culmination of all of Squaresoft's hard work on Final Fantasy from 1 - 8. They truly mastered the craft of Final Fantasy.
