FTL is a great rogue like game that features many creative, interesting, and "evil" gameplay elements
FTL is a space based top-down roguelike game where you take the place of the crew of the spaceship that is fleeing the advances of the rebel fleet. Where you jump from beacon to beacon, making decisions at the beacon
Do i fight this person? Will i gain supplies i need from him by defeating him or letting him live? CAN i even fight them?
You gain scrap, the in game currency, fuel, used to jump from beacon to beacon, missiles, used to fire projectile based weaponry, and drone parts, used to activate drones. All of which can be used as currency if the event demands it.
You can easily target enemy ships where you want to hit, and pause the game!... its better than it sounds, as you can do things such as moving crew locations, opening/closing doors, targeting, and panicking, also planning.
You can customize your ship, set crew to man specific parts of the ship to increase their skill, and aid your ships skills. You can upgrade ship systems, buy power bars to power more of the ship at once (there isnt enough to power the entire ship, so you need to ration power, and decide what needs it the most). you can go to shops and buy fuel, missiles, drone parts, repair your ship, buy augments that passively affect your ship without needing power, buy systems that become a room on your ship and need power, like a clone bay, that unless turned off or destroyed, allows your crew to come back from death, albiet with a minor hit to all their skills.,or buy weapons, to more efficiently destroy things, buy drones to defend your ship, repair your ship, or attack the enemy! Buy crew members so you can have more people on your ship ready to assist in repairs, fighting enemies, or boarding enemy ships!
You can jump to the end of a system after passing through enough beacons, and being in one piece, and go to the next sector, which can be a various set of things. It can be civillian controller, safer, but smaller scrap turnouts, and weaker ships. It could be hostile, higher scrap turnouts, and stronger ships. It could be nebulas, which can house deadly aliens that use the blinding fog of nebular gas against you, with the ability to mind control, hack, and see without scanners, allowing more useful systems to be added. And at the very end of that list of sectors, you have taped your ship back together, smacked your crew on the face and told them to roll up their intestines and get back to their posts, and get ready for the LAST STAND.
The federation base, almost completely taken over by the rebel advances, but, there is something waiting for you...
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR
FTL is a roguelike top-down space based battle game where you fight enemies, collect resources, and upgrade your ship to fight in the next sector, housing stronger better enemies. With lots of customization, randomly generated worlds every game, your sure to die in a new, differently infuriating way every time!
Id greatly reccomend this game, its relatively short, at most 1-2 hour playthroughs, but usually ending in under an hour. It provides great fun and challenging gameplay that has seem to be lost with newer generations of gaming, but not so hard that you never want to play it again.

This game was one of the first ones on my mind once I built my PC, due to custom zombies maps. After playing the same maps time and time again on console, the sheer variety and creativity of the maps available make this game nearly timeless. The graphics for a late 2000's release are pleasing enough to look at, and optimization was done well. Very rarely have I ever experienced a frame drop either in single player, zombies, or multiplayer. There are a few issues however. Controller support is available but it must be done through the console commands and even after enabling a game pad, the aiming and movement feels off slightly. Also, there is about a 70% chance your game will crash to the desktop after hosting a co-op match with friends, this was never fixed, so after 10 years I doubt it ever will be haha. Over all I recommend this game to anyone looking for some addicting zombie wave survival. It goes on sale for cheap quite often, too.

Let's go a bit more in-depth into why this game failed. It wasn't because flaws in the mechanics. It wasn't because it offered too little content for play. It was because error after error made on the publisher/developer ends.
1) The product did not meet what was expected of it by its marketting. Everything I heard about this game up until release was that it was 'kungfu-souls'. I purchased it under the belief that it was going to be a game of Dark Souls' length with a story of Dark Souls' quality. That aesthetic is really just a shell for a PvP fighting game, with PvP in-fact being your primary means of progression.
2a) The core design failed upon release due to technical (mostly server) issues. The servers are down so often they may as well be non-existent. The online play has been inoperable for the first three days since launch, and the multiplayer is what the game is primarily designed around. Even the PvE 'singleplayer' experience fails to work as the combat is designed with 1v1 fights in mind, the mitigating factor for being ganged up on by multiple AI opponents being the constant online play in the style of Destiny's instancing system (but with open PvP).
2b) Performance issues, bugs, crashes, etc. I've had times where I've walked past a zone transition only for the next zone to not fully load in and I fall beneath the terrain and become stuck.
3) The PvE content on its face only takes 2-5 hours to complete on a blind run, much quicker if you know where you're going. You travel across around maybe 6 or so very compact (yet somewhat maze-like) interconnected zones before you've seen pretty much all the game has to offer. After defeating all the bosses you can progress in your PvP 'combat trials' ranking and then rechallenge the bosses at higher difficulty levels. See the previous paragraph.
4) The PvE difficulty curve seems unfair/uneven. The PvE enemies scale with you as you level up after you defeat the final boss for the first time. This isn't very noticeable by statistics, they all seem to have the same health and damage, but the AI becomes more and more difficult to overcome. By time I was level 50, the AI seemed to counter anything I could throw into it.
Hopefully this game gets some TLC in the post-launch future because it isn't simply a bad game. It's more of a good idea made mediocre by what seems to be countless errors on the dev's part.
-------
I'll also explain more what I meant with my fourth point and why it seems like an oversight. Combat in Absolver plays out very defensively. Most of the time both you and the opponent want to focus on defense and counter-attack instead. As the AI difficulty goes up, things seem to hit a plateua. Both you and the AI will circle around in guard mode. If you try to use a guard break move, they will parry it (or dodge/absorb) and counter attack. So you just have to bait them out to attack. But the AI seems to read your inputs and will use feinting to animation cancel out of an attack if you try to parry them. So the battles become stagnant and end up lasting way too long. This may just be an oversight with my chosen starting style (Forsaken) because I had much more luck when switching to Stagger as its defensive moves come out near instantly rather than having a significant delay like Forsaken's Parry.
-------
Let's dig into the PvP somewhat, now that the servers are actually online. It's -crap-. People will say it's full of 'skill' and that you just need a fast reaction time. They're wrong. All you need to do it set up a cheap build. There are two meta builds right now that will carry you in PvP. First is just a set that link Jab and Hook with an alternative guard break that links back to your Jab and Hook sequence.
The second is a build to counter the Jab and Hook meta by using a combo of any of the faster 'low' attacks which will dodge 'high attacks' (which most attacks fall into beyond that).
Though the even truer meta is the 'developers that dont understand server management' build in which the netcode is so unstable neither player can hit eachother and become trapped forever in a 1v1 duel arena that only the Alt+F4 combination attack can free you from.

Reign: Conflict of Nations -  A game of " what ifs?"
Its there to offer gamers interested in historical eastern Europe a Strategy game -unlike fantasy worlds this is a harsh climate, the struggle is almost constant but not the fault of its game mechanics. It is missing minor production values and nuances of older games than itself but overcomes this through its choice of nations and almost endearing ruleset.

I do have to admit that the GUI and Stain Glass/Manuscript art  is genuine and of quality. The game knows what it is implying and does so directly without notice of any shortcomings. To relive the Renaissance and Reformation era as Monarch/Head of State of an Eastern European Principality with very accurate names and maps is done adequetely.
Its where the game ends is the drop off. At 1650 the game ends with one popup window describing my loss due to not being as formidable as other leaders, a pity since I was established at top ranking of every nation on the statistics window in game of every category, OK I wasn't maxed out at Diplomatic relations, that is because I had taken over half the map and ran out of people to truance with. In my mind...I won.

First the dissapointment of doing all this hard work with nothing to show, not even a summary throughout the years. I had lasting family dynasties, many brutal conflicts, trustful allies, great enemies, miserable generations, fascinating trades. Not even a list of every leader I had, at least, in a time frame would have let me remember fondly my hours into it.
The game also misses some points  when - someone dies of say,old age. They sure tell you someone has passed away, but who it was and what their duties were in your vast empire, are up to you to remember where you positioned them, needing to check if there is a deficiency in your nation and replace him. The names sound alike over the years and portaits are reused. Confusing.
Great Music  sticks with you throughout the day, and classical guitar. Only a handful of songs play throughout complementing the state of your province, they are good/great - I claim great.
The game is simply simple that meanders into deep engaging and addictive gameplay. I am a fan. High difficulty in that most everything has a cause and effect. Want to boost farming? well be ready to lose out on gold and research for around 6 seasons. Want to buff Research for some seasons, well every other nation gets some too. Things conflict. This is where I now see my misfortunes in my personal game. Poland, historically suffered tragedy in the timeline when this game nears its end. I should have devoted more time at the start of my campaign in the spread of my empire as there was impossible odds against my nation from constant robbers, and instant takeovers by rebel nations and dark times on the regular after roughly the late 1500s. That is the type of attention to detail that I respect from this thought provoking experience. What if this game had a higher budget? I am leaning towards the developers putting out precisely the game they had envisioned.

This game's simplicity seems to be the cause of its excellence. That is, the game is uncomplicated enough that you can easily see the results of your choices: Maybe you need a unit with longer range? Maybe a different path through the environment would help? Maybe trading some firepower for a shield unit really is the way to go? Maybe the shortest path isn't actually the best one?
In all cases, the feedback loop between your choices and game outcomes is short, easy to parse, and fun. When you do make a fatal mistake, the punishment is rarely so high that you become frustrated. Also, the game's "macro" pacing seems excellent. There's always a new tower or new twist to adapt to, and yet there's also always time to get a handle on the new problem. The game beautifully manages to act as its own tutorial without giving you the feeling that it's all strange or forced.
From my perspective, the developers show real genius in their ability to polish and present a "low budget" concept. The game could have felt cheap - but it doesn't.

What the game looks like:
Mysterious Director X is collecting fresh faced talent to star in his new movie. He is notorious for going overboard to get the results he wants. You plus 7 other hopeful actors are in the running to get the role of a life-time, if you have what it takes to take on/out the competition. This is the abridged version of what is written on the store page for the game.
One of the game's listed key features is , "Be a deceitful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! Flush your enemies in the toilet, crash their heads on their plates when they eat, do whatever it takes to maim and kill other competitors in nasty and unexpected ways! "
After reading all of this plus watching the trailer, I'm stoked. I assume I'm going to be getting a game that's somewhere between The Haunting: Starring Polterguy and Tecmo's Deception. The player must decide the most inventive, zany, creative ways to kill off the competition. You're given the option to use environmental executitions OR just go at them with whatever weapon you find lying around.
What the game actually is:
The humor and story of the trailer is no where to be found in the beginning "cut-scene" as you are treated to a 30 second text and still-image intro. No dialouge yet. It tells a vague story of a director who made movies so graphic that they HAD to be real. Do you want to be a star? This is where I started to get concerned.
I'm taken to the main menu, trying to figure out my options as an annoying as F**K voice over spouts taglines on repeat. Think Spider-Man based on the 2000 film "Did I hurt your tusky wusky", except more frequently.
After messing around with the various game modes in Arcade mode I realize that the game is nothing more than a "theme shooter". There is no story mode, no plot or linear gameplay. One of the best Sonic games since the classic and dreamcast era. As with all Sonic games on steam, it is recommended you play with a controller, but you can use keyboard as well. Sonic Generations is an amazing experience, letting you play with both Classic Sonic and Modern Sonic - Classic is your standard 2D platformer, running through zones, collecting rings, and bashing up badniks. Modern, on the other hand, is a mix of 2D platforming and a 3D fast-paced run, boosting through loops and performing tricks through colourful rings.
The game takes zones from all of Sonic's games, from
, and allows you to run through them from the two different angles of Sonics. Not only that, you fight a variety of bosses from each area,
.
If that isn't enough for you, then throughout each level in both versions (Classic and Modern) there are 5 red rings to collect and thousands of missions to complete.
If you really want more, then there is a section of Generations which is the modding side. Although not akin to the original game, modding allows the game to not only look nicer but run levels that normally wouldn't be in the game, for example the Unleashed Project which adds all the day stages from Sonic Unleashed (to be honest this was the reason I bought the game on PC, since I already own the game for both 3DS and Xbox 360)
All in all, Sonic Generations is a celebration of Sonic's history and is well worth the buy. Add it to your collection today, and start running through those zones at the speed of sound.

One of my favorite RPGs, this title is easily a 9/10 for me when it comes to plot, characters, and mechanics.
My background with Final Fantasy: My first of the series was FF8, which I enjoyed at the time and have since thought "meh." I've also played 7, 10, and 13 (*hate* 13). I played the spinoff Crisis Core in full, have some experience with Tactics and VI, and have seen a full playthrough of 15. VII and IX are tied for my favorites.
+++
+ Compatible with a controller, including accurate button prompts! (This is such a huge deal when compared to the FF7 port.) Plug and play, no extra setup required.
+ IX has a really enjoyable cast of characters. I feel they're unique, and this isn't a game where I find myself making parallels between them and other games in the franchise.
As I replay, I'm reminded how often you don't have a choice of party members. It's predetermined because all of the characters have a role to play and are busy with their own tasks. To me, this is an advantage to character and plot development.
+ I hadn't thought about it until replaying, but this is a rare cast that includes several non-humans, and the world itself is full of diverse species.
+ Turn-based battle system is familiar to its era, but with some alternative mechanics to vary it up. I like the ability system, actually... though it can be frustrating.
Abilities must be learned through various equipment (maybe 0-3 things a character can learn on each item). Characters cannot use all equipment nor learn all possible abilities (e.g. summoning is limited to two characters; steal is available to one main character and three temporary characters). Learning abilities will take place at different times. For example, it's not until late "Disk 2" that an armor makes it possible for Zidane to learn "ability up."
+ The plot flows together well and draws on all playable characters - and very enjoyable secondary characters - to make a cohesive story and rich world. As I replay, I'm remembering how much of the story centers on choice and finding one's place.
+ Chocobo mini-game "hot and cold" is both worthwhile and not nearly as arduous as, say, the infamous FF7 chocobo breeding.
+ Card game is super simple to learn and easy to play. No real rewards, except card-collecting, though.
+ Moogles!
---
I've had with the Steam edition: Very randomly, out of the blue, a battle won't load - music plays appropriately, border is still present, but the center is black as if the game forgot to do its little spin-in to start up. In the ~35 hours I've played, this has happened 10-15 times. Annoying as hell, but not game-breaking. Until I remembered that the PC has checkpoints ("continue" option), I dreaded how this would affect things. However, between the continue option and my own obsessive saving, it's a mild problem. The biggest annoyance, actually, is the lack of a soft re-set.
1) Keep in mind that the checkpoints seem to occur whenever you enter a new screen. Use the "continue" option to your advantage.
2) If you're like me and grind for XP and AP, make sure you save fairly frequently on the world map. The checkpoint there is only for your first entrance so it's easy to lose everything.
- As mentioned above, lack of a soft reset or ability to go back to the main screen.
- While the character models have been nicely updated, the backgrounds can really look like crap in comparison. It would have been nice to see those cleaned up a little.
- Jump-rope mini-game. Screw it.
- Not a big complaint, but I would have liked to be able to do a purposeful save between "disks" rather than count on the checkpoint system.
I feel like this game has been highly under-rated since it came out. Certainly it won't be for everyone (the party system and ability system is semi-limited in terms of choices), but don't let its sort of cutesy graphics fool you. There's a lot going on with the characters and plot.

I really wanted to love this game.  The primary promise of the developers, to break away from the the typical, "wizards are fragile" paradigm is a really appealing one, and frankly, far more in line with most of the popular fantasty stories out there.
But, Lichdom:  Battle mage doesn't deliver the fantasy of a powerful battlemage, as promised.  The biggest reason for this is that enemies absorb too much damage before going down.  How am I to believe that I am a baddass when random moster x takes three hits from my fire spell before going down.  Have you ever played a FPS, scored a headshot on a human, with a .50 caliber rifle, and then watched him return fire?  It feels silly, and that was how a great deal of this game felt for me.
I am pretty sure that the shield system is supposed to make you feel more powerful, by giving you an alternative to retreating from enemies while you charge a spell, but the feedback from that style of spell is poor, and so it is difficult to know when you are "doing it right."
The result for me, is that I found myself giving up on the shield system and just back pedaling from monsters as I tossed (too many) spells at them until they dropped.  This was tedious, and made and certainly did not make me feel like the badass spellslinger that I thought I was going to be.
Other issues are also frequent.  The game does not seem to be well optimized in terms of performance.  I find that my system chugs while playing this game, wheras I can play other, more graphically intense games with no trouble.
The gameplay starts to feel reptitive, as while there ARE technically thousands upon thousands of spells to create, most of them are just minor variations on each other.  This fire spell has a bigger area, this one burns for longer, that one has a stronger impact, et cetera.  There is little motivation to create lots of varied spells, as most enemies can be approached in exactly the same way.  Hence the tedium.
If Magicka, Skyrim and Dark Souls had a threesome then Lichdom Battlemage would be the resulting love-child.

, A.K.A. 20th century GTA, is a really awesome game which exceeded my low expectations.
Its strongest quality is the story. Characters, voice acting and the dialogue were on point. It had great jokes, intense moments and tragic events. The
is highly comparable to GTA just in different time period and with no side activities. Fist fights are simple, cinematic but a little bit repetitive as every NPC fights the same. Driving wasn't appealing to me as I was using a keyboard. I strongly believe that it's better for joystick users. In spite of this, I loved the design of cars and the fact that you have to fix the engine if you crash hard into something. Furthermore, interactions with the police are more thoughtful in this game. They'll chase you if you hit somebody or even drive too fast. You may pay fines, bribe or resist them. If you're on the run and want to completely lose the cops you must change your license plate and clothes.
Lastly, I really loved the small details that were in this game. People are slipping on the snow and falling on the ground, random guy offers you a shoe shine in the park, radio broadcasting recent events in Europe during WW2 and more. It fully represents its time period with appropriate clothes, vehicles and music. In the midst of the game you'll experience a time-skip which will change the environment and will bring in new vehicles.

TL;DR:
This is a simplified, faster-paced successor to The Ship. If you're not familiar with that, think of it as a cartoony, multiplayer Hitman game for 8 players/bots on small maps. It can be a Bloody Good Time, but unfortunately, it has just 3 maps and suffers from dumb bots, a lack of instructions and some cheap weaponry.
Full review:
Bloody Good Time is a simplified, faster-paced successor to The Ship, which isn't surprising because it's from the same developer. The meat-and-potatoes of this game is called "the hunt", a gamemode requiring you to murder a different target each round, all while avoiding guards, cameras and your own hunter. To do this, you can pick from a large roster of weapons spawned throughout the map, each with a randomly-assigned star value which changes every round. This means you have to pick up new weapons often in order to stay on top of the scoreboard. Whoever has the most stars at the end of 12 rounds wins the game. In addition, you'll find "murder aids", which do just what their name implies; they can either be used to assist you in a murder or to defend yourself in a bad situation. There's a glue gun to freeze someone for a few seconds, a holographic decoy to mislead your hunter, even a camera to steal stars. You also have to take care of your "needs" - sleeping, pooping and eating, respectively - and if any of these gets too low, it lowers your speed, defense and strength. You're pretty much defenseless while taking care of these needs, but when fully refilled, they give you an added stat boost. There are also traps littered around each map and while difficult to pull off, the reward is high.
Your target moves all around the map during the round, indicated on your HUD's mini-map by a red crosshair if they're off-screen or a flashing yellow area if they're in proximity. Each gives you an indication of the area they're in, rather than an exact position. This is another important thing the game fails to explain. Also indicated on the map are weapon spawns with different colors indicating star values, and when one of your needs is low, places to take care of them also pop up there.
Every few rounds of "the hunt", the director throws in a random mode to mix things up. "Scene stealer" grants you stars by holding an award and you're defenseless as the other players try to take it from you. "Hunt the leader" pits everyone against the 1st place player in an attempt to level the playing field again. "Infection" is like a game of tag where the infected must bump into a clean player to pass on the disease, then avoid the same happening to them. "Deathmatch" is a free-for-all - also a gamemode of its own - allowing you kill anyone for stars; just don't get caught by the guards or cameras. Besides "the hunt", you have the aforementioned "deathmatch" and "revenge" gamemodes. Revenge first assigns you a random target, but the more you kill, the more will be pursuing you.
The graphics are cartoonish and fitting and the characters, maps and weapons all adhere to that style, which works in BGT's favor. But not all is well in BGT. It took me two sessions to actually enjoy start enjoying it and it seems I'm not alone. It has a "how to play" section, but could have really benefitted from a tutorial level. Far too little is explained, resulting in confusion and frustration for new players. It does explain how certain weapons and murder aids are used when you first equip them, but fails to explain things like when it's ok to kill someone in self-defense, which is a massive oversight.
The bots are dumb; even when I played on hard difficulty the first time, not really trying to maximize my stars, I ended up beating them by a stretch. The main problem is they seem to pick up whatever weapons they stumble across, not caring about their value. Therefore, this game is best played with friends.
But despite that, getting killed by bots often feels unfair, thanks to a plethora of unfair weapons. The bat, frying pan, tazer and more freeze you in place once hit and though they take several hits to kill you, there's no window of opportunity between them for you to retaliate. Bots also activate traps with literally no one in their proximity, ruining your chances to actually make use of them because they need a moment to recharge.
The game also suffers from having too many controls and not explaining how useful they are. FYI, you only need shoot, use, draw/holster, switch hotslot, change weapon and change murder aid.
I've had a lot of fun with Bloody Good Time, but a fair amount of frustration as well. The lack of maps is a big obstacle to its replayability, but that could have been added as well as some balancing changes. It's too bad Outerlight Ltd went under because both The Ship and BGT did some things very well, pulling off unique, yet flawed visions of multiplayer murder mayhem.

Sonic Generations is critically acclaimed. Many Sonic fans call it the glorious return of good Sonic games. I’m not quite a super Sonic fan myself, but I’d say I enjoy my fair share of games like Sonic. That being said, I’m lukewarm on Sonic Generations. Perhaps I just don’t get it, but I’ll detail my experience so you can be the judge.
Sonic Generations is composed of two playstyles. Classic Sonic is pure 2D platforming where you use things like ramps to launch off of or gain speed from. Modern Sonic mostly plays like a game where you run down hallways with occasional 2D sections thrown in. For gameplay, I think Classic Sonic is fun. You’re constantly in control and you gotta manage your speed to make sure you don’t make a potentially-fatal mistake. Modern Sonic is…lackluster. I suppose the main appeal of it is to feel fast, but that’s the only joy it seems to offer. They aren’t bad and you still do stuff in them like dodge things and homing attack enemies which can be fun, but I suppose it doesn’t really feel like you’re playing much of a game. The 2D platforming sections are alright, but I don’t quite understand why they exist when Classic Sonic exists alongside the fact that they kill the whole ‘going fast” feeling I thought they were going for with Modern Sonic.
A problem with this game is that, for the main section, it’s very short. You only have nine levels (18 when splitting the two Sonics, of course) and seven bosses peppered in (which are actually pretty solid overall). The levels are pretty long and don’t overstay their welcome in length, at least. Even then, it felt like I should’ve only been a fraction of the way through the game by the time I reached the final boss (which is dreadfully tedious). However, don’t be alarmed! The game makes up for this short story mode with a ton of extra missions for both Sonics. These extra missions aren’t just going through a level with a specific task. They usually have their own stages with fun and unique twists on objectives. You’re actually required to pick a few every so often to progress the story, but I personally think they’re my favorite part of the game.
As for the story itself, it’s terrible. Not even funny-bad like a lot of aspects like, say, the Sonic Adventure games. The only really enjoyable parts to me where Classic Sonic’s reactions to things and the Eggmans. The rest was just groaning and wishing it was just a collection of levels instead. Thankfully, you most likely wouldn’t be playing this game for the story even if it was good, so it’s not a dealbreaker or anything.
In the looks department, Sonic Generations is gorgeous. The Classic Sonic levels look great, but I think the environments and effects really pop in the Modern Sonic levels. The soundtrack is great throughout as well, and the remixed tracks are really done justice (even if I much prefer the original City Escape).
I’d say Sonic Generations is good, but not as great as many people say. Classic Sonic is fun but I kinda wish he had more levels. I’m just not a fan of Modern Sonic’s playstyle, but for what it is it still works for parts of his levels and the looks. The Missions are plentiful and unique for an extensive and fun postgame. And, of course, the game looks, sounds, and plays great with no glitches or troublesome controls (though I’d play on a controller). I wouldn’t write this off just because of the negatives I brought up, especially since there are plenty of other people that adore this game and you might disagree with what’s fun or not. I think the takeaway is that the game is enjoyable and worth playing, but don’t expect it to be flawless.

Controls are sloppy and all over the place. Level designs emphasize speed without telegraphing what is and is not a hazard. Hitboxes and timing seem inconsistent. "Classic" Sonic feels comfortable platforming in the early remixed zones, but feels like he's platforming on rails in the later zones. "Modern" Sonic works well in parts, but the game never really explains or shows off how to use moves that it then expects you to master at later portions of the game. It does, however, natter on endlessly with unhelpful "advice". Bosses and Rival fights can only be taken on as one Sonic, making the switching mechanic feel hollow.
The story is shallow and annoying; it would have been better to have unvoiced cutscenes without trying to explain anything. The final boss confrontation was a sloppy mess, where there wasn't any clear indication of what was going on, and everything looked like a technicolor nightmare. If anything, the game felt like a series of quick-time event cutscenes with a dash of mediocre platforming thrown on top. Blundering through stages at top speed while making countless mistakes still earned "A" and "S" ranks on most levels.
The only thing this game really served was to highlight how tacky and uninspired the modern Sonic stages felt. And because the stages are all taken from different games, there was no real connection between them, meaning the game was all over the place tonally and thematically. Unless you're a die-hard Sonic fan, I'd stay away... and even if you are a die-hard Sonic fan, why don't you just play the original games themselves?

Frankly, I love this game, and it's not just because I can be kind of a sucker for this kind of style.
It's a really well made platformer that allows you to play it in many different ways. If you don't  like the story or how it's told, just start it in Classic mode, and you don't have to sit through it (not my recomendation, ya ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥). I also love how the cutscenes are done with the same sprites as in game, taking many of the poses available during gameplay, and it reminiscent of older games (even if, or rather especially, when it doesn't fit perfectly, like when they crouch to bow. Carol's basically doing push-ups)
Levels aren't strictly linear (they tend to have multiple paths or at least places to explore), so you can try to search every nook and cranny for secret cards that unlock sound clips, music, and concept art, or you can just try to blaze through them as fast as you can, or even try for a survival run. The game also present a good amount of challenge, even on normal difficulty. While you might not have to particularly try during most of a level, there are bosses that will kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you don't focus. It was never unfair, tho, and they are proper bosses, where you have to use different moves and tactics, as well as, of course, get their pattern down.
The sprites and artwork are just phenomentally done. The character sprites are very finely made, expressive and there's lots of little details that gives the game more charm. Like how Lilac's eyes just turn into 1 dot pupils when you try to abruptly stop from running at high speeds, or how Carol is stuggling to hold herself AND her bike up while hanging form something (which to me just makes her seem like a badass. If she had a normal facial expression I'd be like "yeah, sure, of course she can do that, it'd be stupid do take away a gameplay mechanic in favor of another one when you don't need to". Like this she seems like an actual character)
While most of the soundtrack isn't 'catchy' enough to have you whistling it in your sleep, per se, It is still pretty great. I deffinitely see myself using some of it as background or fight music for, say, a D&D game.
Multiple playable characters (and a couple exclusive cutscenes to them) make sure that there's replay value, and the levels are well made to accomodate for them (the shared ones, anyway. The characters have a level unique for them). And that's before you try the different playstyles I mentioned earlier.
As anything (except my opinion, of course), it's not perfect. It is a bit silly how you can run verticaly or upside down at a snail's pace, but that's probably cause it'd be annoying if you had to walk back to get a running start or add needless things to think about in level design.
The voice acting, while pretty decent, could have been better, particularly Carol's lines. And I can deffinitely see how some people might think the story and cutscenes are cheesy (I enjoyed it, screw you)
And this might be a resolution issue (haven't tested it out to make sure), but sometimes during cutscenes, the text can get out out the dialogue box.
All in all: excellent game, clearly made with lots of passion and effort, recommend it for anyone and everyone.

As years go by, we tend to have a more globalized society, with friends and family members living in different countries, and that is indeed a great step forward. And Project Lounge, is Globalization, in a game form.
With that said, you may be wondering, 'why?'. Project Lounge is a game where you can create unique 'Lounges' which may vary from a simple house, to a whole islands, skyscrapers, mountains, beaches, anything YOU want!
So, your imagination is the limit. And the most unique innovation that Project Lounge brings, is the ability of interaction of literally anything. ANY object, ANY furniture, ANYthing.   Taking that into consideration, inviting your friend to your lounge, is like having him to visit you at your own house. You'll be able to chat, enjoy a cool environment of your choice, play around with draw-boards, Arcade machines, sport balls(soccer, basketball, etc).
The interaction doesn't stop there, using the Steam inventory feature, each one of you can carry your own objects to each lounge you visit. So each world you go, it's most likely to be UNIQUE, since each player has their own objects, and their own creativity.
You are also able to share your lounges so other players can download them, so if you find some place nice for you and your friends to hang out? Go ahead and download it!
Project Lounge is not limited to having only friends in your lounge, you also have the option of setting your lobby public, so you will start meeting people from around the globe, and start interacting with them on your lounge. It's like meeting new people, and having a good time, with strangers, friends, family... Anyone you want, directly from your PC.
Character creation ATM is still only limited to choosing your character's color, however, I believe that would be an astonishing thing to come in future updates.
Long story short, Project Lounge is still a Project as the name says itself, but it has a lot more than just potential. Project Lounge is able to bring all of your friends together, alongside(or not) with strangers, to a meeting, a party, a parkour track, social games. The sky is the limit for Project Lounge. If you are looking for a game to have fun with your friends,or meeting some new friends, do not hesitate to buy it.

, A.K.A. 20th century GTA, is a really awesome game which exceeded my low expectations.
Its strongest quality is the story. Characters, voice acting and the dialogue were on point. It had great jokes, intense moments and tragic events. With an even pace and a cliffhanger ending this is one of the best story based games out there. Even for me, who doesn't really enjoy movies and shows about mafia, it was a truly enjoyable ride.
The
is highly comparable to GTA just in different time period and with no side activities. Fist fights are simple, cinematic but a little bit repetitive as every NPC fights the same. Gun fights are a different story. There's a good amount of guns to use and the mechanics aren't exaggerated with overcomplicated features. It's fun, what can I say? Besides, there are some stealth for our dear ninjas out there too.
Driving wasn't appealing to me as I was using a keyboard. I strongly believe that it's better for joystick users. In spite of this, I loved the design of cars and the fact that you have to fix the engine if you crash hard into something. Furthermore, interactions with the police are more thoughtful in this game. They'll chase you if you hit somebody or even drive too fast. You may pay fines, bribe or resist them. If you're on the run and want to completely lose the cops you must change your license plate and clothes.
Lastly, I really loved the small details that were in this game. People are slipping on the snow and falling on the ground, random guy offers you a shoe shine in the park, radio broadcasting recent events in Europe during WW2 and more. It fully represents its time period with appropriate clothes, vehicles and music. In the midst of the game you'll experience a time-skip which will change the environment and will bring in new vehicles.

This game is fairly good for its price, beat the game in the time you can see by this review and profile. I believe there is more to come for this game but the way it is currently the game is fun, it did push the limits of my current PC which is fine but nothing too unbearable/unplayable. People I have met thus far into my playing experience are helpful for the most part, I know some people will try to kill you but I think it was because my HP was fairly low and they just wanted to replenish what I lost. So in a way they are still helping you out. Hopefully there will be more to come since this game is rather enjoyable for a Dark Souls x For Honor baby. I would recommend this game to small group of friends, theres quite a few sets of gear to find, secret passages to find more gear/masks. The whole experience is more enjoyable with friends. btw the max number of people you can have to a cooperation group is 3 (including yourself). You should not need more than yourself, and 2 buddies to take on the mobs in this game. Every group is broken off into groups of 2-3 and theres enough space inbetween them so you won't accidently pull a 2nd group, unless you are sprinting through hordes of goons. Thus far the game is fun, I have not tried much PvP since I was more focused on the coop side of the game, so I cannot say for certain how well that performs. The leveling in the game is almost perfect, it doesn't feel like the levels take too long nor do they take no time at all. They seem to have made it where the leveling system is just right to make you feel like you did enough to move on. As for the way to level, the mobs will be your main source of EXP (of course) the mobs respawn fairly decently after wiping them out if you are not in their field of vision or area. Maybe 30 seconds at most of a respawn time? Maybe between a 30 sec and 1 min. So potentially you can get a group of pals and go to an area packed to the brim with enemies and farm them to your hearts content. You can also grind and learn different attacks if you block and dodge enough foreign attacks that you do not yet know of. Enemies can also drop gear, most tend to be duplicates if you have already gotten an item from a certain enemy of a certain region, and theres no way to drop or discard extras of the same item. But sometimes getting the same item can yield different stats or a different color or both. So its not all useless. The game is coop until you have to go in and fight 1 of the story bosses, then you have to fend for yourself. If you are wondering how easy the game could be since I have finished it in 5 Hours, most of the game I did alone, and that makes it more difficult on its own. I have tested the enemies and they seem to fix their patterns when fitting against you, even if you beat the game and have leveled up significantly and return to 1 of the starting areas the enemies are still able to kill you, just as the end game enemies can. So there is always a sense of fighting for your life against every single enemy you fight. So all in all theres always a reason to fight a couple of mobs on your way to progress. If this game gets more added to it then I will be most definitely statisfied with my purchase even more so. And if you are wondering what can be done after you finish the story, you can PvP, Return to old zones and help new players while you level yourself in the process. and returning to older areas and looting them for possible items you may have missed. If you get this game, enjoy it! I know I enjoyed my 5 hours of gameplay.

Unique and incredible.  Update:  Haven't run into any server downtime since the patch.
Even when I'm maxxed out on stats and armor, the AI can still provide challenge somehow due to everything being in the moves themselves.
Lots of timing involved and lots of split second choices to make.  Due to simplicity of input (attack with X, X, X, X, X, X if you want, sometimes mixing in Y) you can potentially button mash but you'll be missing the point of this.  The game rewards skill in a variety of ways, one of those being timing between attacks and another between strategizing what you'll be doing.  The right stick on the controller can be flicked in different directions to activate whatever your class ability is, and sometimes you'll feint a move to get to your next combo row.
You build your own movesets based on your desired playstyle, choose what and how much armor you're bringing as you find it around the world, and have fairly tense fights to the death with countless enemies.  There is 1v1 but that is often reserved for PVP - often in story, you'll be attacked by 2 or 3 enemies.  You'll get used to dodging/blocking/parrying these guys or die trying.  You can bring along a co-op buddy or two - or just find some roaming.
As you build your moves out, you may find yourself thinking about all the possible strategies you might need to win.  Charge attacks to blast through flurries of fists, high or low spins to dodge while still throwing your feet out, hard hits that stop charge attacks, or really fast attacks to interrupt your enemies.
There's a rage-meter type thing that allows for spells.  As you fight, you can build it up.  When you defeat bosses you can unlock different spells to slot.
It's "like Dark Souls" in the sense that you can tinker with your build endlessly, and there are ruthless players running around who might just strike you at an inopportune time.  Or maybe you'll be running around with a couple strangers helping each other.  It's all free-flow, and friendly fire is always on.  Unlike Dark Souls, death has little consequence and gear does not determine your moves as much as you do.
Lots to find.  I've put 50 hours into the game and I haven't learned all the moves yet.  I love PVP, and it appears there will be other modes as they are currently locked.  I'm still finding gear for my guy that's new and strategizing on how to learn more sword moves.
The story mode itself is short, but as you rank up in PVP you can take the bosses on again for more unlocks.  PVP also grants rare unlocks sometimes, like cool masks.
Looking forward to the additional content and modes.  Looking forward to server fixes and potentially more zones to explore.  Personally hoping for a cooperate horde mode of impossible odds.

Every time I find myself of a mind or in a mood to play it, I go and look for updates only to find they have at best released a handful of minor bugfixes, usually for bugs they created with their last major patch. No new content, no new levels, none of the mechanics that were originally promised, nothing. No multiplayer, no story mode, no maps or map editor...

And my interest in the game, despite it's potential, despite the fact that it SHOULD be the kind of game I'd love, my interest is basically the same as the game's development pace, which is to say, next to non-existent. Actually, the very fact that it has inspired me to go out of my way to write what is for me a rare negative review should say it all. I have no idea what they do over there at Sauropod Studios, but it most certainly isn't anything remotely like what I'd call "work", I can only assume that they've happily taken the $700k they made off the Kickstarter and are laughing at us all the way.

This game has one major problem that is unnoticeable in the very beginning, but soon becomes an overwhelming tumor killing the game. It's the fact that you have to manually control the resource production. The most optimal strategy is producing ±0 food and throwing the rest of the city population into gold and knowledge production. However, because the food production changes all the time because of various reasons, it have to be manually changed, otherwise you cause starvation or waste resources. And everything affects food production – moving troops, growing population, settlers, religious unrest, disease. It's no big deal if you have 1-5 cities, but if you control half of the map, it's just boring and painful to deal with the mess. Thus the actually interesting and unique parts of the game drown in the micromanaging tedium.
I cannot recommend this game.

Reign: Conflict of Nations is not a bad game. But it suffers from comparison with a great number of A-titles in the same class. If you enjoy epic historical battles and tactical thought, go for Medieval: Total War 2 (or any game of Total War series); if you enjoy historically truthful political simulators with high degree of complexity, go for Crusader Kings 2. If, however, you are not a fan of great battles and CK2 are too complicated for you... go for Knights of Honor. I'd really recommend Reign only to medieval eastern Europe enthusists as myself.
Reign: Conflict of Nations is an empire-building 4x strategy, depicting happenings in Eastern Europe between 1300 and 1700. Your ambition will be to unite one of the leading powers of the region (Poland, Lithuenia, Sweden or Russia) and become a hegemon. To this end, you'll need to build up a powerful economy, use diplomacy and spycraft, convert population to your religion, gather knowledge to make technological progress, and - of course - wage wars. Sounds promising, doesn't it? So... what's wrong with the game?
Firstly, you will be required to do ALL these activities at the same time and that's - even with the help of action pause - is extremely difficult for bigger empires.
Next, the battles are resulted by the computer, without giving you a chance to lead your troops or even influence the outcome. Moreover, the results are often unpleasantly random, so you'll find yourself kicking and screaming many times, after your highly superior army of knight has been wiped out by a rag-tag band of peasants.
Third, you control basically all aspects of the game from the very beginning and none of them (to my knowledge) grows any more important later in the game, so it basically feels all the same when you control a miniature princedom in the heart of Poland, and a huge empire of the late-game. You just do A LOT MORE of the same stuff. And this is a recipe for boredom.
Lastly, the game does not give you much choice of how you will rule your empire. In other game of this kind, you can choose to be a pieceful diplomat and trader, or a vicious tyrant, spying and assassining your enemies, or a steeled knight, conquering the world with fire and sword. Here, the game strangely pushes you into doing all - you can't win by the means of diplomacy, but you can't hold too many provinces with brute force (for unhappiness spawns infinite number of quite powerful rebels, who will finally defeat you anyway).
All and all, R:CoN is quite playable, enjoyable and challanging in the beginning, but largely boring, time-consuming and repetative later in the game. It might be good springboard for those who want to jump into Crusader Kings, but feel intimidated by their complexity. And it might entertain you if you're fan of Sienkiewicz and history of Polish and Russian empire. In nearly all other cases, don't waste your money here!

I was not expecting great things from Mafia 2 as I rarely hear much about the game but i was pleasantly surprised by the quality of this title.
Positives
Story/Setting: In my opinon the story and setting of Mafia 2 are the best qualities of Mafia 2 as the story is a richly crafted experience that last for about 12 hours. The story takes place through the 1940s and 50s which is an awesome time period for a mafia setting. The characters and locations within the main storyline are well done with great voice acting (Joe is amazing) and well crafted places.
Graphics/Performance: The graphics in this game are superb for a 5 year old game on Ultra and the performance rests at a consistent 60 fps on a GTX 970 with rare framerate drops when a new area is being loaded.
Negatives
Content: Although the story clocks in at 12 Hours there is not very much to do outside of it which makes this game pale in comparison to the Grand Theft Auto games. If you enjoy free roaming and completing side tasks then this game may not be for you.
Extras: Although i fully recommend this game i cannot say the same for the DLC's. These are quite weak in terms of story telling compared to the main game. They do not offer much in terms of gameplay or additional items/cars either so i would stay away unless they are heavily discounted.
Verdict :7/10 Very Good

Game has a nice combat system. That is it.
The game itself is very unstable. It crashes a few times in a few hours, and trying to exit the game via the menu locks the game in and there's no real way to get out of the window. So basically, exiting the game requires you to restart and or break your computer. The game has over a dozen different, common, ways of crashing which can occur and they are all very frequent and possible at all times. Not even exagerating, the game legitimately can break, crash, or lock up in any one of over a dozen common ways.
The game is designed for controllers yet the sensitivity on the menus is ridiculous and cannot be toggled. Using the directional buttons makes it skip one option, using the analog stick makes it fly around far too quickly. Even in game, the analog stick movement naturally makes the character twitch out slightly everytime you try to turn them. This is all caused by using Steam controller compatibility with regular controllers, a basic concept that apparently the developers forgot to account for in their controller based game.
The controls for using the gesture and interaction menu are unintuitive and barely explained as well. Which is pretty bad since you need to use them to initiate cooperation and such.
The combat, while nice, is literally rock paper scissors. Half the attacks in the game grant immunity to other attacks, which means if you use that attack against said other you will avoid it and land your hit to win the exchange. The game massively favours spamming, especially light or sweeping attacks, and even has a mechanic which encourages button mashing. There's virtually no skill involved in this game, it is exclusively about building a scummy moveset that uses as much of the obnoxious and unfair attacks in the game as it can. That is entirely what controls who wins in a duel, is who has the moveset with the most and the best abused garbage in it. Charging attacks which grant stun immunity, fast attacks which interrupt everything, sweeping attacks which can't be dodged, evade attacks which make players half as likely to be hit. There is no punishment or restriction at all for choosing any of the blatantly superior and ridiculous attacks in the game, it's just reward.
The game loves ganking the player. Maybe seventy to eighty five percent of all pre-designed enemy placements in the game involve ganking. Some involving up to eight enemies. It is obnoxious and borderline impossible to fight against as everytime you hit one enemy another hits you. There is no way to strategically counter many of the ganks as after a certain point enemies become aggressive enough that the ganks literally just involve mandatory damage, winning is barely possible. Maybe it would be easier to respond to with player allies if the games network and servers weren't so broken. The computer enemies have massive proc ranges, which go through walls, so half of the few one versus one scripted fights in the game are not actually one versus one since other enemies nearby will get pulled in. Even when you do get a one on one fight with the computer, it's not fun. Because the computer has the enemy camp behind their block perpetually, spam dodges, spam parries, and then randomly start spamming attacks before reverting back to one of the three previous things. There's no back and forth fighting to it, it's just each extreme end of the spectrum; which is what the player versus player is anyways. The difficulty scaling of the computer enemies is based on how much time the computer allows you to hit the enemy before it reacts and stops you. That's it, that's how they scale the difficulty.
The map design is horrible. It is such a mess of weaving paths, players have no map, players must travel everywhere manually, and players must track down specific opponents to progress. Honestly, four fifths of the games challenge is trying to find where you need to go or where you haven't been. It is so, so, so unenjoyable and tedious to have to randomly run around trying to find where the new content is. It cannot be understated how much this ruins the game.
The main campaign is roughly three hours long, and there are eight or so unique relatively small maps in the world as a whole. The developers ranted about their open world, befriend or attack other players game; yet the world only has three hours worth of content and most of that is padded with dying to ganks and dechipering the poor map design. So the main point of the game is literally just fighting players in the arena mode, over and over and over. There's no random dungeon raiding system players can participate in, no dynamic versus modes or settings, it's thirty dollars for three hours of obnoxious campaign and then a versus arena. And there is only one versus mode, one on one.
Even the loot system is bad. The game can drop duplicates of anything players have, yet players can't actually remove duplicates from their inventory. Screw basic game mechanics right. Enemies in the game itself rarely drop equipment, and they rarely drop unique equipment. There's almost zero reason to replay through any of the singleplayer campaign since players are not actually rewarded in any way for doing any of it save for scraps of junk equipment and maybe some more unlocked attacks; if they grind. The only interesting aspect to the miniscule cosmetic possibilities to the game are the masks. Problem is, most masks in the game can only be acquired as extremely rare rewards for leveling up in player versus. There are maybe twenty masks in the game, and you can go from level one to a hundred and only get one or two. How do you get more, grind versus more.
The game gives players a variety of magical abilities they can abuse in player versus as well. Some can knock players off ledges, others can disable them long enough to get free hits it, and of course you have the classic heal ability. When one player wins a round, the game doesn't hard reset. It heals the winner a bit, then starts the next round right then. So if the winner is hurt enough that they don't get healed to full by said heal, they are literally handicapped the next round. The winner also gets to keep their magic charges as well, so they have that advantage. So the versus is fundamentally imbalanced in the most basic way that virtually no other game has done, because every other developer naturally understood that in order for the game to be fair each round needs to be equal. not these developers though.
And of course, the network connectivity is garbage. Besides the fact that region lock is enforced, the servers constantly go down, and aren't very good when they're up; when the game has a server fluctuation it will reset the health of all the enemies in the area or disable the players ability to attack until they exit the game. Sometimes it can spawn mini bosses twice as well because of it, which would be great if there was an actual reason to kill them after the first time.
This is probably the most broken and badly designed game I have ever seen. It's not the most unfair or frustrating game, but in terms of the quality of its basic design, the balance and structure of the combat, and stability of the game itself, and the amount of content it doesn't have.
This game should not be sold for profit. It is such a shotty piece of utter trash and incompetence, this should not be something any body profits off of and this should not be on a retail store. They should be paying players to experience this, it's clearly an early alpha.

Castle Story is a castle building strategy game with delightful cartoonish graphics and a fun premise.
You order around a group of little yellow warriors, gathering resources and supplies to build a castle, to protect a large crystal that serves as a spawner for your units. All of this on the fairly simple-though-attractive backdrop of some flying islands in the sky.
Sadly, that's about where the charm of the game ends and the problems start to show up.
Charming though it may be, the game has multiple issues ranging from save-games not loading properly, to certain game modes not functioning. There are major slow-downs in the game, and often your AI will become stuck doing nothing, for seemingly no reason.
The beautiful structures you see in the screenshots are nearly impossible to build in the game's current state. (No, seriously, how in the heck did they make those?)
Development is also insanely slow, if it's even progressing at all.
Make no mistake, there is nothing even nearly complete about the game as it is now.
I want to like the game, it shows a lot of promise, and it LOOKS fun; but with issues that haven't been fixed in literally years, and no sign of forward movement, you're much better off saving your money for a different game.
IF things change in the future, I will happily update my review.

As is indicated, I liked this game overall. I played it on one of the lower difficulty settings so that my health refilled itself more thoroughly. I still died several times, but the game handles death well.
Anyway, for more of a review bit:
Things I disliked:
- Inventory Management. This game has a ton of it, primarily due to the way synthesis works. Synthesis is the term they apply to upgrading spell components, which come in two varieties: Shape and Augment. I won't get into full detail of all you need to worry about with these here, but suffice it to say that there is way too much complexity with this upgrade system, which requires a ton of planning in order to use well. I don't think the game is well served by this, but I can see how it would be hard to simplify as the developers of the game, so I have sympathy for why they didn't. They did add a "Smart Inventory" system that automatically upgrades stuff for you, though you lose all control in the process.
- The limited variety in debuffs that enemies could apply to the player. There were basically two of them: two different temporary complete incapacitations and a time slow/snare effect. For the incapacitations, there was a freeze condition and a knockdown effect, both of which lasted for a short period of time and both of which could be extremely annoying when spammed. The time slow/snare effect was far more interesting, as it slows the player down and prevents dodging (but not shielding). As I said, all of these effects get overused primarily because they are the only effects the developers have to lean on aside from damage. I think the game would have been well served with a few more interesting debuffs for enemies to inflict on the player.
- Lack of variety in ranged enemy attack patterns. Ranged enemies typically either fire one projectile at a time or do a burst of four projectiles, and it is very easy to tell which enemy is going to do which. This makes enemies extremely predictable. I would have liked to have seen a bit more variety in this.
- Certain mechanics force specific styles of play. While there are a lot of different types of spells you can make, various mechanics in the game really emphasize playing a certain way over others. In general, damage over time effects are bad later in the game because of the functionality of synergies, which I'll touch on in just a moment. Also notable is that the lightning sigil (name for elements, basically) has a cool special mechanic that really wants you to not use a ray.
- Synergies, while awesome, appear very late in the game and force a specific playstyle. I like synergies. A lot. I'll get into why more in the "things I liked" section below. However, there were several things I disliked about synergies. Probably the thing I had the biggest issue with was the charging method. To explain: To use a synergy, you must overkill enemies; damage beyond the enemy's health pool goes into the synergy meter. When charged, you can then use the Synergy move, which is a powerful, unique spell. In order to get huge amounts of overkill damage--and thus charge up the synergy--you need to build up mastery (a sort of damage multiplier effect), then hit the enemy with a charged destruction (raw damage) spell. Doing this well will result in huge amounts of damage. The result: Damage over time effects are very bad at building up synergy moves because they tend to deal very little extra damage. That makes damage over time effects bad. I also would have liked to have seen the synergies designed such that, for any three equipped sigils, you could have three synergies. This is generally not the case. It isn't a huge deal, but it would have been nice.
Things I liked:
- The variety of spell types. There are a lot of different ways to play, and combining different sigils and how you set them up leads to a lot of variety. It is fun to see how to match different sigils and spell types together to create different playstyles.
- A decent variety of enemies, especially as the game progresses. There are some neat designs among some of the later enemies as well. Additionally there is a skill in learning which enemies to prioritize, how to react to certain enemy behaviors, and what to focus on.
- There is a lot of room to develop skill in the game. Between learning spell functionality, and how to combine effects, as well as how to handle different situations, there is a ton of room for skill and mastery of systems. Understanding how things combine together, and what effects they have, is a key part of doing well at the game, and a lot of fun to learn when those "aha!" moments happen.
- Synergies are awesome. I love having powerful, unique spells to unleash. I also like the consideration that goes into when to unleash them. There is also a pretty reasonable amount of variety in what you can do with them.
- A lot of different sigil effects. I really appreciated how many different types of elements there were in the game. It gives the player a chance to find combinations that they really enjoy, and I appreciate the work that the developers put into the game to make the sigils feel distinct from each other, each with their own sets of strengths and weaknesses.
- A variety of environments. The areas in the game have their own looks and feels, and I think these were done pretty well. While overall fairly standard (swamp, snowy mountain, and desert, to name a few), they were overall visually distinct from each other and had a good feel.
- Challenge arenas for more loot. I liked these, as they provided, well a challenge in how to handle waves of strong(er) enemies.
- I really like the base idea of a Mage-based FPS game.
- They do a good job of implementing an ammo-less FPS game.
- They have skillful defensive mechanics, which is something I really appreciate.
- They handle player failure (death) well, making it part of the game. This is something I really like, and I want to call it out here. I dislike games that rely on quicksave systems and the like; a system like that would be extra brutal in a game like this that has such a huge emphasis on both loot and inventory management. Instead, they have a simple checkpoint/respawn system, and punish death with minor amounts of backtracking, refighting a few battles (which does provide more chances for loot), and a reduced loot quality drop rate (which increases whenever you reach a check point).
The TL;DR is: A solid magic-based FPS game that makes you feel like a powerful mage in a good way--by learning how to use your magic well and how to coordinate your spells. Unfortunately, a complicated spellcrafting system can lead to serious problems with inventory management for those that want more control than the smart inventory system provides.
As a note to all first person games: If you implement camera-bob, please make an option somewhere to turn it off. My stomach thanks you.
Finally, I'd love to see a sequel with a simplified spell crafting system (I like the essence, but there is too much to track, ESPECIALLY with limited upgrades per item) and more synergies.

Lichdom Battlemage is a game I was really looking forward to for a while there. I love games that let you play around with magic and generally allow you to customize your approach in playing the game. The key to having a customizable game like that is to present various equally effective ways to reach the same goal, and allowing the player to decide what they like best.
Let's start with the good: Lichdom presents a multitude of ways for the player to play the game. Through its intricate spell crafting system you could do anything from having skeletons rise of the bodies of your enemies whose attacks cause your eneies to warp out of existence to a simple 'I'M FIRIN MAH LAHZUR' playstyle. Through various comparable stats like charge up time, casting speed, projectile speed, homing, lobs, lasers, traps, pools and much much more, the game allows you to really choose any way you want to slay your enemies. It is a unique battle system which is truly deserving of respect.
The bad part is that despite all of the customizability, I found that there was really only one viable playstyle. All the really difficult enemies are the types that like to get in your face and one-shot you. If you let them. The only way to actually beat the tougher enemies later on is to hide, shield, and fire from cover. Otherwise they will literally murder you. And before any of you other folk think I'm saying that is the only way, I'm not. I'm saying that as an average player looking to run through a game at a reasonable quick speed (not searching every nook and cranny and without total mastery of the upgrading system) that it was difficult to play the game any other way.
Overall however the game does a good job of helping you over that hurdle. It auto-upgrades your inventory to help you get the best items. It also allows you to deconstruct spells and re-use components, or simply reforge them into new options.
My general assessment is that I like it. It's a good, solid game. It's about what I expected and nothing more, but I have high standards. So, should you play this game? It's fun and it's worth a play-through or two.

So, I played this game back when it came out and I was happy to see a port to Steam -- gonna say that my old consoles are not in the best shape to play game discs that are also...not in the best shape. (: You know how it goes. That's the major draw to buying the PC port. That, and of course, NOSTALGIA!
But anyway -- about the game itself -- well, I've got over 50 hours in already, a couple of completed files on old PS1 memory cards, and hey. I mean -- I still stay just as facinated by the different environments and side quests as ever. I remember a few things, but have discovered a few more things just going off of the achievement list here, another plus for the Steam version. The port is good; graphics for the characters are better than they were back in the day, though I don't see as much difference or improvement with the backgrounds. It's not gonna be true full screen, but will center the game as large as possible between black bars to the left or right -- I don't mind that as much personally. I know it can be an issue for some of you, so I thought I'd mention it again. Further, I appreciate the quick save thing that happens when you navigate your character to a different room in a map or dungeon -- useful if you forget to save sometimes. (Getting re-used to autosaves just... not otherwise happening... is difficult, I feel ya! Heh.) Keyboard and controllers are configurable, which is a plus. Mouse control is useful at times, but not my preferred method of playing this game -- I stick to a controller. Sound is fine, sounds like the original, nothing tinny sounding as other ... 'unofficial pc ports', we'll call them ... can be.
Story is as great as ever with the even more HD cut scenes being the best part, even if nothing is said -- see my screenshot showcase to check on some of the art if you need. Character development is okay in terms of narrative -- there are some in the party that could have more focus. The actual narrative gets a bit wild at times, and if you're not really used to the cray cray that a final fantasy game can be, the combination of two very different fantasy worlds and genres...? Yeah, we'll say that, genres -- can pull you out of the story pretty fast. (My advice? Just go with it! Latch on to those characters! They completely drive the story anyway... as it should be!) World building is great, twice over. Do the sidequests. Talk to every NPC. The more information you gather, the cooler the story gets. Take your time with it -- unless, of course, you're doing a speed run. There's so much to be found -- I even found a star trek reference I missed in other playthroughs. Heh.
One thing I found is that the game sometimes hangs when a battle begins. It has happened to me 3 times in 50+ hours, always on world map battles. SO SAVE OFTEN when leveling outside, people. It's a little annoying but definitely not common enough to make this port unplayable -- and hell, it could even be a failing of my old pc, after all. Just keep an eye out and like I said, SAVE YOUR GAME.
I find a few of the sidequests very tedious, like the Jump Rope achievement, or racing Hippaul, or the chocograph finding -- endless clicking of buttons forever does get a bit boring, but I'd say just configure your controls differently when your hands get tired.
Over all, I'd say it's a great title if you are a fan of the series -- a bit different, a bit wild, but produces a memorable story and loveable characters just the same.

Read below for Pro/Con breakdown.
Pro's:
-  This game runs great!  With so many games not actually working, it's amazing to not have a single problem related to how it runs.
-  Fun mini battles, that have different minion attack/buff options.
-  The new changes to the story mode, give more options to play story mode without PvP matches to progress.
-  Bright colors and visual effects are fun. (also see con's)
-  Build a team with lots of different minions that have different attacks, buffs, nice strategy options.
-  NO issues with pay to win minion card balances, so far.
-  NO "Buy this" pop ups. (Thank you so much, Dev's!) Please note, I have not spent any money on this game yet, but will, to help support the dev's and game.
-  Dev's are continuing to combatt cheaters and bots. (I've seen an improvement in PvP matches)
-  Dev's are currently active with game updates and in the community.
Con's:
-  No information about the stats on any match played.
Possible fix: Adding an after match stats screen, with things like how many mini game hits and how much damage was dished out or taken, could help players understand why they won or lost, or how they might improve game play.
-  Bright colors and visual effects can cause issues seeing the board to make matches. I've noticed this when both side are hitting each other with multi minions at about the same time. (Not great if you have issues with flashing bright lights or color blindness)
Possible fix: Adding a low particle effect or color blind options.
-  PvP matches are only random.
Possible fix: Adding friend invite matches, without effecting PvP rank.
-  No PvP rank info. Currently there is no way to know if I'm being matched up with a level 5 star, heroic, or new level 19 ranked player.
Possible fix: Add rank/player name to PvP matches.
-  Minor issues with camera angle changing for some minions attacks, not game breaking but not pleasant either.
Possible fix: Not move the camera? I have no idea, I'm not a dev.
Please note, I just play games, so take all the possible fixes with a grain of salt, since I have no idea how to make any of it happen. I try to keep things constructive.

An absolutely phenomenal platformer that will be familiar to you if you enjoyed any Mega Man or Sonic titles. Although to me it feels more like something I would see on the Amiga, rather than a Genesis or SNES title.
Despite having a cool plotline, the story isn't conveyed as well as it could be, and the voice performances are a little inconsistent in quality. But it's all good enough to keep you playing and wanting more.
You'll find that enemies and bosses can be incredibly difficult, especially near the end, but with enough tries, you'll get through just fine.
The platforming is very fun, but hindered by a slight flaw: You can't move "a little bit" in a specific direction, like a controller's analog stick would usually allow you to do. You're either in "moving" mode or you're not, and this can get tricky to work with when you're doing precise platforming. Despite this, the platforming feels tactile and nicely tuned.
The graphics and sound are amazing and lush, with an engaging soundtrack to boot. You won't forget many of the songs in this game, and the pixel art is spectacular as well.
GalaxyTrail has proven themselves to be more than capable of making an awesome game the first time around, and I can't wait to see what's in store with Freedom Planet 2. But in the meantime, pick this up and you certainly won't be disappointed.
