Freedom Planet is a Sonic type platformer. Before playing this game, from Sonic platformers I played a few classic old ones, like Sonic CD, but was never a big fan of them(but newer one's like Sonic Mania look very interesting), so I expected it to be like those Sonic CD, maybe a little better. But this game turned to be a way better than my expectations, which really surprised me, and this game turned to be an amazing platformer.
Game has 3 different characters to play as(third unlocked after beating certain levels) I played as Lilac, who I chose, a dragon monster girl with similar to Sonic abilities, but there is a cat and a dog girl too. I had a lots of fun playing through the game.
I really enjoyed it and I could say the strong points of the game are:
- The graphical design which looks very nice with lots of pretty details in the background and foreground.
- An enjoyable story about alien invasion, cool battles, friends, different fantasy and futuristic stages.
- The combat is also pretty good in this game, makes it very enjoyable to go trough the maps and battle bosses.
- Developers even thought about little things like your character starts to dance in a specific areas, lots of secrets to find, and you can even replay the game as another protagonist, but only some things will change, playing as the dog girl gives some extra stages and battles not seen as other characters.
- Special challenging game modes that are not related to story, which you can play to achieve some records, which reminded me of the challenges I used to play for example in Super Smash Bros. Brawl, to break all the targets in time or others.
- A good soundtrack makes you go deep into the atmosphere of the story and the stages you are playing.
From  the negative points to me:
- I didn't find the game has much replay-ability, even using different characters, since most of the things remain the same.
This game really deserves the awards it got the year it released, I can say for sure this is one of the best platformers I have ever played, and definitely one of the best you will find on Steam, and for me it's even one of the top 5 best ones. I will definitely recommend this game to anyone who loves Sonic type games, platformers, action games, retro games, games with cool boss fights, awesome indie games, and just games with amazing characters, soundtrack and story.

This game had been on the fringes of my watch list for years. It wasn't until the Sonic Mania Denuvo debacle that, filled with unfulfilled hype to play a good pacey platformer, I finally gave it a chance.
If I'd had any idea the game would be this good I'd have picked it up all all those years ago. The controls and interesting level designs are absolutely spot on and exhibit an absurd amount of attention to detail, and I'm still in disbelief at the excessive effort that was spent on the sprite work and animation of some of the set pieces that are used just once and are often easily missed!
The story and voicework are... not big-budget, it is easy to notice. For the former that might actually be a good thing when contrasted with some games that are (Sonic Forces...) but the game is very much on the labour-of-love side of the scale with all the benefits and drawbacks that brings. As a fan of consistency I do think it's a good thing the same cast are planned to return for the sequel.
Ultimately this game was probably the surprise package of the year for me and now if Sonic Mania ever removes Denuvo I'm not actually sure it'll be better than this.

Do you know what my advisor said to me the other day? “Sire, it looks like Stronghold 2, smells like Stronghold 2, tastes like Stronghold 2… Good thing we didn’t pay retail.”
I do love the Stronghold series, but Stronghold 3 is simply an abysmal failure.
In terms of game play, aesthetics and overall feel, I get the impression that someone just took Stronghold 2 and Stronghold Legends, put it in a blender and hit puree. That could have been a tasty beverage, but someone got the bright idea to strain out all of the detailed play mechanics and structures from Stronghold 2 and throw them away. Why?!
Stronghold 2 was an awesome game, BECAUSE you had so many management options and detailed buildings! There were geese and eels in a pond, which was my personal favorite structure, followed closely by the royal treasury. There were lots of detailed buttons and menus when you clicked on structures…
And while we’re on the subject, since everything in Stronghold 3 feels repurposed, what was so hard about carrying over all of the peasant dialog from the other games in the series!?! What fun is it to be lord of the castle if you can’t click on your peasants and listen to their simple babble? How are criminals supposed to steal from my granary if there ARE NO criminals!? Done away with gong pits? Madness I tell you!
All of that is gone in Stronghold 3… But at least there’s a day / night slider and some weather options in free build… Oh, and you can free rotate buildings… But the walls don’t connect to my castle anymore either… Win some, lose allot? As we’ve heard so many times before: “People are leaving the castle.”

This is NOT a recommendation! This is a warning! I bought this game on sale even though it got back reviews because I am a huge fan of the Stronghold series. This game is absolute crap. Do not buy! Take my word for it. If you'd like more detail, message me.

A lot of people say this is the best 3D sonic yet. And I am tempted to agree. The 3D sections are pretty fun once you get the hang of the controls and how it contantly changes the physics up.
However... this game is still a heaping pile of ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥
It has a lot of technical issues. It requires you to first run a configuration exe before running the game exe, yet it is VERY common for the config files generated by the configuration exe to become corrupted, forcing you to delete the config files and regenerate them or your game will not launch.
Once you get the game running, it still has a lot of bugs just like any sonic game. I was constantly running into invisible walls or falling through gaps in platforms that are too small for sonic to fit in. The physics here are just♥♥♥♥♥♥poor. And nearly every wall in the 2D sections has their physics walls like 2 feet in front of them. WHY WOULD YOU EVER NOT MAKE THE PHYSICS WALLS MATCH THE LOCATION OF THE RENDERED WALLS!?!?!?! ♥♥♥♥ YOU SEGA.
STOP MAKING ME PLAY 2D SECTIONS!!! I hate them all. I really enjoy the 3D but every mother ♥♥♥♥ign 5 minutes you are forced to switch over to the 2D only gameplay. This may sound blasphemous but 2D sonic has always ♥♥♥♥ing sucked even in it's supposed golden early games. It constantly punishes you for moving fast making the game entirely trial-error memory based rather than allowing players to adapt the first time through. And when you are not moving fast, sonic moves like a god damn grandma. There are only two speeds: too fast to control/react-to-danger and too slow to jump on a ♥♥♥♥ing platorm over a gap. Think of all the great 2D platformers out there: Mario, Yoshi, Donkey Kong, Rayman, Super Meat Boy, etc. All of them are designed in a way that you can see the next challenge and prepare for it. Not ♥♥♥♥ing Sonic. Sonic gives you a loop-de-loop, tells you to do a spin dash, but then PUTS A MOTHER ♥♥♥♥ING ENEMY RIGHT AFTER THE LOOP THAT IS ONLY AVOIDABLE IF YOU KNEW IT WOULD BE THERE AHEAD OF TIME!!!! ♥♥♥♥ SONIC GAMES.
And stop trying to make a god damn story line. It sucks. It always sucks. I am tired of mashing the buttons to make your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ing side characters shut the ♥♥♥♥ up. Just make levels and a hub world/menu... PLEASE...
This isn't how you design bosses in games. The bosses aren't horrible, but the traditional point of bosses is to combine things you learned throughout the game up to that point and challenge you. Instead all the bosses were adding new mechanics that were unlike what you had played up till that point.  And the games knows it. It has pop ups showing you what buttons to press... WHY. Why design bosses that require their own tutorial? You were trying to make this big epic fight that will make the player feel good afterwards, but the player is too busy trying to learn the new♥♥♥♥♥♥and not be annoyed with the pop up tutorials.
After ever set of 3 3d/2d levels, it makes you do ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ challenge crap to unlock the bosses. WHY? The challenges suckand the all take place in the levels you already beat. It is lazy and stupid.
Another issue is just the lack of a place to move around and test the physics/controls. Even back with Mario 64, the hub world let you fully explore the base controls of the game. Not this game. The hub world is 2D only. There is no good way to test and learn the various controls. This wouldn't be sucha  big deal if the games physics didn't constantly change. There is Board Riding (city escape), Water running, Dash sections, 2.5D sections, Rail Grinding, Standard Movement, etc. and they all handle very differently physics wise. And then you add the moves: Ring Dashing, Platform stomping, Homing attack, Standard Dashing, Sliding, etc. The only way to practice any of these various sections and moves is to play the small sectios where they appear (often only lasting a few seconds long for stuff like water running)... There are some good mechanics here, but GIVE US A PLAYGROUND SO WE CAN TEACH OURSELVES THE GAME ENGINE AND HOW TO PLAY. Yeah, from the hours on this game, you can probably tell I like this game a lot. And usually it's because I come back to replay levels again. So, here are some things worthy of mentioning.
- Two Distinct Gamemodes: In this game, you can play as Classic Sonic and Modern Sonic. Classic Sonic returns to the Sonic series' roots, going back to the 2-D platforming it originally was. Modern Sonic takes the boost formula and like any other 3-D sonic game there is, is very fast paced. So, this game is a good combination of 2-D and 3-D.
- Story: Nothing much to say about it, and really the story is not really dazzling. But is very lighthearted and with some "jokes" and references.
- Music: The music is outstanding. Despite being remixed versions of past zones throughout the history of Sonic, the music is still very pleasing.
- Visuals: The zones and places look real beautiful. It might not match Unleashed's quality, but it's very well made.
- Re-imagined stages: Generations returns old stages from the past and remaster/re-imagine them to fit the two gamemodes. And they are in fact quite interesting. Either way, the stages are still very fun to play and some can still be very challenging (though this game isn't too hard).
- Lack of bosses: There are 3 rival battles and 4 bosses. Given that previous games had at least a boss every zone, this is really a small amount of bosses/battles.
- Short?: There are 9 stages (18 levels total). Generations is quite short, as I had finsihed the main stages in one day.
- Extra Stuff to do: You can unlock skills, complete challenges, find red rings (optional things you can collect), and more. This may add a few extra hours to your experience.
-Outlet for fan projects: Many fans have made mods to this game, and all of them are free. Mods like the Unleased Project, give out all the day-stages in Sonic Unleashed (so, you're basically getting a taste of Sonic Unleased for free).

Visuals: 8/10 (Amazing quality, but hub-world looks a bit bland, and game might drop quality at times)
Music: 9/10 (Not much original tracks, but the music is still very pleasing. They also bring back music from previous games)
Gameplay: 9/10 (Very well made stages, and have diverse obstacles to blast through)
Lasting Effect: 10/10 (A game you can go back to, especially with the mods many fans are still making)
Overall (Average): 9/10
Any Sonic fan should add this to their collection, and a good introductory for newcomers who are interested in fast-paced platforming and action-adventure.

Final Fantasy IX is the last game in the series to bear the fingerprint of creator Hironobu Sakaguchi, and it shows. That said, I can't number myself one of the series' "old guard" in good faith, as my favorite title is XIV, and while a polarizing opinion, I consider VII to be the magnus opus of the Squaresoft years.
Even still, IX holds a special place in my heart. Everything in the game oozes magic and charm, from the characters to the music to the beautiful pre-rendered backgrounds that look almost more like paintings than CG. The battle system is more restrictive than others in the series, giving each character a static, individual job, but in many ways this works to the game's benefit, allowing some linear focus and a feeling of progression and rewards while still offering some freedom.
The plot, while arguably going just a bit off the rails in the game's final act, still hits the right emotional beats and enables some wonderful character development throughout the story. The characters are perhaps the game's strongest point, as while some are infamously bizarre (Quina) or underdeveloped (Amarant), all feel real and memorable despite the often cartoonish designs, including (if not especially) its supporting characters, from the swashbuckling actors/thieves of Tantalus, to the conflicted legendary knight Beatrix.
It's not all perfect - the personal arcs of some otherwise great characters seem to be forgotten halfway through the game (Freya, Amarant), there is an infuriating amount of missable content, and taking full advantage of what the combat system has to offer can quickly make the game far too easy - but as a such an incredibly beautiful game, and a perfect last hurrah of the "classic" Final Fantasy games, I can't in good faith give it anything less than a
perfect score.

I've been following this game for years, but the launch product is ... quesitonable.
Pros ---
> Amazing visual atmosphere and lots of places to explore.
> Challenging to a degree that most games don't dare to be these days, and very rewarding to learn.
> Generally solid-feeling mechanical combat with nice audiovisual cues.
Cons ---
> You're going to be exploring that atmosphere, a lot.  Mandatory objectives are more hidden than secrets and the map may as well not exist.  Even as someone who knew a decent amount going in I spent my first 4 hours wandering the starting area trying to find a boss needed to progress.
> Basically every fight with mobs is a 3+ v 1, and even basic mobs seem to have a massive statisical advantage on you, with truckloads of hp, nearly infinite stamina, and almost instant hitstun recovery.  This is compounded by randomly ocurring "minibosses" which are a great deal tougher and visually indistinct from regular mobs, so you won't know you've got one until it 2-shots you with jabs.
> The UI is minimalist to an extreme and tells you next to nothing. It's a good thing combat has such good visual design, because otherwise you'd never know what's going on. This is aggrevated by the fact that literally everyone is a dude in a mask and tunic, so good luck telling mobs / bosses / players apart until you start wailing on them.
> The tutorial explains intuitive things ad nauseum (ie, moving with WASD and attacking with the mouse), but doesn't bother to touch on things like the "mana" resource generation, combo / combo breaking mechanics, etc. that aren't so easy to figure out.
> Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥target locking is busted. You kinda just swing at random and re-target at random as well. Sometimes mobs just aren't "detected" by the locking system and can't be targeted at all, meaning they can murder you while you have no ability to respond.
> You're gonna fall through the map, a lot.
---
All that said, I'll probably keep it and boot it up from time to time.  It's still very skill-based and rewarding in so many ways, just hindered by cataclysmically awful level design and a lacking UI.
That said, I got this game for the combat and the PvP, and so far that's been around 5% of my playtime next to the incredibly huge amount of wandering the landscape and scratching my head, so maybe I won't.

I have heard of a lot of people who insist that they disliked Final Fantasy IX's return to a 'cartoony' sort of game after so many more realistic, harsh, and darker games before it. I have even heard people say that it was their least favorite of the Final Fantasy franchise (at least until much later games came out... but I digress).
I am here to say that I honestly, genuinely can't disagree with it more. This game is, by far, my favorite of the entire franchise. It has approximately two things going for it that I genuinely hate: the card game (which tried so hard to match or surpass Triple Triad, only to fall flatter than a postage stamp under a steamroller) and the ending, which comes so far out of the blue that even NASA is going, "There's not a telescope strong enough...." Seriously. I refuse to put spoilers in a review, but I can only say that the ending and aftermath *both* made me tear my hair out and shake my head; it's like someone punked the dev team and they didn't notice that it had been changed until it was too late.
But I digress.
What it loses in those two (admittedly *HUGE*) black marks, it so much more than makes up in everything else. Amazing humor. Great characters. *CHARACTER ARCS*! My God! Actual *CHARACTER ARCS* in a game where the animation and the light-hearted tone of so much of it makes it feel more like a Looney Toons adventure than a game. You seriously have to just ride through the sillier bits, because stuffed in there is *so* much genuinely harsh, dark storyline that the light tone just makes the more tragic when it comes up, and yet softens the tragedy to make it comfortable and accessible to everybody.
And the *music*! Uematsu is untouchable on his worst days, and to me, this was his Magnum Opus for soundtracks. The game's music has so many good tracks that I can't even begin to name them all off.
Well, I can begin to: "You Are Not Alone." Easily the greatest of the bunch, and yet saying that makes it sound like the rest of them suck. They don't, though; there's barely a dud among them, and they all seem to fit their areas gorgeously. An entire OCRemix was made of this album, and it was made for a good reason.
Gameplay-wise, it is simple, and yet involved enough to be interesting, it gets back to the basic feel of a Final Fantasy game (IMO, anyway), falling way more back on a high fantasy feel than the technological and steampunk 'darkness' that a lot of the Final Fantasies both before and after went into, and I don't find that a bad thing. The side games are incredibly fun, as well, keeping you on your toes as you get to explore and find secrets both accidentally and guided. And the customizing of your weapon's 'learning' system is something else for the collectors in us, being able to give your characters all the more in the way of skillsets and crafting new tools out of old appeals to the hoarders.
There are so many hours upon hours upon *hours* of fun in this game, and something for everybody. I sincerely *try* to understand why so many people dislike it, and unless one is that badly hung up on the ending, I can't understand why. It is, plain and simple, brilliant. Absolutely brilliant. It's an epic game on an epic scale, dressed up in chibified clothing. Please, for the love all that is holy, give it a try. Or at the very least, get the soundtrack, listen to it, and then try and tell me that you aren't at least a little curious about the world that such incredible music helps draw a picture of.

Usually when I write up a game, I start with all the good points and then transition to the bad stuff. I feel like this makes for a more positive reading experience overall, and should make my impression of it whole and clear by the end. I'm not going to do that this time, because the first thing you need to know about Lichdom is that it is too damn long. Now, this is not "the new Shadow Warrior is too damn long" or "the Hobbit trilogy was too damn long" or "presidential primary season is too damn long". This is an entirely new paradigm of too damn long, and you really need to understand this before even considering this game. My first playthrough took 22 hours. That's certainly long for an FPS, and short for some other genres with a little overlap here, but those 22 hours were stretched over eight levels. That's it! Furthermore, those eight levels play more like five, because three of them are continuations of the previous level. There's a lost city level, two ice levels, two desert levels, two swamp levels, and a proper city level. With each of those lasting 2-3 hours, you're going to be wandering through huge stretches of glacier and sand and muck.
But what really makes this game feel like it takes forever is the level design itself. Lichdom is constructed in the vein of an arena shooter, much like Shadow Warrior or Bulletstorm. Hallways lead to conspicuous arenas where you fight whatever spawns in, after which you take another hallway to another arena and so on and so forth. There are no puzzles, no doors, no interactables, almost no alternate paths, and very little reason to explore off the main trail. There are some side fights and usually one or two secret dungeons that can get you valuable piles of spell components, but in terms of gameplay you're just getting harder versions of the fights you're doing normally. So yes, the cardinal sin of this game is that it is 20+ hours of the same damn thing. What you get in the first two hours is what you're going to get times ten, with arguably even less variety as you progress.
Still with me? Good, because if you can get past that admittedly enormous flaw, there's a pretty great game in here. The whole reason to play Lichdom is to make good on the whole BADASS MAGE thing, and the magic system delivers. Instead of guns or swords, you fight solely with magic that you can customize to an impressive degree. Over the course of the game you unlock eight sigils, which are elements like fire and ice but also more curious concepts like corruption and delirium, and you can have three equipped and ready to use at any given time. Each sigil has three spells attached to it for you to use. There's a targeted spell that can be built as a homing missile, a bomb you lob, or a channeled beam. There's an AoE spell that can be an explosion, a pool, or a trap that must be triggered. And there's a nova that has conditions for triggering it depending on your shield (more on shields later). On top of that, you can determine the EFFECT of each spell, either direct damage, a status effect, or a damage multiplier, which also varies in its function by sigil. Fire spells can knock down and burn over time, lightning spells can stun and chain across enemies, delirium spells can mind control and make enemies flee, and so on.
And honestly, that's just the basics. Spells can critically hit for additional effects, or be charged before casting for a guaranteed crit. Charged spells can do a special crits charmingly named "apocalypticals" which give you a bonus effect based on the inflicting sigil. You can craft special synergy spells that use two sigils instead of one and have awesome room-clearing effects like collapsing black holes or summoning exploding zombies or conjuring a hurricane. You also build a shield spell for yourself that represents your hit points and determines additional abilities like teleporting and blocking. Spells are crafted out of Diablo-style loot drops from enemies and chests, color-coded by rarity (white-green-blue-purple-orange-red, of course). These components can be combined up to higher grades, disassembled for specific parts, or gambled away for a chance at rare components. If this sounds overwhelming, there's a Smart Inventory option that will upgrade your spells and combine up your components for you. Honestly though, if you're not in it to♥♥♥♥♥♥♥out over your spells, you're missing a huge part of the game. You've got a ton of control over your arsenal, and experimentation is incredibly fun with the enormous range of effects and combinations your can produce.
As hard as I slagged the level design, I have to say they are pleasing to progress through. The CryEngine makes for some gorgeous scenery, and a lot of love went into rendering the battlegrounds and cesspools you traverse. The levels themselves can be pretty creative, even if their layout is not. The third level is particularly impressive once you figure out what it is. While there is a lot of detail, it's worth mentioning that there are no destructables or physics objects. This felt particularly disappointing while slinging around devastating spells, even if the spell effects themselves are meaty and satisfying. There's a pretty good variety of enemies as well, or at least there would be for a shorter game. About half are introduced early on and the rest are slowly sprinkled in so there is some variety to the battles, even if you're going to be fighting every possible combination of foe at least twice.
The story is nothing special, classic fantasy revenge story, but the voice acting is pretty great. You get to play as Troy Baker or Jennifer Hale, and whichever one you don't pick becomes your NPC traveling buddy. And let me tell you, they are some clever, snippy jackasses. The other characters mostly talk like Tolkien characters but these two love cursing and quipping at each other and everything in a perfectly charming way. Your mentor figure is Clancy Brown (swarthy Lex Luthor from the Superman cartoons!), and the villains and side characters all turn in quality performances as well. I will say that the plot does something dumb in the swamp levels that cuts into the voice acting fun quite a bit, but by that point you're probably just trying to power through to the end. There are some pretty good and challenging boss battles, and the New Game Plus mode if you manage to beat the game is great for dicking around and tricking out your mage; it's a big series of challenge portals with different randomized fights and scaling difficulty.
So there you go, a writeup almost as long and meandering as the game itself. I've certainly gotten a lot of enjoyment out of it, chiefly because the spellcrafting and combat are excellent and the presentation is fantastic. But even I was getting sick of the game by the ten-hour mark, and that wasn't even halfway. I really pushed myself to finish it, and I'm glad I did, and I still kinda want to play it now and then. It's just important to know what you're getting into, and prepare for a lot of monotony if you want to get to the meat of the game. Pick it up on sale like I did ($5 is a steal for a game of this quality, at least!) and give the first level a try, and if you're cool with that for another 20 hours, enjoy depopulating a faraway kingdom with fire and locusts and zombies and time rifts. Forever.

Stronghold 3 may look like a medieval fortress simulator where feudal armies throw themselves against vast layers of fortifications with thick walls and towers that look as if they reach the skies. This is unfortunately only true if you play one of the scenarios that feature already constructed fortifications. Throughout the rest of the game you will never get to build anything more than a few haphazardly placed walls and the occasional watch tower.
The problem with Stronghold 3 is it's speed. Everything moves at a dreadfully slow pace. Gathering resources and building structures seem to take forever and most of the game seems to take place without any interaction from you, simply waiting for something to happen. The extremely tiny maps doesn't help either, making every town feel cramped.
You play as a feudal lord starting every map with your, very small, castle and some starting peasants. As you build resource gathering structures or conscript soldiers those peasants get used up and to attract more you need to provide them with adequate housing, food and not as much plague as you would like to inflict upon the lazy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
As your town grows you start to get involved in the more costly resources as well as the more complicated resource chains letting you equip your army better and feed your populace more sufficiently. Along the way and depending on the scenario or campaign mission you're on you might face the additional threat of invading armies or super aggressive wolves that'll kill your poor defenseless peasants and put a stop to production until you can attract some more.
The problem with economic and city-building aspects of the game is as mentioned before, the speed. Everything happens at a snail's pace. You place your initial resource gathering buildings, got get a cup of coffee, come back and place the another resource gather. You repeat this process until you get enough of an income to start placing the more advanced resource harvesters as well as building the beginnings of an army and then you go get a cup of coffee and come back when you've got enough resources to place another advanced harvester or recruit another soldier. You spend more time waiting than actually playing the game and that is a serious design flaw.
I am normally all for slow paced intelligent games but this is just ridiculous and the slow speed adds nothing to the game's depth.
The military aspects of the game is predictably simple. You harvest resources to construct weapons and then use those weapons to conscript your peasants into military service as a variety of different types of soldiers. The actual combat however pretty much boils down to box selecting your army and clicking attack on the enemy army, hoping you got the right numbers and combination of troops.
Graphically there is nothing wrong with the game but not much right either. It neither adds nor detracts much from the experience. The sounds are comfortably boring although the soundtrack does feature some neat flute music that fits the genre very nicely.
All in all Stronghold suffers from two serious design flaws that takes it from being a great idea to a bad game. The slow speed makes the game boring and any sense of accomplishment you get from finally getting a proper economy working is instantly removed when a new map starts and you are thrown back to square one having to rebuild. The lack of proper fortress building however is what truly kills it for me. You will never come to a point in the game where building those mighty fortifications that is the game's trademark becomes natural. It takes far too long to get there and once you do you could probably have won the map three times over.
Stick to the older titles in the series or looks elsewhere, this is not a game that delivers what it promised.

I could start with the fact that graphics are unpolished, often times are stretched over meshes obscenely, or straight out glitch on a regular basis but that wouldn't do the terrifying experience that is stronghold 3 justice.

DPEJ is a charming game where you get to explore various Disney Princess realms, customize your own princess, fight some loser evil ex-princess, and (in an ending ripped straight from the Shining) get sealed into a portrait with all the other princesses. (Sadly, "Midnight, the Stars, and You" doesn't play during this sequence).
The gameplay is fairly simple. After character creation, you enter one of several princess worlds and resolve to help the people there with whatever problems they might have. You are armed with a magic wand, with which you can fire magic bolts or flourish it to trigger different environmental effects. Occasionally you will be called upon to fight Heartless (not their real names, but I never bothered to remember what their stupid name was and they're basically the same as Heartless); however, they pose no challenge as you can basically spam the spacebar to rapid-fire your wand and clear all foes off the screen.
The graphics are pretty nice, for the time the game came out. There are worlds that (to a youngster) would be quite large and fun to explore (as an oldster myself, I was able to sprint through most everywhere in no time flat). There are lots of cute animals all over the place, the one true metric of a good game.
The game scatters gems all over, whether sitting out in the open, squirreled away in chests, or rewards for completing tasks. The most you can hold is 999, and they have no discernible use.
At one point, there's a minigame where you have to save the memories of the merpeople from Ariel's world from sinking deep into the ocean. It's fun to just let the rocks sink down, since there's no penalty for a miss anyway. Take that, memories.
Snow White only has four dwarf friends. Sneezy, Sleepy, and Bashful were presumably killed and eaten.
All in all, this is a good game for children, and a fun game to ironically play for adults.
I nominated this game for the 'Defies Description' Steam Award. I really think it deserves it.

Bought this game to play it with my 3 year old daughter, who loves the Disney princesses. I have to say that I am very disappointed.
The game lacks controller support. There are simple workarounds to that, by using third party software to map controller buttons to keys and mouse events, but out of the box, the game is far too difficult to control for a small child.
There isn't much story, which is acceptable given the audience. The gameplay feels clumsy much of the time, as well as the controls, in sequences where timing is of some importance. The game interface shows symbols of what keys to press (on the keyboard), but because we have mapped these to a controller, it provides us with nothing but confusion.
When the game has been completed (which doesn't take very long), it is possible to revisit all locations, but there is absolutely nothing to do. All the enemies and tasks are gone, making it really boring to play afterwards. We started over from the beginning, but it quickly became boring to revisit the game.
I appreciate the fact that this game is one of very few which are available in our native language. The princess theme is interesting for young girls.

This is a first-person "caster" game (as opposed to "shooter"), where magic is the only weapon. There are no cool-downs, no mana potions. Just a limitless well of magical ability, abetted by a unique spell-crafting system, good graphics, great voice-acting, long (occasionally boring) levels, great boss fights, and a serviceable-but-not-special story.
First the magic. There are no other weapons. There are nine elements; each can combo with the others in different ways. Only three elements can be equipped at a time, so there are limits. Results can be explosive (like 27,000 points per combo). The spell-crafting system is deep. Guides are a must, but only the most rudimentary tutorials are provided in-game, so prepare to trawl the forums looking for tips. Fortunately, all spell elements have detailed descriptions; you can spend hours in the crafting window, tweaking and building new spells or breaking old ones apart.
Unfortunately, the combat can actually get boring after a while.The enemies are don't vary much from beginning to end; you'll be fighting the same baddies in the final level that you fought in the caves early in the game.  While general level combat is "same-y", bosses offer a lot of variety. Several of them are hard as nails and require strategizing and careful spell-crafting to defeat.
The path through the game is linear . Arcade levels with massive loot drops hide in caves and corners, so explore throughly. You can only save via checkpoint. Graphics are glorious; it's CryEngine 3, so expect the game to look as good as Crysis 3 (it will also strain your hardware). The voice-acting is superb; Jennifer Hale and Troy Baker have an excellent rapport, presided over by the somber tones of Clancy Brown (remember him from the original Highlander movie?). The story is passable, but after a while I stopped caring.
While the repetition wore on me after a while, I still had great fun with Lichdom: Battlemage. It's kind of a hit-or-miss game, though; get it when it goes on sale if it tempts you. If you like it, you'll think you got a bargain. If you don't, then you won't have spent much.

What began as a Sonic the Hegdehog fangame was reshaped into a game that stands tall and proud on its own. When I bought the game, there were only two characters for the story, the third one only available for Classic and Time Attack modes. But it was enough. Freedom Planet plays like the old games I played back when I argued with my older sister that my SNES was better than her SEGA Genisis. I encountered no bugs during normal play, no sudden slow-downs, and it worked fine with my generic GameStop PC controller. There are a few difficulty settings to choose from, so if you don't like the game to be hard like I do, you can turn it down. The game won't mock you for it with a "you must play on a higher difficulty" message like many older games we all have nostalgia glasses for.
However, the story can be a bit.... well, the story can sometimes give you whiplash in the tones and moods it has, going from Saturday Morning goodness to something much darker. No blood is present in the game, but it dosen't have to be for the cutscenes I'm thinking of. Voice acting didn't bother me at all, but it may evoke PS1 era laughs or cringe, though I disagree about it being "Jill Sandwich" bad.
All in all this is a great, fast-paced sidescroller. I heavilly recomend this.

This is my favourite sonic game since sonic 3 and knuckles. This game is a nostalgia trip if you are a sonic fan, and if you are not, it makes you discover the "good" side of sonic games.
I will start by the negative points to get them out of the way. This is a short game, even if you want to 100% it. You can get through the main story in about 4-5 hours, but there are a lot of side missions, bonus content and red rings to collect and complete your collection of various items from sonic's history (more on that later).
This game was released at first in 2011, celebrating sonic's 20th anniversary on xbox 360 and ps3 and was intended for these consoles. This is a port, and port are known to have some issues, but this is a good port! The only problem I found is that I have a Nvidia GTX graphic card and at first, the game didn't detect the card (since I have a gaming laptop). The config tool is a pure mess: it sometimes won't save your configs when you start the game (like your controlls), but you need to go through it because this game is meant to be played with a controller. Don't even try with a keyboard...
Now let's get to the good points! This is a really pretty game graphically. Sega really gave it all in here! I have nothing else to say about that. The story is pretty simple, like most sonic games, it consists of Sonic and friends doing their usual stuff, when something bad happens and the time is all mixed up because of a mysterious creature, and it's up to classic and modern sonic to restore the world and destroy this evil creature. The story is very light and fun, but that's not this game's selling point, the gameplay is.
For some years preceding this game, fans have split up in 2 categories mostly: the ones who stick with the classic sonic games on the genesis (sonic 1, 2, cd, 3 and knuckles and knuckles chaotix if some remeber that) with memorable 2d platforming and iconic music and the ones who like modern sonic (like sonic adventure 2 and sonic unleashed). To compensate for this, Sega decided to give us both sonics! Classic sonic is all about the platforming and the 2d. The controlls are not identical to the classic games, but they feel close enough. I think I read somewhere that classic sonic was not compatible with modern sonic's physics, so they needed to modify the engine to suit him. Then there's modern sonic, with his blazing speed and boost, mixing 2d and 3d platforming. Fans of the day stages in sonic unleashed will feel very at home here.
There are 18 levels, 4 bosses, 3 rival battles and tons of missions representing sonic's history over the years, like the iconic green hill zone to city escape. 3 levels per era (the genesis or classic era, the dreamcast era and the modern era) sum up each game nicely. There is also the bonus room, which contains music, character descriptions, concept art and cutscenes you collect throughout the game. What I like about this is that you can use the music to collect to replace the usual level in question theme by that music, so you can feel like a boss playing "endless possibilities" in rooftop run :)
This would be the end of the review, but there is one more element I need to talk about. The number of hours written here don't represent the time I've spent on this game. I think it's more like half the time, because there are a lot of mods for this game, and I mean it. From new levels to new characters, the modding community is still going (more calmly, but still alive). One of the mods I will talk about is the Unleashed Project. This mod ports levels from the Sonic Unleashed day stages to Sonic generations and it does it very nicely! This project is still going: the creators are making the Unleashed Project 2.0, looking to port EVERY level and dlc to Generations (I honestly don't even know how they will, but work is beeing done on their channel.
This is the end of my review on Sonic Generations. I absolutely recommand this game, though 30$ may seem a little expensive, I think you should buy it, Sonic fan or not...
Pros:
-Great graphics
-Satisfying gameplay
-Good replay value
-Nostalgia trip for sonic fans and a good way to introduce people to sonic
-Lots of collectibles and easter eggs
Cons:
-The config tool is annoying, but you still need it
-Some issues with detecting graphic cards (for me at least)
-A bit of the short side, but still very enjoyable (there are a bunch of mods to mess around with)
-A controller is pretty much needed, playing 3d stages with 4 directions feels ackward

One of the greatest 3D Sonic games ever made.
The experience of thrill with Classic Sonic with his plattaform, almost identical physics and good level design give some pretty good vibes of nostalgia. Truly captures what Classic Sonic was all about, also on the cutscenes he is the cutest thing ever.
Modern Sonic brings Unleashed Day Stages to the maximum level. Level design on the new stages is more open, you can go different paths of the stage and each one will be exciting and fast, making the different paths worth checking out by going to the stage again and again.
There are also red rings which encourage even more exploration. That is good on my book. There are also trials that you can do, these are mostly required for getting keys to unlock tne boss of the era. But you can still do the rest of these to have fun and check them out, most of these are challenging and pretty fun to get through. The trials also give special abilities for Classic and Modern Sonic, which you can then buy on the item shop, and equip them. Like Modern Sonic gets more boost meter (basically infinite meter) or actual infinite meter, but you won't be able to collect rings, at all. 0 rings while using infinite boost.
Classic Sonic will get elemental shields, and even he gets the homing attack! You can also unlock super sonic when you defeat the final boss, for modern and classic. So there are a lot of fun things to do in this game. Although story mode is too short and a bit bland.
If you are a Sonic fan, you will love this game to death. If you are new to the series, this is good for getting to know a bit how the classic games controlled, and what stages where the most iconic on 3D Sonic. If you do get interested on the series, check out the classic games, Sonic 1, Sonic 2 or Sonic 3 and Knuckles. Or also play the adventure games if you want.

Do you remember booting this up, and discovering all four discs.
If you still have them, then skip this utter trash port.  After a decade, we've been subjected to an utter half-way mistake.
They finally support 1920x1080...but only with huge bars at the side.  The visuals were remastered...on the character sprites.  The background is still hand drawn, and boy did it not age well.  The hidden chests are now easier to find...because they've had their pixels count increased so they stick out like a sore thumb.  The battle system is still working...except every 30th or so sequence when the enemies fail to load and you are staring at a blank screen.  At least there are new features...only those features are buried in a backwards menu.  If you press start it pauses the game.  To exit you have to enter the inventory, go to config, scroll to the bottom (because pressing up once is apparently too easy), then exit out of the program.
At least whenever there's a crash the game starts you from somewhere close to where you died...except it's basically just a saved state for a transition between areas only.  Saved states in emulators do the same thing, but better.
The underlying game is as good as it ever was.  It hasn't aged great, but it's still a blast to play.  "Remastering" this game is a joke.  The publisher/developer have functionally done what an emulator does, only worse in almost every conceiveable way.  Avoid this port.  It isn't worth the money.  Find an old PS2 or PS classic, and buy a copy of the original game.  It's better in every way that I can think of.
Update:
At about 3/4 of the way through the game, very little has changed.
Random encounter battles are about 80% of this game.  Walk from town to town, and it's roulette as to whether an encounter crashes the game or not.  Care to spend some time grinding for that last little bit of AP?  Hope you save frequently.
I've also discovered that more than a little bit of this game is directly tied to resolution settings and frame rate.  It's frustrating to be trying to do the arthritis inducing mini-games, but even more so when a minor fluctuation in frame rate can lead to a failure because the game did not detect something.  Namely, the Hippaul and jump rope games can go directly to purgatory.
Sigh.  I remember utilizing an automatic button clicker on an emulator to get these...travesties...to work.  The same doesn't work now, and the detection for button presses is just a mess.
Listen Square, I have no love for you.  You continue to forget what made you great, and delegate important projects to third tier developers.  I'll make a deal with you.  While the FF7 remake remains in development limbo, take about 7% of their staff off of the project.  Put them on a remaster of this game, with just PS3 level graphical fidelity as their goal.  Quietly anounce it's going to happen, two days before it hits store shelves.  It'll give you enough good will to prevent the massive black-hole that FF7 will inevitably generate in the community.  You are going to need something else, given that the FF7 release could cure Alzheimers at this point and there would still be disappointment because it doesn't also generate free energy.
Seriously, you've already done better.  The version this is based on was the poorer port from the past.  I'd still gladly take good old 4:3, but spending the money on a remastered port and only focusing on the FMV and character models was...let's call it odd given that "high" poly creatures appear on a background that looks like a resized JPG is just baffling.  The FMVs are a very small slice of this game, and most notably are not a game.

I love a lot of the features of this remaster/PC port. It has some decent convenience stuff, like a 'continue' that seems to pick you up from the last room change, and a speed-up mode for easy grinding.
But.. One really big, significant, constant, incredibly game-breaking bug totally and utterly ruins it, hands down, without any hope for the upsides countering it.
At random, sometimes after one battle sometimes after 5 sometimes after 12, the game will do the random battle sound/graphical effect, fade to black.. and never, ever fade back in. You can't Alt-F4, you can't continue where you left off, there's no save states to load or anything. If you were grinding for the last half hour and the final enemy froze like this? You're screwed, unless you save after every couple fights - and that's assuming you even can, and ignoring that it's kinda super tedious (call moogle, wait, choose save, wait, choose data slot, wait, choose save slot within data slot, wait.. exit.. exit.. exit.. exit.. )
The only "fix" I've found is to overwrite the x64 version of the game files with the x86 ones, which is a ridiculous fix to have to attempt, and it didn't fix the issue for me, anyways.
It is absolutely game-breaking to have random, and even sometimes non-random battles, completely lock the game and lose your progress, in this kind of game. Utterly and totally inexcusable, and reasonably common of an issue based on the number of folks posting about it without any full resolution.
tl;dr - when changing into battle the game will sometimes stay faded to black and you lose all progress since your last save, period. It happens sometimes right away, sometimes after a couple battles, sometimes after 10, doesn't matter if it's a scripted or random battle, all of them can break.

Lichdom: Battlemage is a fast-paced, spell slinging action combat game. It's very visually appealing, and the story takes you through a decent variety of good-looking environments where you fight waves of enemies with a number of pretty fun spells. The difficulty of the game scales quite well and can be very challenging on the higher difficulties - though if you choose to put the difficulty up, you will want to take advantage of the rather versatile "custom inventory" instead of the more streamlined "smart inventory".
However, the game does have its flaws. It is very linear - while there are some interesting things tucked away in the corners of the map, there is only ever one path forward. The game sort of encourages you to pick one set of elements and stick with it - higher level elements do more damage, so if you switch around a lot you'll eventually find yourself underpowered.
It can also feel very repetitive; the format of every level is the same (fight through smaller enemies, fight a miniboss, repeat until boss fight). This is amplified with the optional 'loot machine' fights. They're generally worth it due to the sheer amount of sigils you can obtain, but they are tedious and repetitive. I also feel that they distract from the sense of urgency that the narrative tries to convey - if someone I care about is in mortal danger, I shouldn't be stopping to fight some optional skeletons.
There is some interesting worldbuilding and backstory, but you only catch glimpses of it in the game's narrative. Most of it is delivered via collectible - and optional - journal entries. Despite the tags, I do not consider this a role-playing game. There is only one narrative choice in the game, and that is whether you play as the male or female character.
I personally enjoyed the game, although I did take a fairly long break around the middle because of how repetitive it was. I had fun with the sigil crafting system and experimenting with different powers, and the higher difficulties provided a nice challenge one I'd gotten the hang of the combat system. It is not, however, something I can see myself playing again anytime soon.
TL;DR version -
Pros:
- Fast paced action
- Very pretty, varied environments
- Cool spell effects
- Difficulty scales well
- Decent crafting system
Cons:
- Very linear.
- Repetitive
- Game encourages you to stick to one set of elements
- Worldbuilding not really presented in the narrative
- No significant replay value
In conclusion, if you like fast-paced action games and a bit of a challenge, give Lichdom a shot. If you're looking for something more tactical or with more role-playing elements, you might want to look somewhere else.

I tried so hard to like this game.  I always gravitate towards mages whenever a game allows, but there are just so many flaws that love of  magic isn't enough.  If you love hard games, magic, boring stories, AND grinding, pick the game up when it's on sale for no more than 20 dollars.  Now that that's out of the way, let's begin.
The voice acting is good, but they didn't really try with the story, or the ending.
The graphics are pretty, depending on how you feel about rather obnoxious film grain.  Spells look pretty spectacular, they got this part right.
There are 8 Sigils in the game (think magic schools), 3 of which can be equipped at one time.  Killing enemies is how you'll get most of your spell components.  The crafting system is undeservedly complex.  The game claims to have thousands of spells, which is nonsense.  Nova spells comprise your shield effects, and have no variation.  Shields themselves come in three varieties.  AOE spells come in two varieties.  The third slot can be a missile (like a fireball), a lob (like a grenade), or a ray-type spell.
And that's it.  Components are found, combined, upgraded, reforged, broken down, and possess a wide array of randomized stats, but there is no ignoring how basic the magic system is in the game, which is shrouded in poor explanations (if any).  The inventory system is terrible, designed to artifically inflate the amount of time spent sifting through your components through horrible organization.  Farming exists through fast-travel to previous areas, but voice-overs will play again and again as though you had never been there before.
Synergy spells are special spells you can create for when you have two specific sigils equipped.  As you kill either of the enemies with either sigil you a bar fills and you can cast a special spell.  The most synergies you can have equipped at one time is 3.  Some of these are pretty cool, but the learning curve of figuring out exactly how to make the spell in the first place was unnecessarily obtuse.
The entire game is a monster-corridor.  Environments are just as beautiful as the magic, but the game is almost on rails.  In a game where there are powerful spells but no such thing as a mana bar, they had to compensate by throwing in ever-increasing numbers of cheap enemies.  It's gripping, and fast-paced, but the entire game feels exactly the same.
It's not quite as hard as Dark Souls, but the game lets you know when you need to upgrade your spells or try a new combination of sigils by using your eye-sockets for pleasure.  The problem is it will do so completely without warning through sudden random spikes of difficulty, which will probably break the pacing of an already mundane story by making you go farm.  The only incantations the game makes you utter are long streams of cursing and the mumblings of boredom.

Pros:

Cons:

- RNG on summoning new monsters

Although I don't recommend this "early access" game, I want this game to be a wild success and hopefully the devs at Reentry Games will read this review. I know I only have 5 hours into the game and at only level 35 w/all my monsters are level 12, I stopped playing PVP when I got to rank 20 because I can already see how RNG will kill this game.
If you could implement a system like League of Legends where everytime you win a PVP match you get some sort of in-game currency to save up for a monster of your choice.  Right now, it is all luck of the draw. I could put $50 into the game and still end up with 2-star cards. That's no fun.
Yea yea, I can keep playing story mode to level 40 to test my RNG (and probably get another 1-star card), then keep playing PVP to grind gold so I can get to level 60 to test my RNG again (and probably get another 2-star card).
Ember Strike has another form of currency called "essense" where you can actually pick which monster you want.  I think this is Reentry Games way of getting rid of the RNG, but it actually promotes it. You achieve essense at the end of PVP season or when you get duplicates of the same monster. The higher rank in PVP you are, the more essense you get.  So if you have good monsters from the get-go, you will be racking up essense no problem. Snowball effect.  As for getting duplicates, RNG is also a killing blow here.  If you're lucky, you'll get a new card. If you're unlucky, you'll get a duplicate of one of your many 1-2 star cards. Then the vicious cycle repeats. You stay ranked low in PVP arena, get miniscule essense, grind PVP to get gold to level up your monsters to get 100 summoning stones in story mode. Get another crappy monster or duplicate, repeat.
The gameplay in this Ember Strike is so unique. I hope Reentry Games can find a new way to gain cash to make this game a wild success!

-The sound assets are brilliant. You can feel every blow as it connects.
- The Combat Deck system. It's just so much fun making your own fighting style.
-The Feel of it all, but I'll touch on that at the bottom.
THE BAD:
-Region Locking, if you hate that sort of thing. personally I dont. Fighting games need it, and this IS a fighting game.
-The challenge. It can be steep. Don't be put out if you lose. Figure out why, and fix it.
-Its a PvP game. It just is. You can play the whole thing offline, but you'll lose a LOT. Play it online. That SAID, playing online you will encount assclowns. This is not the game's fault, it's just a human thing. Some people like to be tossers. The devs have said there's a "friends only" mode on the way though, so that's neat.
So, Absolver.
It's easily, EASILY, one of the very beast fighters I've ever played. Every single moment in battle is tense, heart pounding, and beautiful, and with each enemy you put down you can FEEL yourself getting better. The progression is palpable, helped in part by the fact you learn new attacks by blocking/dodging them in battle. But by far what I adore most about the game is how well it hit what it was aiming for.
The world doesnt have a big sprawling story. It doesn't need one, it's a fighting game.
It doesn't have big groundbreaking photorealistic visuals. It doesn't need them, it's a fighting game.
It doesn't have a massive open world filled with quests and adventure. It doesn't need one, it's a fighting game.
Absolver is a game wherein every interaction is carried out not through spoken word or written dialogue, but by the power of your punch and the strength of your arm. It is a blood-soaked arena where champions are born and I genuinely believe it could grow to be an incredible game.
If you like fighting games and wanna try something with a bit of a new edge, give this a go. It's fun as all hell. Just don't play it if you're looking for a perfect game.

I still really like Absolver, this game has amazing depth and is a very deep rabbit hole to go down. As you learn more moves and unlock more slots for those moves the complexity can increase simply by trying to chain together a series of attacks that feel right to you and expresses your fighting style. There is no perfect set of attacks or optimized type of equipment.
For example, every piece of clothing has a weight and protection value, the heavier your clothing the slower you are. There are multiple types, styles, weights, protection values so simply choosing what pants or belt, or elbow pads becomes a risk reward proposition.
Each type of move also scales differently, some are affected more my strength or dexterity or overall mobility.
You will build a character that suits your style of play and you will be unique in the game and that is very satisfying.

A pretty innovative game (although see also The Ship and a couple of others in the same ballpark) that has its flaws, but can be pretty fun once you get the hang of it all. Basically you play an actor that needs to kill the other actors in the movie so you can be the star.
Although there are a few game modes, the core is The Hunt - you have one opponent to kill, while someone else is tasked with killing you. So essentially you have a FPS version of Chompy Chomp Chomp and you rush about collecting weapons and items to help you, heading to where your target is on the minimap (or you get regular notifications when they move to a new area of the map), while trying to avoid traps and other people who might be out to kill you themselves.
The learning curve is pretty steep - you really need to know the maps intimately, including what each area is called, and what the quickest routes to get there from where you are is (there are usually dozens of routes as there are ladders, stairs, doors, corridors - pretty much every room/area has 4 or 5 ways out, and many have 10 or more. You also need to know where the weapons and traps are and how to use some of the more esoteric weapons like the rat bomb (and when to use it), and how to best use the bonus items which can be game changing when properly applied. Plus you need to know where all the traps are, and critically where they can be triggered from so that you know when it is safe to pass through. And then you need to track which weapons are currently good to use, as well as knowing the ins and outs of the different game modes, which will be switched every few minutes.
The weapons are not really balanced, but this is kind of as designed - this is mitigated somewhat by the scoring system - the good weapons usually get enough use they rarely ascend to a being a high scoring weapon after the first round, but in practise getting an easy kill for average score beats a strategy of trying to successfully use every awkward weapon in a cycle as they get to 5*. Another issue is the Blood Money round, which basically scores way to highly, such that most of the rest of the game often becomes a tie breaker between the people that did well in that one round.
Once you have the hang of it, and have some friends who also do, things finally click and you will probably start having a Bloody Good Time, but I can see plenty of people deciding that getting to that point isn't worth the payoff, as even then this game is quirky, flawed and not particular well balanced.

The new age of SimCity has arrived in SimCity 4: Deluxe Edition. EA has created yet another fantastic game for the PC and they have succeeded in making it work. SimCity 4: Deluxe Edition is a marvel, because it's like you are building a real city on real terrain. You control the city in every way possible. I got this game because I am a SimCity fanatic and I couldn't wait to try it out. Once I finally installed the game I did the Tutorials (which are optional) and finally got to create an entire region! That's rite I said region, an entire state seems to be at your fingertips! You can make Oceans, lakes, rivers, mountains, cliffs, and even plateaus with GOD mode. Forests and animals alike can be created as well! In this game you are finally in control.
Graphics 9/10
Now I'm not one to judge a games graphics, because to me, that doesn't make a game what it is but this game is different. It looks as though you are in an airplane looking down on real forests and buildings that you yourself created, now that is what I call the work of EA.
Game Play 9/10
Now this is what makes SimCity what it is, you have control of everything on your map, the terrain, the animals, and obviously your city. You make your city from the ground up, you start with nothing but level land and then you make residential, commercial, and Industrial areas along with a power plant. You work your way up and begin adding schools, police and fire stations, library's, water plants, and so much more. Before you know it your small village where everybody knows everybody becomes a bustling metropolis, complete with towering sky scrapers and traffic problems, which brings me to my next topic. The expansion Rush Hour comes complete with the Deluxe Edition making it possible to drive cars, boats, and airplanes in your city. You can be a police officer chasing down a thief or you can be an evil scientist attempting to transport dangerous chemicals across your city. You can really be anyone and do anything in this game. There is also a mode in which you can move your sims into your city, where they can gather opinions from civilians that live in your city about how good of a job you are doing. In MAYOR mode you build your city and make complex road systems, airports, seaports and massive bridges to cross seas. You can design a sewer system or even create a vast country side of ranches and farms. The best part is in GOD mode, where you can unleash a hoard of disasters on your city, from fires too alien invasions you can re-create judgment day on your defenseless sims.
Replay Value 8/10
You can never finish the game but after a solid good 6 months of playing it you will feel like you have done everything there is to do, but in this game, the sky is the limit. If you had the energy and lived in a decent sized city you could recreate it rite on your computer, that is just how detailed this game really gets. This game gets more complicated the bigger your city gets and sometimes you get so confused that you just give up playing for awhile.
Do not rent this game, just don't buy it if you don't like simulation games. It goes for about forty dollars and it is a good buy so if you are really into the SimCity games you can mow a couple of lawns, but if you just like any good simulation game go ahead and buy it if you have forty bucks laying around.
Overall rating 9/10

Super Blackjack Battle 2 Turbo Edition - The Card Warriors:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Fans of Blackjack, here is your chance to become the best player on the planet and play the ultimate game against the notorious godfather and owner of the largest casino in Las Vegas. But before reaching this final match, you will have to face champions around the world to book your ticket to Las Vegas. The number 21 is all you must think of. . . Blackjack!
Super Blackjack Battle 2 Turbo Edition - The Card Warriors is essentially a card game combined with Street Fighter 2 style of artwork and the fact that you have to beat several opponents to reach the ultimate face off with the godfather himself.
The game offers four modes of play – Single player combat, Simply Blackjack, Versus unranked opponent and World Championship (the last two are online modes).
Upon selecting the single player combat mode, you will have to choose one of the ten characters to play with. There are another two characters but you have to unlocked them. If you don’t know how to play Blackjack, what you have to do is to get to 21, or as close as possible, to win the round if you play against the house. However, if the house has a number closer to 21, or exactly 21, you lose. In Super Blackjack Battle Turbo Edition – The Card Warriors, you play against the house and an opponent. Each battle has up to ten rounds to complete, but it might take only one round to win or to lose.
At the start of each round, you have to place a bet. Then the house will distribute two cards each to you, your opponent and itself. If you think your number is too low, you can ask for another card or stand if you are happy with your number. If the house is the one who is closer to the magic number, your opponent and yourself will lose your bet. If you are the one who is the closet to the number then you win. To beat your opponent and move on to the next round, you must have the highest number of credits after ten rounds, or your opponent will lose all his or her credits before the end of all the rounds. Whether you win or lose, you will be treated with a cheesy comment - a flashback to the Street Fighter 2 comments. Beat all your opponents to win the game.

If you like to play just against the house, select the Simply blackjack mode. As I mentioned above, the remaining two modes are online but I didn’t have the opportunity to play against another user.
The artwork is great and nostalgic. In regards to the soundtrack, it’s pretty much the same style as in the iconic fighting arcade game.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great and nostalgic artwork
-	Interesting combination
-	Several modes
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
-	Repetitive
Fun combination and great homage to an iconic arcade fighting game.
6/10

I bet anyone who heard of a crossover between blackjack and SF would be genuinely interested, so lets see how this game holds up.
Design, graphics and music
-----------------------------
No doubt, Super Blackjack Battle 2 Turbo Edition - The Card Warriors borrows alot from a certain game, even its title is straight from Street Fighter. It adds, in my opinion, to the charm of a classic game and also makes it stand out from a sea of blackjack games online. Characters look like they belong into a 90s arcade and the music fits every stage. All in all the overall design is well executed.
Gameplay
-----------------------------
It's blackjack. Plain and simple. There is a single player campaign, where you travel around the world, beat the other characters and get rewarded with a silly quote after each battle and an individual ending after the campaign. Also there are multiplayer modes, with a 4 player mode and ranked and unranked matches. Haven't checked them out yet, as I was playing the campaign only but nevertheless I liked it. The first couple opponents play overly aggressive and beat themselves most of the time, the later ones act more cleverly. But since it is blackjack, it happens that sometimes either you, your opponent or the dealer get lucky. My guess would be that I would like playing against human opponents as much or even more as playing against the AI, so no major complaint regarding the gameplay either.
Verdict
------------------------------
An entertaining little game with an special appeal, it delivers what it promised: A blend of SF and blackjack.

I must admit that this game caught my attention the first time I stumbled upon it. The combination of Street Fighter 2 and Blackjack is rare enough and promising.
The artstyle is on point, the different nods and references are well done and detailed and anyone who played Street Fighter back in the days will get that fuzzy feeling of nostalgia in their tummies just a couple of seconds into the game. The characters, the cutscenes, the cheesy dialogues...everything's there.
At heart, it is a Blackjack card game, each round you bet money and try to get a combinated card value of 21 (or near). But here comes the twist:  Not only do you play against the house in classic Blackjack tradition but also against an opponent from some corner of the world. You win by either your opponent going bankrupt or you having more money than him by the end of round 10. Here, some strategy is thrown into the mix: Betting high right from the beginning so you win big and your opponent won't the able to catch up? Playing safely by only betting as much as your opponent or hoping he gets unlucky? Many ways to play. Of course the game shines the brightes in online multiplayer as human opponents are way more interesting to play against. I think more and more players will show up over time and I was also being able to play a couple of rounds against others with a little patience.
It will take you some time so see all the endings and get all achievements and after that you will have a nice and cool looking time waster for inbetween.

Final Fantasy IX, way I see it, is among the best of the Final Fanasy series. Great characters through what can be described as no less than a fantastic journey which moves across an amazing world. The various cities, landmarks and strange places you find across your journey all have no only that nostalgia behind them, but a real depth is found in not only the lives of the party of characters you'll get to know, but the people who surround them and their own arcs cleverly put in by an interesting story telling system called "active time events." Some of which indirectly change certain variables creating dialogue that could otherwise go unknown, hiding the bits and pieces FF-IX leaves strewn about for you to find.
The graphics and artwork for this game remain beautiful and appear to have been touched up for a higher resolution over it's original Playstation release. Along with that, the game runs beautifully, not that it isn't expected, as even with the touch ups, the game is shouldn't be much of a bother to run on any machine unless there is something tremendously wrong with your computer. As a note here, there isn't much in the way of graphics options other than resolution.
The game runs just fine using an Xbox-360 controller, zero issues here on that front. If you have an issues, my only advice would be to uninstall the controllers driver and reinstall.
As for combat, skills and magic and the such, nothing that is to far out of tradition when it comes to a J-RPG. Though the characters are class based in a sense, this limits what each character can do, making certain characters more appropriate for certain areas based on whether they can use white or black magic, have strong phsyical attacks or have unique abilities more suited to the present situation. Along with that, most weapons and armors for characters can teach the character certain abilities which you can activate in the menu which give certain buffs. Things such as auto-regen, certain attack resistances, various other buffs and debuffs that you can change at your leisure, but are limited to how many of these abilities you can have active at any given time too.
As for collectables and end game content, FF-IX is brimming with it. Chocobo side quests, a few smaller story arcs with other NPC's, rewarding collectables and that horrible thing in the sky.
All in all, FF-IX is a great J-RPG experience and is worth playing. I've played it several times back during the days after it's original release and played it on Steam and the experience never really gets old. I sure had fun and I can certainly guarentee you will too. If it's on sale, get it. If it's not, get it. It's worth every penny.

If you like 1 on 1 fist fights with many different combos and your own move sets this game is for you. Almost every attack flows into the next in a satisfying deal of blows. The combat is similar to For Honor in that you have multiple stances and you switch between them during the fight to get different move sets. The gameplay is smooth and fun, its what the game excels in, but if you came in looking for rich lore or story you came to the wrong place. First off one of my main issues is the coop system, you can join friends or other random players in a group, normal right? That is until one of you die and that person is then removed from the group until you find them in the game world again or you go back to an altar to waste time reinviting a fallen friend. The main campaign which consists of fighting every boss in each area took me and my friends 5 hours to complete. After that you can go into leaderboards with your own school. There isn't much end game content added as of yet, but at the moment there is a hidden move set that you can find by exploring around the relatively small map (3 main large areas). The 1v1 fights versus friends are a blast and combat keeps getting interesting with learning new moves, or trying out any of the other classes (3 main and 1 hidden for now). The move set deck is perfect for personalizing your fighting style and making every fight with another player unpredictable, add that with weapon combat and this is Absolver.
Pros:
- Fluid motion
- Fun deck building system
- great visual asthetic
- good combat and bosses
- Fun 1v1s
- Leaderboards when you beat main story
Cons:
- Short campaign
- small map
- more than 2 enemies when alone is sometimes unfair.
- alot of lag issues, some enemies teleporting everywhere, and falling off the map like Nightcrawler just got his powers. Many times ruins the experience for pvp or pve
- Awful coop system where when you die you leave the group and wastes time when you want to rejoin.

So, two and a bit hours into my playtime and I have to say I am having an absolute blast playing this so far! First impressions are always the most important for me and this really hits the nail on the head in breaking you into the world of Absolver. Its very darksouls-esque from what i've seen this far but instead of people invading your world, you seamlessly meet people throughout your journey and can choose to fight or aid each other...friends can become enemies and enemies friends in a few clicks depending on your playstyle. I personally am the friendly type, i'll help others and just let them get on with their lives! The more Darksouls-y side comes in with the world itself, with no loading times between zones and plenty of loot to pick up, its somewhat of a semi-open world experience where you can choose whatever order you want to do things and work to the ultimate goal (that of which I still don't really know yet, looks like you have to defeat a bunch of mini bosses to unlock some sort of pathway to another area? I haven't gotten too far yet, just taking my time and enjoying the game).
The first few minutes of figuring out the combat and the combo deck may put you into a bit of a blunder at first depending on how quickly you take to it, but its easy to understand after you play around with it all, then its just a case of mastering your chosen fighting style and understanding what type of equipment you need to wear to get the most efficiency from it. I went for Windfall, which has a focus on dexterity based attacks and using timed avoidance mechanics...i'm pretty bad at it right now but practise makes perfect!
For anyone more interested in the PvP but dont want to go around bashing everyone up in the overworld all the time, fear not! there are "combat trials" where you can do some good old fashioned 1 on 1 with a random and you can do it whenever you want. It looks like there is definitely more you can do later on but right now for me it was just 1v1 sparring where its best of 3 wins. I tried my hand at a match and won 3-1...the map we got was a little cheap as my first point was by accidentely knocking them off a flight of stairs into the abyss, made sure we had a platform for a proper fight rather than cheap quick wins.
Honestly, hats off to the creators of this marvelous masterpiece...trumps For Honor any day of the week! I'm really looking forward to making more progress and seeing what kind of updates and content come along in the coming weeks/months!
