I expected more than just Borderlands: Wizard edition. I thought maybe my prayers for an incredibly polished mage only combat game have been answered, but I guess it's back to the praying for me. Not terrible, but not what was promised.

Pretty fun, the interface is simple and easy to learn. The levels as mentioned by previous reviewers are huge but with only a few waves of enemies with large gaps between. Some of the wave challenges feel drawn out to fill space and create a time sink.
The crafting and upgrading of the spells are fun and interesting allowing the player a lot more control than in previous games. You do feel like you have a whole ton of hidden power just waiting to be unleashed on your foes. I do find in the earlier levels I have to groups of enemies then use the fire aoe to stop being swarmed but good use of the teleport and enviornmental objects makes this more than achivable.

It is an interesting concept but the actual gameplay is slow and doesn't live up to the tagline of "empowering the mage". The crafting system is more of changing small numerical bonuses into other slightly less small numerical bonuses. All in all, I don't see myself playing it in the future.

Lichdom: Battlemage offers a prospect that many other games don't offer: "What if magic was as easy as normal fighting? No cooldowns, and the limit to your power is how strong of spells you can form".
The problem with this is that, while that premise of the game is delivered upon, most of the rest of the game just isn't anything beyond pretty at best. Honestly, that's about the nicest thing I can say about this game, because it's in Cryengine, it's rather pretty. However, all of that is lost when you have as many other things that are just NOT very good.
The largest gripes I have with the game are:
- Enemy variety is basically non-existent
There are MAYBE 9 varieties of enemy, and about half of those don't show up till around 1/2 through the game
- There are only really 24 spells
You can craft many different spells with different stats, but there are only 24 different effects, and many of those overlap.
- Difficulty is very poorly balanced
I literally ACCIDENTALLY killed the 4th boss (there are 5 total) in one shot, without any sort of crit beyond charging my spell. On the flip side, some normal mini-bosses will one-shot you and take multiple apocalypticals (double-crits) to kill.
- About as linear as you could possibly imagine
This game offers basically no choice, all the game play takes place in what is effectively hallways. To give an idea, it's about as linear as Bulletstorm or Gears of War 1
- The game is about 2X as long as is necessary
I've played it for around 32 hours, and about 14 hours of it felt boring/repetitive/pointless
That being said, the game is definitely worth around the first 10 hours or so, as experimenting around with synergies and sigils can be quite fun. It just gets boring, as I quickly realized that most of the spells do effectively the same things with different particle effects. Some do actually do completely different things (i.e. Phase & Necromancy), but in the end, it is most effective to just grab a big DPS sigil, like Fire, an then some means to stop enemies in their tracks, and then blast them with mastery (which is a gameplay element that allows for amplified damage) until you are ready to blow them to kingdom come.
I can't recommend the game at full price. However, if the game is on sale for ~$10 or less, feel free to buy it, as it is worth that in my opinion.

More than a building blocks game, Castle Story s a civil engineering game. Your structures need to stand on something, and if that something is blasted, all the dependencies will possibly be afected if not secured somewhere else. No more hiding on floating towers like Terraria.
Play it on survival for the most fun with management AND structural design.
If you want to play a cosmetic building game, I suggest you to go for Minecraft or the likes that do not use a physics engine outside the grids, so you won't be limited by performance demanding calculations.
If you want to watch minions do your bidding flawlessly, maybe something like The Sims would be better.
Survival is based on waves, and more predictable than Space Engineer's asteroids. I liked it because you can improve your management and not ruin a good run by random chance.
AI may seem dumber than some other games, but they have a lot more to adapt to. Play it like it's 2015 and recon the complexity of this game. The rules are simple and few, yet you'll find building a defense is not that straightforward like other games make you believe. Your minions are not overpowered and will be shot down from high towers.
Give it a go, don't expect a mind blowing experience, but do expect an awesome one nevertheless. It's architecure with focus on function over form.

Absolutely fantastic game. I'll start off with my first impressions, followed by a pretty cool story.
So, I was just coming out of the prologue area, not really sure how to play or what my ultimate goal was, but I noticed a random player struggling to fight off four npc's. He quickly became swarmed and I ended up joining into the fray. We kicked some asses, he bowed and went on his way.
I remembered his name and ended up running into him down the line a few minutes later. This time he had been attacked by a player, or he had instigated a fight, either way, I was on his side. We quickly took down his opponent and I never met him again.
This was in the first 10 minutes.
I've had lots of moments like that so far, but the one that I love the most is the most recent, and the reason why I'm writing this review. Essentially me and this guy met up somewhere in the game, similar to the previous story, and we went into cooperative mode for about 45 minutes. We encountered several groups of NPC's, several players, and no one could take us down. We ended up fully exploring one of the areas and reached a dead end. He decided we should no longer be allies. Betrayed I fought him to the death and ended up winning. With my last gesture I resurrected him and we both split up never to see each other again.
It was awesome that I met some random person, we tanked through about 50-60 enemies, and then he betrayed me at the last moment. I haven't had many moments like that in video games so I'm super impressed.
Visually, the game is fantastic. Aesthetics are on spot and the whole feel fits the genre perfectly.
Audio is excellent, you can even rely on audio cues for certain moves to better anticipate.
Combat is fantastic, it's honestly one of the best of it's kind.
High player population, never had an empty map so far. (This can be disabled for those who want to lose out on some of the awesomeness)
Relatively okay story, I haven't really progressed through it much nor felt the need. I've been enjoying just travelling and exploring the world.
If you're into fighting games this is something you need to pick up. Absolutely fantastic game, highly recommended.

As much as I hate to say it, the game is not good in its current state.
The loot is very unrewarding. If you want more armor, you're going to have to EQUALLY take away from your strength and mobility that you gain armor, and it feels the exact same for every piece of gear you find. It never feels like I should pick it up unless it looks cool.
The enemies are far too easy. It can be fun to wreck noob AI, but only to a certain extent. The bosses I were able to kill were easy, the only difficulty is that they throw in extra enemies to keep your hands tied.
But the most disappointing thing to me is that the co-op just doesn't work for this type of game. If you encountered a group of enemies in single player, you would encounter the same group of enemies at the same difficulty level that you would with 2 other people in your party. When the game is as easy as it is already, that's a poor gaming experience.
Also, the game needs a progression system. I would want a reason to keep playing after beating the poor story.
The PvP is great, but I'm not going to pay $30 for a seemingly unfinished 1v1 brawler.

This game is a nostalgia rush for sure.  I dig some of the classic era stages being re-imagined the most.
Overall the remixes of the original tunes isn't bad but they can occasional sound a little weird if you heard the originals a lot as they tried to modernize some of them a bit.
The game has stages from 3 eras:
Classic Era: Green Hill, Chemical Plant, Sky Sanctuary
Dreamcast Era: Speed Highway, City Escape, Seaside Hill
Modern Era: Crisis City, Rooftop Run, Planet Wisp
Each era has a total of one boss and one rival battle with 5 challenges and 2 acts for those challenges.
Classic Sonic plays act 1 of each stage and challenge.
Modern Sonic plays act 2 of each stage and challenge.
There is two different play styles:
Classic Sonic acts are 2D stages with 3D graphics and 2.5D elements here and there.  Controls similar to how he did in the classic Genesis games.
Modern Sonic acts are 3D stages with some 2D sections here and there.  Controls like the Sonic from Unleashed, Colors, etc. with boost to win elements.
A gallery for unlocking some artwork, music, and secret room for unlockable statues of various characters from the franchise.  Cutscenes can be re-watched here as you progress through the game's story.
Bosses and rival battles have a hard mode.  The ranking system mostly judges you on time and if you died at all during the stage or boss.  Rankings in order from the highest to lowest: S, A, B, C, D.
The story is lighthearted and simple enough.  The plot doesn't really get that deep here.
The PC version does have issues that the Xbox 360 and Playstation 3 versions do not!  It is recommended you get the console versions if you can. It's a good game overall.  So it's worth it
Make sure you pick up a controller that supports XINPUT!  I recommend one that's similar to a Xbox 360 or PS3 dual shock style controller.

The flawed-yet-thrilling Sonic title that we've wanted all along.
The game attempts to find a compromise between the style of gameplay Sega and their devs seem to want the series to have and the style of gameplay that people fondly remember the series having.
The game really doesn't actually accomplish either, but at least seems to land close-to-target.
For what it is, the game is fantastic.  There's a lot of nostalgia thrown around, but a lot of fun if you don't mind a little bit of jank and are willing to work with the game to make it do what you want to do.
The levels are all cover versions of past Sonic stages, along with some awesome renditions of the music associated with those levels.  There's some iconic sights and sounds that have been bizarrely omitted, but we can't have everything and even if we asked Sega probably wouldn't care (and would throw in a new animal friend or sidekick for good measure).

I realized that I’ve never given this game a proper review, which is disappointing, because it holds an easy spot in my top 10 favorites.
This game is, in a word, brilliant. It’s a Star-Trek/Firefly simulator rougelite that puts you in the captain's seat of your own starship. While the game may lack eye candy, its minimalist presentation is effective. The soundtrack is stellar, the gameplay is deep, and even the writing is pretty great. FTL has all the elements of a modern classic.
You play this game for the victories, and the emergent stories that come with them. Winning this game is not easy. I’ve attempted over 600 runs and have only won about 5% of them. But those 5% are some of the most triumphant highs I’ve experienced in gaming.
Of course, just as in life, winning isn’t everything. Losing in this game is fun too, because your losses help you grow. FTL is one big try/fail cycle. Every time the game knocks you down, you come away having learned something new about its mechanics, so that when you start a new game, you make it a little farther. And a little farther after that. Until finally you see that victory screen and decide to play your next game on Normal instead of Easy, because you want more.
FTL might be the only game I’ve ever played in which I actually try to beat my high scores. I haven’t logged as many hours on this game as I have with other titles, but I’ve continued to come back to it every year since the day I bought it. Few games have had that kind of staying power with me.
I bought FTL for a buck during a humble bundle way back when. I’ve since purchased a second copy at full price to support the developers.
To Subset Games, thank you for the fun.
To anyone who reads this, consider giving this game a try. It can be frustrating at times, but when you tap into its depth, it’s immensely rewarding.

One of the best games of my childhood, and having played it again on Steam and EA's Battlefront 2 on Xbox, I can say hands down that this game is still better by far, albeit without the movie quality graphics. Despite the age, the graphics are actually pretty good, and for a FPS, Vehicle, Objective based game, it plays rather smooth. It is also worth pointing out that it doesn't have loot boxes ;)

Being someone who had never played this game before (and told my friend that recently) he found it was on sale and gifted it to me on the spot. Although I cannot compare it to the 2017 Battlefront 2, I would like to say it holds up INCREDIBLY well.
Story: As a medium star wars fan (read alot of books, but not hyper-fan in that I own every book and have read every book/comic) but I do consider myself slightly above the level of dedication of an average fan. With this knowledge in hand, the story mode holds up very well. It doesn't completely hold up to the new cannon (the recent spinoff movie kinda messes with some of them), but you have to keep in mind that that movie wasn't written at the time, or even concived. Ironically, it looks way better then the same amount of story content in the new 2017 version, which I have seen videos of. The cutscenes are better made in the new one, the visuals are better in it, but the star wars feel goes 100% to this game. If I were to pick a more star wars game, it would be this one, because quality and realism isn't everything.
TLDR - Story almost entirely avoids conflict with cannon and way better put together then in the 2017 version to my knowledge. Even where it could mess with it, I didn't end up caring enough as it was put together more then perfectly, and it serves as a great introduction to the game if you're into the multiplayer side. 9/10
Gameplay: Holds up pretty nice as well. No notable negatives. It's great in the veriety of tasks you can do. I will admit to being bad at these types of gams normally, but the unchaotic nature of inital gameplay prepared me for the more chaos that came later, and allowed me to slowly get into it. There wasn't a big learning curve for this game at all as a player new to ANY of the battlefront star wars games. I got into it suprisingly fast, and I want to play it more as I speak, but the only limiter right now is how much time I have on hand for myself to play it. 8/10
Visuals: Ok, what do you expect? it's 2005. Even so, I consider this almost as good as the 2017 for the time, so I'll give it an extra point over what I would normally give it. The style as it is is pretty nice, and it manages the best it can with what computers could handle back then. Great designs and classic sights from the movies don't quite come to life like in the 2017, but it's also from 2005 and taking up only a few GB on your hard drive. Honestly, watching videos of the 2017 Battlefront 2 gives me a severe case of "uncanny valley". I'm a little weird in that I can see how hard they are trying, but it unsettles me where they are at. In this game, it is clearly digital, giving my brain no problem deciding at all. 7/10
Hardware compatibility: I only wish to note this in a positive manner, as many 2005 games I have had serious issues working on newer machines, and I would never attribute that negatively to a game. However, not only does this work great on my brand new 2017 laptop, it works without any compatibiliy modes or any tinkering at all, and perfectly at that. I noted only one minor visual error that didn't impact gameplay, which is absolutely amazing. I've had more issues with minecraft (I had to get a mod for it to even work correctly. So much for being such a great game.)
Overall, I'd give this game a 8/10 in a regular rating system, or in my book, extremely above average. Worth every penny of $10 even today. If you have not played it - BUY IT. Play the story mode as if it was half priced DLC for battlefront 2 2017 if that makes you feel better. Nah, one third priced DLC - they'll find a way to charge $30 for it, I'm sure. And don't tell me they aren't doing DLC, they're gonna do it. Either that or doom lootboxes to a death of fire and angry lawmakers. This game - while limited in scope at times - is great, and I yet again HAVE advised all my friends to get if they haven't already.

Probably the best Sonic inspired game you can find out there.
But don't mistake them to be too similar, as each title does things differently for best and worse.
Freedom Planet's levels composition is more complex, unlike Sonic which is more linear and speed focused with less road blocks.
This game puts more emphasis on combat, be it your own various attack moves, trash enemies having hp (every mob in Sonic is one hit) and more diverse boss patterns.
There's also a story + dub, but honestly it's so ♥♥♥♥ing cringe that you wouldn't miss a thing if you simply skip it all. Unless you're into that "fighting for my friends" (actual quote) stuff.
If you're looking for different modes, the game also offers time attacks (chapter select basically), different difficulty settings - from casual to hard, and 3 different characters with their own adventure paths and story variations.
Overall Freedom Planet delivers a great adventure with unique worlds that keep the gameplay fresh with new enemies, hazards and interactive objects per each zone. Definitely recommend for everyone, regardless of your platformers experience.

It's a great game all around. The story isn't anything special, but the high-quality amateur voice work is absolutely charming. The artwork and animation is very well-done as well. If you like 2D platformers, and especially if you like the Sonic games, I cannot recommend this title enough. It's a must-have.

Ok, to start, I'm going to say that I grew up with nintendo. You'll find no classic genesis comparisons here because I have little to no experience with that. Anyway, this game is fantastic. Great level design paired with fast and fun gameplay. Replayability is pretty good with the three characters playing similarly but different enough to have variety, plus the collectable cards that are hidden pretty well throughout each level. The specific character abilities are fun and unique, each making me think of different ways to fight the same boss or get around the same obstacle. One minor complaint I have in the gameplay department is that the levels can sometimes go on maybe a bit too long. I counted three levels where I had a time under ten minutes after playing Lilac's story, one of which being the final level,
After the great gameplay, we have the not as great story. It's not bad, but about halfway through it takes itself way too seriously. I like the first bits where the game is more lighthearted because the writers and voice actors can really do decent comedy and fun dialogue, but later, it can become funny for the wrong reasons. specifically, the voice acting can be good at times, but it usually makes things worse due to the voice actors not really being able to convey certain emotions well in my opinion. A good specific example would be after a certain spoiler boss in Lilac's story. There's potential for some actually good emotion, but the VA ruined it because she overacted and made it hilarious. I feel like if it didn't have voice acting, and just had a little more animation, it would've come off a LOT better. However, like I said before, I feel like when the game tries to be funny or lighthearted, it succeeds, even when it comes to the voice acting. Funny, now that I think about it, this game is such a successful homage to sonic it even manages to get the cheesiness of the story and voice acting in the early 3D games down, so maybe it's intentional. Either way, I'm thankful for the classic mode, where cutscenes are cut off and you just go from level to level.
After that, there's the characters themselves. I honestly have no complaints here besides what I've already written. The designs are cute, the personalities are fun, and there isn't one intolerable♥♥♥♥♥♥in sight, not even the one who's meant to be an intolerable♥♥♥♥♥♥ (that being mayor zao, who's cocky and narcissistic, but has plenty of humor surrounding him and never goes too far with those character traits)
Lastly, there's the graphics. I freakin' love the art style in this game! The backgrounds are lively and colorful, and while the environments aren't always original, they're done really damn well! The animations are smooth and often funny or cute, plus really well detailed! Yeah, I really don't have much to write in this bit because it's literally just that. I love it.
One last thing about the voice acting: it may be my computer, but the VA volume seems extremely low for some characters. Sometimes, I could barely hear any voices, let alone make out any words from them.
Overall, the game is great, even if the story sometimes gets too serious and will often fall into a giant pit of cheese. 8/10 I would definitely reccomend it to anyone who likes platformers!

This here’s a lengthy and informational review on the game Castle Story.
Please note that this game is still in development, and can and, in fact, probably will change (seeing as this game is far from finished and there’s lots of work to be done).
What is Castle Story? Its the story of, well, a castle. You get these cute little guys called bricktrons who want to defend themselves from ever increasing waves of little ankle-biters known as corruptrons. How exactly? A castle (duh). There are 3 types of bricktrons currently in game. The first is the worker bricktron. This cute plump little guy is the backbone of your fortress. He will gather resources such as wood from trees and rocks or orange and blue crystals from mines (or pits if your playing in sandbox mode). They can also place bricks (automagically converted from rock in stockpiles) to form your castle. There are also various structures you can build such as doors, pillars of wood, planks, lanterns (trust me, you’re gonna need them), etc., as well as stone structures such as stairs, pillars of stone, half-bricks and arches. The next kind of bricktron is the knight bricktron. He is armed with a sword, shield and helmet who defends the castle. They have a HUGE amount of health compared to the other bricktrons, and work well with the last kind of bricktron, the archer bricktron. This bricktron is armed with a bow, quiver full of arrows and a sexy Robin Hood hat. These bricktrons are able to shoot corruptrons at range (albeit not as accurately as you’d think). However, their health is rather weak, so their main use is on top of battlements.
Then you have the antagonists of the game, the corruptrons. There are only 2 types currently implemented. The first and most common type is called the, well, corruption (it doesn’t really have a name). They are short, stocky, weak little guys who go for your bricktrons and structures. They can also throw rocks at archer bricktrons to stun them for half a second. They are one-shot-killed be arrows, and two-shot-killed by a knights sword. The other type is called the big corruptron. This guy has HUGE health and can one-shot-kill knight bricktrons. However, he is really slow.
Wood is used in wooden structures, stone makes bricks, yellow crystals make lanterns, and blue crystals make more bricktrons. Simple resources.
That there’s the game. Now to my analysis.
The game idea itself is FASCINATING. Its stronghold meets minecraft in a way. But it takes a LOT more time than you’d think to build your castle, and it really is VERY difficult to build a castle and defend it like the one in the advertisement. Heck, your corruptions wont even come through the front door, they’d rather just pummel through your walls, right under your archers where they cant shoot the attackers to defend the wall. In fact, it is nigh impossible to get a castle even closely similar to it. You might see only one in your entire game experience. That is, however, NOT the most outstanding issue, that being the AI. The AI is completely broken, ironically through a huge patch that featured ‘improvements’ to the AI. How you ask? Here’s some reasons.
Corruptrons, once they’ve found a target (which is right when they first come into being far, far away) will NEVER NEVER NEVER NEVER NEVER pick a new one until he’s updated through being blocked from his target or the target being destroyed. Even worse, knights can’t attack moving targets because they have to stand still for a second to rev up their attack, and by the time he’s ready, the target has moved out of range. So its impossible to hurt enemies with a knight unless they pass right by you or are attacking their target (which could be the knight). Even WORSE, this mechanic makes big corruptrons completely overpowered. Since they one-shot-kill any bricktrons, knights are not an option unless the big guy is attacking a building. Archers are supposed to be the counter, but fail for 2 reasons. Archers have a TERRIBLE accuracy, and so are useless until you have LOTS of them (which is FAR beyond when the big corruptrons come out). Secondly, Big corruptions have LOTS AND LOTS of health. It ill take you at least roughly 10 arrows before you could DREAM of killing one of these things. Fortunately, since these guys are slow, they come after the much more spry corruptrons already die, so all your archers should be able to pick out the big guys. But thats REALLY hard in the early game when you may only FRANTICALLY save up blue crystals in order to get maybe one or two archers. The only viable option is to hope he targets a bricktron, then use it to kite the big guy around while your archers hurriedly fill him with arrows.
Your worker bricktrons are dumb as rocks (BA BING BAA, JUST GO PICK UP THE WOOD LOGS! I KNOW YOUR SAD ABOUT THE TREE YOU CHOPPED DOWN GOING OVER THE CLIFF BUT COME ON!), and they run away from corruptrons…sometimes straight into the claw of another corruptron.
Thats not all. The UI is TERRIBLE, and organizing stockpiles is pretty important (especially to make sure not to stockpile blue crystals so that they put them straight into the great crystal (It’s so uncomfortable to type crystal)), but annoying. Once your castle really gets going, builders take at least 3 seconds to decide where to put the brick they just picked up. The graphics are not great. The developers are too busy fixing the mess to actually add a lot of content. Nobody’s on the multiplayer. Planning a castle before it’s actually built takes a long time. Because of the targeting system, its really hard to defend your workers before you have a castle (before the 4th wave or so). Sometimes, workers decide to play fair and let a corruptron hit them. Archers give friendly fire, and are VERY naive about it. etc.
Now on to the suggestions to the developers. I’m thinking that either the big corruption should be slower, have less health (or boost archer attack), or deal less damage (COME ON, ONE-SHOT-KILL?!?). I think that instead of making different types of bricktrons, your bricktrons should be able to ‘arm up’ either with craftable weapons or automagically. This would allow you to have more kinds of resources to find, and allow you to have different tiers of weapons. The game should definitely have more of something to it than castle building I think. I myself am a game designer, and so feel qualified to make a couple suggestions/propose some ideas.
So what do I think? Don’t get this game until the developers hopefully fix it.

The tower-offense idea behind this game alone makes it worth playing if you're a fan of tower-defense games. The graphics are good and the gameplay ideas are unique enough that it stands out.

This lack of control makes this a tentative recommendation, it's worth a playthrough but be prepared to be frustrated sometimes with how stupid your units can be. Make sure to pick it up on sale.

Lichdom: Battlemage offers a prospect that many other games don't offer: "What if magic was as easy as normal fighting? No cooldowns, and the limit to your power is how strong of spells you can form".
The problem with this is that, while that premise of the game is delivered upon, most of the rest of the game just isn't anything beyond pretty at best. Honestly, that's about the nicest thing I can say about this game, because it's in Cryengine, it's rather pretty. However, all of that is lost when you have as many other things that are just NOT very good.
The largest gripes I have with the game are:
- Enemy variety is basically non-existent
There are MAYBE 9 varieties of enemy, and about half of those don't show up till around 1/2 through the game
- There are only really 24 spells
You can craft many different spells with different stats, but there are only 24 different effects, and many of those overlap.
- Difficulty is very poorly balanced
I literally ACCIDENTALLY killed the 4th boss (there are 5 total) in one shot, without any sort of crit beyond charging my spell. On the flip side, some normal mini-bosses will one-shot you and take multiple apocalypticals (double-crits) to kill.
- About as linear as you could possibly imagine
This game offers basically no choice, all the game play takes place in what is effectively hallways. To give an idea, it's about as linear as Bulletstorm or Gears of War 1
- The game is about 2X as long as is necessary
I've played it for around 32 hours, and about 14 hours of it felt boring/repetitive/pointless
That being said, the game is definitely worth around the first 10 hours or so, as experimenting around with synergies and sigils can be quite fun. It just gets boring, as I quickly realized that most of the spells do effectively the same things with different particle effects. Some do actually do completely different things (i.e. Phase & Necromancy), but in the end, it is most effective to just grab a big DPS sigil, like Fire, an then some means to stop enemies in their tracks, and then blast them with mastery (which is a gameplay element that allows for amplified damage) until you are ready to blow them to kingdom come.
I can't recommend the game at full price. However, if the game is on sale for ~$10 or less, feel free to buy it, as it is worth that in my opinion.

After having played through Lichdom once and having done some stuff in the new game + mode I can say that this game is one the one side really awesome, on the other side however the devs ruined it with bad design decisions and elements that  easily make you hate a game.
First off, the graphics are quite good. Strong explosions, epic vistas, lighting effects, cry engine 3 has been used well and the game is one of the best looking out there at the moment, probably te best looking mage-game that exists.
Now, the magic. In the game you can use 3 magic types at the same time switching between them by mouse wheel, there are eight magic types overall reaching from mind control to necromancy to fire and ice. All of them feel quite well implemented and they all bring their purpose, however the "spellcrafting" sounds cooler than it is. If you think you can mix elements or do your completely own spells youre wrong. You have control spells, mastery spells that increase critical damage you deal and normal damage spells. Those types can be delivered in special shapes: rays, missiles, lobbed projectiles, AoEs, AoE pools. Thats it.
There are special spells called synergies that can be used when crafting spells with legendary items, however those require two spell sigils to be equipped (e.g. kinetic and fire calls a meteor). What I missed were some more inspired ways to deliver damage like throwing frost shards, a flamethrower or life-leeching spells. Especially the necromancy sigil is very one-sided as all ways of augments have the same effects.
Spells are crafted from items that frop from enemies, making the spellcrafting lichdoms biggest strength and weakness at the same time. Loot is random and you will find tons of junk, this feels cheap and does not motivate.
The combat in the game is skill-based(casuals might die once or twice, I for myself did not find it that hard, only died 4 times at the second boss and then never died on a boss again, battlemage difficulty) and feels actually very good, however there are not many types of enemies and you will get bored really fast. There are some "elite" mobs with special prefixes, loot rarity increases with every checkpoint you pass without dying but that's it already. 99% of the game you are throwing fireballs on enemies or melt faces.
That's where we come to on of the bigger negative points of lichdom: repetitiveness. Some levels fell so large that they never end or you just think "gosh, I know that this swamp is beautiful and all but I want to keep going".
The story is classic fantasy blabla: bad man kills wife (male player character way), mage gives you cool braces that can do magix, you kill everything that moves -> boss etc.
So, can recommned this game? Yes and no. Yes for the time I spent experimenting with all the spells and combos exploding enemies in gory clouds of blood and sucking them into black holes. No for the really repetitive gameplay and the wasted potential because of the linear level design. Overall I had fun even though, it got a bit worse to the end.
I'd say it deserves a 7/10 with my emotions reaching from "what a bad game" to "OH MY GOD IS THIS AWESOME"
Give these people your money, hope they will learn from their mistakes and if lichdom 2 is a thing I know it's going to be awesome.

This is one of the last games Square made before edgy protagonists dressed in more zippers than an airplane's luggage compartment and bad voice acting took over. If your only experience with Final Fantasy has been with the sci-fi influenced titles like VII, you might be in for a bit of a surprise, but if you played any of the SNES era titles, you'll be in familiar territory. Even during its original release in 2000, FFIX is a throwback to the more traditional Final Fantasy titles and the golden age of JRPGs.
To start, FFIX was not ported the same way as FFVII and FFVIII. Those two titles had PC releases back in the day, and the Steam version is just a patched and updated version of their PC releases, complete with localization errors and minor differences from the Playstation titles. FFIX, on the other hand, is a complete port in Unity of the original Playstation release with minor graphical updates to the UI and textures to facilitate both a PC and mobile release. This means that you have the original Playstation audio and controller-friendly input, unlike VII and VIII.
The first thing you'll notice about this game is the artwork. Even after 17 years, it has aged remarkably well. I do wish for a few more pixels of resolution in the pre-rendered backgrounds, but the world is still beautiful. Square did touch up some a lot of the textures for the in-game models, and they still blend quite well with the world. Unfortunately, due to the nature of the pre-rendered backgrounds, you're locked into a horrible 4:3 screen ratio, and Square decided to mock us all by adding ridiculous textured bars on either side of the screen to emphasize the fact.
After that, the next thing you'll notice is just how slow combat is, particularly at the beginning of the game. It does get better as your characters level up and become faster, but it is definitely an exercise in patience at times. They manage to redeem themselves because the battle mechanics are well-refined. They are simple enough for a child to grasp them but still encourage strategy and experimentation.
The characters are very likable. They exhibit a level of character development and growth that you don't typically find in video gaming, which makes the story that much more immersive. Even after years of playing this game, Steiner's little fits and tantrums make me smile, and I still find Vivi's realizations about life and mortality quite moving.
The story itself is a little on the weird side. If you were expecting something normal, you shouldn't be playing JRPGs. That being said, it is enjoyable and significantly less convoluted than what you find in some of the other Final Fantasy titles (VIII, anyone?). You'll probably be more weirded out by the fact that Queen Brahne looks like a blue Jabba the Hutt in drag than you will over any particular element of the story.
Value-wise, it's a pretty good deal. You can get from start to finish in under twelve hours (it's the only way to get a particular weapon, in fact), but you're more likely to take twenty to thirty hours on your first playthrough, possibly more if you decide to go through all the sidequests, and it's enough fun to play that I've been able to replay it multiple times and enjoy it each time.
If you're on the fence about buying the game, just cough up the dough and get it. It's probably better than the other game you were looking at.

After (too many) years playing this game, I could sum it up like this :
Pros :
- Free to Play.
- Unique RvRvR gameplay.
- Fun fort and open field wars.
- Mostly open-world.
- Freedom of being able to do whatever you want at any time.
- Simple and straightforward.
- Nice community.
- Free of Asian-MMO nonsense.
- Light on system resources.
- Premium not directly influencing gameplay.
- Linux support.
Cons :
- Rubbish controls. (eg: not able to rebind spell keys)
- Grinding nightmare. (And you need to be fairly high-level (>45) in order to get fun from the RvR.)
- Really stale, boring and partially broken combat mechanics.
- Omnipresent luck and randomness. (Enjoy having your spells and hits randomly being resisted and evaded for no reason)
- Game of numbers with no diminishing returns system of any sort. (Usually the realm with most numbers will always stomp while outnumbered ones will be completely helpless.)
- Very dull quest system riddled with bad translations.
- Extremely basic guard and mob AI.
- No crafting or jobs.
- Very limited and crappy character customisation.
- Fundamental design flaws leading to perpetual class and map imbalance.
- Premium indirectly and increasingly impacting gameplay.
- Out of date graphics.
- Dull and repetitive sounds/music.
- Worriying direction the game is taking (such as ruining RvR by implementing instances).
- Support system sucks.
- Same map that will appear boring and small after a while.
- Not many capturable buildings.
- Many hours of boredom before a few minutes of action happen most of the days, at least in the International server.
- Not much to do in this game outside of grinding and warring.
- Developers track record not really good, and sometimes acting in very unprofessional manners.
- Major ignored problems, imbalances and bugs still ruining this game after so many years.
- Lacks a ton of polishing in many aspects.
- Linux and OpenGL support partially broken, many extra bugs and missing graphical features.
I would have recommended this game a few years ago when it still had an interesting and unique potential, however not much improvement, and instead a lot of regressions have happenned in the past few years, while the root issues haven't been cared about so far.
So as a conclusion, if you're looking for a well-made polished and complete MMO then you should not even bother with this. If you don't mind most of the aforementioned cons (especially grinding) and look for something simple, you might get some fun and new friends from it.

It's hard to review a game like this.
As a game in it's own right, if you've never played it before, it's a good game. Typical crazy Final Fantasy story (although it takes a bit to get into it), interesting characters, and simple but fun real-time turn-based combat. Final Fantasy games are known for their stories and characters, which are great in this member of the series.
If you've played the game before on PS1, then it's good for nostalgia. However, many people complain about it being a bad port. It has built-in cheats, in case you just want to be able to enjoy the story, characters, and side-quests. I played this years ago on PS1, and I really enjoyed my trip down memory lane with this game.
If you're an achievement hunter, this game is horrible. There are achievements that, unless you're literally following an online scripted step-by-step walkthrough, you will miss some random little thing, not know it, and then have to play the entire game over. Another achievement requires you to speed through the game in under 12 hours, which means you will grind through the game you already played, watching the same story you just watched, all over again, wasting six hours (that's how long it took me), just for the sake of one achievement... There's also another achievement to kill 10k enemies. when you can play the whole game and not even kill 1k enemies... You might think, "oh they just want you to play the game through 10 times then". No. It's 10k enemies in one playthrough. You run out of content, and have nothing to do, except grind battles, for literally dozens of hours. It's terrible.
Despite my bitterness about the achievements, it's a really enjoyable game. Considering the FF series are mainly known for their stories, it lives up to its reputation. If you're an RPG fan, this is definitely on the list of "must plays".

The community on here is rather small, but it is both active and kind.
Basis of Combat:
There are three classes to choose from: Melee, Archery, and Magic, which can further be divided based on how you wish to play.  It's been a while, so I don't quite remember the class names aside from the warior's subclasses of Knight and Barbarian.     It doesn't get exceedingly difficult as far as combat mechanics go.  It's simply click, click again to attack, and pick a number for a quick technique.
The Leveling:
At first, the grind is not as apparent as you'd think.  You tend to level easily for the first ten levels or so upon simply turning in quests.  However, it becomes a monotonous slaughterfest trying to grind out enemies to reach the next level.  Quests begin to be more trouble than reward, so grinding enemies becomes the best option.
Pay To Win Aspect:
People see you are able to but items with real money, so they immediatelly critisize the game for being a
game.  This couldn't be further from the truth.  There is
thing that seems mandetory to buy; that is a mount.  All a mount does is allow for quicker travel
, because trying to use a mount in PvP WILL get you killed in most cases.  The most commonly bought items, aside from mounts, are vanities:
I have invested quite a bit of time in this game, not even counting outide of Steam, and I have not
bought an item from the market.  It has a market, but it is not
.
Other Notes:
This game has an amazing soundtrack, though there aren't many songs.
My Thoughts:
I've invested a decent amount of time in this game, mostly outside of Steam.  I've played as each kingdom, race, and class.  I do like this game.  The RvR aspect doesn't quite speak to me as much as it does many; I simply love partying new people, showing them the ropes and a few tricks, and just chilling listening to music.  I could almost be called the Human NPC.
The game is a very casual game for the most part, until you decide to go into the RvR area.  The combat is pretty much relian on your level, your weapon, and your chosen skills.  Most of the people will be in the upper 40s, 50s, and 60 (which was the cap when I last played), so you will have to be sure to grind a lot before going RvR.
This is one of those games I pay half-attention to.  I watch a movie or just chill in general when I play.  There isn't a need for serious attention unless you're doing RvR.
Why I Can't Recommend It:
There are a few reasons as to why I can't recommend this game.
First-Though the community is active, there are nowhere near as much players at a time as a few other MMOs.
Second-While I'm used to grinding, most people will not feel that it's worth it.  It takes a long time.
Third-The quests are nothing special.  Most of the time, you will get a quest with the same structure over and over in different areas, and the rewards become worthless, aside from money.
Who Do I Recommend It To:
-People looking for a very xasual MMO
-People looking for a small but active community to play with
-People who don't mind a monotonous grind.
I do like this game, and I will continue playing it until the servers shut down, but it's not for everyone.

Freedom Planet is a solid 2D platformer with heavy influence of the Sega Genesis-era Sonic the Hedgehog games.  The gameplay allows for you to dash through levels as quickly or possible or take it slow and explore around for various secrets.  Both options are pretty satisfying, which isn't something I could always say for the side-scrolling Sonic games, since those had an emphasis on speed and a 10 minute time limit.
The gameplay, visuals, and music are all very good and are definitely things I want out of a modern-day 2D platformer trying to recreate an experience one might get from a Genesis game some 20-plus years ago.  The boss battles can provide for some meaty challenges at times, but it never feels too unforgiving or makes you want to quit playing.  I completed the game in about five hours, but your mileage may vary, and there's different characters you can choose to play that adds some variety.
The story is more of a mixed bag from me.  The voice acting can feel really out of place, and the quality of each character's dialogue/voice is very noticeable, as if each voice actor recorded their parts in different environments.  Also, some of the cutscenes can really feel like a drag, and considering how short this game is, it almost feels like overkill.  This can all be skipped by playing Classic Mode, which features gameplay only and cuts out the story entirely.
Overall, I had a lot of fun with Freedom Planet, speaking as someone who grew up playing the 90's Sonic games.  There was a lot of effort and passion in the development of this game, and it really shows.  While maybe not as memorable as the source material, it's still worth your time to give a look.

With the release of Sonic Mania, i feel that it is time to talk about this wonderful game.
"What is Freedom Planet?" you may be asking. Freedom Planet was a game that originally was a Sonic The Hedgehog ROM Hack, but after the creators deciding that they could make a unique game out of it, they built a new engine from scratch, removing all the likenesses of sonic, and after they did that, they went to kickstarter to fund the game. After some overwhelming success, they went on to produce and publish the game today, known as Freedom Planet.
Freedom Planet gets its roots from Genesis/Megadrive-era Sonic games (which if you havent played those, i recommend them, as they are really good.), and thus, the gameplay is similar to its core. The key difference from freedom planet is that its a much more "Recent take" on the classic sonic formula, and since they made this game for PC instead of a limited console like the megadrive, they had much more to work with.
Lets start with the story. The game starts up with an introductory cutscene where the main antagonist, Lord Brevon, invades the palace of shuigang, one of the major monarchal lines of the planet avalice, killing the king and enslaving his son, Prince Dail. Since dad is dead, Prince Dail takes up his namesake as ruler of shuigang, and begins to ensue war with the other rivaling monarchs, with Lord Brevon playing the puppet master. We then cut to our two female protagonist, Sash Lilac and Carol Tea, both of which respectively are a Water Dragon and a Wild Cat. They notice a ship crashing into orbit, and they decide they should go check on it to see if everyone is okay. The game starts up with whichever character you chose, and you load up into the first level of the game, Dragon Valley.
Now its time for the gameplay, and as i said before, its a sonic game to its core, being the original concept being a rom hack of a sonic game. What makes the game different, however, are the characters. The way the game works is that when you maneuver the levels, you start to notice a few differences. One of the first differences you may notice happens in the first level, when you come across your first enemy, and the difference is that the enemies cant hurt you simply by touching you. The enemy has to make an effort to damage the player by doing an attack, which you will learn almost from the get-go that you, the player, also have an attack button. Thats where alot of main differences between freedom planet and sonic the hedgehog end, but thats only the difference between the two games, a not the actual character you chose.
Lilac is a good first choice for a first timer of Freedom Planet, as she is the most familiar character gameplay wise. Her attack hits a bit harder than most characters, can jump a bit higher along with her added ability to double jump, and she has a charge attack that allows her to rocket herself at mach speeds, similar to the spinball of sonic, except its almost instant. Carol plays alot differently than Lilac, as she has a unique set of skills that differentiate from Lilac. instead of a charge attack, Carol has a special move that allows her to kick furiously, which also provides a bit of immunity frames. Instead of being able to jump freely, she has the ability to wall climb Megaman X style, and she can roll into a ball to gain momentum while going down slopes. Carol deals less than most damage, but the bonus is that she can attack much faster.
Now, i feel the game nails everything else, like the Music and sound effects, which sound amazing and makes it feel good to hit things. The graphics are whats amazing about this game, because it feels like an unbound genesis game, where the visuals are nice and appealing, and the animation quality is excellent, where even the most minor thing, like running up to and climbing a ladder have a starting animation where the character will run past the ladder, only to grab the ladder, and swing themselves back onto it. Theres also a few secrets in the game, where you could hear a few bloopers in game, and they took the time to animate the characters to do unique things during these hidden moments. If you want to do that, then simply hold the down arrow and the C key during specific story cutscenes to hear them.
My only gripe with the game is the Voice acting, which at times feels a bit campy and weird. now, if youre playing the game today, you probably wouldnt notice it, but in earlier gameplay of the game's story mode, there were times where the characters would talk about certain events the NEVER HAPPENED or was simply cut from the game to make sense. An example was after the third zone, where it was a palace dinner scene, you had two of the characters agree on liking sushi, and lilac pitched in about them finally agreeing on something, where those two characters never made it visually apparent that they disagreed on something. There was also another moment after completing the second zone that carol chimed in about a question on how they were gonna make money, which struck me as odd, because they never talked about needing money beforehand. it was only until i found out that a cut moment in the game showed the two main characters as theives, where they were gonna steal money from the rich, which never made it into the full game. You have some minor plotholes, and the time line is kinda wonky when you play multiple campaigns with different characters, the whole game story-wise becomes a mess. However, if you dont like the story, and the campy dialogue, you are given the choice to play the game as if it were a sonic game, where you just play zone after zone with no story in between.
If you are on the fence about getting this game, i recommend it, as it is fun, and gets a bit challenging later on. It still has a few flaws, but if some dialogue or some plot inconsistancies are in the way, you can just play the game in classic mode.

I really really love this game!  I bought it about a year or so ago and constantly go back to it.  To be honest, I think I enjoy it even more than I enjoyed any of the actual Sonic games back in the Genesis days.  The boss battles are certainly much better than any Sonic game.  The characters are all quite nice and give lots of variety to the gameplay.  If I had one complaint I'd say that even though the story cutscenes are very well done, I do think they could be cut down a bit perhaps.  Sometimes they seem a bit longer than you'd like, especially when you just want to get back to the game.  It's not a big issue though because you can play the game without the cut-scenes which makes this a much more free-flowing old school style Genesis game.

I'm very nearly not recommending this, but it gets a pass. If you've already played Sonic Generations and Sonic Mania (which isn't out yet but reviews are great so far), and you want a Sonic-feeling PC game, then this is a good pick. It's fun and fast, with great art and music.
Unfortunately it's far from perfect. The story and voice acting are cheesy and weird and not really in an enjoyable way. I wish the levels were shorter, as you kind of have to commit yourself to a half hour every time you sit down. The cut scenes are quite long, and if the levels were split up a bit like the zones in Sonic games, it might make the cut scenes easier to get through.
The hit boxes sometimes behave strangely, and there's next to no invincibility after you get hit, so getting juggled and losing most of your health is common and not fun.
Also the collectables in the game are completely pointless. To compare, in Sonic the rings are also your health, you drop rings when you get hit, if you collect 100 you get an extra life. In Shovel Knight, a different indie pixel art 2D retro-style platformer, the money you collect is for upgrades and you lose some when you die. In Freedom Planet, you collect crystals. You never lose crystals, and if you collect 200, you gain an extra life. Now in Sonic, if you lose all your lives- that was it- game over. In Shovel Knight, they've done away with lives and given a well-designed check point system that takes money when you fail and rewards risk-taking. In Freedom Planet, if you run out of lives you gain five more. That's it. There is no penalty whatsoever for losing lives. Meaning lives don't matter, meaning crystals don't matter. Why do the crystals exist? No one knows. What a bafflingly stupid design choice.
The difficulty scaling is also way off in my opinion. The levels are all incredibly easy, since death means nothing the only goal is really to get to the next checkpoint, so health is a minor concern. So the bosses are the real challenge of the game, with the quality of them varying greatly. The first few bosses are quite easy, and then there is a sudden difficulty spike. All of the bosses are manageable until the third phase of the final boss, which suddenly gives no tells and is completely randomized in how to operates. I beat it, but if felt more like I got lucky than anything skill-based.
Damn, that is a lot of bad things for a positive review. I'm a very negative person. There are a lot of games to play before Freedom Planet, and it's "Overwhelmingly Positive" score is unearned in my opinion. But it feels like Sonic 3 when you're speed through the world, and that's what I was looking for. Get it on sale.

Bloody Good Time is what I consider one of my (albeit many) guilty pleasures. Do I recommend it? Well... sort of.
First and foremost, what all potential buyers need to realize is the game never really finished development, may as well be considered 'dead' in terms of the online play (though there are a few groups that do planned game nights), and is far from perfect.
That said, it can be a very enjoyable game to mess around with now and then, as it does have bots for singleplayer experiences. Is it the ultimate in difficult or varied gameplay? Absolutely not. Is it stunningly beautiful with some kind of mind blowing story? Hardly (though I'm quite partial to the graphical style). But CAN YOU HAVE FUN IN A UNIQUE ENVIRONMENT AND EXPERIENCE? YES.
I think most folks that bought BGT initially were expecting a much more expanded experience from the developer's previous game: The Ship. However, the development was prematurely ended. They had *no chance* to make this a game that would meet expectations, so complaints about that should be summarily tossed out in my opinion.
What the game DID end up providing was a framework that is fun to play, unique to experience, and a base of inspiration for future developers.
So here's the low-down:
Graphics
Pretty good (I'm a huge fan of the style, personally, but I'm kind of weird :P). Nicely stylized and well-themed. Not AAA standard, but who cares about that nonsense.
Sound
Another "pretty good". Not a lot to say here, as it's a pretty straight forward game that doesn't have a whole lot of chances to show its chops.
Gameplay
I REALLY like the gameplay, and while it could have definitely been expanded upon, the version available isn't all that shabby. There is a good amount of weapon variety, map layouts, environmental traps, game modes, etc. Certainly not infinite potential, but a fair amount (depending on price). The bots aren't exactly the smartest AI in the world, but if you intentionally prevent yourself from exploiting their shortcomings they can be quite fun.
Difficulty
This is kind of a toss-up. It really depends on how you play and how much you exploit mechanics that will *never* be fixed. Basically: you can have as much fun as you allow yourself to have... if you get greedy and elitist, you'll find that fun-factor and difficulty plummeting quite quickly.
Multiplayer
Again, the game is 'dead'.... but if you have friends at a LAN party or whatever, this can be an absolute blast to play. Just don't expect to find any random pick-up games outside of dedicated Steam Groups that hold organized game nights.
Overall I'd say the game is fairly good if you're looking for something new and interesting to mess around with now and then. If you have friends that you can play with, the game can be freakin fantastic.. but bot play will work in the short term (though will definitely get tiring after awhile). But hey, depending on the price it may be worth it for something you can install and play a few hours every now and then (like I do).
Is "The Ship" better? Yeah, most likely... but BGT is quite a bit different in theme and style, so it's hard to compare. If you want the ultimate in 'murder party' experiences, go with The Ship... if you want a more deathmatch-y, ridiculous setup go with BGT (or just go with both and have all your desires satisfied).

Hot damn, Xaviant have crafted something really beautiful with Battlemage: gorgeous environments and vibrantly repugnant enemies coalesce with a deep and engaging spell crafting system which rewards experimentation and creativity to produce a gauntlet of frenetic action which rarely risks monotony. The combat system itself consists of only a few basic elements, but these can be utilised in quick succession, rewarding quick reflexes and tactical planning and punishing those who assume that spamming the flame spells will achieve victory; it won't, genius. It also demands mentioning that the spells themselves are positively... well... spellbinding (deal with it), wild motes of colour dancing, arcing, bolting and exploding in vivid spectra from the bare hands of your avatar to pierce, bludgeon, restrain and, often, utterly decimate the wonderfully lively monsters and undead you face throughout Battlemage.
All this said, the tutorial systems are an eggregious state of poor: shortly after beginning the game, having been just introduced to the four or five most basic combat features of the game, Battlemage simply gave up on tutoring me at all, instead directing me to the in-game journal for a lovely dump of boring text to sift through and educate myself on what are, honestly, the far more interesting aspects of the game, such as crafting and the three key types of spell damage required for combos. Endless Legend suffered from much the same issues with its tutorial (100 hours and I am still having to learn obscure mechanics through experimentation). Fortunately, Battlemage's mechanics are far simpler and easier to experiment with and, thus, thoroughly learn, but it still saddens me that this will likely turn many people off through lack of easy accessibility born from a lack of simple tutorials.
Obviously, highly recommended. Additionally, the 1.2 hours currently listed for my playtime for the game are false. It is significantly more than that.

Your not a student of the arcane who spent years reading through ancient tomes to learn how to throw just one tiny spark of fire across a room or a knowledge theif who broke into a wizards library and too their secrets for your own. Nope you are just some idiot that got themselves killed and now has magic handed to them.
Right off your not so much a mage as you are a dude who throws a few fireballs around. The second problem I ran into is that some of the game controls do not work as described in the tutorial videos(which themselves are disruptive to gameplay). The game tells you to hold down space while targeting to do a combo slide spell attack. This never worked for me after several minuets of trying all different combinations of the controls. The game also tells you that you can attune different elements to change how they fire but does not explain how to actually do this. It seems like something that is suppose to open up later in the game leaving me confused as to why it is brought up at all.
The game boasts being able to mix and match magic but right away you are locked into only using fire or ice and have to cycle between them. Trying to adjust this at one of the waypoints(the only place you can make changes apparently) the slots are all locked at the begining. Some master magicial huh?
These issues might be forgivable if the gameplay felt at all exciting or interesting. The few levels I played where all linear rail shooters designs with really predictable enemie A.I. In fact old school rail shooters like Serious Sam, Duke Nukem, and Doom have more inspired and open world designs despite being graphically dated. Additionally the 3 shield health system is an unessary break up of a normal health bar into 3 arbitrary bars. If they regenerated over time or gave you more power the fewer bars you have it might make it meaningful. Maybe this happens later in the game but I couldn't be bothered to struggle through many boring levels to get there.
And to everyone out there who thinks I was not paying attention or just didnt give the game enough of a chance to figure thigs out the truth is the game didn't hold my interest enought for me to care to dive deeper and learn more. Also reading other reviews it looks like the gameplay stays the same throughout and you MUST have mastery equiped to a spell to even make it worth using.
TLDR: I felt like more of a badass master mage plaing Darksouls and Magica.

Short Review: The game is a lovingly crafted, inventive masterpiece with a few flaws still lingering.
8/10
Long Review:
-Singleplayer: Short and sweet. A hand-crafted world with difficulties that throw you in, and see if you will swim. The plot of the entire world wrap you in a veil of mysteriousness that you honestly want to know more about. Who are these people? What happened to Adal? Are these masks some magic voodoo? Who knows, but if you can finish the singleplayer you have a great start in the multiplayer, which is somewhat spoiled at the moment by server downtimes. (9/10)
-Multiplayer: Aggravating, and rewarding. At some moments there are times where you have no idea how this guy is beating the crap out of you, and then you realize they are 30 levels ahead of you. In my honest opinion right now there is quite a bit of balancing that needs to be done between either matchmaking, level/dmg/whatever caps, or simply server stability (actually atleast server stability lol). If you do get matched up with someone on even ground with you (50/50 chance) it is an intense, and heart-pounding experience. (5/10)
-Other Pros:
I have spent an hour of my in-game time going around and taking screenshots of random things simply because the artstyle is so uniquely beautiful. There are very little games made that have this strictly low-poly world that still manages to look stunning.
To see this game grow into a competitive space would be a leap for fighting games everywhere. Chivalry tried to make this 3D Fighting game space a reality, then For Honor, and now Absolver is trying to do the same thing with an inventive, like, everything. The combat, the world, the artstyle, is all Absolver. There is no other game like it, and with the right devs (I think these are them xD) it can grow into something bigger.
-Unfortunate Cons:
Server Downtimes(devs working on it so we'll see), Server stability(server-side lag in matches, etc.), Matchmaking shenanigans(unfortunate matches with people 20 levels higher, and lower than me), and a few balancing issues (any competitive game has balancing issues, but things like mobility > equipment, shockwave on small maps, etc.).
-Overview:
There are simply things that hopefully with devs that stay with the game after release the problems it has now will leave, but this game is overall a dope, and unique experience, and I will continue playing it with as much free-time as possible, and I hope you do too, peace! 8/10

TL;DR: Great game with horrible connection issues.
BUT what's there online, essentially the single player component, is awesome. The more you learn about the combat decks, the more in-depth they get and with practice, you'll be switching stances and really feeling just how tight Absolver's fighting it.
Picking up new moves is like picking up new weapons in Dark Souls. They scale of different stats and you chain them together to build your own combos. So your starting class pretty much determine which counter you'll be using, because you can eventually learn all the moves.
The game is exactly what it says on the box. It's a simple world that's meant for limited exploration, but mostly serves as the back drop to find opponents and fight them.
It has all the best parts of Dark Souls pvp. In fact, imagine the maps as Dark Souls maps where if you invade or get in invaded, you want to find the host or the invader quick. The smaller maps lends themselves well to this.
As good as the game maybe, it's all bout the online combat, and if that's a bit wonky right now.

Warning: May crash from time to time. I'm running it on Windows 10 with a GTX970 and an Intel i7. May just be a little janky with new hardware. It autosaves so it's not a big deal. Sometimes it will save you in a glitched state, but you can start from chapters so it isn't a huge loss.
Make no mistake you are here for the story. The combat and driving is okay, but the sandbox is hardly a sandbox and the story is the big draw.
I don't usually play heavily story-based games, much less get into them, but the characters and world of this game draw me in. Think of the plot a bit like GTAIV but polished and with a lot less of the silly ♥♥♥♥ing around.  The character has a history that actually makes his line of work believable, and he has a simple straightforward goal that could easily be summarized as "The American Dream"
Story (Maybe implied spoilers?)
This game has a lot of stereotypes (The Chinese characters are fairly offensive, but they take their fair share of♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the Italians and Irish too, and I think the game is actually made by Czech developers for the most part)
Despite the stereotypes, the characters seem to have goals and depth that I feel a lot of games like GTA forego with its side characters. There are a lot of cliches that I feel like it avoids entirely. The drama feels real because you don't get monologues about character deaths, there's no betrayal that seems sudden or to add shock value. Every action that the characters take feel like it has an almost real world motive.
The gameplay is fine. Shooting is fun, you get lots of toys, but the Thompson is naturally the best thing you can use (Why bother with anything else if you're gonna be a hardened mobster?) The combat is incredibly easy to exploit and for some reason they add more to it about halfway through even though you use it like... 3-4 more times in the main story after that point. The driving is functional (I admit I don't play driving games but it wasn't particularly aggravating if you have the right car)
The sandbox is a bit of a shame. Not that it's boring. It's lovingly crafted and from how nice it is, may be up there with my favourite sandboxes to walk around in. The detail is amazing. The people sit down and eat, they park and get out of their cars, posters and things change depending on what era you're in. During WWII you'll see veterans and the like in the streets. You can walk into eateries, and they'll all look different and have different clientele. And frankly, it is beautiful for a 6 year old game. (selectively, some people have very low res textures in their faces, but vito is gorgeous. Moderate to high levels of homo intended)
You just can't do anything in the sandbox. It simply acts as a hub world to go from main mission to main mission (the dlc expands on it a bit) There are pick ups but I have no clue how to find them in a world that big without a guide, I've only found one so far and I beat the game. The main stories take place in the hub world but for combat sections usually have really special little portions of the map you're locked to, full of cover and the like. Speaking of collectibles, playboy pinups are pretty fun to collect. They even all have different covers (quite an eye for detail!)
My wishlist for Mafia III is to have a sandbox I can interact with. New Orleans is such a fun city and I want to experience that.

It's hard to review a game like this.
As a game in it's own right, if you've never played it before, it's a good game. Typical crazy Final Fantasy story (although it takes a bit to get into it), interesting characters, and simple but fun real-time turn-based combat. Final Fantasy games are known for their stories and characters, which are great in this member of the series.
If you've played the game before on PS1, then it's good for nostalgia. However, many people complain about it being a bad port. It has built-in cheats, in case you just want to be able to enjoy the story, characters, and side-quests. I played this years ago on PS1, and I really enjoyed my trip down memory lane with this game.
If you're an achievement hunter, this game is horrible. There are achievements that, unless you're literally following an online scripted step-by-step walkthrough, you will miss some random little thing, not know it, and then have to play the entire game over. Another achievement requires you to speed through the game in under 12 hours, which means you will grind through the game you already played, watching the same story you just watched, all over again, wasting six hours (that's how long it took me), just for the sake of one achievement... There's also another achievement to kill 10k enemies. when you can play the whole game and not even kill 1k enemies... You might think, "oh they just want you to play the game through 10 times then". No. It's 10k enemies in one playthrough. You run out of content, and have nothing to do, except grind battles, for literally dozens of hours. It's terrible.
Despite my bitterness about the achievements, it's a really enjoyable game. Considering the FF series are mainly known for their stories, it lives up to its reputation. If you're an RPG fan, this is definitely on the list of "must plays".

Game has some problems.  Its age shows.
Game is in a 4:3 ratio.  The textures of the main characters, and other significant characters were redone, but the static background scenes were not.  The effect is a little jarring but its better than block hands.  The "scenes" paradigm is a negative for the game, lack of changeable camera angles and no indication that anything is interactable make collecting items without a walkthrouhg tedious.  Navigation is not as bad as FF7's horrible scenes, but still feels very dated.  The view distance is also suprisingly low in the overworld.  I imagine this is because this is a mobile game port.
A fun adventure, probably the strongest FF story besides 6 or 4.  But like all Final Fantasy games they're more fun to start than finish.
Frameskip is very useful for the Chocobo minigame, and generally getting to the creamy center of the game.  You can bulldoze past the filler and time consuming hurdles the game puts up to actually enjoying the adventure, which is quite charming and a lot of fun to play through.
Not a remaster and might should have been for the price tag.  A few soft-crashes (eternal battle loading screens).  Autosave behavior is unintuitive.  If you save after the autosave (which occurs each scene transition) the "Continue" button will pick you up at the autosave, not your more recent hard save.
A fun game whose good qualities outshine its annoying ones.

This game is exactly as the title states; it's bloody fun to play. The rules are simple (kill or be killed), and the gameplay is easy to pick up on and fast-paced. There are several game modes with varying levels of difficulty, but I tend to play Deathmatch most often. Basically, you're an out of work movie actor/actress looking for a part in a new film by the hottest horror movie director in Hollywood. This director demands bloodshed with style; he will constantly critique your kills and advise you on your techniques. You can choose to kill any way you want, and whomever you want. However, if you don't pay attention to which murder weapons are considered "hot" at that time, you won't earn as many points per kill. Your true goal is to become the director's darling, after all.
As far as weapons go, the variety is as fun as playing in a more twisted version of Tom & Jerry: there's anything from katanas, axes, syringes, stun guns, flamethrowers, frying pans and more at your disposal. There's also a multitude of "murder aids" (like mines, lures or lullaby-inducing sheep) that can be helpful. The environments themselves can also be used to your advantage, with plenty of creative traps to use on your victims. Another fun mechanic is the fact that you have to pay attention to your current state of energy, hunger and...need to use the bathroom for lack of a better term. It will effect your speed and performance, so be sure to catch up on sleep, eat, or use the toilet when needed...just don't be surprised if someone catches you in a moment of weakness.
From the characters to the settings, the game itself is a parody on the horror genre, and a throwback to all the ultra gory and cheesy b-movies I love. There's nothing deep to this game, nor should there be. It's a guilty pleasure kind of game, satisfying and simple.

I've been excited about this game for awhile just from the screenshots and descriptions, I didn't really follow the development or the forums because I didn't want to build up too many expectations. Even as excited as I was, this game has surpassed my hopes. It's clean, smooth, and beautiful, and the combat is fluid and realistic while also feeling satisfyingly dramatic and skillful. It's surprisingly Soulslike, given the mostly-empty interconnected regions of the world, strategically placed NPC opponants, and the combat system putting heavy emphasis on patience and precision. The controls (I'm using gamepad) are complex but also intuitive, affording the player a wide range of actions on a relatively small number of buttons without making them frustrating or difficult to navigate; it took less than a half an hour to get a grasp on how the controls work.
I'll update my review as I play further and likely discover more things that annoy me, but for now, very glad to have gotten this when I did.
