From its speed-based gameplay, to its anthropomorphic cast of characters, Freedom Planet is a game that clearly takes inspiration from Sonic the Hedgehog. But that's where the similarities end. You can rest assured that Freedom Planet is more than a mere "Sonic clone". It's a game that perfects and refines the formula and morphs it into its own unique identity.
An intergalactic villain named Brevon crash-lands on our heroes’ planet, as he seeks the power of the planet’s Kingdom Stone to rebuild his ship and continue his domination over galaxies. He invades one of the planet’s three kingdoms, beheads their king, and brainwashes their prince to do his bidding. He is pursued by an alien named Torque who requests the assistance of our main characters to retrieve the Kingdom Stone, prevent a full-scale war between the three kingdoms, and defeat Brevon once and for all!
The story has a plethora of cutscenes that are fully voice-acted, and they’re pretty well done for the most part. It won't win any awards, but it more than gets the job done. An honorable mention goes to Brevon, who really shines through as a sinister-sounding foe.
While the story presents itself as something grand, it ultimately boils down to standard save-the-world fare that we’ve seen countless times already. What the story does excel in is the fantastic dialogue and likeable cast of characters. The tone is light-hearted for the most part, but it does have its dark moments as well. The presentation is top-notch and keeps the game flowing nicely. I will admit the cutscenes are a tad on the lengthy side, but you can skip them any time you wish.
There are three characters you can play as in-game (two from the beginning + one unlockable), and each of them are quite different in how they play.
The first is Lilac, a dragon girl who plays the traditional main character role. Lilac has a double-jump that also functions as an attack to shield yourself from enemies. But her most defining feature is her special ability, which grants her invincibility and zips around at high speeds for a short duration. You can even control the direction she flies in! It’s about as fun as it sounds, and she’s easily my favorite of the three.
The second is Carol, a sassy green wildcat who serves as somewhat of a foil to Lilac. She has access to a neat wall jump ability (think Mega Man X), but otherwise is a bit awkward to use. Carol has no double jump and her special ability (a flurry of weak kicks) is really underwhelming. One redeeming feature she has is the ability to ride her motorcycle whenever she touches a gas canister on the map. It’s actually really fun, as it gives her a double-jump and she can move around really fast. Unfortunately, they’re limited in quantity, and they get destroyed rather quickly. There are also these pads that let her jump around like a ninja, but they’re not too useful. All-in-all, Carol has some fun ideas, but I don’t find her to be as wholly satisfying as I do with Lilac.
The third and final party member is Milla, a timid dog who is easily the most carefree of the group. Let me tell you: she is without doubt the hard mode of the game. First off, she has access to a shield which, in a fast-paced game that involves beating up hordes enemies, is instantly not very useful. It does do damage at the end of the animation, but it’s delayed. Secondly, she has an ability that creates phantom blocks, and it’s also pretty useless. It takes about a second to charge and it requires aiming. It does do good damage if it connects, however. Lastly, she has access to a flutter-jump ability (think Yoshi’s Island) that lets her scale tall heights. This is the only thing I like about her. She’s easily my least-favorite of the three as I feel that her playstyle contradicts with what the game is expecting of you. But I can least respect that it gives the player another way to experience the game.
Contrary to its “Sonic-esque” appearance, Freedom Planet does not utilize a ring system. It instead has a more traditional health system, where you have health points that can be replenished as you go throughout the stage.
Freedom Planet has about a dozen main stages to choose from. Many of the stages are shared by all three characters, with one being exclusive to Lilac and one being exclusive to Milla (Carol doesn’t have an exclusive stage, curiously enough…). Now while that sounds kind of small, the stages are MASSIVE! It can easily take over 10 minutes to beat each one. They’re also varied and well-designed, with a wide array of branching paths to keep them from feeling too linear. The end of every stage culminates with a boss battle, and I have to say, the bosses are quite fun in this game. They all present a unique style and they’re challenging, yet fair. All of the stages (with exception to the final stages) have 10 cards hidden within their worlds, which further promotes exploration and increased replay value. The cards unlock stuff like music, sound clips, and concept art, so it’s a nice treat for perfectionists.
What really makes Freedom Planet shine is with its intuitive design. Let me explain what I mean by that. One of my major frustrations with Sonic games is how they are always made with speed in mind, yet you are always crashing into enemies and spikes because you didn’t have the stage perfectly memorized (see Metropolis Zone). Or worse yet, you fall into a bottomless pit and that forces you to restart part of the stage. These types of issues I’ve long had with Sonic are FULLY addressed in Freedom Planet, and is why I consider this game to be better than most Sonic titles. There is no collision damage in Freedom Planet. Enemies can ONLY hurt you if you run into their attack animations. This is extremely smart design and it makes running through stages a lot less cheap and so much more enjoyable. Instant death is also kept to a minimum, and there is only one stage that prominently has bottomless pits, and even then it’s still easily avoided. The people who made this game had a clear understanding of what worked (and more importantly, what didn’t work) in Sonic and made a game that meets (and perhaps succeeds) the level of quality seen in Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
Lastly, Freedom Planet gives you the option to adjust the difficulty at any time, with “Casual” mode making the game a literal breeze to play through, and “Hard” mode seriously testing your reflexes. Both casual and hardcore gamers can thoroughly enjoy this game because it’s as difficult or as easy as you want it to be at any time!
If you are an avid fan of platformers, you are doing yourself a disservice by not adding this gem into your collection. Everything from the tight gameplay, to the well-designed stages, to the fantastic soundtrack, to the amazing sprite-work, to the gaggle of achievements and collectibles make this game a blast to play. Heck, it even has a mah-jongg mini-game for crying out loud! Some indie developers are absolutely worth supporting and GalaxyTrail is no-doubt one of them. Buy this game already.

Some have used the term "Star Trek Mission Generator." You Start the game with a ship and a crew (with unique abilities based on their species) and told that you must get vital information to the main fleet 8 sectors away. You jump from beacon to beacon in each sector until you reach the exit beacon to the next sector, all while gathering fuel and resources to upgrade your ship and weapons in preparation for the final battle. Oh and by the way, the rebel force is after you, so you can't stay in each sector for too long before their fleet catches up to you, or block your escape. Each sector is randomly generated so no two playthroughs are ever the same, which accounts for its replayability.
I have played at least 800 hours of it. Though, my total time is over 1100, but I am deducting a big chunk for occasionally leaving the game on overnight or on the background. Still, it is my go-to game for when I want to play something, but don't know what.
Even on Easy setting, the game is very challenging. You will need to master your strategy to make it through to and defeat the final ship.

This is my absolute favorite game of all time. I have 2 copies of the PS1 version, and this port as well. I've played through the game to full completion approaching a dozen times now, and it still hasn't gotten old.
The characters- memorable. They actually develop quite a lot over the course of the game. This is most noticeable with Steiner and Garnet, but Vivi, Eiko, Zidane and even Amarant get some noticeable moments. Freya and Quina don't change too much, but they were already stable, well-rounded characters. This is Zidane's story, and the character focus is largely on how his interactions with the other characters change them as the game progresses. Vivi get a lot of really poignant moments as well, especially in the ending. Supporting cast? Tons of amusing lines- this is a very light-hearted game, but it doesn't shy away from some heavier themes, again mostly with Vivi and parallels to him.
The soundtrack? I've listened straight through it so many times by now, it's a little ridiculous. The main battle theme still gets me pumped, every single area has a fitting theme, the use of leitmotifs throughout the game with both the title screen and credits theme weaving throughout the entire game... it's just fantastically done. Outside of those two melodies, You're Not Alone and Assault of the Silver Dragons, among others stick out as some of the best tracks.
The battle system? Well, that's admittedly nothing too special... but FF9 has some of the best balancing in the series. It does start to fall apart near the end of the game, as physical attacks can get many more multipliers than magic, and there are 3 fixed damage attacks that can be easily farmed up to 9999... but you don't need to do this at all. For the majority of the game, nearly all characters are equally viable, and even in the endgame all characters have their uses. It's simpler than the surrounding FF games, but it does its job well and there are some interesting encounters along the way.
The sidequests? Chocobo Hot and Cold is the best. End of discussion.
I guess Tetra Master is pretty fun when you understand it, too.
So, with all of that praise, are there any complaints? Well, yes. The beginning of "Disc 3" takes quite a long time to get through and not a lot happens there. It's fine the first time through, when all the plot is new, but on subsequent playthroughs it does kind of drag on. The Trance system is Square's answer to abusable limit breaks in previous games, and as you can't control when it happens, it can be a little annoying to see a Trance happen in a random battle when you really would have liked it to occur on the next boss... but when it does line up, that boss is in some serious trouble.
Personally, I still think the PS1 version is the way to go, but this is a good port. Some of the sounds are a little degraded in quality, there's no analog movement for some reason, and you can't navigate menus as fast as you can push the buttons either. The convenience features (no encounters, speedup) are very nice for breezing through storyline sections you just want to end on a replay, or getting certain treasures without worrying about interruptions. The other boosters (always trance+always full ATB, always 9999, instant level 99, instant max gil) lean too close to cheating for my liking, but they're there if you get truly stuck. (No encounters doesn't cross that line because it's possible to run through all screens without an encounter anyway)
So that's how it is. Why are you still reading this when you could be playing instead?

I got this game a while ago when it was on sale, expecting a few cheap laughs and a bit of a placebo for my dearly departed "The Ship" game*. So after a quick download (as it is a rather small file) I was thrown into a pixar-esq world high on the promise of comedic violence...
Does it deliver?...
kinda...sorta... not really
There isnt really a dedicated tutorial, you are left to piece together a basic control scheme through a quick "loading screen button mapping" picture and through occasional tool tip pop ups
But even when you get past the awkward controls you find that most of the budget for the game was put into the weapons (that dont come with instructions). There is a good assortment of weaponry ranging from the several generic melee weapons, all the way to the esoteric "sleep sheep" (that you will have no idea how to use, or even what it is)
There are 3 maps total, and they feel too big... and at the same time too small.
They feel far to big to only have 8 people max playing at any one time, and you will find yourself lost pretty easily.
But they feel so small because you keep backtracking to the same spots over and over again to spam a deathtrap or to pick up a weapon that doesnt require you to be right next to your victim
The characters are full of life and their own personal charm, with nobody feeling like a reskin or palate swap of another. Thats  a two edged sword as it makes it INCREDIBLY easy to find your prey... but also makes evasion boil down to "bring bigger weapon against your attacker" or "run in hopes of losing them"
So between an awkwardly specific cast, confusing weapons and set designs, as well as a totally dead online, I cant in good faith reccomend this game

Good fighting game. The learning curve and the controls are tough and lots of people are probably going to whine about it when they die (including me), but it's still a fun and challenging game. It's harder than all fighting games I played. You have to time your blocks/evades and they're directionnal, which is tough to master.
You unlock new moves and such by learning them from your opponents when you successfully block/evade them (different types of evasion too), be they NPC or players. Eventually you also unlock weapons, which you find in the world along your equipment, but you learn the weapons moves the same way you learn fist fighting moves.
There are also 4 fighting "schools" we could say, each emphasizing a different gameplay to some extent. Only one of 3 can be selected at character creation, so I suppose there's another to unlock somewhere. One school emphasizes on fluidity and actively dodging hits, another parrying hits, another is about absorbing the damage. In all schools you can also simply block.
There are also 4 different fighting stances, you can switch from one to another at will, and your sequence of attacks will often move you from one to another. There are special attacks in all the different stances, for example one that breaks block, an attack which at the same time lets you evade vertical attacks, or one that lets you dodge in one direction, and such.
You can modify the attack moves that constitue your attack chains, each of the 4 stances' basic attacks forming an attack chain (so 4 in total). You can unlock more slots in the chain, and each stance also has an alternate attack (like special attacks described in the paragraph above).
I only played like 3-4 hours, but I can see there's much strategic depth already. Easy to play (and get killed!), very hard to master.

TL;DR - Great classis JRPG with lovable characters, an awesome story, decent gameplay mechanics to keep the player immersed and interested, and as far as I know it doesn't require a square enix account to play
This was my favorite game as a kid and I still have a lot of love and nostalgia attached to it so of course I recommend it.  That being said there are still some things to get into with this review.  When I saw this game on steam along with other FF's I was pumped and wanted to get some of the others I never played through or don't remember that well.  Well, reading the reviews for those games (particularly 7 and 8) I come to find out that they have many, many flaws like broken audio, scaled-down cutscenes and requiring a square enix account and login to play.  So needless to say I was a little bit hesitant to buy and play this FF9 update.  I'm glad I said "F*ck it" though because so far I have experienced no problems.  Matter of fact, this steam version is a pretty solid update that improves on graphics (especially the character models) and adds achievements.  Now idk if this is the case for everybody or if I'm just very lucky, but at no point was I required to make a square enix account and login to play this gem.
OK, so let's get into the actual game.  One thing I will address right now is that this FF might not be for everybody.  I remember being the only one out of my group of friends who really liked this installment of FF.  A lot of my friends felt it was too cartoony and childish looking, and tbh, it can be in parts.  But once you get to disk 2, say goodbye to all the cutesy whimsical stuff, sh*t gets real and these adorable little cartoon people start getting into some real existential messes.  Gameplay is just about the same as any other FF, you have a party of 3-4 people and run around towns, cities, dungeons, and a vast world map.  Combat is a more fleshed out version of the class system that prevailed in earlier FFs but also incorporates specials called Trance that are unique to each character (e.g. Zidane gets a new skill list called Dyne, Vivi can cast 2 black magic spells instead of one).  Aside from the main story there a lot of subplots to follow along with in what is called Active Time Event (ATE for short).  Basically while exploring, you'll get a prompt to press a button and view a scene usually involving minor characters that is happening as a "meanwhile" or as a follow-up to events that happened earlier.  Sometimes these ATEs are humorous, other times they tie up loose ends.  Then there are the sidequests that will have you traversing the entire world map in search of treasure, card battles, and character development.  One thing I loved about this game as a kid was every playthrough I found or learned something new just by exploration and pure chance.  While nothing is really "hidden" (fan made walkthroughs all over the internet will tell you how to get/ do everything) there are still a lot of cool secrets that can only be uncovered by some good thorough exploration.
EDIT: I forgot to mention one thing, if you can, buy this when it's on sale - unless you are delusional like me and pretend all your $$$ is going to Zidane, Vivi, Dagger, et al.  I love FF9 and old-school squaresoft but square-enix is starting to become a real shinra inc. (if ya know what I mean) who tend to cater to fan-service, rush getting products out into the market, and end up ruining great franchises (e.g. Thief, FF, and now Dragon Quest is on some slippery slope bs)

For some, Early Access has come to mean "take the money and run".  I don't think that was the case here.  This game's history followed the theme "we bit off more than we could chew, and made promises we couldn't keep."  After years of trying to fix pathing and UI problems, the game was shoved out in a mostly-complete state.
The game features a team of tiny yellow people that follow your orders, which involve mainly gathering supplies, building simple bock structures, and defending those structures. The problems with the game are simple.
* The pathfinding is strange and sometimes fails Pathfinding problems increase exponentially if you create structures of any non-trivial complexity. Creating systems of stairs and layers of fortifications eventually causes your minions to become useless.
* The game has virtually no content. You can chop trees and mine, and build blocks. You can build a few very basic structures, which are periodically attacked by roving bad guys. The enemies are uniform and boring. Terrain is unrelieved grass and identical trees.

There are aspects of the game that are well worth criticism. The AI is horrendous, especially on driving missions. I cannot count the times I've failed a mission because an AI car crashed into me trying to pathfind itself out of my way because of my siren. Or the times an AI car has magically appeared on top of me, making my vehicle exploed. Or the times I've started a mission that finishes within seconds because the AI target spawned right next to the city border. Or the train missions that were initiated on the wrong side of the tracks (how can I travel east if the train is spawned facing west on a one-way track?). Or the times I've failed a mission because I have angered Uncle Vinnie for no apparent reason.
But these results of the game's age should not and cannot discourage players away from the immersive city planning, the multitude of factors that influence construction, the possibility of building and terraforming an entire map from scratch, and, above all, the customizability of the game's resources that allows for stellar modding.
If you have lots of free time or you're just looking for some mindless yet mindful fun to relax after work or school, SImCity 4 is well worth its meager price. And, much like the hopefuls still expecting Half-Life 3, I will forever wait for that worthy sequel that will take the best elements from this game and dress them in modern graphics and intelligence.

TL;DR - Great classis JRPG with lovable characters, an awesome story, decent gameplay mechanics to keep the player immersed and interested, and as far as I know it doesn't require a square enix account to play
This was my favorite game as a kid and I still have a lot of love and nostalgia attached to it so of course I recommend it.  That being said there are still some things to get into with this review.  When I saw this game on steam along with other FF's I was pumped and wanted to get some of the others I never played through or don't remember that well.  Well, reading the reviews for those games (particularly 7 and 8) I come to find out that they have many, many flaws like broken audio, scaled-down cutscenes and requiring a square enix account and login to play.  So needless to say I was a little bit hesitant to buy and play this FF9 update.  I'm glad I said "F*ck it" though because so far I have experienced no problems.  Matter of fact, this steam version is a pretty solid update that improves on graphics (especially the character models) and adds achievements.  Now idk if this is the case for everybody or if I'm just very lucky, but at no point was I required to make a square enix account and login to play this gem.
OK, so let's get into the actual game.  One thing I will address right now is that this FF might not be for everybody.  I remember being the only one out of my group of friends who really liked this installment of FF.  A lot of my friends felt it was too cartoony and childish looking, and tbh, it can be in parts.  But once you get to disk 2, say goodbye to all the cutesy whimsical stuff, sh*t gets real and these adorable little cartoon people start getting into some real existential messes.  Gameplay is just about the same as any other FF, you have a party of 3-4 people and run around towns, cities, dungeons, and a vast world map.  Combat is a more fleshed out version of the class system that prevailed in earlier FFs but also incorporates specials called Trance that are unique to each character (e.g. Zidane gets a new skill list called Dyne, Vivi can cast 2 black magic spells instead of one).  Aside from the main story there a lot of subplots to follow along with in what is called Active Time Event (ATE for short).  Basically while exploring, you'll get a prompt to press a button and view a scene usually involving minor characters that is happening as a "meanwhile" or as a follow-up to events that happened earlier.  Sometimes these ATEs are humorous, other times they tie up loose ends.  Then there are the sidequests that will have you traversing the entire world map in search of treasure, card battles, and character development.  One thing I loved about this game as a kid was every playthrough I found or learned something new just by exploration and pure chance.  While nothing is really "hidden" (fan made walkthroughs all over the internet will tell you how to get/ do everything) there are still a lot of cool secrets that can only be uncovered by some good thorough exploration.
EDIT: I forgot to mention one thing, if you can, buy this when it's on sale - unless you are delusional like me and pretend all your $$$ is going to Zidane, Vivi, Dagger, et al.  I love FF9 and old-school squaresoft but square-enix is starting to become a real shinra inc. (if ya know what I mean) who tend to cater to fan-service, rush getting products out into the market, and end up ruining great franchises (e.g. Thief, FF, and now Dragon Quest is on some slippery slope bs)

Overall this game is a must play for final Fantasy lovers and story rpg lovers alike. You will have no regrets.

Everyone has that one game from their childhood that has shaped who they are, and stuck with them their entire life.. Final Fantasy 9 is mine. I have loved this game since the day I first played it when I was but a wee lad. I remember getting stuck in the Ice Cavern as a child for DAYS before finally beating it (That's not an issue these days.. I found a way to five shot Ozma using Vivi and auto reflect x3).
The story of Final Fantasy 9 makes me tear up even thinking about it. Enemies become friends, friends become enemies, and unlikely companions end up lifelong friends that have bonds running deeper than blood. Through a trench of corpses and unforgiving environments, a group that would NEVER be friends by any means become a powerful and unstoppable band of Goonies style buddies. (I'm looking at you, Steiner and Zidane)
Alright so the characters in this game rule. Zidane and Kuja's design are ♥♥♥♥in' weird and I'm not a huge fan, but everything else is fantastic. The big two.. Dagger and Vivi. DAGGER IS A FREAKING BABE and has the magic to back it up, so 10/10 would marry and never let go. Vivi is just an adorable scared lil kitten that grows into an empowered badass black mage that has the balls to stand up to God himself. This is a guy who couldn't even move when his friends were attacked because he was so terrified, and now he's the one that stands against a FREAKING GOD and says "No more, I'm not going to let you hurt anyone anymore" and initiates the fight. Good lord, what an arc.
Amarant is one of my favorite designed characters of all time. His character is standoffish and strange, but over time you grow to respect him as he clearly has his place in the FF9 roster. UNFORTUNATELY, Eiko shows up in the game WAAAAAAY too late to do any real impact other than being a secondary white mage (who, by the way, outheals Dagger 11/10 times she rules) but she's an adorable little girl with a heart of gold and a love for Moogles.
Quina is bizarre and doesn't impact the story much, but is a good comic relief character. Not much else to say about him/her.
Steiner is DIE HARD "Protect the princess" at the start of the game, like any good Captain of the Knights of Pluto should be. However, over time, he grows to respect and care about Zidane and his friends. His desire to protect the princess doesn't go away, not by a long shot, but it does expand to include the rest of the troupe. You need a guy that hits REALLY freaking hard and can take a beating, Steiner will always be there to stand on the frontlines for you.
Freya is the standard dragoon (or lancer) character. Jump to break defenses, stall out battles, and deal some massive damage. She's sturdy (but not too much) and quick, however I found myself only using her when the game made me. Her story is all about her ex boyfriend Fratley that disappeared and discovering where he went and honestly I never really cared all that much for it. I think I might be biased, though, because the first time I sat down and seriously played FF9 she beat me in the Lindblum hunting contest four times in a row.. I might just be bitter.
Kuja is the main villian and he's just... yeah.. he's just Kuja... he's not bad, but he's no Golbez.
BUT THAT'S NOT ALL. The supporting characters in this game are really what makes it shine. HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ HOW DID BRAHNE BIRTH SOMEONE AS GORGEOUS AS DAGGER I JUST DON'T GET IT. She's a fat pig with a thirst for power and no sense to realize she's being played. She's a great antagonist and someone worth hunting, every time she shows up you can feel that♥♥♥♥♥♥is about to go down. Her two sidekicks, Zorn and Thorn, are HILARIOUS and always crack me up. Although their boss fight is kind of hard.. because it comes out of nowhere and (at least for me) there was little to no preperation the first few times playing the game.
Tantalus. Freaking Tantalus. You know when I first played this game I didn't care about any of them, but by the end I loved ALL OF THEM.. even Blank.. ESPECIALLY Blank.. Tantalus is Zidane's crew of criminals that help Princess Garnet escape Alexandria, and end up in the midst of this interdimensional plot to take over Gaia. They don't really care, though, all they care about is saving their friend Blank who was petrified in the Evil Forest. It sounds strange but trust me, it's awesome.
The other supporting characters I can't really talk about.. because.. spoilers.. but Garland is really freaking cool. He shows up extremely late in the game, but he's worth it. GARLAND WILL RULE THE WORLD.
I can't even say anything about the environments in this game, because there are no words in the English language or any other known langauge that can describe the feeling of awe you get looking out over them. The excitement of exploring this world that truly feels alive, the joy of accomplishing your goals and saving your friends, and the dread of knowing that this is not nearly the end.. I'm tearing up just thinking about it. ♥♥♥♥, I love this game.
The same goes for the music, except for OH MY GOD. If you could choose one soundtrack to play forever in the background and follow you wherever you go, it would be THIS one. 10/10 times you would choose this one. There has NEVER been a soundtrack that can even BEGIN to compare to the beauty of it. The main title is stellar. Like, seriously stellar. And it was a bold move to change it from the traditional Final Fantasy title theme (You all know it) but DAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAMN did it pay off. The battles in this game would be UNBEARABLY slow if the battle theme wasn't so ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic.
Now, graphics. Okay this is gonna be unpopular, but.. Final Fantasy 7 is OLD and DATED, and both looks and feels clunky. This is not the case for Final Fantasy 9. It looks ♥♥♥♥ing amazing, despite coming out only THREE SHORT YEARS after 7. Everything, from the sprites in the overworld to the FMV cutscenes.. ♥♥♥♥ me, man.. video games truly are art.
I want to live in this game. The lore, the characters, the music, the look, the dialogue, the random races of creatures you don't even interact with.. the world is amazing.. the game is amazing.. I teared up just writing this review thinking about how much this game means to me. Please return to this style of game. It's. ♥♥♥♥ing. Amazing.
This is the game that taught me that video games can be art. It taught me to forgive people when they don't deserve it, and to pull yourself through whatever trials life may throw at you. In times of trouble, that main theme chimes in my head, and man.. everything is alright. PLEASE PLAY THIS GAME.

This is a spiritual successor to Outerlight's previous title, the Ship and because of that, I will be doing a comparative review. There are a slew of differences but some of the first things I noticed are how much the game is simplified compared to the Ship and of course how wacky and silly it is. The 8 stereotypical slasher victim characters are generic and cheesy for comic relief, the weapons are more diverse and creative, and the graphics are much more colorful and vibrant. In a nutshell, The Ship is much more serious and realistic, but it was preciously this fast-paced crazy chaotic play in Bloody Good Time that made it so enjoyable to me. I'll elaborate.
Bloody Good Time has 21 different weapons, while The Ship has a whooping 44. The weapons in TS are more typical items that focus on melee weapons like a hammer, knife, crowbar, ect. The weapons in BGT however are more unique like a flame thrower, a futuristic laser, a remote control exploding rat, and a powerful taser with one hell of a shock. However, a lot of the weapons in BGT need ammo, and they come with very limited ammo (four, in a lot of cases) causing weapons to quickly become useless. You now also have things called "Murder aids" which don't do any damage but have helpful affects. To give examples, there is a dart gun, glue gun, hologram decoy, pills to temporarily boost stats, and there is also what's called a "Lullaby Sheep" which causes everyone in the surrounding area to doze off. There are more traps in this game, and they are much more noticeable and useful, compared to the few discreet out of the way traps in TS.
The security in this game has fewer consequences and is less punishable. While you were immediately apprehended in TS upon sight, fined, and sent to jail with your entire inventory wiped out, in BGT you are now given the chance to run away from security guards. If you can get out of their line of sight for just ten seconds, they will give up their search. If you are caught, only the weapon equipped is confiscated. I felt like there was also less security in this game but there was one map, Las Vegas, where security seemed very unbalanced compared to the other maps. It later got very frustrating after repeatedly getting tasered and having one of my weapons confiscated while in the middle of trying to kill my quarry only to watch them get away. However, I feel that may have been intentional since it's set in a fancy ritzy place with rich casinos.
While TS has 8 different needs, you now need to only worry about hunger, exhaustion, and using the bathroom. This may sound like a huge difference in gameplay, but it actually isn't. In TS the needs decrease far too slowly to get in the way much as long as you didn't allow them to pile up and have to treat them all at once. In BGT, the rate is much quicker (an average of 3 minutes or one round), but with only three needs to look after, this was easy and not a big deal.
There is no story mode this time around, and there are only four different modes (Hunt, Death Match, Elimination, and Revenge) compared to TS's 9. You are compensated however with different "scenes" within BGT that give a break from the usual gameplay and to keep things fresh. These can not be selected and will occur randomly after a match. It's a round of a new gameplay type with a different objective such as murdering the leader with the highest score. My favorite scenes were Infected where certain cast members who chase after you have an infection you need to avoid and Scene Stealer where you have to nab a golden statue. Everyone will be gunning for you and unable to attack while holding it, you have to run away and try to survive as long as possible with the statue in your hands.
Being rewarded with money (in TS) has now been replaced with Fame (the new point system), where each weapon is assigned a number of stars (up to 5 stars) that give you fame instead of each weapon being assigned a money figure upon kill. Since there's only 5 stars, there are more weapons in each category. This means you don't have to search high and low for a high-scoring weapon.
There's only 3 maps instead of TS's 12, and when it comes down to it, that's exactly why I got bored in the first place. I logged ten fun packed hours into this game, but I can't help but feel that I would still be playing if only there were more maps. They were also much smaller compared to the massive maps in TS with no secret passageways, false walls, or hidden secrets to discover.
If you're anticipating the multiplayer in this game, don't because it's extinct. The servers are completely dead, but as added knowledge, they would only house up to 8 players, compared to The Ship's ability to hold 32. I unfortunately never had the experience of playing in a BGT server but I will say that I was impressed with the AI. It's greatly improved from what it was in TS (which was poor). I ran into very few hiccups with it, and it did a pretty good job of emulating players.
There isn't nice tutorial to show you the ropes like in TS but instead just 15 pages to read through that doesn't even elaborate upon things it really should have. I found myself learning more useful tidbits from the pop up tips on the loading screen than from the instructions.
I should also warn about a big glitch. Steam never registers that the game is shut down, and so it's impossible to play another game or even close Steam until the computer is reset.
It definitely shows that less work went into this than did The Ship, and that's easy to tell from a vast array of things. There's a handful of features missing that were once in the preceding game. In TS, you were able to customize your character's outfit instead of choosing from pre-made characters. There was a money system with banks and ATM's sprawled across the map in which the currency could be used to buy soda, pay for medical treatment, or to purchase wardrobes from boutiques and outfitters. There was an entire sick bay where you could visit doctors or physicists when injured or ill to heal. There were NPC's aside from security guards like restaurant and bar staff, sailors, engine crew, and innocent cruise passengers. When caught by security, you were sent to jail. BGT has none of this, and I miss it, but at the same time it allows you to jump right into the game with very minimal confusion. Going from over whelming complexity (in TS) to the simplicity (in BLT) was both comforting and lovable. Due to the lack of previous content and extra features, BGT is more laid back and quickly to adapt to. The biggest differences between this and TS is that this game is less complicated, easier, more wacky, and faster-paced. Everything is simplified, from your inventory to more importantly the HUD that used to be cluttered with tons of icons, indicators, and information (in TS) which I considered to be an eyesore and hard to keep up with. The screen in BGT is now more organized and clean, displaying only the necessary details, and the map is much easier to read.
And for those of you who haven't yet played The Ship and are thinking about getting it, I actually suggest playing BGT first. Since The Ship is more complex and intricate, BGT is a really good starting game to first get you used to the gameplay and how things work. And being that it's only five dollars, it's a good way to see if you'll like this type of game. If it's something you enjoy, then you can upgrade to The Ship later on. To end my review, I do recommend Bloody Good Time. It's an amazingly fun game, and I've had a great time playing it.

Having lived through the Maxis downfall of the late 90s and eventual handover to EA, and having played every Sim City but the newest one, having loved different things about all of them and having realised I'd spent more time on Sim City 4 Deluxe than any other, I felt I owed it to this game to give it my retroactive review.
Like most of us city-builder fans I tried out and fell in love with Cities Skylines shortly after it came to the limelight and like all new and improved game interfaces and technology, my expectations for a City Builder have increased along side them. So it's hard for me to appreciate the Sim Cities now as much as I did then but SC4D, despite having many annoyances with UI and a lack of some modern freedoms does still offer an unprecedented amount of control in the Sim City range.
Small things like different zoning densities and diagonal roads don't seem like a big deal, but because Maxis was basically the only big company doing these titles, it was a game-changer for the time and playing around with those limited complexities is still incredibly satisfying in 2017.
The other thing SC4 does better than many other games is the introduction and tutorial of the concepts and screens. Everything is intuitive, even to non city builders and I remember always loving Maxis' ability to produce fluid gameplay from start to finish, it's held up just as well today.
Ultimately most of the things I don't like about this game are because more modern titles have done them better, added more freedoms and removed small annoyances, but to criticise a game by comparing it to something that didn't exist at the time is a fools errand. Yes, I would recommend other titles above this now if you're new to the genre or have limited cash, but I would also very much recommend trying out some of the older Sim City titles because they're still engrossing and satisfying and stand up well today.

This game is great. I bought it the moment it came out, and I don't regret it. If you read the negative comments, they mostly focus on 3 things, 1) Too hard, 2) Spell making isn't great, or 3) too repetitive.
Well, It's hard. There are boss fights and even mini boss fights which I will slam my head against for hours. If you don't like a challenge, don't play. This game wasn't meant to be a stroll through the park, it was meant to really challenge a mage-type character. I enjoy difficulty, so I enjoy this game.
The spell making is much more than what the negative comments would make you think. Yes, there are only three basic types of spells (Area, Target, Nova). However, there are multiple types of each spell. For example, targeted spells can be rays, missiles, a lobbed bomb, etc. Then, once you've chosen the type of spell, and it's category, you can choose modifiers. You can go for super fast, super destructive, crowd control, etc. AND that's not even all. Don't forget the sigils, each sigil is a different type of magic with different effects and usages. To top it off, when you're crafting spells, the most powerfull spells use two sigils, and that mixture brings epic destruction.  There is plenty of spell variety if you're looking for it.
No, it is not repetitive. There is quite a bit of grinding, I won't deny that, but that is only due to how difficult the boss fights can get. The more you kill the more spell components you get, the better spells you can craft, the more powerful you become. When you get to boss fights, different bosses require different strategies. Some you have to cc and kill quickly, others you have to dodge and run and hit hard when you can. Some bosses you have to walk right up to them and just hit them non-stop until they slam into the ground and explode (It looks awesome).
p.s. I forgot to mention when it comes to spells, there are also sheilds.

An hour and a half in, I'm bored out of my brain.  The spells are all the same, casting is slow, ui is overwhelming with 0 explanation, and the controls feel terrible.  The only pro to this game is the beautiful graphics.

There's even a Smart Craft systen in place if you can not be arsed to deal with the more complicated crafting system.
Only... the game punishes you, especially on harder difficulties, for not doing so. In fact, trying to learn and experiment is never really encouraged because your resources are finite and the new elements you unlock start with weakly powered versions.
It's incredibly disappointing to find out a certain element doesn't work together well with the others. Which makes choosing them (an irreversible choice) all the more disappointing. Guess you'll have to suffer through your terrible build for another chapter and see if you can get lucky!
Now, truth be told, that issue could be alleviated with proper information. But at the time of writing, Googling answers for specific questions is absolutely ineffective. The best you can find is the same articles explaining the basics of the game you already know. I get it, charge up damage with the one skill and activate it all with a damage skill. BUT WHAT DOES THE SKULL DO? (apparently the Necromancy's skull, will fully negate any damage during block for a period, a fresh steam guide had to inform me of that)
If you want a game where you can mindlessly be a mage, this game is not for you. It's not "Skyrim 2, the linear hallway shooter."
Sticking to the classic setup will not carry you, even if you use Smart Cast to upgrade the levels. (which is a huge waste of resources by the way)
No, instead you need to figure out the best synergies with, again, too few information on any of them. And the information provided often proves confusing. The game simply makes poor work of conveying the information regarding it's mechanics.
Fine, you start experimenting. Hey, some combinations work and some elements are interesting in concept. It's like the game wants to reward you for thinking for yourself!
Only, they barely prove to be viable when the combat really gets heated. Which can suddenly happen, as well.
You'll be pitted against Bosses and Minibosses that, for some reason, are perfectly capable of withstanding your combo. Freeze is ineffective, Fire doesn't do enough damage... Meanwhile their skills overpower you and you can't figure out why you can't even dodge them.
The excuse that is being made then, when complaining about the bosses, is that you can actually easily beat these bosses with SPECIFIC COMBATIONS. This goes against the idea that you can craft any combation of spells in this game. Yes, you can craft them, but very few will be viable on long term and you won't even realize your combination is faulty until you've respawned 10 times wondering if you're just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dodger.
The game really doesn't inform you well on HOW you died either, or what is to blame. Just that you took enough damage (or with some cleary overpowered enemies, just take ONE hit right as they spawn) and died. You can't even look around for a final glimpse.
The lack of information, more than anything, is what infuriates me. It took me five respawns (not counting the respawns just trying to get to that point) to realize that it was a huge worm spawning in a direction I never was looking in, spitting it's insanely powered, slowing goop. Leaving me up as prey for the crocodile-like creatures to be chewed on and knocked back. Dear God, I shudder at the idea of being knocked back AND frozen at the same time.
Lichdom: Battlemage has an insanely interesting concept and completely falls flat on executing it by making only a specific set of combinations strong enough to take on anything. That counters creativity, a game that shamelessly says it WANTS you to create and experiment. What use are a 100 combinations when only 2 work?
The worst thing is, in some cases it's just the default spells being underpowered and you just need to craft a better version. But when that's not the case, you just wasted resources on an element that you won't end up using anyway, and have to go back to your slightly underpowered elements you were using before. Praying some enemies may drop some Rare parts that you can use. It's not fun to constantly die just to pick up scraps. Especially considering that dying once will reset the rarity chance, meaning that once you start losing, you'll have to get lucky or scrape by.
Storywise... It's nothing to write home about. You can pick between a male or a female. The character, then nicknamed Dragon, gets wronged by an Antagonist and is joined by a the other charater now nicknamed Gryphon.
Then you go on a tour of destruction through several settings while the plot dumbs down to "follow the trail to your target and kill them at the end".
If you can deal with constantly respawning with no satisfaction or feeling of progress, the game might be worth it. Yes, indeed, the crafting is interesting and it's probably a lot of fun on the easiest difficulty where efficiency doesn't matter a single bit. Doubt it'll be challenging or satisfying.
But if you want to get serious and play a harder difficulty, you'll need information that's poorly conveyed and hard to find on your own.
What use is innovation if it's poorly implemented.

All in all this will probably turn into a great game once the developers get to work on the post-launch feedback, but as it is right now it's not a game I will be playing and not a game I will be recommending to others.

Not only FFIX holds up well against modern day games, but manages to amaze with a narrative excellence, lovely characters, thought-provoking themes, amazing art, wonderful soundtrack, depth of immersion and exploration, sheer fun and longevity, that is simply unmatched by even the most titanic AAA titles of today.
No game, no book, no movie, no story, no soundtrack, has ever managed me to move me like this masterpiece. Tears of joy, tears of sadness, so many laughs, so many hearthfelt smiles. I've been all through this while (re)playing it. This game is worth every second, every moment. It's a must-play for everyone who cares about gaming, an unforgettable experience that positively sticks with you forever!
To conclude, Final Fantasy IX once again proves itself to be my favourite game ever. And I hope it will be yours, too!

I traded for this game when it was being offered for free, and I was happy with the deal.
If you like tower defense games, especially reverse TD, then you will really like this game.
I've played TD-games since I was a child, and Anomaly plays as a reverse TD, where you must keep your army alive while they navigate past enemy towers on their way to the end checkpoint.
The aesthetics are very nice, the weapon effects are nice done well. The sound and music is decent.
The tutorial is not too long and helpful in ensuring that you understand how to play the game. The controls are very simple and the learning curve is minimal. The main mechanic you will be using is to go into the map screen and select which routes you want your army to take - you can order them to continue around in a circle to destroy the stronger towers, or skip them altogether.
Your army arrangement will be important, as the enemy towers follow a "fire on first enemy you see" targeting pattern. Typical strategy is to deploy your APC (tankier unit) first to soak up the damage. Be warned, that enemy towers may also attack the last unit in your convoy if you haven't destroyed the tower on your way past it.
You act as the convoy general and have 4 skills that you unlock as you progress through the game. For example, you can heal your units, set up a smoke screen, or place a decoy to divert enemy fire. You will have plenty of these as you destroy towers because allied planes will drop many pickups for you.
Units are upgradable, and you unlock more the further you progress through the story. Admittedly, I did not care so much for the story - it's interesting but not quite enough to keep me deeply engaged..
A very fun reverse TD game, give it a try if you are interested.
Recommend.

Originally a Sonic fangame, Freedom Planet has made a name for itself as a game title and, now, a series. With a definite focus on speed but also an emphasis on exploring and story, Freedom Planet tries to expand on its origins as a fangame of the popular blue hedgehog. The choice of three characters allows for diverse gameplay and a multitude of experiences throughout the game. The inclusion of many different levels -- including some character-exclusive levels -- keep the replay value going, with each character giving a different experience of the world. The soundtrack (which I purchased on Bandcamp) is fun and fast-paced, reminding me of the days of the Sega CD.
I thoroughly enjoy this game and recommend it to anyone who enjoys fast-paced platforming.

Freedom Planet begins with our two, anthropomorphic heroes, Lilac the Water Dragon and Carol the Wildcat, who save a duck-like creature known as Torque after he crash-lands on their planet. He instructs the two to protect a powerful relic known as the Kingdom Stone, which serves as the energy source for their entire planet. Later on, it's revealed that a nefarious warlord known as Lord Brevon is not only after it, but has manipulated the three nations, Dail, Shuigang and Shang Tu, into warring with eachother. So Lilac, Carol, Torque, and another ally they meet later on, Milla the Hound, must stop him at all costs in order to not only save the planet, but the entire universe.
An interesting tidbit is that Freedom Planet, an indie game developed by the small studio GalaxyTrail, actually started development as a Sonic the Hedgehog fangame, but later on ended up becoming its own thing.
And it definitely shows, because Freedom Planet is more or less a retro throwback to the classic Sonic games on the Sega Genesis, and fully encapsulates the adrenaline-fueled gameplay and solid platforming that made those game so good. The only large difference is that while you can go fast, it mixes speed with combat and obstacles as well, making it feel more like an action-platformer, such as Metroid.
While the story may seem simple at first, it goes far beyond the plot of any Sonic game. The story takes its time in order to make those truly feel connected to this world, its inhabitants and their figt to free their planet from the control of a maniacal overlord. It's well-written, isn't afraid to be dark at times, and the characters have strong backstories and are very memorable.
Except Neera. Faq that betch.
Lilac is more or less a female Sonic, being that she's a strong and determined hero who always helps those in need. Then there's her close friend, Carol, a tomboy who's also impatient and a theif. And last but definitely not least, Milla. The cutest, most adorable and pure thing in existence that must be loved and protected no matter what.
My favorite character was actually Torque. Not just because I thought his voice actor outshined everyone else, but he was intelligent and down to earth as well, and has a somewhat tragic backstory that fuels his determination to stop Brevon at all costs.
Then there's Spade, who is more or less Shadow, being that he's snarky and cold, is seeking to avenge the death of someone close to him, and even SOUNDS like how he did in his debut in Sonic Adventure 2. So he basically is him.
As for Lord Brevon...calling him a clone of Dr. Eggman would be entirely inaccurate. Unlike him, he's MUCH more cold, callous and sarcastic, doing any means necessary in order to achieve his goals no matter how cruel his actions may be, and for a game like this he was definitely a fantastic villain. He was like Zor from Sonic Lost World, but done even better.
As for the level design, it is FANTASTIC. Each one uses an East Asian style that's both culturally rich and gorgeous to look at, and are fun to run, spin and soar through.
Also, in the classic Sonic games, each level or "zone" was divided into two acts, while here it's just one, large level with two different segments, each with their own boss. And because of this, they feel incredibly satisfying to complete.
Instead of rings, you instead have health system marked with red leaves. Taking damage causes your health to deplete, while collecting more red leaves casues it to replenish. This suits this game a lot better, being that it's more action-oriented, as I said before.
In the normal Adventure Mode, you play through the story as Lilac, while in Classic Mode, you simply go right through levels as either Lilac, Carol, and eventually Milla.
Lilac uses her hair like a whip as her standard attack, while her Cyclone attack causes her to spin her hair at all sides in order to float into the air. But her best move is an ability that works very similarly to the Lazer Wisp from Sonic Colors, where she goes hurtling in a single direction, destroying any enemy and bouncing across any walls she comes into contact with.
Carol's standard attack is clawing enemies, but she can also use a strong attack kicking attack, pounce, climb walls and in certain parts of the stage even get her motorcycle and blaze right through the level until its destroyed.
Milla plays a little, well...more unique than the two. She can flutter through the air by flapping her ears, much like Cream (which's what her character is closest to, even if she's surprisingly even cuter), but her attacks reolve aroune....slime. That was unexpected. But yes, she can materialize and throws slime blocks at enemies, and a slime shield that can both block enemy attacks and fire energy blasts.
The sprite-styled is phenomenal, and is entirely fluid, colorful and vibrant as the characters are very expressive. The soundtrack uses a chiptune, 8/16-bit style, and is incredibly catchy and very melodic to listen to.
As for the voice acting...its fine for what it is. There are times when the quality of the voices can be either too quiet or too loud, and I thought the line delivery wasn't very good at times...but it's at least not entirely terrible. *flashbacks to the Sonic Adventure games.*
Despite its iffy voice acting, Freedom Planet is an amazing retro throwback to the classic Sonic games with an engaging story, likeable characters, fast-paced and fluid gameplay, vivid sprite-art visuals, and an incredibly catchy soundtrack. I entirely recommend it for fans of the classic Sonic games or Sonic series in general, or even anyone else so they can enjoy a very solid 2-D platformer.

While some may write this off as just Sonic fan service, it's actually much more than that. Sonic Generations if the perfection of the boost formula seen in Unleashed and Colors while also bringing back Classic 16 bit Sonic (albeit he isn't as fluid as the original). These 2 different forms of Sonic gameplay actually blend really well together and give us the best of Sonic's past.
However good gameplay means nothing without level design and thankfully Sonic Generations has some of the best, if not the actual best levels in the entire series. Sure, there was copying and pasting going on here but even with that the levels still feel new and fun to playthrough, with many alternate routes available for replaying levels. That being said the butchering of Wisp Planet from Colors is almost unforgivable. What'd you do to it? Also speaking of copying and pasting; the music is phenominal. These are fantastic remixes of past tracks and the game even allows us to assign whatever music we want to each level. You know what that means? City Escape on every single level obviously.
It's easy to see this game was rushed to meet a deadline and while I would have liked more, what we got is still top notch. This is the Sonic game I come back to the most which is saying something since I've been a fan since the Megadrive. Let's hope the upcoming Sonic Forces is even half as good as Generations.

Sonic Generations is the Sonic game you've always wanted to play and then some. Classic levels, familiar and new bosses, unlockables, special stages galore, and lots of achievements! This game has so much gameplay that I was very surprised. It certainly is a lot better than most modern Sonic games that have come out recently.
The graphics are really nice, and you can play in two different modes, in a "classic" mode where you control sonic in the traditional 2D style, but with 3D graphics, and the other where you get to control him in full 3D. The levels take place in many different stages from various games, and include new versions of music from those games as well. The Casnio Night DLC is now free, and provides a nice distraction if you're getting tired from trying to get all those S Ranks!
The unlockables give you a gallery of sketches from the production of the game, and others, history of the characters, classic music in it's original format, etc., and of course cinematics. It's hard to find fault with this game, except that at times it can be hard for a "kids" game.
Regardless, all of the special stages are optional, you only actually have to do a couple of them, and they range in difficulty greatly. So, don't worry too much if you need to choose a different one.

Unfortunately the gameplay design of this game is terrible, you'll spend way too much time desperately thumbing around trying to make a spell thats actually worth using and making one thats still weak and confusing. And the fact the game limits how much stamina you are alowed to have makes it to be very difficult to dodge enemy attacks while you stumble around uselessly.
Comparing this to games like borderlands and diablo and you'll see what I mean, in those games when you pick up a weapon its almost automatically identifiable whether is worth using or not. But seeing as you have to assemble these weapons yourself in this game you have no idea what kind of weapon you'll end up with or if it will be any better than what you already had, compounding this even more is the fact that there are multiple elements that completely change the function of all the weapons which makes it even harder to understand what decisions you are making. In one situation I used all the best components I had and accidentally made a 'fire' weapon that did NO DAMAGE, but the game did not make obvious what mistake I had made until it was too late.
One little detail that also never gets explained in any practical fashion is that there is a third kind of attack thats associated with shields, but this attack is only possible with one specific type of shield equipped, but the game does not give you this shield when you start!  All this together makes a very stunted, frustrating and unsatisfying experience.
For people who enjoy high octane magical combat with weapons and spells you can actually use and understand, the ability to run nonstop without penalty and player choices that actually make sense: look up Ziggurat instead.

I've had this game for a long time, but it has been sitting on the shelf.  I finally completed this game and now it is review time.  I still play Jagged Alliance 2 1.13 from time to time, so I am a seasoned JA player.  I also liked Back in Action, it was a refreshing modernization of Jagged Alliance, and I could only wish the developer took more time developing and polishing THAT game.  Then out comes Crossfire.  You would think that this stand alone addon would overhaul some aspects of this game that fell flat with BIA...but...*kerplunk*.  This game still has bugs, even with the rebalance mods that say they fixed it.  This game is years old and out of development, and the mod community is pretty much dead.  So newcomers beware.
The character interactions are still terrible.  AI pathfinding is terrible.  AI strategy is too easy, just set up firing lines or ambushes and watch the dummies fall for your diversion every time, which is the same problem BIA had.  Increasing skill level only makes the enemy soldiers more bullet proof and you more bullet prone.  The story was terrible too.  The game wanted to feel like Afghanistan / Tibet, but the map was small and uninteresting.  For a JA game, it is short.  A decent player can finish in 12-16 hours, much quicker if you keep pushing your mercs to the limit.  The ending was garbage.  Just some flyers and weird colors that made me feel woozy and horribly written English.  The game was made by Germans, and they don't bother trying to use proper gramar, spell correctly, or match NPC text to speech.  Quite frankly, it's lazy.  The whole game had great potential, but it's obvious they had to cut corners and rush because of budget constraints.
PROS:
-You can finish the game.
-Some fun tactical gun battles every now and again.
-No CTDs in my play thru....
-More maps to fight in
-Feels like a JA type game
CONS:
-I got weird video/monitor flicker playing on some maps.  Like, the video turned off and on.  My computer crashed once playing this game.  Unsure if it was me or them.
-Broken quests
-Grenade Launchers blow up your merc 90% of the time.  Like, standing in an open field and aim the weapon down range, and your merc blows up.
-English localization is awful
-Game needs the rebalance mod to be 95% playable
-Story and characters are uninteresting
-Maps aren't all that great.  The Harbor (first level) is a good map.  The other maps feel empty.
-The game just feels rushed.
Summary:
If you absolutely love JA, and really liked Back in Action, you probably have this game already, but if you don't, try to get the game as cheap as you can.  It's old, unsupported, and not a complete game.  It's still fun to play if you are a diehard tactical combat fan.

When I saw the trailer, I wasn't very impressed, to be honest. The game looked too frenetic to me. If the trailer was the only soruce of information, I would not buy the game. Luckily, it wasn't.
Lichdom: Battlemage is a fantasy action game. You are a mage who is not limited with the amount of mana. A powerful mage who can destroy thousand of enemies, yet can't jump nor swim. You do not have a sword either, so casting spells is the only way you can fight enemies.
There are 8 sigils in the game, each with three spells- Nova, a spell activated when you defend yourself, Targeted spell, which is a standart one and AOE- Area of Effect spell. Each spell can be atunned to destruction, control and mastery. The effects of these attunements vary from sigil to sigil, but in general it's reccommended to combine them in order to hurt your enemies more.
The powers of sigils can be combined, which is the main fun of the game in my opinion. For example, I casted a time bubble on an enemy, which absorbs damage from other spells. Then I casted a spell which sends bugs to the enemy, eating them alive from within. Finally, I used a teleport spell. The enemy was teared apart with it. The bugs then went to other enemies, hurting and teleporting them through the battlefield.
You can also craft your own spells from resources you'll find on the way, upgrade the spells and even the resources and craft synergies. Synergies are spells which combines power of two sigils. They can summon powerfull creatures or deal huge damage to enemies.
In general, this game is very good. Yes, it can get sometimes a bit repetetive and the levels are basically corridors with few other ways to go. I think the story can't stand on it's own, it serves more like a motivation to go further, killing enemies down the road. But this is a debut of Xavian, and as such is really good. I reccommend this game.

I like the concept but I can't really recommend this game - or at least not at full price. It's not a bad game but I didn't find it particularly good either.
The story is pretty basic, as least as far as I got. You, Generic Townsperson, were hanging out doing one day doing townsfolky things when your relative was tragically killled by Lord Evilguy and his evil followers, the Cult of Evil. You then gain magic powers and set out to kill Lord Evilguy and avenge your beloved <InsertRelativeNameHere>. There are a few other cutscenes along the way but they don't seem to tell us much we don't already know.
Level design is also fairly straightforward - the entire game seems to be one long corridor with the occasional short sidepath, although it looks decent enough.
The combat is clearly the meat of the game, but for me it just wasn't that interesting. A lot of people who like the game will claim that if someone doesn't like the combat, it's because they're "doing it wrong" - they don't know how to combine spells properly and just throw the one fireball spell over and over. In my case I don't think that's true. I've seen the videos, I've read a couple of guides, I'm using the mastery and control spells, I'm using my blink and block, and I still dodn't find it terribly exciting.
Generally, spells work best if you charge them up a bit, and it usually takes several spells to kill an enemy - at the very least, applying "mastery" (which increases the power of subsequent hits) and/or a control spell before going for damage is normal. Combine with the fact that the game doesn't really require precision aim - the standard bolt spell actually homes in on enemies! - and combat felt a little sluggish to me.
Compounding this is that there is a
of combat, but all the enemies and environments seem to be basically the same. Once you've got your combos down, the only thing that brings any variety to combat is that enemies spawn with random "affixes", similar to the unique monsters in games like Diablo or Path of Exile. This make choosing which enemies to prioritise important - which I assume is what they were aiming for, since there's not a huge emphasis on manual dexterity - but I didn't find it enough to prevent combat become repetitive fairly quickly. Some of the spell effects are pretty flashy if you like that sort thing, however.
The other major part of the game is the crafting system, which is potentially interesting but more of a chore than it needs to be. Prepare to spend a lot of time on inventory management, because you're going to amass large piles of junk which you'll need to sort though using an interface which could be better. Again, it's not the worst but it could have been better. If you're really into min-maxing and comparing stats you'll probably love it, though.
Overall I think this game is competent but underwhelming. It doesn't really have glaring faults, but I just couldn't get into it. If you love flashy special effects or complicated crafting systems and don't mind a bit of repetition you might get more out of it than I did.

This game doesn't try or pretend to be anything it isn't, while very strongly delivering on what it does want to be. It gives you a very large and highly customizable toolset that allows you to be an incredibly powerful battlemage in lots of very intense combat situations that really keep you on your toes. If you don't make use of your entire arsenal, or if you let your concentration lapse, you will fail quickly. But if you do it right, you are every bit as badass as advertized.
The latest "Use your tools" video is I think a pretty accurate description of the reviews you see here and elsewhere. Most negative reviewers find themselves fleeing around the battlefield charging up their fireball spell and spamming it at the enemy, Whenever I find myself casting a fireball more than 3 times in a row, I wake up to the fact that I'm a badass battlemage and then I go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and destroy everything and anything in my path.
The combat is great and versatile. You'll need strong situational awareness to make sure you're targeting the enemies that need to die asap and that you're crowd controlling whatever you're not killing so you don't get overwhelmed. You've got both targeted and AoE spells to freeze, stun, DoT, burn, explode, you name it, and you can always decide to let the enemy attack so you can go for a timed shield block and nova the entire area.
Customization is strong, with lots of options to tune your loadout to your liking depending on whether you prefer to go for a freeze + destroy build, a slow + bleed build or any other style you can think of that synergizes well together. You'll need to figure out a well balanced set of spells to use, not just stack up destruction-only spells and hope you won't get your face smashed in.
The story so far isn't very special. It's very black and white but I've never needed an excuse to be a badass before.
The crafting is in-depth, but my one gripe is that the menus don't really support the huge number of items and variety that the game has. It's a little hard to know whether this item you're looking at could be best recycled or used in a spell somewhere, simply because the list of options is so large that only a tiny set is on-screen at a time.
Level design is fairly predictable (oh look, a combat arena type of space, I wonder if there will be enemy spawns) but the combat arenas are well balanced and the visuals aren't terrible. They're not too special but they don't detract from the experience at all.
Spell visuals are great and you feel really powerful vaporizing groups of enemies at a time.

I follow a lot of early access games and this is the
I am aware of at the moment.
(As of June 2015 with 'bleeding edge' version)
-The way the UI is set-up for building, placing items, etc, is atrocious. You have to drill down through so many selections to reach what you want to reach, then you have to get back out if you want to do something else.. it's a bit like torture.  (This is the worst thing about the game for me)

I remember first seeing this game way back when it first came out. It looked fun & I was interested in playing it. It took me at least a year & a really helpful review by one Somecallmejohnny to finally play it...on the Wii U (R.I.P. 2012-2017). It was fun, and I bought it again on Steam because it was on sale and because why not? I haven't played the game in over a year so I think i'll buy it & play it again for old time's sake.
And here's what I have to say about it.
To put it bluntly, I think this game's weakest link is its plot. Its not because of voice acting (I actually like a lot of the voice actors they got for this game, and their acting is acceptable at worst), but because the story they're trying to tell is confusing. You think it would be simple: "Alien warlord with an absurdly large monobrow steals important gem & its up to a purple dragon, a green cat & a dog to get it back."That's all fine & good, but it tries to flesh out its characters in a way that poses more questions than answers. Don't get me wrong, I'm completely ok with character development, but this game likes to mention a character's past instead of explaining it, which makes it even more confusing when these pasts are
. The two main leads Lilac & Carol (mostly Lilac) will bring up things that happened in the past during certain scenes that genuinely leave me confused & eventually annoyed.
Now you might say, "well, if you don't like the plot then why not play Classic mode?" Well, its probably because the first thing you see when you boot up the game is the main villain decapitating the king of one of the game's three kingdoms & brainwashing his son into waging war (you heard that right, that's literally how this game starts). That alone engaged me to play Adventure mode to discover this game's plot, which brings up another flaw of this game's weak story...its tone. This game has no idea what kind of story it wants to tell here. Is it a light-hearted adventure or a dark & ominous epic? Hard to tell thanks to it shifting between the two constantly. In some scenes we see the three heroines hangning out & enjoyng themsevles, and in others we get the lead being electrocuted & screaming bloody murder (again, you heard that right). Its almost like a roller coaster of tone, going up & down between light & dark storytelling. Overall, I think this game's plot would've been better if they just picked a tone to stick with & left out certain lines of dialogue that give this game more plot holes than a fine swiss cheese.

Animations are fluid & fast to match the high-speed antics this game thrives on. Good lord the soundtrack is SOOOOOOOOOO good! I love almost every piece, from the bouncy stage themes to the catchy as hell boss battle themes.

Sonic Generations offers all the elements a fan of the series could want. This PC version is by far the smoothest version, and properly demonstrates this game's stunning visuals and gameplay.
Outside of the glorious scenery and amazing soundtrack (including several remixes of classic sonic tunes), the level design really stands out as one of the best features. Expertly crafted 2D and 3D sections reimagine classic and modern stages throughout sonic's history, and offer high speeds, hidden shortcuts, collectibles and a time attack mode that will keep fans coming back again and again. It's the small features of generations that make it appeal to fans of the series such as me, including an option to change the music of a stage, and new skills that make enjoyable changes to the sonic formula.
It is worth mentioning that some sections of the game can be long and tedious, and despite many being extremely fun, some of the "challenges" (though largely optional) are frustrating and/or boring. Some long 2D sections in a few of modern sonic's stages take away from the thrill and excitement of the 3D sections (such as Crisis City & Planet Wisp), and a handful of the bosses are unsatisying.
Like many other sonic games (primarily 3D entries and thus, primarily the 3D sections of generations), this game does have a tendency to glitch out at times and kill you by mistake, but overall, these points combined are nowhere near strong enough flaws to consider this a 'bad' sonic game, as the title pays an outstanding tribute to a gaming icon, and offers a speck of hope in the future of the series.

Have you ever wondered what it'd be like to play Diablo with poor English and horrendous movement? Well you're in luck, because here's Magician's Apprentice! Magician's Apprentice is an early access Action RPG that attempts to give that old school Diablo feel. What it actually comes out as is something that looks like it was run through Google Translate (note: with English set as the ONLY language), and combat and movement that feel extremely clunky.
Movement is available in 8 directions through WASD usage. As of now, there is one area in the Prologue where you can climb to the top of a building to kill some zombies and skeletons. Once you're up there, have fun getting down. I was stuck for several minutes out there as I tried to find the exact right angle to get down, nearly giving up thinking I was just stuck there for good.
Combat comes through setting up runes (spells) for use. Certain runes will let you continue chaining them across and down, while some will only let you continue down. Once you've set a rune, it's stuck there unless you set one that will end the across setup. I couldn't find any sort of key that would let me remove them from being set without doing that. You can also set special abilities to these runes which are extremel useful but do increase the MP cost (MP cost also increases based on how many pieces you have set for that key). If there's any sort of melee combat for those times you run out of MP, I couldn't find it. MP and HP do recover fairly quickly however, with HP often recovering faster than enemies can hurt you!
Right now, I don't see much hope for Magician's Apprentice. The developers have not responded at all in the discussion board. They do state that the price "will increase over time", and right now the game doesn't even feel like it is worth the $10 asking price, even if you do get "all future updates for free once you buy it". Unless the game improves by leaps and bounds, you're much better off just avoiding Magician's Apprentice and finding a better Action RPG to play instead.
